11735-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Scientific American Supplement number 481, dated 21 March 1885, opens with engineering: the Righi railroad, the Chinese pump, the water clock, and new self-propelling torpedoes. Dobson and Barbour's improvements in Heilmann's combers and a boot-polishing machine follow.

Technology covers gas in the workshop, by T. Fletcher, with burners, shades, blowpipes, furnaces, and engines, plus the gas meter and a Geneva school for watchmaking. Electricity brings personal safety with currents and W. H. Preece on electricity in America in 1884, noting fire alarms and telephone protection from light wires. The number is a practical 1885 survey.
11761-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Scientific American Supplement number 514, dated 7 November 1885, opens with chemistry: chlorides in the rainfall of 1884, and an apparatus for evaporating organic liquids. Engineering follows with fluid and solid fuels, steel castings, and science in diminishing casualties at sea.

Technology covers the blue print process, reproductions in blue lines on white ground, and a plan for a carbonizing house. Later pages describe timber treated with dry powder, twenty pounds to a thousand feet of lumber, heated until fermentation, a process first used for a steamboat in 1879. The number is a working technical journal.
12490-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Dated 6 June 1885, Scientific American Supplement number 492 gathers engineering, mechanics and science for a technical audience. Contents list new Spanish artillery, tests for steel rails by Tetmajer, and a small Bessemer plant by Trappen. Triple compound engines by Seaton, the early steam jack and a bridge over the Adige at Verona follow.

Mine pumps, direct-acting steam pumps by Leavitt, gun pressure gauges, boiler plate measurement and express engines follow, with figures and engravings. The supplement, five dollars a year alone, served engineers, makers and curious readers. This number captures 1880s applied science in mid-stride, practical, illustrated and fond of machines.
13401-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Scientific American Supplement No. 520, dated December 19, 1885, leads with steel structures and the best use of different grades of steel, from a paper by James Christie. Andrew Carnegie reads a paper on natural gas fuel for manufacturing, covering wells near Pittsburgh, the extent of gas territory, piping costs, and analyses of gas.

Other articles cover a gas engine water supply alarm, the water supply of ancient Roman cities and their aqueducts, and Lieut. Fiske's search light, which lit Philadelphia during the electric exhibition and let him read fine print from a station tower. The issue joins heavy industry, ancient engineering, and new electric light in one weekly survey.
13939-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Scientific American Supplement number 484, April 11, 1885, covers engineering and mechanics in depth. A bridge over the Blaauw Krantz Ravine in Cape Colony opens with engravings. Torpedo ships, the gas engine by Dugald Clerk, and rapid construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway follow. The Osgood Mammoth Excavator and capstan navigation add detail.

Clerk traces combustion engines from Watt's experiments to the first gas engine. A note on fire engines explains motive power derived from fire, not mere extinguishing machines. The supplement served engineers, inventors, and curious readers. Its diagrams and tables show Victorian technology in action. The issue suits historians of engineering.
14097-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
April 4, 1885, brought this Scientific American Supplement, priced at five dollars a year with its parent journal. Chemistry leads with graphite in minerals, sulphocyanide of potassium, and notes on remelting cast iron and the hardness of metals. Engineering follows with a jet ventilator, boiler feeding, and the Honigmann fireless engine, which runs steam engines on a solution of soda hydrate.

Practical danger and invention share the pages. A boiler passage warns that cold feed water, spreading thin on a shell while fires are banked, can rupture plates three times in six weeks. A spring motor answers with cheap power: wound springs drive elevators and small yachts, with a winding station costing under one hundred dollars a week in fuel and wages. Readers meet Victorian technology as workshop news, clear, hopeful, and alert to risk.
14131-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-2-no-:
January 1885 brought this Massachusetts magazine, opening with a profile of Governor George Dexter Robinson. Fred W. Webber presents him as the thirtieth governor under the state constitution, praising character, ability, and education. Public service, dignity, and steady judgment mark the portrait, in the booster style of the age.

Country life fills the later pages. A Berkshire agricultural society, founded in 1811, inspects crops, offers premiums, and stages plowing matches, with a quarter acre turned in thirty-five minutes by one winner. Dr. Holmes read a ploughman poem to the show in 1849, and William Cullen Bryant wrote an ode for it years before. Another long sketch follows an acquitted adventurer fêted by nobles and king, then sunk by vaulting ambition. State pride and good stories share the number.
14132-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-2-no-:
February 1885 brought this Massachusetts magazine, opening with Arthur P. Dodge's life of William Gaston. Victor Hugo supplies the motto: historians of morals and ideas serve no less than historians of battles and crowns. Gaston's career then unfolds against unwritten Bay State history, the interior life of people who work, suffer, and wait.

Colonial enterprise fills the later pages. A Nashaway company, led by Dr. Robert Child of Cambridge and Padua, chases mineral treasure in New England hills while its politics offend the colony. King's widow, debts from Indians and John Prescott, and a second husband named Cutler add domestic detail. A Bermuda section praises Captain John Smith's 1624 map of the Summer Isles, with forts, bridges, and a market-place stocks. State history, biography, and antiquarian notes share the number.
14509-lippincott-s-magazine-october-1885:
Lippincott's Magazine for October 1885 opens with an essay on a Texas sheep ranch, musing on how words like ranch win fashion and fade. The Philadelphia monthly mixed fiction, travel, and criticism for a general audience.

Other items include a lady lawyer's first client, poems, a salt-mine sketch, and serial fiction, all in the magazine's polished late Victorian style. The issue reflects American magazine culture at its height, when monthlies carried the nation's reading. It offers a pleasant cross-section of what educated readers enjoyed in a single autumn month.
14530-lippincott-s-magazine-august-1885:
Lippincott's Magazine for August 1885 carries serial fiction, essays, and gossip for Philadelphia readers, with a contents list added by the transcriber. F. C. Baylor's serial continues, beside Margaret Bertha Wright's Our Ville.

Other pieces include a primitive couple tale by M. H. Catherwood, pioneers of the Southwest, Scottish crofters, fishing on Elk River, and monthly gossip on Webster's moods and Southwestern feuds. The issue mixes high and popular tastes in one cover. Its gossip columns and literature notes round out a full summer number. It captures a summer month of American magazine reading, varied and unpretentious.
14689-the-bay-state-monthly-volume-2-no-:
The Bay State Monthly for March 1885, a Massachusetts magazine, opens with George L. Austin's profile of the publishers Lee and Shepard, a firm whose name had graced millions of volumes for a quarter century. Austin traces the senior partner from Boston's North End.

Other articles cover Rodney Wallace's start in life, business, and politics, and the gold mines of California and the West, whose annual product had fallen from tens of millions in 1853. The issue mixes biography, business, and mining statistics. It offers a neat portrait of Massachusetts publishing and enterprise in the 1880s.
15840-lippincott-s-magazine-december-188:
Lippincott's Magazine for December 1885, a monthly of fiction, travel, and essays from Philadelphia. Lippincott's mixed short stories with sketches of places and people, aimed at a broad middle-class audience. A transcriber's table of contents lists each piece with its page. The December number balances home and abroad.

Philip A. Bruce writes on a tobacco plantation, while Theo. Wolfe follows Charlotte Bronte's life in Brussels. Margaret Bertha Wright sketches Cookham Dean, and Edward C. Bruce notes birds of a Texan winter. The Ferryman's Fee, letters of Charles Reade, and a suppressed Tuscan monastery complete the variety. The issue reads as a Victorian magazine at ease: curious, genteel, and wide-ranging.
16792-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
This September 26, 1885 number of the Scientific American Supplement, volume twenty, number 508, gathers short technical pieces. Chemistry leads with the Cowles electric smelting process, an electric furnace for boron, silicon, and aluminum, light's chemical action, salt alloys, chinoline, urea tests, and glaze assays. Engineering follows with deep shafts and deep mining, including a French working shaft sunk with many figures.

Each piece is brief, plain, and rich in figures and shop detail, aimed at makers and keen readers. The issue shows 1885 science chasing cheaper metals, deeper mines, and better light. Readers can dip in by topic for period craft, or read through for a snapshot of a technical age in full swing.
20955-the-international-monthly-magazine:
The finest portrait yet of Louis Kossuth fronts The International Monthly Magazine for January 1852. Hungary's hero then stood in America, set to mark a bright page in liberty's tale. Taller than most supposed, with a face of piercing intellect, the Tribune's words are quoted.

Kossuth's tour for Hungarian freedom gripped the United States that winter. This monthly mixed portraits, tales, essays, and news for parlour reading. Volume five's first number froze that fever of welcome in print. Readers can feel how a foreign cause fired American crowds before the Civil War split their own house.
26185-lippincott-s-magazine-november-188:
Lippincott's Magazine for November 1885 opens in mid-story with The Lady Lawyer's First Client, part two. Mrs. Tarbell, a woman attorney, faces the Stiles family at her office before trial. Mrs. Stiles, on a cane, brings daughters Georgiana and Celandine, while Celandine pays the case costs herself and proves hard to manage.

The case, Stiles against a railway company, reaches court at the September term after delays over an ankle and the law's slow pace. Later pages turn to Philadelphia brickwork, praising Flemish bond, stepped gables, and moulded string courses. The issue mixes popular fiction with solid craft writing, as a general magazine of its day should.
2654-the-papers-and-writings-of-abraham-:
Abraham Lincoln's second volume in the Constitutional Edition covers 1843 to 1858, edited by Arthur Brooks Lapsley. It opens in Springfield in May 1843, with a warm letter to his friend Joshua F. Speed, gladly received and not a bore at all.

Through law practice, Congress, and the long road back to politics, Lincoln's letters show a man growing into his powers. The volume ends on the edge of the great debates that made him famous. Readers get the private Lincoln, funny, loyal, and ambitious, before history claimed him. Speed remained a lifelong friend, and their letters stay warm throughout.
27662-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Dated May 9, 1885, this weekly supplement to Scientific American gathers illustrated articles on chemistry, engineering, physics, art, and hygiene for general readers. Its table of contents runs from Chinese fixed oils and the Creusot ironworks to electric light for military use.

Other pieces describe the Cathedral of the Incarnation at Garden City, a new seismograph, electrotyping, and the stone pine, with engravings throughout. The issue captures the magazine's role as a bridge between workshops, laboratories, and curious readers in the late nineteenth century. The issue closes with patent notes and short miscellaneous items.
29074-the-american-missionary-volume-39-:
The American Missionary Association published this issue of its monthly journal in February 1885. The association ran schools and missions for freedpeople in the South, for Chinese immigrants, and for Native communities, and the journal reported that work to donors and supporters across the North.

This issue covers the freedman's case in equity, industrial education and what the association was doing in it, its showing at the New Orleans exposition, and the outlook for its Chinese missions. It also prints a letter from an Indian boy, lists missionaries and teachers, and closes with receipts. Readers get a detailed record of post-Civil War missionary education, in the association's own voice.
29158-lippincott-s-magazine-september-18:
J. B. Lippincott Company published this issue of Lippincott's Magazine in September 1885. Monthly magazines of the day mixed a serial novel with essays and short fiction, and this issue follows that pattern. Its serial, On This Side by F. C. Baylor, reaches chapter nine, opening with two bachelor brothers in Caroline County, Virginia, receiving an English visitor.

Other contents include F. N. Zabriskie's essay on the truth about dogs and a piece titled Rena's Warning. Together they show the magazine's range: regional fiction, natural history, and short tales side by side. Readers get a single month of a busy Victorian literary magazine, readable as a time capsule of American popular writing in 1885.
30158-the-american-missionary-volume-39-:
The American Missionary for July 1885, volume 39, number 7, gives one monthly number from the American Missionary Association in New York. Editorial pages treat figures and finance, the exercise of benevolence, and colored people at the New Orleans Exposition. Notes follow on the Congregational Association of Ohio, the grave of Lovejoy, and what to do with the Chinese. The association, led by President William B. Washburn, sold the journal at fifty cents a year.

Southern reports follow, from Fisk University, Hampton Institute's anniversary, Gregory Institute, and religious interest at Talladega, plus a letter from Austin and a student's letter. Obituaries, the Bureau of Woman's Work, a true incident, and a children's page on a little black girl's sacrifice close the number. The issue records missionary education and charity in the postwar South, in its own earnest voice.
30459-the-american-missionary-volume-39-:
The American Missionary for March 1885, volume thirty-nine, number three, gathers reports, editorials, and letters from mission work in the United States and abroad. Editorial pages cover figures and finance, the death of Rev. G. D. Pike, paragraphs, and a word to ministers, plus a test applied to preaching as the main feature of missionary work.

Southern reports include an itinerary from Austin to Corpus Christi, views in Texas, a week of prayer, and a letter from a student. Chinese sections follow Lou Quong at home in China and a bride and bridegroom worshiping ancestors. A bureau of woman's work adds societies, a lady missionary's letter, and a teacher's monthly report, giving a full picture of the mission field.
31169-the-american-missionary-volume-39-:
Volume thirty-nine, number eight of The American Missionary, dated August 1885 and published in New York by the American Missionary Association, reports the association's work across the United States. Editorials take up finances, farewells and greetings, the higher education of Black students, and general opinion, at fifty cents a year in advance.

Section reports follow from the South, with Berea College, Talladega, Tougaloo, Tillotson, and Avery Institute. They then come from Indian missions on an Apache raid, and from a tour among Chinese missions, with a bureau of woman's work and a children's page. The issue is a compact record of Reconstruction-era mission schooling and its supporters.
3195-mark-twain-s-letters-volume-3-1876-:
Albert Bigelow Paine arranged this third volume of Mark Twain's letters, covering 1876 to 1885. The section on 1876 turns largely to William Dean Howells, with literature and politics sharing the page. Plans for a play with Bret Harte appear among the projects. Hartford's Monday Evening Club, an association of the city's literary talent, forms the social background.

Writers, editors, lawyers, and ministers made up that club, many of them men of national standing. The letters show Twain mid-career: famous, busy, and testing new work on friends before the public saw it. For readers of the novels, the volume fills the gaps between books with the talk, jokes, and worries that surrounded their making.
7117-memoirs-of-sir-wemyss-reid-1842-188:
Stuart Reid edits the memoirs of his brother Sir Wemyss Reid, 1842 to 1885, inscribing them to Lady Reid, the devoted wife of his brother. His introduction confesses personal loss still keen and vivid, and says he must write out of the fullness of his heart, since duty demands it. His earliest memories begin when he was a child and Wemyss a bright, self reliant lad in the Newcastle home, described with artless realism in the opening pages.

The brothers grew up in an atmosphere of love and duty, under a studious father rich in a library of dry theology the children never read. Among those tomes they searched in vain for fairy books, a small detail that says much about the household. The memoir that follows traces a journalist and man of letters from that home to public life.
7530-the-renascence-of-hebrew-literature:
Nahum Slouschz wrote this history as his doctorate thesis at the University of Paris, published in book form in 1902 and translated here from the French. Its period runs from 1743 to 1885, the years when Hebrew, long believed to have no place among modern languages as a literary vehicle, found new life. Jews of the West had given up their national language outside the synagogue, and many thought that settled the matter.

Slouschz shows how writers, scholars, and journals proved otherwise, building a modern Hebrew literature before Hebrew became a spoken national tongue. A few years after the French edition, the author himself put the essay into Hebrew for the Tushiyah press. The book remains a pioneering study of the Haskalah, the Jewish enlightenment, in letters.
9666-scientific-american-supplement-no-4:
Scientific American Supplement number 497, dated July 11, 1885, gathers the week's science and craft for general readers. Chemistry pieces take up making sea water drinkable, wool oil acids, and nickel on zinc. Engineering reports cover foundations in quicksand, a lift bridge over the Ourcq Canal, and a new canal making St. Petersburg a seaport. A French dispatch boat and sidewise ship launching follow.

Later pages treat high-speed engines, oil pipe lines to the seaboard, and the fuel of the future, with figures and engravings throughout. The supplement cost five dollars a year beside the parent weekly. A reader gets a lively snapshot of 1885 invention, when steam, steel, and chemistry remade daily life.
addison-steele-spectator-selections-1885:
Joseph Addison and Richard Steele were English writers who changed daily reading in the early 1700s. Together they ran short-lived journals: the Tatler, the Spectator, and the Guardian. Each issue carried brief essays on manners, books, and town life. This volume, published in 1885, gathers a full selection of those papers.

The essays teach through humor, using made-up clubs, letters, and characters like Sir Roger de Coverley. Addison and Steele aimed to make philosophy lively and polite talk smarter. Their clear, balanced prose became the model for modern English essay writing. Students read these selections for over a century as a style guide.
alexander-of-cappadocia-from-the-epistle:
Alexander led the Church first in Cappadocia and then in Jerusalem. He died a martyr in the persecutions of the 250s. His letters survive only in scraps quoted by the historian Eusebius.

An 1885 Fathers volume gathers those fragments under his name. Warm greetings to Origen, once his student, stand among them. Friendship and faith breathe through the brief surviving lines. Brief as they are, the pieces touch readers across the centuries. They keep the voice of a bishop who faced death for his belief. In a shelf of heavy treatises, such small human traces carry a weight of their own.
annals-cakchiquels-brinton-1885:
Daniel G. Brinton edited and translated The Annals of the Cakchiquels in 1885 for his Library of Aboriginal American Literature. The annals, also called the Memorial de Solola, are the chronicle of the Cakchiquel Maya of highland Guatemala. Brinton prints the original Cakchiquel text beside his English, with notes and an introduction.

Cakchiquel lords kept the record from mythic origins through migration, kingship, and war. It runs on through the Spanish conquest, told from the conquered side. Plague, tribute, and forced labor enter its later pages without flinching. Brinton, a pioneer of American anthropology, prized such native histories as primary sources. The annals remain a key voice of the Maya past.
aristides-the-apology-of-aristides-the-p:
Aristides, a philosopher at Athens, presented his Apology to Emperor Hadrian. The presentation came around the year 125, early in the Church's life. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers carries the elegant defense in English.

Aristides sets Christians beside pagans, Jews, and Greek thinkers for comparison. In morals and in worship, he argues, Christians come out ahead. The work then vanished for centuries from Western knowledge. Scholars recovered it only in the 1800s, to wide excitement. It now stands as the earliest Christian apology that we possess whole. Its calm and reasoned tone still impresses readers who expect ancient polemic instead.
artefii-arabis-philosophi-liber-secretus:
Artefii Arabis Philosophi Liber Secretus, printed in 1685, gathers Latin alchemical secrets under famous ancient names. Its first work, the secret book of Artephius the Arab philosopher, opens the magic fire hidden from all. With it stands a little book by Saturnus Trismegistus, or Brother Elias of Assisi, which teaches the manner of operating openly.

The volume also includes the Libellus de Lapide Philosophorum and other works by Friar Elias of Cortona, with twelve woodcuts inside Elias's text. Such added pieces, some printed here for the first time, made the book a small library of the philosophers' stone. It shows the seventeenth century still binding medieval friars and Arab sages together as authorities of the art.
arxiv-2509-00285:
Mir Tafseer Nayeem and Davood Rafiei present OpinioRAG in 2025, a framework that builds user-centric opinion highlights from thousands of online reviews. Popular products can draw more reviews than anyone can read. Past methods either fail to scale or give generic summaries that miss what a given user cares about.

OpinioRAG is scalable and needs no training. It retrieves evidence with a retrieval-augmented method and uses a language model to draft tailored highlights. New reference-free metrics check factual consistency with a fine, context-aware eye, tuned for sentiment-rich text. A new data set pairs entities with over a thousand reviews each with expert summaries and hand-labeled queries. Extensive tests support the approach.
arxiv-2509-00585:
Euan T McGonigle, with three co-authors, Matthew Pawley, Jordan Richards, and Christian Rohrbeck, tackles change point detection in extreme dependence, finding moments when the joint tail behavior of several series shifts. Such breaks matter, but most methods watch the whole distribution, not the tails, or assume strict parametric forms.

McGonigle and his co-authors propose MOPED, a nonparametric moving sum method for pairwise extremal dependence in multivariate data. A multiscale variant pools estimates across threshold and bandwidth choices, avoiding a single hard threshold pick. Simulations show good performance, even for subtle tail changes with no correlation shift, and the method finds changes in brain signals from seizure-prone newborns.
arxiv-2509-00785:
Elena Masserini, with two co-authors, Daniela Micucci and Leonardo Mariani, explores audio bug reporting for mobile apps. Bug reports help developers collect faults that escaped testing, and letting users record a spoken message on the spot is simple to implement and could raise the number of reports teams receive.

Masserini and her co-authors note that audio reports have specific traits that challenge existing techniques for reproducing bugs: speech is unstructured, may lack precise steps, and varies in clarity. Based on a preliminary experiment, they discuss these challenges and motivate further research on collecting and analyzing audio-based bug reports. The paper is a position and exploration piece, arguing the channel deserves dedicated tools.
arxiv-2509-00985:
Alexandre P Costa and Alexandre V Dodonov present a study of resonances in light-atom interaction. The interaction of atoms with light fields is central to modern physics. It also underpins emerging quantum technologies. The Rabi models give the simplest basic description of it. They come in semiclassical and quantum versions.

The authors derive both models concisely. They show how one- and multiphoton resonances arise in the semiclassical regime. They then analyze how these resonances appear in the quantum Rabi model. Similarities and differences with the classical picture are discussed. Special attention goes to the three-photon resonance. Textbooks usually neglect it for its relative weakness. Yet it is intrinsic to how radiation and matter interact. The goal is a clear reference for students and researchers.
arxiv-2509-01185:
Long documents strain language models, and progress is held back by a lack of good, varied long-context data for training and testing. Seganrasan Subramanian and Abhigya Verma present a modular framework that creates such data synthetically, by prompting language models themselves. The system can be extended and serves several training goals, from fine-tuning to preference-based methods.

Four kinds of data are covered: multi-turn dialogues, document-based input-output pairs, instruction tasks with checkable answers, and long reasoning examples. Templated prompts, a design that works with any model, and rich metadata make the output scalable and controllable. Subramanian and Verma aim to give builders a steady supply of purpose-aligned long-context material, so models can learn to handle books, files, and long records with more care.
arxiv-2509-01285:
Surrogate models stand in for costly simulations, but they need good sample points, and wide state spaces make sampling wasteful. Julen Cestero, Marco Quartulli, and Marcello Restelli propose sampling a simulated environment with agents trained by reinforcement learning. Those agents visit states in ways that plain random draws may miss.

The team compares their approach with Latin hypercube sampling and with active learning paired with Kriging, checking results across all sampled data sets. A mixed data set worked best, combining samples from random agents, expert agents, and agents trained to seek states where transitions are least predictable. Cestero and the co-authors conclude the method improves on the prior state of the art and opens the way to surrogate-aided policy learning, where cheap stand-ins guide costly training.
arxiv-2509-01485:
In the study of dynamical systems, a recurrence set holds points whose paths return near their start. Its size is measured by Hausdorff dimension. Hiroki Takahasi introduces a new condition, called W-prime specification. It is defined through language splits of subshifts, symbolic models of dynamics. The aim is to cover systems that lack the classic specification property.

Takahasi proves a strong result. Any recurrence set of a subshift with this property has full Hausdorff dimension, the largest size possible. The result reaches a wide class of systems. It covers all S-gap shifts, some coded shifts, and coding spaces of many interval maps with positive entropy. For many expanding interval maps, the same conclusion follows. A known effect thus extends far past its first setting.
arxiv-2509-01585:
A Loschmidt echo measures how faithfully a quantum system can retrace its steps when its evolution is reversed, and noise makes that return decay. Takato Yoshimura and Lucas Sa study echo dynamics in noisy quantum many-body systems with no conservation laws. They first show the operator Loschmidt echo under noisy unitary dynamics equals the operator norm of the matching dissipative dynamics, once noise is averaged.

Two decay regimes emerge, set by time and noise strength together: a Gaussian fall at early times, then an exponential fall whose rate no longer depends on the noise. A heuristic picture for generic driven systems ties echoes to operator growth and to out-of-time-order correlators, tools that track how information scrambles. The authors then prove all their claims exactly for a solvable chaotic circuit, the dissipative random phase model, giving firm ground in dissipative quantum chaos.
arxiv-2509-01785:
Philani Rodney Majozi revisits a model theory result that leaned on the Continuum Hypothesis, a disputed claim about infinity sizes. His topic is FN bases, structures tied to Frechet-Nikodym ideas, and traits called flatness and nonforking. Past work from 1991 used the hypothesis to guarantee certain heir structures under filter conditions. Majozi asks which parts survive in standard set theory alone.

He shows many of the traits can be recovered by studying special ultrafilters, which are tools that pick out large sets. Counted, good, and regular types each play a role. With the right model traits, ultrapowers of flat bases stay definable and nonforking. Examples and counter cases pin down where each filter trait matters.
arxiv-2509-01885:
Zhimeng Luo, Abhibha Gupta, Adam Frisch, and Daqing He pull a structured pain assessment from messy health records using language models. The target format covers onset, triggers, quality, spread, severity, and timing of pain. Records are unstructured, so classic tools miss key details and strain clinician time. The team recasts extraction as text generation, letting the model show reasoning steps like a doctor would.

Showing steps lifts clarity and helps when labeled examples are scarce. Judging free text output needs new scores, so they adapt classic entity metrics with a semantic similarity measure. The blend checks both exact facts and clinical intent. Results point to a scalable aid that can sharpen records and support care choices.
arxiv-2509-01985:
Eduardo Espindola and Yu Tang design sliding mode controllers for mechanical systems with symmetries. Sliding mode control drives a system onto a chosen surface and holds it there robustly. Symmetric systems evolve on principal fiber bundles, layered spaces that split motion into base and group parts. Working directly on the full space forces awkward coordinate choices.

Their design splits the job: reaching happens on the base space, sliding on the structure group. A sliding subgroup built from a kinematic controller anchors the sliding stage. A reaching law built from the mechanical connection drives the state toward that subgroup. Stability proofs give near global convergence plus local exponential speed. Tests cover a spacecraft with reaction wheels and a wheeled unicycle robot.
arxiv-2509-02085:
Natalia Gorobey and Alexander Lukyanenko revisit whether the EPR paradox is truly a paradox within quantized field theory. The classic puzzle involves two photons in a singlet state measured at separate detectors. If exciting a field system with set quantum numbers is impossible, the source trigger amplitude vanishes. They analyze the source plus two detector system in full detail.

Operation of one detector with a given photon polarization fixes the adequate choice for the second detector. That determination follows from motion laws and conservation of excitation quantum numbers. No nonlocal influence is invoked in their account. The conclusion reframes the correlation as a selection effect inside one global field system. Their stance adds to long running debates on quantum foundations.
arxiv-2509-02185:
Takahiro Hayazaki, Daisuke Kadoh, Shinji Takeda, and Gota Tanaka compute entanglement entropy with tensor renormalization group methods. Entanglement entropy measures how strongly a subsystem links to its surroundings in quantum systems. Tensor networks compress quantum states efficiently, and renormalization coarse grains them step by step. Their method represents the reduced density matrix as a tensor network one dimension higher.

An explicit algorithm for one dimensional systems handles subsystems of arbitrary size. Tests on the two dimensional Ising model tensor network recover the central charge with striking precision. The central charge is a key fingerprint of critical behavior. Agreement with theory within error bars validates the approach. The method opens entropy computation for larger tensor network studies.
arxiv-2509-02985: Fang-Ting Tu and Yifan Yang wrote a 2025 number theory note giving a concrete form of the Jacquet-Langlands correspondence for certain non-Eichler orders. That correspondence matches two kinds of symmetry objects, one built from quaternion algebras, which are number systems with four parts. The authors focus on indefinite quaternion algebras over the rational numbers. They study a special index-two suborder inside an Eichler order of a given level, in an algebra whose discriminant is even.
arxiv-2509-03085:
Emin Ablyatifov and Georgy Lukyanov studied optimal taxation in 2025 when citizens doubt their government. In their model, people value a public good paid for by distortionary taxes, taxes that also shrink economic activity. But they credit the government with honesty only part of the time, fearing it may divert all funds instead.

That simple doubt produces a sharp trust threshold. Below it, any positive tax lowers expected welfare, so the best policy is no tax at all. That holds even when people value the public good. Above the threshold, the usual logic of tax design returns, with the value of public money scaled down by trust. A worked example gives direct formulas linking trust to the best tax rate. The lesson is that credibility reforms may need to come first in low-trust places.
arxiv-2509-03185:
Debopom Sutradhar and 5 co-authors applied reinforcement learning in 2025 to cleaning low-dose CT scans. Lower radiation doses make scans safer but noisier, and standard denoisers can blur away detail that doctors need. Their framework lets an encoder-decoder network learn its denoising policy from image quality feedback as it goes.

An advanced policy optimization algorithm, a method that updates behavior cautiously, runs inside a custom training environment modeled on a gym. On a low-dose dataset drawn from scans and projections, the system beat traditional and deep rivals on standard fidelity scores. Scores stayed strong on a well-known public challenge dataset. As a further check, cleaned COVID-19 scans fed into a classifier raised its accuracy above the no-learning baseline.
arxiv-2509-03585:
Louise Welsh and sixteen co-authors consider how metal absorption systems cluster near the end of cosmic reionisation in a 2025 research paper. Reionisation was the era when early light re-energised hydrogen across the universe. The authors trace carbon and silicon ions, seen as absorption dips in quasar light, using the E-XQR-30 survey at high redshift.

A two-point correlation function measures how often absorber pairs appear at each separation. In velocity terms, clustering barely changes across cosmic time when compared with lower-redshift quasar surveys. In physical distance terms, clustering strength grows with time on scales below about 1500 kiloparsecs. That growth is reported here for the first time so close to reionisation. Simulated galaxies from the GAEA model match the carbon-traced structures best at a particular halo mass, suggesting the absorbers live in similar environments.
arxiv-2509-03885:
Topotein, a framework bringing topological deep learning to protein learning, is the subject of a 2025 research paper by Zhiyu Wang and five co-authors. How a protein's structure maps to its function is a central question in biology. Sequence and graph methods capture much, but miss the hierarchical organisation built into protein structures, from residues up to the whole molecule.

Their Protein Combinatorial Complex represents a protein at several levels at once: residues, secondary structures, and complete proteins, keeping geometric information at every level. A companion network, TCPNet, passes messages across that hierarchy with geometry-aware updates that respect rotations and translations. Four protein learning tasks test the framework against leading geometric graph networks. TCPNet wins consistently across them. Its clearest strength appears in fold classification, where recognising how secondary structures are arranged matters most. The results validate the value of layered topological features in this setting.
arxiv-2509-04085:
Stanly Wilson and eight co-authors propose a second-hand marketplace for building materials in a 2025 research paper. Construction throws away huge amounts of usable material, which wastes money and resources. Their design uses blockchain records, a shared tamper-evident ledger, to track where each used item came from. Files describing items sit in a distributed storage system called IPFS, so records stay open to checking.

Buyers and sellers would trade through shared rules rather than one central operator. The team lays out how listing, checking, and handing over materials would work in practice. Clear tracking should make firms more willing to reuse beams, fixtures, and other leftovers. That shift supports a circular supply chain for construction.
arxiv-2509-04185:
Itai Gat and eight co-authors present a faster way to run large language models in a 2025 computer science paper. Standard models write one token, a word piece, at a time, which makes long answers slow and costly. Their method, Set Block Decoding, mixes ordinary next-token writing with masked prediction, where hidden tokens get filled in. A single pass can then propose several future tokens at once, not always in order.

Solvers borrowed from diffusion research, a family of generation methods, pick good token sets. No change to model structure is required, and ordinary caching still works. Fine-tuned versions of two open models needed three to five times fewer passes for the same quality. Deployment costs could fall sharply.
arxiv-2509-04285:
Henry Mittenzwey and one co-author, Andreas Knorr, propose a new mechanism that scrambles exciton spin in atom-thin semiconductors in a 2025 physics paper. Excitons are bound pairs of an electron and a missing electron, and their spin state matters for future devices. In flakes of transition metal dichalcogenides, atom-thin layered crystals, uneven surroundings create local electric fields. The authors build a many-particle Rashba Hamiltonian, an energy description capturing how motion and spin couple under such fields.

Pair interactions between excitons emerge from that description. For one material, molybdenum diselenide on silica glass, the fields relax spin in under a trillionth of a second above a modest temperature. Sister materials with bigger bright-dark energy gaps barely feel the effect.
arxiv-2509-04485:
Chris Sainsbury and one co-author, Andreas Karwath, build a transformer model that predicts cardiovascular risk from patient records in a 2025 research paper. Their model, ASCENDgpt, reads long-term electronic health records as token sequences, like sentences. A phenotype-aware mapping turns tens of thousands of raw diagnosis codes into fewer than two hundred clinically meaningful phenotype tokens. Semantic content survives while the token list shrinks by over three quarters.

Pre-training used masked language modeling on records from about 19,000 people. Fine-tuning then aimed at five outcomes, including heart attack, stroke, and cardiovascular death. Test scores averaged strongly across outcomes on the C-index, a standard ranking score. Clinicians also gain predictions they can read through the phenotype tokens.
arxiv-2509-04585:
Y M P Gomes, writing alone, extends spontaneous collapse ideas into relativistic quantum field theory for fermions in a 2025 physics paper. Collapse models modify quantum theory so that wave functions occasionally localize on their own, easing the quantum-to-classical transition. Gomes applies that assumption to Dirac fields and solves the Lindblad master equation, the standard open-system evolution rule, through the Keldysh formalism. The result is an effective action where collapse shows up as a self-interaction term with an imaginary part.

Loop-level equations then yield an effective mass with startling character: mass turns complex. Lorentz symmetry, the backbone of relativity, breaks at low energies yet recovers at high ones. A conserved charge survives, though the energy-momentum tensor does not.
arxiv-2509-05485:
How much a classifier trusts its own answer can be judged by how close a test image sits to its training data. That is the proposal of Maksim Kazanskii and Artem Kasianov in a 2025 machine learning paper. Models often give confident answers on images unlike anything they were trained on.

Their Embedding Density method measures that distance inside the model's internal representation space, without retraining the model. Predictions from sparse, low-density regions are flagged as low confidence and can be filtered out. Filtering those cases raised classification accuracy significantly in their tests. The method was checked across several architectures against leading out-of-distribution detectors, and the authors suggest it may generalise beyond image tasks.
arxiv-2509-05585:
Links between written requirements and the code that implements them are recovered better with domain knowledge than with wording alone, Zhiyuan Zou and four co-authors show in a 2025 software engineering paper. Traceability links help engineers check coverage and manage change, but natural language and code describe the same thing very differently.

A large empirical study first exposes where plain text similarity fails across link recovery tasks. The authors then add several domain-specific strategies to two models, a graph transformer that uses edge types and a large commercial language model given extra inputs. On requirements-to-code recovery across twelve open projects, both upgraded models beat their plain versions and the prior leading method.
arxiv-2509-05785:
Cameras and radar together locate objects in a top-down view with less depth confusion, in a 2025 paper by In-Jae Lee and five co-authors. Camera-radar fusion is cheap and complementary, but backward projection methods, which spread image features along viewing rays, suffer depth ambiguity that creates false detections.

Their model, CRAB, fuses sparse but precise radar depth with the dense, less reliable depth guessed from images during the view transformation. Spatial attention with radar context further sharpens the three-dimensional scene reading. On the nuScenes driving dataset the method reached leading performance among backward projection fusion approaches for both detection and segmentation.
arxiv-2509-06085:
Pre-trained models have become a new kind of software dependency, and Jerin Yasmin and three co-authors study how open-source projects actually live with them in a 2025 paper. A reused model brings learned behavior and extra artifacts, not just code, which can threaten maintainability and reliability. The team calls this shift Software Dependencies 2.0.

From a dataset of over twenty-eight thousand repositories reusing models, they sampled four hundred one projects for mixed-methods analysis. They document how projects structure and record model dependencies, what reuse pipeline stages and organizational patterns appear, and how models interact with other learned components along the way. The study maps a dependency practice that tooling and documentation habits have not yet caught up with.
arxiv-2509-06185:
A shopping assistant should ask questions when a request is vague and recommend when it is sharp, and Firas Jarboui and Issa Memari make that call from entropy in a 2025 paper. Conversational recommenders over huge catalogs must balance exploring a shopper's needs against exploiting them. Their method measures the breadth of interest from the score distribution of a neural retriever.

High entropy in the re-ranked scores signals ambiguity, so the dialogue policy asks exploratory questions; low entropy signals a specific intent and triggers direct recommendations. The routing keeps a language-model agent aware of an arbitrarily large catalog in real time without stuffing the catalog into its context window. The authors present the entropy signal as a simple, effective steering rule.
arxiv-2509-06485:
Sorting waste on a moving belt is the idea behind a 2025 computer vision paper led by Andrea Marelli, with four co-authors. The workers who already pick items off the belt supply the help. Factories still rely on people to spot unwanted objects in mixed streams. Full labeling for training software is too costly across many sorting jobs.

The authors define before-after supervision: a camera sees the belt before a worker removes an item and again afterward, and the difference itself teaches the system. They release a dataset of more than eleven thousand high-resolution frames from several camera views, the first of its kind for this task. A full processing pipeline is included, and several weakly supervised methods, which learn from rough hints rather than exact outlines, are benchmarked on it.
arxiv-2509-06785:
The symmetry group hidden in a family of cubic surfaces is computed by Eric Pichon-Pharabod and one co-author in a 2025 algebraic geometry paper. A cubic surface famously carries twenty-seven lines, and as the surface varies in a family, those lines get permuted. That permutation group, the Galois or monodromy group, measures the family's symmetry.

The authors describe a method using certified numerical computation, meaning numerics with guaranteed error control, to find this group for linear systems of cubic surfaces. Applying it to every family invariant under a subgroup of the symmetric group on five letters, they find the group is often much smaller than the full Weyl group that bounds it. Discriminants of the families come out as a byproduct. The method extends to monodromy on the homology of any family of smooth hypersurfaces, illustrated with symmetric quartic surfaces.
arxiv-2509-06985:
Caz L. Czworkowski and John W. Sheppard present VIGPSO in a 2025 paper on improving particle swarm optimization. Particle swarm methods search for good solutions by moving a swarm of candidate points through a space, and they are widely used for real-valued optimization. They face challenges in high-dimensional search spaces, where variables interact in unknown ways.

Variable interaction graphs have proven effective when problem structure is known, but their use in black-box optimization remains limited. VIGPSO dynamically learns how variables influence each other by analyzing how particles move, then uses those learned relationships to guide future movements. Evaluated against standard particle swarm optimization on eight benchmark functions across dimensions from ten to one thousand, it achieved statistically significant improvements in most test configurations.
arxiv-2509-07085:
Nirmalya Brahma and 3 co-authors study how magnetic white dwarfs can make light dark-sector particles in a 2025 paper. The particles at issue are axions and dark photons, both still hypothetical, with very small masses. A white dwarf is the dense, burnt-out core of a dead star, and some of them carry strong magnetic fields.

Inside such a star, the field twists how light waves move through the hot plasma. That twist can line up a photon with an axion or dark photon, a match known as resonance, in spots where no such match would occur with no field. The team find that the field opens fresh zones in the star where this match can happen. Past limits on such particles, drawn from stars, may thus need a fresh look for strongly magnetic cases.
arxiv-2509-07185:
Jordan Cotler and 1 co-author prove a new form of Egorov's theorem in 2025, recast for quantum mechanics. Egorov's theorem links how quantum states evolve to how their classical counterparts move. The new version is stated in the Schrödinger picture, where states carry the time change. Distance between states is measured with a Wasserstein metric, a tool from optimal transport that prices the work of reshaping one distribution into another.

The proof uses Husimi functions, which give each quantum state a smooth phase-space portrait. With distance index one, the result is a low-regularity theorem, meaning it needs few smoothness assumptions. Larger index values give stronger bounds. Along the way, the authors prove an optimal transport inequality like one known in mean-field quantum theory. The work gives physicists a sharper ruler for comparing quantum and classical motion.
arxiv-2509-07285:
Xiang Tang and 1 co-author develop a unified framework in 2025 for proving that certain cohomology theories do not change under Morita equivalence. Cohomology theories assign algebraic summaries to geometric objects, and Morita invariance means the summary depends only on the object's essential structure, not its presentation. Lie groupoids, the objects here, generalize both spaces and symmetry groups.

The approach views each theory as coming from sheaves of modules on the nerve of the groupoid, a layered construction that records how the pieces compose. The authors give criteria for when such sheaves yield Morita invariant cohomology. A single framework that covers many theories at once saves each new case from needing its own bespoke proof. The result is a piece of infrastructure for geometers who work with stacks and groupoids.
arxiv-2509-07485:
Jeongwoo Na and 3 co-authors present MVP in 2025, a faster and less biased way for language models to rerank search passages. Reranking takes a first list of candidate passages and reorders them by relevance. Current language-model rerankers generate text step by step and scan with sliding windows, which gets costly as lists grow, and they suffer position and selection biases from the input order.

MVP instead encodes each query-passage pair into several view embeddings, distinct numeric viewpoints, without generating text. An anchor vector per view yields relevance scores in a single decoding step, and an orthogonal loss keeps the views distinct from each other. With only 220 million parameters, MVP matches much larger fine-tuned models of about 7 billion parameters in the reported experiments. Cheaper, stabler reranking could improve search quality in everyday systems.
arxiv-2509-07685:
The BESIII Collaboration measures the space-like transition form factor of the neutral pion in a 2025 paper. A transition form factor describes how a pion converts into photons under momentum transfer. It is a basic test of quantum chromodynamics at low energies. The measurement uses electron-positron collision data from the BESIII detector. The collisions were taken at a center-of-mass energy in the GeV range.

The process under study is two-photon fusion. The colliding particles exchange photons and produce a pion. A single-tag approach detects one scattered lepton. Both the cross section and the form factor are measured across a range of squared momentum transfers. The results agree with past measurements. They improve precision at the lower end of the range in a marked way. Such data sharpen tests of pion structure calculations. Those calculations feed into broader precision physics.
arxiv-2509-07785:
Niklas Frederik Schmitz and 2 co-authors present a differentiation framework for plane-wave density functional theory in 2025. Density functional theory, or DFT, is the workhorse for computing material traits from quantum mechanics. Plane-wave versions expand the electron states in waves. Derivatives of outputs with respect to inputs are often needed. Inputs range from geometry to model parameters. Such derivatives usually demand hand-derived formulas for each new case.

Their AD-DFPT framework merges two tools. One is forward-mode algorithmic differentiation, which propagates derivatives through code on its own. The other is density functional perturbation theory. Derivatives of any output with respect to any input then come out with no manual gradient work. The framework is implemented in the Density Functional ToolKit. Examples include inverse design of a chip band gap. They also include learning model parameters and carrying input uncertainty to relaxed structures.
arxiv-2509-07885:
Ottavio Khalifa and 3 co-authors survey methods for grouping categorical time series in a 2025 scoping review. Such series record states over time, like a patient's daily status or a customer's changing segment, and they appear across epidemiology, sociology, biology, and marketing. Analysts need guidance on which clustering method fits which data.

Searching three major databases up to November 2024, the team screened over fourteen thousand studies and kept 124 articles describing 129 methods. Methods fall into distance-based, feature-based, and model-based families. Each is judged against practical challenges: uneven sequence lengths, missing data, several variables at once, and very large datasets. The map should help researchers choose tools deliberately instead of by habit.
arxiv-2509-08185:
Faint gravitationally lensed galaxies hide in Herschel survey data, and Juan Alberto Cano's 2025 paper with 7 co-authors presents a new way to find them. Earlier searches favoured bright, strongly magnified submillimetre galaxies, leaving dimmer, mildly lensed systems to statistics alone. The new method pairs high-redshift Herschel-ATLAS sources with nearby WISE elliptical galaxies that could be doing the lensing.

Candidate pairs within a small angular separation become targets for individual study. Each confirmed lens is a natural telescope: the foreground galaxy magnifies a background galaxy too faint to inspect directly. Building a fair sample of weak and strong lenses matters because lensed galaxies reveal star formation in the early universe at resolutions no telescope reaches alone.
arxiv-2509-08285:
Software in cars and medical devices now carries safety-critical duties, and it changes faster than safety paperwork can follow. Carmen Cârlan, Daniel Ratiu, and Michael Wagner argue for safety factories in a 2025 manifesto paper. Software teams already work factory-style, with build systems and automated pipelines. Safety engineering still relies on disconnected tools and manual documents.

The authors propose investing in formality up front. Safety work products should live in rich, machine-processable models. Automatic consistency checks can then guard them, and documentation can be generated rather than hand-written. Safety tooling would plug directly into the software pipeline. The manifesto is a call to transfer software's best habits to safety work. Faster releases, the authors argue, should not require slower or weaker safety assurance.
arxiv-2509-08385:
Designing a quantum circuit that generates realistic financial data is a search problem with many dead ends. Yaswitha Gujju, Romain Harang, and Tetsuo Shibuya let a large language model do the searching, in a 2025 research paper. Their target is the quantum circuit Born machine, a generative model built from a parameterized circuit. The circuit's layout, called its ansatz, must be expressive yet shallow enough for noisy hardware.

Prompts to the language model include qubit connectivity, gate error rates, and hardware topology. Feedback on accuracy, circuit depth, and validity steers later rounds. The test task modeled daily changes in Japanese government bond interest rates. Circuits the model proposed were much shallower than the standard baseline. They also generated better data on real IBM quantum hardware. The work points to language models as practical architects for near-term quantum devices.
arxiv-2509-08485:
Unknown cameras joining a network announce themselves in their traffic, and Priyanka Rushikesh Chaudhary with Rajib Ranjan Maiti build a detector in a 2025 network security paper. Consumer internet-of-things devices rarely give administrators monitoring or control, so simply noticing a new streaming camera is a security problem in itself.

Their zCamInspector identifies known cameras with supervised classifiers and flags zero-day cameras, models never seen before, with one-class classifiers trained on normal patterns. Roughly forty gigabytes of traffic across three datasets, commercial cameras, open-source cameras, and conferencing applications as decoys, support the evaluation. Homes and offices full of silent lenses need exactly this kind of flow-based census before any policy can be enforced.
arxiv-2509-09085:
Jifeng Shen and 6 co-authors present IRDFusion for multispectral object detection in a 2025 paper. Multispectral cameras combine visible and thermal views, but fusion often keeps background noise. Their method contrasts cross-modal features and screens out shared interference.

Two new modules refine features within and across modalities, then feed back difference signals as guidance. That feedback loop, inspired by differential amplifiers, amplifies salient relational signals step by step. Common mode noise is suppressed while complementary object information is kept. Tests on FLIR, LLVIP, and another benchmark reach state of the art results. Robustness holds across diverse challenging scenes.
arxiv-2509-09385: Milutin Obradović and 1 co-author wrote a short 2025 paper on symmetric Toeplitz determinants. The work concerns univalent functions. It gives bounds for these determinants in the class U. It also treats the wider class S. Both indices run through whole values from one upward. The authors work through selected cases of those values. Readers get a compact set of bounds for a classic object in complex analysis.
arxiv-2509-09785:
Moslem Yazdanpanah and 7 co-authors adapt 3D object classifiers to new conditions without any retraining in a 2025 computer vision paper. Point cloud models lose accuracy when the world shifts, and most fixes update the network at test time, which costs speed and memory. Their idea, token purging, simply throws away the internal tokens most damaged by the shift before those tokens reach the attention layers.

Two flavours are offered: one guided by stored source statistics, and one fully source-free that leans on the classification token. On three corrupted benchmark sets the first beat other update-free methods by about ten points of accuracy on average. The approach also ran many times faster and leaner than its baseline.
arxiv-2509-10185:
R. Montalà and 6 co-authors let a learning agent discover how to control airflow over a wing in this 2025 paper. At a steep angle, air breaks away from a three-dimensional wing, lift collapses, and the wake turns turbulent. The team coupled a fast graphics-card flow solver with multi-agent deep reinforcement learning, and let the agents search for jet actions that fix the separation.

The learned strategies reattached the separated shear layer to the wing surface. In the reported tests, lift rose sharply, drag fell by about two thirds, and overall aerodynamic efficiency multiplied several times over. Flow pictures confirm the fix. The authors present the result as evidence that learning control can handle genuinely complex, turbulent flows.
arxiv-2509-10485:
Paul Alexander Bilokon studies when new denominators first appear in the Calkin-Wilf enumeration of the positive rationals in this solo 2025 number theory paper. That enumeration lists every positive fraction exactly once in breadth-first order. Bilokon defines a first-appearance map recording, for each denominator, the earliest position where a reduced fraction with that denominator shows up.

His main theorem is a symmetry he calls simultaneous novelty. Around the natural starting index of any level, first appearances of two denominators placed equally far below and above that level mirror each other exactly. The proof compares this pattern with a simple denominator-first array, using a local-coherence analysis and a discrete intermediate-value argument. He also restates the result in group-theoretic language tied to the tree structure behind the enumeration.
arxiv-2509-10585:
A mega-constellation with a failed satellite needs a spare, fast. Seungyeop Han and five co-authors design the spare-parts strategy for large satellite fleets. They present it in this 2025 operations paper. Their focus is the direct insertion strategy. Replacement satellites go straight into constellation planes. A reorder-point, order-quantity policy governs the flow. The policy is borrowed from inventory management.

Failures are random. Launch delays are random, too. The authors model each as a Markov chain. They combine the chains into one framework. It is efficient to compute with. It is accurate enough to optimize against. They then solve for the spare policy that minimizes operating cost. A case study uses a real-world mega-constellation. It shows the method working at practical scale. Operators gain a principled way to decide two things. How many spares should they keep? When should they launch them?
arxiv-2509-10685:
Jiayou Zhong and four co-authors argue that aligning AI with human values in healthcare cannot mean aligning with one average patient in this 2025 paper. Medical choices are steeped in personal, cultural, and situational values, and existing pluralistic alignment schemes, such as Modular Pluralism, were not built for that setting.

Their framework, EthosAgents, is a lightweight, general approach that simulates diverse perspectives and values through role-driven agents. Tested across seven language models, open and closed, of varying sizes, the framework improved pluralistic alignment in all three modes the authors measure. The broader message travels beyond medicine: in high-stakes domains, alignment methods must adapt to who is speaking and what situation they face, rather than smoothing disagreement away.
arxiv-2509-10985:
Sofia Zinzani, Francesca Baletto, and Kevin Rossi link a nanocatalyst's shape to its performance with machine learning in this 2025 paper. Designing catalysts by trial and error is slow. Their demanding test case is the oxygen reduction reaction, central to fuel cells. They predict the mass activity of platinum nanoparticles, estimated by a microkinetic model.

Accurate models emerged from two very different descriptions of structure. One is available only in computation: the distribution of generalized coordination numbers across surface sites. The other is measurable in the lab: the pair distance distribution function. Coupled with Bayesian optimization, the model then found the ten and one hundred most active structures in a pool of over fifty thousand candidates, after testing only a few thousand. The pipeline is a blueprint for faster catalyst hunting, theoretical and experimental alike.
arxiv-2509-11285:
Teaching a neural network new classes over time without erasing old ones is the problem behind this 2025 machine learning paper by Alejandro Dopico-Castro and three co-authors. The usual approach, repeated gradient training, is costly, touchy about settings, and prone to catastrophic forgetting.

Their framework, CIFNet, takes a different route: with a frozen pre-trained feature extractor, each new class can be added by an exact closed-form ridge regression update, with no backpropagation at all. A small calibration buffer in feature space, plus density-aware oversampling, keeps the decision borders fair between old and new classes. On three standard benchmarks the method matched iterative rivals while learning smoothly, never collapsing midway, and using far less energy. The results make a case for analytic, formula-based continual learning.
arxiv-2509-11485:
Vinícius Yu Okubo and 4 co-authors measure how magnetic stripe patterns evolve in a thin magnetic film, in a 2025 study combining deep learning with geometry. Labyrinthine stripes appear in many physical systems, but their lack of long-range order makes them hard to quantify.

A U-Net segmentation model, trained with synthetic noise, first isolates stripes in magneto-optical images despite occlusions. A pipeline then skeletonizes the patterns, maps them to graphs, and fits curves to measure local length and curvature. Applied to hundreds of images from annealing trials, the analysis tracked a shift from a quenched, disordered state to a more parallel, coherent one. Two distinct evolution modes appeared, linked to field polarity.
arxiv-2509-11685:
J. S. Alvarado, M. Hoballah, and E. Voutier assess a proposed probe of hadron structure in a 2025 paper on double deeply virtual Compton scattering. Generalized parton distributions encode how a hadron's parton momentum and place correlate. That link reveals mechanical and spin traits of the hadron.

The known single version of this scattering reaches those distributions only in a narrow kinematic region. The double version offers broader access but is still unmeasured. The authors study how feasible its observables are with polarized electron beams at Jefferson Lab and the future Electron-Ion Collider. They focus on sensitivity to one family of distributions and on extracting linked Compton form factors. Projections support that measurements at both sites are feasible.
arxiv-2509-11885:
Francis Xiatian Zhang and 5 co-authors estimate depth inside airways during bronchoscopy in a 2025 medical imaging paper called BREA-Depth. Knowing depth from a single camera view could improve navigation accuracy and safety in complex, branching airways, but depth models often overfit local textures and miss global airway structure.

Their framework adapts a depth foundation model with airway-specific geometric priors. A cycle-consistent generative model, refined for depth awareness, translates between real bronchoscopic images and airway geometries from anatomical data, bridging the domain gap. A structure awareness loss enforces depth consistency inside the airway channel while preserving smooth transitions. A new metric judges anatomical realism. Validation on ex vivo human lung data and an open dataset beat existing methods.
arxiv-2509-12185:
Choosing between forecasting models by score alone ignores luck, and Argimiro Arratia with three co-authors revive a classical variance test for the job in 2025. Their subject is the Morgan-Pitman test for whether two error streams share the same variance.

Raw forecast errors misbehave: they carry heavy tails, outliers, and dependence that the textbook test cannot stomach. The authors harden it accordingly and add a strategy that renders machine learning residuals statistically independent, a precondition for honest testing. Simulations and real-data applications then show the adapted test working as a dependable instrument for evaluation and selection. The pitch is modest but useful: give model choice a sampling-variability yardstick instead of crowning whichever score happened to land higher.
arxiv-2509-12385:
Mitchell Plyler and 4 co-authors present SENTRA in a 2025 paper on detecting text written by large language models. As these models spread, undeclared machine-written text becomes harder to spot. SENTRA is a general-purpose supervised detector, meaning it learns from labeled examples rather than relying on a single trick.

SENTRA is a transformer-based encoder that uses selected next-token probability sequences, the model's own estimates of what word comes next at chosen points. It also uses contrastive pre-training on large amounts of unlabeled data, learning by comparing similar and different examples. Across three public datasets covering twenty-four domains of text, SENTRA significantly beat popular baselines when tested on domains it had not been trained on.
arxiv-2509-12485:
Falling into a rotating black hole, a traveler's clock can be repackaged into Lemaître time, a coordinate that stays smooth across the horizon. A. V. Toporensky and one co-author generalize that time in 2025 to wider families of rotating metrics, and to the charged Reissner-Nordström hole, then probe its behavior right at the horizon.

Four properties turn out to be linked: whether the time stays finite, whether it runs forward, the sign of a generalized energy, and a censorship principle banning literally infinite collision energies. That link explains an old puzzle, why two particles colliding inside the horizon cannot release infinite energy in their shared frame.
arxiv-2509-12785:
Alexis Mousseau, Soizic Terrien, and Vincent Tournat study how thin plates can shift sound to higher frequencies in a 2025 experimental paper. Classical sound absorption methods face basic limits that non-linear effects may overcome. Thin clamped plates are strongly non-linear elements capable of transferring acoustic power from an incoming airborne wave toward higher frequencies.

The tests show varied vibrational behaviors depending on the amplitude and frequency of the excitation signal. Low levels produced harmonic generation in a weakly non-linear regime, while higher levels produced quasi-periodic and chaotic regimes. Those regimes govern the frequency-up conversion process. A parametric study across plate thicknesses found the effect is mostly guided by the plate's resonance at its first natural frequency, which depends on thickness and on static tension from clamping.
arxiv-2509-12985:
Alessandro Casini, Adam McCloskey and two co-authors track dynamic treatment effects over time in 2025 with instrument tools. Instruments shift treatment for some cases only, called compliers. In time data those cases can now be named one by one.

Smoothness and local contrasts do the naming. Named non-compliers allow a direct test of the core exclusion rule. A survey finds weak instruments rife in top journals, yet strong pockets often exist. A dynamic search finds the strongest pocket for sharper estimates. Use on money policy splits past results and supports the exclusion rule.
arxiv-2509-13385:
Charlotte Beylier, Parvaneh Joharinad and two co-authors use sectional curvature in 2025 to grade shrink maps and gauge true data dimension. Curvature here reads metric links among triples and further points. A profile sums those links for a discrete space in full.

A quantitative score grades representation quality from the profile. Tests show the profile also estimates intrinsic dimension well. Large empirical networks are explored with the tool. Shrink methods are graded on real sets. Geometry thus gives a shared yardstick where error alone misleads. Dimension calls gain a check that is apart from the shrink method itself.
arxiv-2509-13785:
Bingshen Mu and ten co-authors summarize a community challenge in a 2025 speech paper, the Interspeech 2025 Multilingual Conversational Speech Language Model Challenge. The goal was to push models that can hold spoken conversations across many languages, a step beyond single-language voice assistants, and to give the field shared data and baselines.

The organizers released roughly sixteen hundred hours of real multilingual conversational speech and defined two tasks with baseline systems. Seventy-eight teams from thirteen countries entered, producing hundreds of leaderboard results and fourteen technical reports. The summary distills what the submissions taught about building such models, from data handling to training recipes, as a reference for the wider speech community.
arxiv-2509-13885:
Tugce Pekacar Calci and Serhat Emirhan Soycan investigate a new class of rings in a 2025 algebra paper. Their objects are called delta-quasipolar rings. A condition defines them. Each element links to an idempotent, an element equal to its own square. The idempotent commutes with the element twice over. Their sum lands in a special subring built from the Jacobson radical.

The pair develop a general framework for these rings. They work out the fundamental properties of the class. They also examine how it behaves under standard constructions, such as matrix rings and polynomial rings. And they map its relationships with better-known families. Those include strongly delta-clean rings, uniquely clean rings, and J-quasipolar rings. The new class takes its place within the broader landscape of ring theory.
arxiv-2509-14085:
Matheus Hostert and Salvador Urrea survey spallation sources as hunting grounds for new light particles in a 2025 particle physics paper. Spallation facilities smash protons into heavy targets for neutron science. Their intense beams also produce floods of pions, muons, and kaons. Decays at rest of those particles could emit long-lived particles beyond the standard model. Nearby neutrino detectors might catch them decaying.

The pair catalog spallation sources worldwide and estimate each detector's reach. At J-PARC, the ND280 gaseous argon detectors could set leading limits on particles decaying to electron pairs. The JSNS-squared liquid scintillator detector can exploit double and triple coincidences from kaon decay products. Smaller detectors at Los Alamos and Oak Ridge also show promise. Some models are testable more than ten times beyond current limits.
arxiv-2509-14185:
Yongji Wang and twenty-one co-authors report the first systematic discovery of unstable fluid singularities in a 2025 paper. Whether smooth fluid motion can blow up into infinite gradients is a foundational open problem. It is tied to the Euler and Navier-Stokes equations. Known numerical examples were stable singularities, robust to perturbation. The key open cases are expected to need unstable ones. Those demand infinitely precise starting conditions and so stayed hidden.

The team paired custom neural networks and training recipes with a Gauss-Newton optimizer tuned for high precision. Some solutions reached accuracies near double-precision machine limits. They found new families of unstable self-similar blow-ups. The equations covered are the porous media equation and three-dimensional Euler flow with a boundary. A simple empirical formula links blow-up rate to the order of instability. The work lays groundwork for future computer-assisted proofs.
arxiv-2509-14385:
Gabriel Nixon Raj, writing alone in 2025, proposes a regime aware learning system for long term investing. Markets shift among hidden regimes, such as calm growth or stress. A portfolio agent that ignores regime change can hold the wrong mix at the worst time.

Raj builds test environments where the agent reallocates capital as latent economic regimes shift. Rewards penalise wild swings, include capital resets and add tail risk shocks. Several learning designs compete, including transformer and memory based variants of a standard policy method. Classic equal weight and Sharpe optimised portfolios serve as baselines. Transformer agents earned the best risk adjusted returns under stress in the tests. Memory based agents traded some return for clearer behaviour and lower training cost.
arxiv-2509-14485:
Marko Tesic and four co-authors look past raw scores in 2025 to profile prosocial skills in groups of AI agents. Social skills such as working together and following shared rules decide how agent groups fare. Game scores alone hide which skills drive success.

The Melting Pot contest gives social test scenes where joint work can be scored. A Bayesian tool called measurement layouts infers a skill profile for each agent group from contest play. Profiles foretold later scores inside the suite. They also showed which prosocial skills each group truly held. For builders of agent groups, a profile beats a rank table: it names the social skill to train next.
arxiv-2509-14585:
Minh Vu and Konstantinos Slavakis introduce in 2025 an online reinforcement learning framework built on sparse Gaussian mixture Q-functions. A Q-function scores actions by long term reward. Mixture models give a structured, interpretable form for that score instead of a black box network.

Earlier mixture Q-functions were trained offline from fixed data. The new online scheme learns from streaming experience and encourages exploration as data arrive. Sparsity is induced through a Hadamard overparametrisation that curbs overfitting while keeping expressiveness. Parameters live on a Riemannian manifold, so updates follow its geometry with online gradient descent. Interpretable value functions that learn live suit control settings where operators must audit why an agent favours an action.
arxiv-2509-14785:
Kentaro Seki, with five co-authors, tackles a gap in audio AI in a 2025 paper. Contrastive language-audio pretraining, called CLAP, links sound recordings with text descriptions. Older CLAP systems handle only one sound source at a time, so they miss where each sound comes from. Seki and the team propose Spatial-CLAP, which learns embeddings that carry both content and location.

Their method adds a content-aware spatial encoder, so each source keeps its own position in the learned representation. A training strategy called spatial contrastive learning forces the model to match each source with its correct location. Tests on downstream tasks and on unseen mixtures of three sources show the embeddings stay reliable. The results mark a shift from single-source training toward true multi-source training.
arxiv-2509-14885:
Georg Schildbach and Hossam S. Abbas extend deadbeat robust model predictive control to systems whose dynamics change with parameters, in a 2025 control theory paper. Model predictive control plans inputs over a horizon while respecting limits. The deadbeat idea wipes out disturbance effects within the first few steps, so the rest of the plan can be made with certainty.

That trick removes the need for a robust invariant terminal set, which is often hard or impossible to compute. Earlier work proved guarantees such as recursive feasibility and input-to-state stability for plain linear systems. The new paper covers linear parameter-varying systems with bounded parameter uncertainty and added disturbances, keeping the full guarantees. Simulations show the scheme performs well with the origin as terminal set and a slightly longer horizon.
arxiv-2509-14985:
Arda Kabadayi, Senem Velipasalar, and Jiajing Chen present PRISM for finding products in shopping cart photos in a 2025 computer vision paper. Retail retrieval is harder than generic image search: rival brands look nearly identical, and shopper photos come from odd angles compared with catalog shots. Foundation vision-language models often miss the small local differences that separate products.
