PRISM combines the strengths of two approaches in three stages. A vision-language model first pulls a shortlist of the most similar catalog items, narrowing the search. Pixel-wise matching, accurate but slow, then runs only on that shortlist to settle fine distinctions. The hybrid keeps the speed of learned retrieval and the precision of direct image comparison, a practical balance for checkout and inventory applications.
arxiv-2509-15185:
Xiaoyu Yue and seven co-authors teach image models to grasp a scene before they draw it, in a 2025 paper. These models build a picture one token at a time, a recipe taken from text models. A close study finds three blocks to grasping high-level meaning: too much weight on near tokens, meaning that drifts from step to step, and weak sense of spatial layout.

Their fix adds self-taught goals to training, with no outside model of images needed. The model builds its own grasp of visual meaning as it learns to draw. Grasp and drawing then boost each other. Tests show the self-guided training lifts the semantic quality of the output and narrows a known gap with models built just to read images.
arxiv-2509-15285:
Mikhail Korobko and five co-authors show a speed-based readout next to a place-based one in a single bench interferometer, in a 2025 paper. Quantum push noise from light limits the low-rate reach of gravitational wave detectors. The standard cure, squeezed light tuned by rate, needs long filter cavities and much extra gear.

A speedmeter dodges the noise at its source by gauging a test mass's speed, not its place. None had been shown with a moving mass in a lab optomechanical setup. The team's mixed readout cavity pulls place and speed signals from two ports at once. Matching the light transfer curves of both ports proves true speedmeter action in hardware. A working bench speedmeter firms the case for the concept in future detectors.
arxiv-2509-15485:
Ahmed Abdou, writing alone, grades how hard Arabic texts are to read. His entry in a 2025 shared task sorts texts into nineteen levels of reading ease. A plain model pick can land far from the true level, and far misses cost more than near ones. Abdou wanted a method that admits doubt and stays close when unsure.

His fix works after any base model has run. A method called conformal prediction gives a set of levels that likely holds the true one. He then averages those levels, weighted by the model's own scores. Scores rose by one to three points across base models. Sentence level results beat document level ones. Reviewers can focus on a few likely levels.
arxiv-2509-15585:
Akanksha Sarkar, Been Kim, and Jennifer Sun ask how many known classes a model needs to find new ones. Finding new classes in unlabeled data helps fields from science to robotics. Real data mix many tangled factors, which makes the question hard to study cleanly. The team build a controlled test bed to isolate it.

They use a data set of simple shapes made by a program, with factors they can vary at will. They then change how many classes are known and how well those known classes cover the space. Gains from more known classes reach a ceiling, past which finding new classes stalls. The pattern gives users a way to weigh cost against gain.
arxiv-2509-16085:
Screening thousands of traits for the few that matter is a core step in large data work, but the standard screen scans every row for every trait. Xiaxue Ouyang, Kejun He, and Cheng Meng speed it up with a method that grows its sample bit by bit, in the spirit of bandit problems. Traits with weak links to the outcome are dropped early, which saves work.

Their method cuts the scan cost sharply while keeping the trait-finding promise of the older screen. Clear theory shows how sample size trades against accuracy. On made-up and real data, results match the standard screen at much lower run time.
arxiv-2509-16385:
How far young organisms drift before settling shapes whole ecosystems, and rare long trips matter most. Luis F. Gordillo and Priscilla E. Greenwood show that a simple drift model can yield those rare long trips if its settings vary from case to case. In their model, each organism wanders in two dimensions for a random time, with the wander and timing traits drawn fresh each time.

That modest variation alone produces heavy-tailed spread patterns, where far settlers are much more common than a fixed-setting model would give. The result offers a clean frame for grasping long-distance dispersal in movement ecology.
arxiv-2509-16585:
Ta Giang Thuy Loan and co-authors tackle tracking a hidden signal space from dirty data, in a 2025 signal paper. Data streams often span a low-dimensional space that shifts over time. Real samples, though, can be sparse and hit by harsh, non-standard noise. The team build a method that tracks that space while resisting the noise.

Their method beat prior robust trackers in tests. It did so with low computing cost and small memory use. Trials also covered finding the direction that signals arrive from. Both tasks showed clear gains. Such tracking sits behind radar, sonar, and many sensor systems, so gains in speed and trust matter.
arxiv-2509-16785:
Maxime Martin, Levi Pereon, Quoc Tuan Truong, and Victor Teboul stretch time steps in liquid simulations in a 2025 paper. Simulating molecules step by step is costly when steps must stay tiny. The team treat the simulation as a random process and coarsen time, much like others coarsen space. A tweaked force law is the key.

They swap a sharp short-range wall in the force law for a smooth curve. With that swap, a much larger step gives the same motion as the old law with small steps. Tests compare both laws head to head. Bigger steps could cut the cost of liquid studies in chemistry and materials work.
arxiv-2509-16885:
Haomiao Huang and co-authors take deep spectra of two compact planetary nebulae in a 2025 astronomy paper. A planetary nebula is a glowing shell shed by a dying star. The team used a large Canary Islands telescope for long, detailed exposures. Their spectra span a wide range of wavelengths, catching many faint emission lines.

Line strengths reveal the chemistry and state of the gas. Both shells fit the radial oxygen pattern seen across our galaxy's nebulae. Comparisons with aging-star models point to low-mass parent stars. Deep spectra of faint shells help trace how stars enrich the galaxy with new elements as they die.
arxiv-2509-17185:
Bence Soóki-Tóth and five co-authors wrote a 2025 arXiv paper on bribery attacks against the Ethereum blockchain. The long-term health of such systems rests on paying validators fairly for honest work. Smart contracts can now offer bribes without trust, which puts that honest bargain at risk.

The team builds and tests three bribery contracts. The first buys votes to fork the chain onto the briber's blocks. The second pays validators to quit, which raises the attacker's share of what is left. The third runs an open market that auctions control over Ethereum's randomness beacon. The authors add an early game-theory study of one market. Their work shows, in running code, how cheap trustless bribery can be.
arxiv-2509-17585:
Viola Negroni, Davide Salvi, Alessandro Ilic Mezza, Paolo Bestagini, and Stefano Tubaro built a detector for fake speech. Their 2025 arXiv paper answers a growing abuse: AI speech now powers helpful tools, yet it also feeds impersonation, misinformation, and biometric spoofing. As fakes near human quality, detection has become urgent.

The system, the ISPL team's entry to the SAFE challenge, joins several leading detectors in a mixture of experts. An attention-based gate weighs each expert per clip, since each expert learns a distinct facet of the shared training data. That division of labor beat single detectors in tests. The entry ranked first across all tasks at the challenge. The authors present the gating idea as a general way to make audio forensics sturdier as synthesis keeps improving.
arxiv-2509-17885:
Saad Mokssit and 3 co-authors train deep nets that can answer early, before all layers run. Their 2025 paper calls the plan Confidence-Gated Training. Early exits save cost when a net is sure, but joint training lets deep exits hog the work.

Their rule sends deep-exit lessons back only when the early exits fail. That makes the shallow exits the first choice, and saves deep layers for hard cases. Tests on two bench sets cut mean run cost and raised total score at once. The plan suits places with tight compute, such as small devices.
arxiv-2509-17985:
Geonung Kim, Janghyeok Han, and Sunghyun Cho make videos of 3D scenes from rough shape and one photo. Their 2025 frame, VideoFrom3D, aims to speed up 3D design work. A plain video model fed just shape tends to blur detail, drift in motion, or break flow across frames.

Their plan pairs an image model with a video model, each for its strength. The image side makes sharp anchor views that agree across angles. The video side then fills frames between anchors, guided by shape and camera path. No paired set of 3D scenes and photos was needed to train it.
arxiv-2509-18085:
Sudhanshu Agrawal and 5 co-authors speed up diffusion language models with a graph of draft tokens. Their 2025 method, Spiffy, deals with a new class of models that write in blocks, both ways at once. Such models could write far faster than step-by-step ones, if draft checks keep up.

Spiffy drafts from the model itself, so no second draft model is needed. Draft states form a directed graph, tuned off-line for high take rates and pruned live for speed. Paired with cache and threshold tricks, it cut model runs by large factors on three models. The output spread stays provably the same.
arxiv-2509-18585:
Fine-tuning a large model on every parameter is costly, so low-rank adapters train only a small part. Yu Chen, Yifei Han, Long Zhang, Yue Du, and Bin Li present TsqLoRA, a smarter adapter scheme, in this 2025 paper. Older schemes treat all layers alike and use whatever training data is at hand. Layers, though, differ in how strongly updates affect them.

TsqLoRA has two parts. A quality-aware sampler picks the most informative training examples. A rank allocation module then gives each layer a rank matched to its sensitivity. Layers that matter more get more capacity; quiet layers get less. Tests across varied language tasks show better efficiency with equal or better scores than standard adapters. The authors say the pairing of data choice with layer-wise ranks is the key. Code is promised in public.
arxiv-2509-18985:
Elisa Composta and three co-authors built a fake social network and filled it with AI agents to see how online talk unfolds. The agents run on large language models, so they can read and write posts in natural language. Each agent starts with a profile modeled on real posts from the 2022 Italian election. The setup also gives agents opinions that can shift as they interact.

The agents wrote posts that made sense, formed links, and built a network shape much like a real one. Their views over time moved much as classic math models of opinion change predict. Yet their posts varied less in tone and harshness than real users' posts. Changing the settings barely moved the results, which suggests the agents need richer mental models from the start.
arxiv-2509-19585:
Galaxy centers that flicker over months can betray feeding black holes. Zachary Stone and twelve co-authors hunt for that flicker in the first two imaging rounds of NEXUS, a large JWST program near the north ecliptic pole. About twenty-five thousand sources were compared across two epochs nine months apart. Subtracting one image from the other exposed changes far fainter than single-epoch measures could catch.

The team found 465 high-confidence variable sources. Nearly all look like distant galaxies rather than stars. Their distance pattern matches the parent sample, so the hunt is not skewed to one era. The work also proves how steady the new camera's readings are. Later NEXUS rounds will add spectra and more epochs, letting the team sort true black hole feeding from other causes of change.
arxiv-2509-19885:
Intensive care generates dense time series, yet labeled data for training models stays scarce and siloed. Katja Naasunnguaq Jagd, Rachael DeVries, and Ole Winther pretrain a foundation model on pooled health records without labels. Their Bi-Axial Transformer reads across both time and variables. Self-supervision lets it learn the rhythms of critical illness from raw streams.

Fine-tuned on a fresh hospital set for mortality prediction, the model beat supervised baselines. The edge was largest where labeled cases numbered under five thousand. That regime is exactly where smaller hospitals live. A shared pretrained base could lift care analytics in places that cannot amass big data. The authors present the model as an early step, with transfer evidence to justify the direction.
arxiv-2509-19985:
Anomalies in sensor networks often hide in timing and coordination, not in single wild values. Sepehr Maleki and Negar Pourmoazemi build Pi-Transformer, which watches multivariate series with two attentions at once. One pathway learns from data; the other follows a smooth prior encoding habits such as self-similarity across scales and phase synchrony. The prior ignores amplitude, making it a steady temporal reference.

Training pairs reconstruction with a divergence term that keeps the two attentions close yet distinct. At test time, an alignment-weighted energy score merges with a mismatch score that flags phase and timing breaks. Industrial monitoring and health telemetry both produce such series. A prior that knows normal rhythm can catch disorders that value-only detectors miss.
arxiv-2509-20085:
Peng Gao and Yuetong Zhao wrote this 2025 arXiv paper in analytic number theory. It studies Fourier coefficients of modular forms, numbers that encode deep arithmetic patterns. The coefficients are twisted by quadratic characters, which flip signs in a structured way. The paper bounds the average size of long sums of these twisted coefficients.

The authors bound all high integral moments of such sums. Their upper bounds assume the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, a famous unproven conjecture. They also prove matching lower bounds for all even moments without any assumption. Matching bounds mean the estimates cannot be improved in general. Results like these feed into wider questions about how modular form values are distributed. The paper is short and technical, aimed at specialists in the field.
arxiv-2509-20185:
Alex Bartel and Carlo Pagano wrote this 2025 arXiv paper in number theory. Class groups measure how far a number field falls short of unique factorization. Ray class groups refine that measure using a fixed modulus. The paper proposes a statistical model for how these groups behave on average for real quadratic fields.

The model says the groups are distributed randomly under a natural Cohen-Lenstra type measure, at least near a fixed set of odd primes. The authors work with a refined Arakelov version of the ray class group. They show their model implies the classic Cohen-Lenstra predictions for ordinary class groups. It also predicts how the fundamental unit of a field is spread modulo an integer. The predictions match known results on the average size of three-torsion parts.
arxiv-2509-20385:
Security data is too dense for plain tables and text, so researchers draw it instead. Ishara Devendra, Chaman Wijesiriwardana, and Prasad Wimalaratne review that field in a 2025 arXiv systematic review. Software security visualization turns threat and compliance data into pictures analysts can grasp. The authors set out to map the techniques and their uses.

They examined more than sixty recent key papers. The techniques fall into four families: graph-based, notation-based, matrix-based, and metaphor-based. Two broad application areas stood out, covering software development views and operational security views. The review records recent advances and the field's open issues. Its message is that visualization must keep evolving with the threat landscape. Better pictures, the authors argue, sharpen detection and speed response.
arxiv-2509-20485:
Judging synthetic speech still leans on crude yardsticks, and Ismail Rasim Ulgen and four co-authors propose sharper ones in a 2025 arXiv paper. Word error rate gives only a rough text-based sense of intelligibility. Pitch error measures describe melody narrowly and need a reference recording. Their framework, TTScore, needs no reference at all.

Two predictors, each conditioned on the intended text, score a synthesized utterance. One reads content tokens to judge intelligibility. The other reads prosody tokens to judge rhythm and tune. Each score is the likelihood the predictor assigns to the matching token sequence, an interpretable quantity. On three standard benchmarks, the scores tracked human judgments of overall quality more closely than existing focused metrics. The split design also tells developers which aspect failed.
arxiv-2509-20585:
Small mammography datasets starve deep learning models, and Farbod Bigdeli, Mohsen Mohammadagha, and Ali Bigdeli feed them cropped regions instead in a 2025 arXiv paper. Their region-of-interest augmentation replaces some full training images with random crops. The crops come from a precomputed bank of label-free bounding boxes, with optional jitter for variety. The strategy adds nothing at inference time.

Evaluation respected strict patient-level separation, so no patient appeared in both training and test folds. The dataset held nearly ten thousand images from about twenty-four hundred patients. Augmentation gave modest average gains in ranking accuracy, though results varied by fold. A ranking measure for positive cases stayed flat to slightly lower. The authors present the recipe as a cheap, label-free boost for constrained medical imaging settings.
arxiv-2509-21185:
Complex-valued neural networks handle the phase of speech naturally, but they cost more compute, especially in small models. Luan Vinicius Fiorio, Alex Young, and Ronald Aarts test a hybrid design in a 2025 paper on monaural speech enhancement. The hybrid keeps parameters matched against purely real or complex rivals.

One branch processes magnitude with a real-valued mask. A second, complex-valued branch adds a correction, and domain conversion functions couple the branches at the bottleneck. The design is applied to both a convolutional denoising autoencoder and a convolutional-recurrent network. Averaged over four noise levels, the hybrid models beat the counterparts considered on intelligibility and quality. They also use substantially fewer operations, a practical win for hearing devices and phones.
arxiv-2509-21385:
Concept bottleneck models predict through human readable concepts, so experts can check and fix them. Fixes at test time do not cure deeper misalignment, such as shortcuts learned from biased data. Eric Enouen and Sainyam Galhotra propose a debugging framework for that problem in a 2025 paper. Their process has two steps: removal and retraining.

In removal, experts use concept explanations to find and drop unwanted concepts. In retraining, their CBDebug method turns concept level feedback into sample level auxiliary labels. Those labels support supervised bias mitigation and targeted augmentation. That reduces the chance the model relearns the same shortcut. The framework is general and uses the interpretability of bottleneck models as a bridge to better training data.
arxiv-2509-21685:
Creative experts must weigh trade offs and invent mitigations, not just list ideas. Yaqing Yang and 5 co-authors present an AI augmented ideation system in a 2025 paper. Existing tools either expand the idea space or evaluate ideas, without supporting mitigation reasoning. FlexMind scaffolds multi threaded trade off mitigation chains in a structured workspace. Users surface concrete trade offs and generate actionable mitigations inside it.

Multiple idea branches can be navigated and expanded in parallel. A controlled study with twenty participants found deeper exploration without sacrificing breadth. Domain experts judged the resulting ideas higher quality than a baseline tool. A case study with six experts further examined how the system supports creative thinking. Continued reasoning over new trade offs is the core design bet.
arxiv-2509-21785:
Sharing data often starts with binning: raw values, like income, are grouped into ranges. Abolfazl Asudeh, Zeinab Asoodeh, Bita Asoodeh, and Omid Asudeh show in this 2025 paper that this step can quietly bake in unfairness. A poor choice of bin edges can skew group shares and harm later decisions. The authors set out to bin without that bias.

They define the unbiased binning problem: find the grouping closest to equal-size bins that keeps group shares even in every bin. They prove the best edges must come from a small candidate set, then give an efficient algorithm to search it. Fair bins sometimes cost too much accuracy, or do not exist at all. So the paper also defines a relaxed version that allows a small set bias, with a fast optimal method and a scalable search method on top.
arxiv-2509-21985:
Yoh Maekawa, Ryuna Nagayama, Kohei Yoshimura, and Sosuke Ito split the flow of information between two coupled systems into two meaningful parts. Their 2025 paper works in information thermodynamics, the study of how information and energy trade off in small systems. The setting is an autonomous pair of subsystems whose jumps follow a Markov process, a standard model for thermal machines and sensors at small scales.

The split uses the geometry of probability currents and the thermodynamic forces paired with them. One part, the housekeeping component, comes from cyclic modes that break detailed balance, and it maintains the correlations between the subsystems. The other, the excess component, comes from conservative forces, and it changes how much information the two subsystems share. With this split, the authors generalize several known results: the second law of information thermodynamics, the cyclic decomposition, and trade-off relations that bound what such systems can do.
arxiv-2509-22485:
Guohui Zhang and 8 co-authors focus training effort on the image tokens that matter most. Reinforcement learning with checked rewards has improved autoregressive image generators. Yet most methods train all tokens alike, though some tokens shape the final image far more. Early tokens steer later ones. Tokens at structure boundaries carry extra weight. Tokens that differ across samples add diversity.

Their method, GCPO, finds such critical tokens from those three angles. It then weights their advantage by how far the policy strays from a reference model. Using under a third of the tokens, GCPO beat full-token training. Tests spanned several text-to-image benchmarks and model types.
arxiv-2509-22785:
Tuhin Ghosh, Mark Wyatt, and Oliver Shorttle show that the debris from giant impacts keeps eroding atmospheres long after the crash. Giant impacts between planetary embryos shape planets and their orbits. Simulations price the immediate loss, but cost has blocked study of the aftermath. The team followed the debris thrown out by primary impacts and tracked how much falls back onto the growing planet.

About a fixed small mass returns across a wide range of Earth-like planet traits. Each returning fragment is a small impact, and together they strip air over time. Debris from the Moon-forming impact could have erased an Earth-like atmosphere in tens of millions of years. Planets growing by giant impacts likely face heavy erosion.
arxiv-2509-22885:
Jarno N Alanko and Maximo Perez-Lopez open a new line of work on short strings inside labeled graphs. A k-mer is a string of length k found along walks in the graph. They ask how hard it is to count distinct k-mers. Counting turns out to be very hard in general, even on simple layered graphs.

For one neat class, deterministic Wheeler graphs, the pair give fast counting methods. They also discuss ways to reshape a graph into a Wheeler graph while keeping its k-mers. As a use case, they build a compact store for the de Bruijn graph of the k-mers. For large k, their store can beat older build methods.
arxiv-2509-23085:
Standard weight starts assume wide networks, and narrow deep nets with sigmoid units suffer for it. Hyunwoo Lee, Hayoung Choi, and Hyunju Kim propose a start tailored to odd-sigmoid activations. Gaussian starts push early signals into saturation there. Gradients then collapse before training gets going. Their method preserves signal variance on the forward pass.

It also keeps gradient norms alive on the backward pass, across many variance scales. Image benchmarks showed far less sensitivity to depth, width, and activation scale. In physics-informed networks, the pairing beat Gaussian setups on loss. The authors offer it as a practical fix when standard starts break down.
arxiv-2509-23385:
Simulator-trained inference breaks quietly when the simulator differs from reality. Pierre-Louis Ruhlmann and 3 co-authors correct posterior estimates with a small calibration set. Their FMCPE framework works in two stages. First, a posterior approximator trains on abundant simulated data. Second, flow matching moves its predictions toward the true posterior. Calibration observations guide that transport.

No one needs to know the form of the mismatch in advance. Which part of the model is wrong also stays unknown. Synthetic and real data sets show bias and overconfidence both shrink. Accuracy and uncertainty quality beat standard simulation-based baselines. Compute cost stays modest.
arxiv-2509-23585:
Explaining an image model's choice means showing which pixels mattered, but detail and clarity pull apart. Emerald Zhang and 3 co-authors tune one explanation method, Layer-wise Relevance Propagation, with an evolution strategy instead of hand-set rules. The method traces relevance backward through the model's own layers. Its settings are usually picked by habit, not by measured quality.

Their EVO-LRP search adjusts those settings against scores for faithfulness and sparseness. The tuned method beat standard explanation tools on those scores and on visual coherence. It also reacted strongly to features specific to each class. The team argues that attribution quality can be raised by principled, task-specific tuning rather than fixed rules.
arxiv-2509-23985:
A walker hopping on a line of sites, each with its own frozen random depth, can slow to a crawl in deep traps. Silvio Kalaj and 3 co-authors study continuous-time random walks in a Gaussian random potential on a one-dimensional lattice. Three models spell out how the site depths set the hopping rates. Their analysis tracks five quantities on a finite chain: the current, its reciprocal resistance, a splitting probability, the mean first-passage time, and the diffusion coefficient in a ring.

Moments of these quantities tell a split story. Current and resistance are not self-averaging, so their typical and average behaviors part ways. The other three quantities do self-average in long chains, though finite chains fluctuate strongly.
arxiv-2509-24085:
Phones that talk direct to each other must pick radio settings that save power yet stay fast. Ju-Hyung Lee and 2 co-authors present PEARL, a system that puts a large language model on the device to guide those choices for Wi-Fi Aware links. It builds on the team's past work on single-device models.

PEARL uses the state of both peers, not just one side, to pick settings. Its training reward scales delay by what each app can bear and scales energy by battery level. A fuller variant scored best overall. A lighter variant answered in well under a blink with near-equal scores and cut energy use in low-battery paired cases.
arxiv-2509-24385:
Three-dimensional scene questions usually need three-dimensional input data, which limits how widely models can be used. Haijier Chen and 5 co-authors built Vid-LLM, a compact model that reads plain video instead. Geometric priors from reconstruction guide its scene perception. A cross-task adapter aligns those priors with vision-language features in a compact way.

A metric depth model recovers true-scale geometry from the reconstruction output, keeping the scene consistent and whole. Two-stage distillation then speeds convergence and steadies training. On question answering, dense captioning, and visual grounding benchmarks for three-dimensional scenes, the model showed strong multi-task skill. Video alone, the results suggest, can carry much of what 3D data gave.
arxiv-2509-24485:
Generative AI tools now write code from prompts, which tempts teams to let agents replace developers wholesale. Vlad Stirbu and 10 co-authors propose the opposite move, a framework they call shift-up. In GenAI native development, the point is to push human effort toward high-value activities while AI agents handle the rest under direction.

The paper sets out the framework and reports a preliminary study that tests its ideas with current tools. Early evidence is offered rather than proof, and the authors are plain about that scope. They close with research goals for studying shift-up in depth. The frame aims to keep developers on judgment work as automation grows.
arxiv-2510-00085:
Simon Ternes wrote this 2025 paper on drying thin liquid films evenly across wide wafers. A narrow jet of air, called an air knife, sweeps over the wet film to dry it. For films such as perovskite layers, the drying speed at one key moment shapes final quality. Uneven thickness across the wafer makes that speed hard to keep steady.

Ternes derives equations for the knife path that holds the key drying speed constant. A two-stage least-squares method solves them and yields the best speed profile over time. Films that grow thicker along the travel direction can always be dried evenly this way. Films with bumps or dips cannot always be fixed by path changes alone. Even then, the method finds paths that give far more even results than a steady sweep.
arxiv-2510-00185:
Gabriel de Olim Gaul and three colleagues at Imperial College London published this 2025 paper on explainable image classification. Their system, SAA-CBR, pairs a neural network with symbolic case-based reasoning. The neural part uses slot attention to split an image into separate objects. The symbolic part then argues from past cases, in a framework built on abstract argumentation.

The authors add several extensions, including a one-versus-rest scheme for many-class problems. They also shrink the case library by keeping only representative samples. On the CLEVR-Hans datasets, which are built to expose shortcut learning, the system proved effective. It stayed competitive with plain neural baselines while offering reasons for each call. Because decisions rest on cited cases and arguments, a user can inspect why an image received its label. That audit trail is the point of the design.
arxiv-2510-00285:
Joseph Kapusta, Mayank Singh, and Thomas Welle wrote this 2025 theory paper on fluid dynamics at extreme energies. When matter crosses a first-order phase transition, it can separate into two phases, much like droplets forming in vapor. That process, spinodal decomposition, may occur inside colliding atomic nuclei or merging neutron stars. The authors write down relativistic flow equations that include this separation.

Their equations keep track of surface effects along the boundary between the two phases. Leaving those effects out would misstate how the mixed region evolves. They solve the system in Bjorken flow, the standard expanding geometry for ion collisions. The result is a working tool for simulating intermediate-energy heavy-ion collisions. The same equations also suit binary neutron star mergers where such a transition is expected. Simulations can now follow phase separation instead of assuming it away.
arxiv-2510-00585:
Zulkaif Sajjad, Furqan Shaukat, and Junaid Mir published this 2025 paper on outlining organs and lesions in medical scans. Segmentation guides diagnosis, yet classic networks see only local patches and miss global context. Transformers see widely but fuse local detail poorly, the authors argue. Their model, U-DFA, marries a frozen vision foundation model with a U-shaped decoder.

A fusion adapter injects spatial features from a small convolutional side network at several stages. The design blends high-level semantics with fine spatial patterns throughout the encoder. Only about a third of the parameters ever need training, keeping costs down. On the Synapse and ACDC benchmarks, the model set state-of-the-art scores. The authors call it a robust, scalable template across imaging modalities. Three-dimensional scans and prompt-driven variants are next on their roadmap.
arxiv-2510-00885:
Ayoub and four co-authors question a default choice in reinforcement learning in this 2025 arXiv paper. Value-based methods learn to predict rewards, then pick actions with the best predicted returns. Almost all of them train those predictions with mean squared error, a habit inherited from standard practice. The authors ask whether that loss actually serves good decisions, and they argue it often does not.

Their theory shows that mean absolute error controls the learned policy's suboptimality gap more tightly. Cross-entropy losses, both binary and categorical, line up with the absolute error objective rather than the squared one. Experiments in linear reinforcement learning back the theory, since methods using cross-entropy losses beat squared-loss methods in their tests. The advantage grew clearest when the best achievable value sat close to the maximum possible return.
arxiv-2510-01185:
Mirvakhabova and co-authors at Qualcomm AI Research fix a quiet failure in models grown by copying one network into many experts. Upcycled mixture-of-experts models gain capacity cheaply, but their routing stays timid and the experts blur together. The router never commits, so specialization never really forms.

Their loss, DPSL, shapes routing probabilities toward a chosen Dirichlet prior distribution. That gives trainers direct control over expert balance and focus, even per modality. Experiments across three language-model backbones in vision-language models beat standard upcycling recipes. The same shaping trick applies to any module that outputs categorical probabilities. Low-confidence routing was measured directly before the fix was proposed. Priors can encode hunches, such as sending image tokens to dedicated experts. No manual intervention is needed once the target prior is set. Balance and specialization stop trading off blindly. The router finally has a teacher.
arxiv-2510-01585:
You and Liu redesign the transformer around three ideas meant to fix long-context weakness and wasteful attention. Standard transformers stack rigid layers, attend everywhere at once, and lean on position codes. Their ReSSFormer swaps stacking for a recurrent memory unit that reasons in bounded loops.

An adaptive sparse attention module picks relevant context at token and expert levels. A self-organizing encoder drops position codes and infers structure from content itself. Tests across language modeling, multi-hop questions, and structured tasks showed efficient scaling. The design suits problems where sequence order matters less than relationships among parts. Bounded loops keep computation predictable even as contexts grow long. Structure induction from content frees the model from rigid order assumptions. Sparsity at two levels trims both tokens and experts. Recurrence replaces depth, trading layers for iterations. Long documents are the obvious beneficiaries above all.
arxiv-2510-01785:
Cheng, Subramaniam, Wu, and Brenowitz present a GPU library for spherical data in this 2025 computing paper. HEALPix grids divide the sphere into equal-area pixels and serve astrophysics, cosmology, and Earth science. Spherical harmonic transforms on those grids are valuable but hard to run fast. Irregular pixel layouts and huge resolutions strain ordinary implementations.

Their library, cuHPX, rewrites the transforms as optimized CUDA kernels for graphics processors. It delivers more than twenty times the speed of existing libraries in their tests. Accuracy stayed high, with rapid spectral convergence in their evaluations. The transforms are also differentiable, so deep learning frameworks can backpropagate through them. Out-of-core processing handles grids too large for GPU memory. Flexible regridding moves data between HEALPix, equiangular, and other spherical formats, which widens the tool's use in climate and sky surveys.
arxiv-2510-01885:
Cotter, Castiñeiras, and Cionca schedule neural network work across small edge devices in this 2025 paper. Phones and cameras increasingly offload deep learning tasks to nearby mobile-edge machines. Those tasks carry deadlines, and the network between devices keeps changing. Their scheduler uses a lightweight picture of device and network state to place each task well.

The design adds priority-aware preemption, so urgent tasks can displace routine ones. A dynamic bandwidth estimator keeps placement choices honest as links speed up and slow down. The team implemented the system on four Raspberry Pi devices watching a waste-sorting conveyor. Against their own earlier approach, the new models cut latency under heavy workloads. Task throughput also rose when resources grew scarce. Under light loads, though, the accuracy edge of slower, thorough methods could still win out.
arxiv-2510-01985:
Almenara and a large team revisit the K2-19 planetary system with ten years of transit data in this 2025 astronomy paper. The star hosts two Neptune-sized planets locked near a three-to-two orbital resonance. Their mutual tugs produce strong transit-timing variations at two distinct frequencies. Earlier modeling of just over three years of data found suspiciously high orbital eccentricities.

The extended baseline confirms the earlier planet masses almost exactly. The eccentricities, however, collapse to a few percent for both planets. Those milder values fit standard planet formation models far better. The old high values trace back to a single transit measured at twilight, which faked an early ingress. That one bad point shifted a midtransit time by twelve minutes. A Fourier treatment of the timing signal independently recovered the masses within two percent. The paper is a cautionary tale about single-point systematics in precision photometry.
arxiv-2510-02085:
Wang and Zhu complete the first next-to-leading order QCD calculation for a fully charmed tetraquark in this 2025 particle physics paper. The exotic hadron X(6900), made of two charm quarks and two charm antiquarks, was found at the LHC. Predicting how often collisions produce it tests QCD in a new regime. Leading-order estimates carry large uncertainties from gluon radiation.

The authors resum gluon radiation effects to push the cross section to a higher order in the strong coupling. A symmetry analysis sorts the possible internal quark configurations in a color basis. Combining LHCb's total cross-section data with CMS spin-parity measurements, they extracted the universal long-distance matrix elements. Those elements encode the step where quarks bind into the tetraquark. With them fixed, the paper predicts rapidity and momentum distributions for future runs.
arxiv-2510-02185:
Amusuo and five co-authors filter phantom crashes out of AI-generated fuzzing campaigns in this 2025 software paper. Tools like OSS-Fuzz-Gen use language models to write fuzz drivers automatically. Many reported crashes turn out to be infeasible artifacts of bad drivers, wasting maintainer time. Their system, FalseCrashReducer, attacks the problem on two fronts.

First, inferred constraints on a function's inputs and state guide driver creation toward realistic calls. Second, context-based validation checks whether a reported crash is reachable from real program entry points, by analyzing callers. On fifteen hundred benchmark functions from OSS-Fuzz, the approach cut reported crashes by more than half. Spurious crashes fell measurably as well. Frontier language models proved reliable as program analysis agents inside the pipeline. The paper shows agentic AI can clean up after generative AI in security testing. Fuzzing programs gain signal instead of noise from automation.
arxiv-2510-02585:
Dashtbani and Tahvildari distill practical lessons for scaling microservice systems automatically. Their 2025 software engineering paper tests leading autoscalers on standard benchmarks. Microservices dominate modern cloud application design. Auto-scaling them well remains surprisingly hard in practice. The trouble often sits below the scaling algorithm itself. Design, coding, and deployment flaws sabotage good methods. The authors sort the pitfalls by lifecycle phase. Architecture choices cover service splits and dependencies. Implementation covers startup cost, metrics, and error spread. Deployment covers resource limits and health checks.

A Sock-Shop case study showed the damage concretely. Broken call graphs and masking errors crippled autoscalers. Fixing those flaws let an advanced method shine. It beat reactive threshold rules on service goals and efficiency. Scaling is a systems problem, not just a formula. Benchmarks must reflect real world messiness to teach anything.
arxiv-2510-02785:
Yang and co-authors detect several battery free beacons at once in ambient backscatter systems. Their 2025 wireless paper builds on the Neyman-Pearson framework. Zero energy devices harvest ambient signals to communicate indoors. Finding many tags together is the hard part. Interference and shaky synchronization blur their signals. Earlier work handled a single tag only. The new detector keys synchronization to a near-perfect code. That code sharpens the peak against its sidelobes. Dual correlators replace the older filtering chain. A contrast metric then reveals secondary tags.

False alarm rates stay under control. Multi-frequency combining adds another view of the scene. Tests ran on the CorteXlab testbed. Detection stayed reliable at low signal to noise ratios. Asynchronous tags still separated cleanly. The near-perfect code beat Barker codes on separation. Indoor location systems need crowds of tags read at once. Battery free sensing becomes practical at that scale.
arxiv-2510-03085:
Boyle and co-authors set up three-dimensional electrodynamics on a curved lattice. Their stage is a sphere crossed with a time line. Radial quantization organizes states by scaling rather than by time. The Quantum Finite Element project pursues such theories on lattices. This first paper studies the free limit of the theory. Overlap fermions carry the matter fields on the grid.

Key symmetries of the continuum theory survived the lattice build. The team derived analytic correlators for the setup. Lattice results matched them, normalization and all. Errors shrank with the expected second-order rate in grid spacing. Counts of descendant states were estimated for early refinement levels. No fine-tuning was needed to reach those matches. The free case thus validates the whole construction. Interacting QED in three dimensions is the real target. Such gauge theories may host conformal phases of matter.
arxiv-2510-03285:
Kara, Faisal, and Nath present a 2025 arXiv paper on testing web agents under real world failure. Web agents are programs that browse sites and finish tasks like booking hotels or filling forms. Standard tests run on calm, stable sites that rarely break. Real sites crash, stall, show pop-ups, and face attacks. The authors built WAREX, a tool that adds such faults to existing agent tests without rebuilding them.

WAREX injects network faults, script errors, delays, and hostile page changes while an agent works. The team ran it with three well known test suites named WebArena, WebVoyager, and REAL. Adding faults caused sharp drops in task success for leading agents. That gap shows that strong lab scores can hide weak real world skill. The tool gives builders a fair way to harden agents before users trust them with real tasks online.
arxiv-2510-03485:
Wen and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on checking whether web agents follow the policies they are given. Agents that shop or code online must obey rules set by people, yet long action chains can drift into violations. The team built PolicyGuardBench, a benchmark of about sixty thousand cases drawn from agent runs. Policies pair with action chains inside and across site areas, each labeled for compliance. A harder task asks models to spot trouble from only the start of a chain.

Their guardrail model, PolicyGuard-4B, is enough to run cheaply beside an agent. It scored on full chains and on the early warning task alike. Guards trained only for safety failed to transfer to this compliance job. The small model held its accuracy on domains it had never seen in training. Cheap guards could let firms deploy web agents with far more confidence in their rule following.
arxiv-2510-03585:
Kavatamane and colleagues present a 2025 arXiv paper on how high temperature annealing affects tiny diamond resonators built for quantum photonics. Diamond hosts spin defects that act as qubits, and those defects are made by blasting ions in and baking the chip above twelve hundred degrees. Nobody had checked what that bake does to the resonators that must couple light to the defects. The team measured optical quality factors before and after annealing and studied the surfaces with Raman spectroscopy.

Annealing in vacuum grows a thin non diamond carbon layer on the surface, and that layer roughens it and adds optical loss. The quality factor drops as a result. A boiling tri-acid wash strips the layer off and restores the resonators' quality. So defects can be created inside finished resonators without wrecking their optics. Quantum networking and transduction devices depend on exactly that kind of safe fabrication step.
arxiv-2510-03785:
Huang and Tzounas present a 2025 arXiv letter exposing a duality between the two ways of discretizing a dynamical system for simulation. Solvers step through fixed time points, while quantized state methods update each variable only when it changes by a set quantum, letting busy variables run ahead of quiet ones. The authors recast the quantized methods as integration applied to a dual model, where time becomes a state dependent variable. That lens lets scheme designs be imported into the quantized world.

As a proof of concept, they build a second order Adams-Bashforth method in quantized form. Combined with implicit solvers, the approach delivered speedups in power system simulations while holding accuracy. Power grids are a natural fit because their activity is localized: most components sit idle while a few switch rapidly. Adaptive quantum control promises further gains. A unified theory of the two discretization families could yield solvers.
arxiv-2510-03885:
Kim and colleagues present this 2025 arXiv paper on giving mobile robots a memory of their rooms. Most robot policies act from current camera images alone, a narrow view that hurts long tasks spread across a room. The authors argue that a three-dimensional map of learned features can supply the missing context.

Their system, called Seeing the Bigger Picture, fuses views from many angles into a grid of latent scene features. The map grows as the robot moves, and it stores observations far beyond the current field of view. A policy then reads global context from the map while choosing actions, trained by imitation or reinforcement learning. In tests on scene-level and sequential tabletop tasks, map-based policies beat image-only ones. One sequential task gained about fifteen success points. The results favor explicit maps as long-term memory for robot manipulation.
arxiv-2510-03985:
Zhang, Gornyi, and Gefen present this 2025 arXiv paper in condensed matter theory, on how exotic particles called anyons respond to small pushes far from equilibrium. Linear response theory predicts currents from tiny disturbances, but it normally assumes the system starts near equilibrium. Anyons carry fractional charge and unusual exchange statistics, and collider experiments now shoot dilute beams of them at each other. The authors build a response theory whose starting state is such a beam.

Their framework yields transport coefficients for charge and heat that directly reflect the anyons' fractional charge and statistics. The theory also predicts finite thermoelectric effects, where heat and charge currents mix. Those effects signal real anyon collisions rather than mere virtual braiding, tied to a broken particle-hole symmetry. The work extends a bedrock tool of quantum transport into a regime it could not previously reach.
arxiv-2510-04085:
Ananth, Bostanci, Gulati, and Lin present this 2025 arXiv paper on building strong pseudorandom unitaries from shorter ones. Pseudorandom unitaries mimic truly random quantum operations while using little randomness, and they anchor quantum cryptography. A gluing theorem from earlier work joins random unitaries on overlapping systems, but security against adversaries who can also run the joined operation backwards was open. That inverse access defines the strong variant of pseudorandomness.

The authors give an alternate gluing method secure against inverse-query adversaries. As a consequence, strong pseudorandom unitaries can generically have their length extended for the first time. If any strong pseudorandom unitary family exists, they show constructions needing only a small polynomial-root share of the qubits' worth of randomness. The work is the second part of a CRYPTO 2025 paper on pseudorandom unitaries in the Haar random oracle model.
arxiv-2510-04385:
Byung Kyu Na, Stefan Possanner, and Xin Wang wrote this 2025 paper on simulating hot charged gas, or plasma. Fusion devices hold plasma that mixes fluid like bulk flow with fast single particles. Waves and particles trade energy in ways that can spoil the plasma and weaken confinement. The team built a computer scheme that tracks both parts at once. Their design keeps the total energy balanced by construction.

The model equations come from a variational principle, a rule that gives consistent links between the fluid and the particles. A tricky energy term from the guiding center approximation needed new time stepping methods, which the team supplied. The code runs inside an open source Python package named STRUPHY. Tests confirmed that the scheme conserves energy as designed. It also reproduced a key wave driven by energetic particles, with no artificial damping or filtering.
arxiv-2510-04585:
Jianshu Zhou and nine coauthors wrote this 2025 paper on a robot gripper that can hold almost anything. Robots grip well when objects share a size and a solid state, and they fail outside that comfort zone. The team built a soft gripper that fuses two tricks: surface suction spread over its skin, and granular jamming inside its body. The mix needs no airtight seal against the target. One device thus spans solids, liquids, and a huge range of sizes.

In tests, the gripper handled targets from a glass bead to a sheet of paper and a woven bag. The largest targets were wider than the gripper contact patch. A sensing layer reads liquid contact and suction pressure, so the device can tell solids from liquids in real time. An algorithm picks the grasp mode from those signals. Trials covered underwater grabs, fragile objects, and scooping liquid, all with steady success.
arxiv-2510-04685:
Shuche Wang, Adarsh Barik, Peng Zhao, and Vincent Tan wrote this 2025 paper on learning algorithms that need no hand set constants. Online convex optimization covers decisions made under shifting costs. One model mixes random noise with adversarial moves, so methods must handle both. Methods for that model ask users for two problem constants in advance. Those are the size of the decision region and a bound on how steep losses can be.

In practice, users rarely know a number. The team built parameter free methods for this setting. Their engine is an optimistic Newton style update that adapts as data arrives. The first version handles an unknown region size, and the second handles both unknowns. They keep regret bounds that track the noise and the adversarial drift in the data. The guarantees match what tuned methods achieve, without the tuning. The work closes a practicality gap in a learning model.
arxiv-2510-04785:
Luca Lazzaro, Manuel Mariani, René Algesheimer, and Radu Tanase wrote this 2025 paper on whether contacts help behaviors spread. Long ties link people who share few mutual friends, bridging circles. Studies have disagreed on whether ties speed or slow contagion. The authors blame clashing assumptions about how people decide. They ran experiments measuring real adoption choices under social influence. The products offered had uncertain payoffs, like many innovations.

At the personal level, uncertainty pushed people to lean on what others did. Yet people differed: risk tastes and feelings about uncertainty split their responses. The team then placed those measured behaviors into network simulations. With heterogeneity in place, long ties promoted diffusion. Their benefit shrank as uncertainty grew, but it did not vanish. The lesson is that diversity in responses, not the contagion type, decides the role of long ties. Marketers and policy makers who seed behaviors should plan around that diversity.
arxiv-2510-05185:
Vrinda Malhotra, Jiaman Li, and Nandini Pisupati model how fear spreads through crowds in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their simulator, AgentZero++, extends Epstein's classic Agent_Zero framework for collective violence. The original agents reacted with simple rules. The new version gives them memory, emotions, and social feedback.

Eight enhancements drive the upgrade, including age-based impulse control and memory-based risk estimation. Agents can flee or fight, retaliate, and align emotionally with similar peers. Small differences in memory or reactivity amplified or dampened unrest through feedback loops. Younger agents activated earlier and swung more wildly in simulations. Longer memories sustained emotional activation, while short ones faded fast. The platform helps researchers probe how individual psychology scales into crowd conflict.
arxiv-2510-05485:
Filipek tackles a slow step inside the training of language models. BLEU is a standard score for judging machine-written text against a reference. Reinforcement learning needs that score for every sentence, right inside the training loop. Standard tools compute BLEU on the CPU, which forces costly data transfers and stalls training.

His tool, TensorBLEU, rebuilds the score for graphics processors inside PyTorch. A compact counting trick keeps memory use low, even with very large vocabularies. In benchmarks against the standard NLTK library, the tool ran far faster on both test cards. Speedups passed thirteen times on a consumer card and forty times on a data center card. That speed turns a major bottleneck into a minor step in each training run. It also gives each sentence its own reward signal during learning. The author released the code openly for other research teams.
arxiv-2510-05685:
Han and Wiesel ask how many samples make entropy-regularized optimal transport trustworthy. Optimal transport compares probability distributions, but estimates from samples degrade in high dimensions. Adding an entropy penalty smooths the problem and speeds computation. Their 2025 paper bounds the sampling error for radial cost functions.

The bound holds for measures with exponentially decaying tails. Radial costs need only a local Lipschitz condition near each point. The rate is sharp up to logarithmic factors. It senses the intrinsic dimension of the distributions through a generalized covering number. Dimension enters through support geometry, not the ambient space alone. Examples include subgaussian and subexponential distributions. Power costs with exponent at least two fit the framework. Earlier bounds covered narrower cases, like quadratic or bounded costs. That matters because practitioners plug transport costs into learning pipelines. The bound tells them how much data a target accuracy demands.
arxiv-2510-05885:
Montoison and colleagues port an augmented Lagrangian solver to graphics processors. Large nonlinear programs with degenerate constraints defeat standard constraint qualifications. Augmented Lagrangian methods handle such degeneracy robustly and detect infeasibility fast. Their 2025 MadNCL implementation exploits the method's natural fit for GPU architectures.

Quadratic penalty terms regularize the KKT systems the solver must factor. Stabilized and condensed formulations both run efficiently on the GPU. Sparse factorization with static pivoting uses NVIDIA's cuDSS library. MadNLP serves as the interior-point subproblem solver inside. Fusing the inner and outer loops plus extrapolation steps improves stability. The design avoids explicitly forming a Schur complement, a first for GPU systems. Interior-point methods need aggressive reformulation to run on GPUs at all. Benchmarks include optimal power flow and security-constrained variants. Degenerate complementarity constraints, long a solver headache, are managed effectively.
arxiv-2510-06085:
Ibrahimov and Heinen let small robots map a room by touch in a 2025 robotics paper. Their design copies the cockroach, which feels its way with antennae in dark, cluttered spaces. Each robot carries a tactile sensor like an antenna and follows walls as it wanders.

Instead of dodging obstacles, the robots record every point where they bump into one. Each robot builds a local map from its collision points, and the team merges the local maps into one global two-dimensional map. Distributed optimization divides the work so robots avoid repeating each other's routes. In Webots simulations with e-puck robots, the swarm mapped a small arena holding three obstacles. The trials achieved high coverage, few collisions between robots, and accurate maps. The approach suits places where cameras and laser scanners fail, such as smoke-filled rooms during rescue work.
arxiv-2510-06185:
Jeronimo and Shagrithaya give a framework for derandomizing random linear codes in a 2025 information theory paper. Random codes achieve excellent parameters, yet randomness only shows good codes exist somewhere. Engineers need explicit recipes they can build and decode.

The framework targets local properties, covering distance, list decoding, list recovery, and perfect hashing. It extends the classical Alon–Edmonds–Luby construction using a modified formalism of local coordinate-wise linear properties. The main theorem says that when random linear codes avoid a bad local property with high probability, explicit codes can too, at a larger but constant alphabet. That yields the first explicit constructions for list recovery and special cases like erasures and perfect hash matrices. Their parameters match random codes exactly. The codes also admit efficient list decoding through recent expander-based decoders. Coding theorists gain a systematic bridge from existence proofs to explicit optimal codes.
arxiv-2510-06485: Hebert, Klimek, and McBride construct spectral triples for Hensel-Steinitz algebras in a 2025 operator algebras paper. In noncommutative geometry, a spectral triple equips an algebra with Dirac-like geometric data. Fredholm modules represent classes in K-homology, dual to K-theory. Existence results rarely supply explicit representatives. The authors fill that gap completely here. For every K-homology element of these algebras, they build an explicit representing Fredholm module and spectral triple. Concrete representatives matter because index computations need formulas, not just existence theorems.
arxiv-2510-06585:
Clément Aubert and Jean Krivine work in theoretical computer science, on systems whose steps can run in parallel. Their 2025 paper starts from a simple idea about causality. A computation counts as valid when every observed event is preceded by the events that caused it. Causality acts like an abstract clock for these systems.

The authors ask whether that rule still works when events can be undone. They extend the standard models of concurrency to cover reversible computations. Their tool is a symmetric operation that lets configurations step forward or backward. Stable configuration structures stay stable under this operation, which is reassuring. The resulting semantics matches a switch operation that swaps conflict and causality. Reversible steps turn out to fit the same causal rules as ordinary ones. That finding supports the claim in their title, that reversible computations really are computations.
arxiv-2510-06885:
Marco Martinez-Cañadas leads a large collaboration measuring a nuclear reaction rate at CERN. Their 2025 paper reports new data for neutrons striking chlorine-35 and knocking out a proton. The reaction matters for three fields. It affects boron neutron capture therapy in medicine, and it feeds into the puzzling origin of sulfur-36.

The team used the n_TOF facility, which times neutrons over a flight path to sort their energies. Their data span from below thermal energies up to 120 kilo-electron-volts, a range never covered. Fitting the yields gave a thermal cross-section of about zero point four seven barns. That value agrees with the standard evaluated library and many measurements. Only two earlier studies disagree with the new result. Resonance strengths for the first two resonances match reports. Higher resonances came out smaller than previously listed. Rates like this anchor medical dose planning and stellar models.
arxiv-2510-07185:
Mazuelas tackles a hidden data cost in a popular method for honest predictions. The 2025 paper concerns conformal prediction, which wraps any classifier in sets that contain the true label with a set chance. The standard split version needs fresh labeled examples just for calibration. Those labels cannot then serve for training. The author asks whether unlabeled data can do the calibration job.

The new method weights unlabeled calibration samples so they statistically match the training data. A two-sample test guides that matching. Theory and experiments show performance close to the labeled version. The price is a modest weakening of the guarantees and some extra computation. Still, the approach frees all labeled examples for training. It could make set predictions practical in medicine, law, and other label-poor settings. The paper gives both proofs and benchmarks to support the claim.
arxiv-2510-07485:
Parpillon and a large team demonstrate the first particle detector chip that filters its own data with built-in AI. Their 2025 paper reports a prototype readout chip for silicon tracking detectors. Colliders produce more collisions than any data system can store, so sensors must discard junk at the source. Prior work designed a physics-motivated edge algorithm on paper. This team fabricated it: signal processing and machine-learning filtering now live inside each pixel's readout circuit. The chip was made in a commercial twenty-eight nanometer process shown to tolerate collider radiation levels well.

The prototype meets the strict power, area, and latency budgets that in-detector electronics face. Real-time reduction at the sensor level slashes the torrent that downstream systems must handle. The milestone points toward intelligent silicon trackers for the High-Luminosity LHC, where collision rates will multiply.
arxiv-2510-07585:
Desai and co-authors compute how topology shapes electric transport in real materials. Their 2025 paper unifies two effects tied to Berry curvature: the chiral anomaly in magnetic fields and the nonlinear Hall effect, a sideways voltage with no magnetic field at all. Sound numbers need band topology and electron-phonon scattering together. The team solves the Boltzmann transport equation. Test cases span tantalum arsenide, a Weyl semimetal, and three nonlinear Hall materials.

In tantalum arsenide the chiral part of the conductance in a field comes out positive and growing with field strength, matching experiments. Electron-phonon coupling reshapes the Berry curvature dipole and how it shifts with temperature and Fermi level, a warning against estimates that skip scattering. The Hall response in the barium compound also agrees with measurement. It also settles a physics point: interactions and topology act as intertwined drivers of nonlinear transport, not separate corrections.
arxiv-2510-07685:
Sun and six coauthors present LiveThinking in this 2025 paper on AI assistants for e-commerce livestreaming. Digital avatars selling products must answer viewer comments at once. Slow replies break the flow of a live show. Large reasoning models answer well but think too long and cost too much. The team set out to keep the quality while cutting delay and cost sharply.

LiveThinking works in two stages. First, a large teacher model is distilled into a smaller one through rejection sampling fine-tuning. Second, reinforcement learning trims the model's reasoning paths while guarding correctness and helpfulness. On a hard reasoning benchmark, their compact model beat its huge teacher while answering more briefly. In deployment on Taobao Live, total computing cost fell about thirtyfold. Correctness and helpfulness both improved, and shoppers converted and chatted more. The study shows careful reasoning can fit real-time commerce.
arxiv-2510-07985:
Egashira and four coauthors wrote this 2025 security paper on a hidden danger in pruning language models. Pruning deletes weights so downloaded models run cheaply, and popular engines make it a one-click step. The authors show an attacker can booby-trap a model before sharing it. The trick starts with a proxy score estimating which weights pruning will remove. Malicious behavior is planted in weights that pruning will keep.

A repair step then uses the doomed weights to cancel that behavior in the full model. The shared model behaves normally until a user prunes it. After pruning, the hidden behavior switches on strongly. Across five models and three pruning methods, attack success ran above ninety-five percent in the strongest scenarios, covering jailbreaks, refusals, and content injection. The paper flags a deployment-time security gap that compression pipelines must start checking.
arxiv-2510-08085:
El Karmi wrote this 2025 paper presenting a fully reproducible simulator for the limit order books that run modern markets. His stack pairs a deterministic C++ order book engine with a Hawkes process generator for order flow. Hawkes processes let each order excite further orders, mimicking real clustering. The generator serves both C++ and Python users, and diagnostics report likelihoods, residual tests, and branching ratios. Scripts regenerate every figure.

He also proves stability conditions for linear and nonlinear Hawkes processes, with intuition alongside. He calibrated exponential and power-law kernels on Binance Bitcoin trades and detailed Apple order book data. Realistic clustering required a subcritical yet nearly unstable regime. The paper maps where Hawkes simulators match market stylized facts and where queue-reactive baselines do better. Released code makes the study auditable.
arxiv-2510-08485:
Chong Mou and the ByteDance Intelligent Creation Team unify image and video editing under language model guidance in a 2025 arXiv paper. Diffusion editors follow written instructions to change pictures, but design choices for guiding them were poorly studied. Video editing data is also scarce, which holds back unified tools. Their framework, InstructX, pairs a multimodal language model with a diffusion generator.

The team ran a comprehensive study of how to integrate the two model types for instruction-driven editing. Two findings stand out from their unified modeling analysis. First, training on image data alone produced video editing ability without explicit video supervision. This transfer eases the shortage of video training data considerably. Second, modality-specific features from the language model let one model serve both media. Extensive experiments reached state-of-the-art results across a broad range of editing tasks.
arxiv-2510-08585:
Ahmed Adel Attia, Jing Liu, and Carol Espy Wilson bring knowledge of mouth and tongue movement back into speech recognition in a 2025 arXiv paper. Articulatory features describe how speakers shape sounds physically, complementing raw audio. Older work used them only with shallow acoustic models, and deep learning largely dropped the idea. The team revisits articulation with modern transformer architectures.

Their framework trains speech inversion, predicting articulation from audio, as an auxiliary task. The predicted articulatory features then enter the recognizer as a query stream in cross-attention. Acoustic embeddings serve as keys and values that the articulation queries attend over. Experiments on the LibriSpeech benchmark showed consistent gains over strong transformer baselines. Improvements were largest under low-resource conditions, where training data is scarce. The authors argue articulation deserves a place in modern recognition design.
arxiv-2510-08685:
Juan Pablo Elía, Lucas Cantarutti, Nahuel Mirón-Granese, and Esteban Calzetta model the reheating era of the early universe with fluid dynamics in a 2025 arXiv paper. After inflation, the inflaton field oscillates and dumps energy into other particles, reheating the cosmos. Tracking full field dynamics is costly, so a macroscopic fluid picture is attractive. Their causal hydrodynamic model treats the inflaton condensate as a background coupled to a relativistic fluid.

The fluid represents the condensate's inhomogeneous fluctuations within a divergence-type theory from kinetic considerations. The model captures dissipative, non-equilibrium effects while staying stable and causal. Coupling between the oscillating condensate and fluid triggers parametric resonance in the tensor sector. This amplifies the viscous stress tensor and generates gravitational waves peaking at a characteristic frequency. Lattice simulations performed with CosmoLattice produce a matching spectrum.
arxiv-2510-09085:
Shree and Jupuru slash the cost of decoding speech with a leading recognition method, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The method, called CTC, scores every possible token at every audio frame, and that exhaustive bookkeeping can eat ninety percent of a system's time. Their decoder prunes instead: at each frame it drops the tokens whose probability falls below a relative threshold, keeping only live contenders.

The pruning is dynamic, tightening or relaxing with the model's own confidence at each moment. On the standard LibriSpeech benchmark, the decoder ran more than ten times faster than the standard one and used nearly three times less memory. Word error rates barely moved, so the savings came almost free. The authors highlight the algorithm's simplicity: it drops into existing decoders across processors and graphics cards alike. That portability targets the small, cheap devices where speech recognition is hardest to afford.
arxiv-2510-09185:
Hess and van Cranenburgh deliver an uncomfortable message about the flexible choice models transport planners love: they fit beautifully and forecast no better, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Mixed logit and latent class models let each person in a survey weigh price, time, and comfort differently. That flexibility reliably improves how well the model describes the data it was trained on, and it reveals rich detail about hidden taste differences.

Using theory plus two case studies, one on real travel choices and one on survey choices, the authors show the advantages stop at the sample's edge. Forecasts from the flexible models were no more accurate than simpler ones, and predicted market shares were recovered no better. The single exception is predicting for the very same individuals used in estimation, using their fitted personal distributions. That trick, by construction, cannot forecast anyone new. Flexibility, the title warns, comes without foresight.
arxiv-2510-09485:
Hrad Ghoukasian, Bonwoo Lee, and Shahab Asoodeh study private sampling in a 2025 arXiv paper. The task is to draw one sample that looks like it came from a sensitive distribution while satisfying local differential privacy, a strong guarantee that any single person's data stays hidden. Earlier work optimised the worst case over a whole class of distributions, a global minimax view.

The authors instead take a local view, measuring the minimax risk in a small neighbourhood around one fixed distribution. They characterise that local risk exactly and show it equals the global risk computed on the neighbourhood alone. To prove it, they extend earlier results to a broader functional privacy framework and show the globally optimal sampler stays optimal locally. They also derive a simple closed-form sampler independent of the chosen divergence measure. The local view fits the common setting where public data supplies the reference distribution.
arxiv-2510-09585:
Saeedeh Mohammadi and seven co-authors, among them Taha Yasseri, review four years of Community Notes in a 2025 arXiv paper. Community Notes, launched as Birdwatch on Twitter in January 2021 and now running on X, lets contributors write and rate corrective notes on posts. It is the first large-scale crowdsourced moderation system, and other platforms are now copying the model.

The authors parse the notes and ratings from the programme's first four years. They detect the language of every note, extract embedded links and discussion topics from the English ones, and build monthly interaction networks among contributors. Their descriptive study covers linguistic diversity, sourcing practices, contributor activity, and rating behaviour. Alongside the analysis, they release a curated dataset and source code for future research. They also review earlier studies, aiming to give the growing field a shared foundation.
arxiv-2510-09985:
Njungle and co-authors present Prismo in this 2025 arXiv paper on privacy-preserving machine learning. Machine learning runs on personal data, which raises real privacy risks. Many frameworks now promise to train models while protecting that data, but choosing among them is hard.

Prismo is a decision support system that helps users pick a framework for their needs. The options differ in privacy guarantees, speed, and ease of use, and no single choice fits every task. Prismo compares the frameworks against the user's setting and requirements. The goal is to make a specialist decision accessible to teams without deep privacy expertise. The authors frame selection itself as the bottleneck that better tooling can remove.
arxiv-2510-10385:
Nizovkina, Larsen, Brown, and Helmi refine open cluster parameters with Gaia data in this 2025 arXiv paper in astronomy. Open clusters are groups of stars born together, so they share age and composition, making them clean tests of stellar evolution and galactic dynamics. Gaia's uniform photometry has sharpened cluster measurements.

Two problems remain: age and metallicity can mimic each other, and many clusters lack spectroscopic observations. The authors use metallicities from Gaia's XP spectra to break that degeneracy. Independent metal abundances pin one side of the age-metallicity trade-off. More precise cluster ages and compositions follow, strengthening the use of clusters as tracers of the Milky Way's history.
arxiv-2510-10585:
Heng Zhang and seven co-authors target wasted duplication inside multi agent systems in this 2025 arXiv paper. Teams of language model agents solve problems together, but agents often repeat each other's retrieval and reasoning. The team's measurements found an average knowledge duplication rate of 47.3 percent across agent communications in the systems studied. They argue the root cause is that current designs never ensure agents share only the minimal sufficient information.

Their framework, D3MAS, attacks redundancy through structure. Task decomposition filters out irrelevant subproblems early. Collaborative reasoning captures complementary inference paths across agents. Distributed memory gives access to non-redundant knowledge, and the layers coordinate through structured messages in a unified graph. On four challenging datasets, D3MAS improved reasoning accuracy by between 8.7 and 15.6 percent across the reported results, while cutting redundancy by 46 percent on average.
arxiv-2510-10885:
Jiajing Guo and four co-authors test which answer time tricks actually help database question answering in practice, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Text to SQL systems let non experts query industrial databases in natural language. Test time scaling strategies, which spend more computation per query, promise better answers. The team benchmarks six lightweight, industry oriented strategies across four language models, including two reasoning models, on the BIRD Mini-Dev benchmark.

Beyond accuracy, they report latency and token consumption, the costs that decide whether a strategy is deployable. Divide and conquer prompting and few shot demonstrations consistently improved performance, for both general purpose and reasoning focused models. Adding more workflow steps, by contrast, gave mixed results. The choice of base model played a critical role in outcomes. The authors frame their findings as practical guidance on the trade offs among accuracy, efficiency, and complexity when shipping Text to SQL systems.
arxiv-2510-10985:
Menghan Yi, Yanlin Tang, and Huixia Judy Wang build honest prediction sets when labeled outcomes are scarce and the target population has shifted, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their method is conformal: it returns sets guaranteed to cover the true outcome at a chosen rate, with no distributional assumptions. A labeled source distribution, related to the target through a shift assumption, supplies the data. If the target has no labels at all, predictions rest on the source alone; partial labels, when available, sharpen them.

Two obstacles are handled head on. The likelihood ratio between domains is identified by matching covariate distributions inside a finite spline space. And to allow skewed or multi peaked errors, the sets are highest predictive density sets. A weight adjusted estimator follows the source density along a quantile process and reweights it toward the target. Theory, simulations, and a MIMIC-III clinical study back the method.
arxiv-2510-11385:
Magnetars, neutron stars with extreme magnetic fields, fire off X-ray bursts whose light usually rises fast and decays exponentially. Yue Wang and a large collaboration checked whether that standard pulse shape is the only one in this 2025 arXiv astronomy paper. They examined burst light curves from the magnetar SGR J1935+2154 recorded by the GECAM satellite between 2021 and 2022.

Alongside the familiar fast-rise exponential-decay pulses, they discovered a new pattern they call exponential rise and cut-off decay, which a mathematical function describes well. Bursts with the new shape are generally longer in duration, brighter at peak flux, and harder in spectrum than standard ones. The pattern is not unique to this magnetar; it also appears in others.
