Dwarf galaxies are common yet poorly understood, and feedback from stars and black holes should shape them most. D. Kakkad and twenty co-authors image nine nearby dwarfs, at redshift below 0.08, with JWST's NIRCam and MIRI instruments plus archival Hubble data, as part of COSMOS-Web. Stellar masses run near a hundred million to a billion suns, with star formation from 0.003 to 0.3 solar masses per year.

Every target is detected in both JWST cameras, showing substantial interstellar material, and the mix of early- and late-type dwarfs looks representative of low-density environments. Mid-infrared fluxes match mass-matched TNG50 simulations, while morphology varies most in MIRI, likely from dust lanes and clumps. The sample offers a clean test bed for feedback prescriptions.
arxiv-2602-09385:
John Bostanci and two co-authors claim to draw a firm line between quantum and classical proof-checking with classical oracles. Their 2026 paper separates languages checkable with a quantum proof from those checkable with a classical proof, a result reached before by more complex means. The new proof is presented as simpler in idea and in detail, and it extends readily to further splits.

The same tools also give the first firm classical-oracle split between choice with quantum advice and choice with classical advice, beating earlier quantum-oracle and classically-accessible results. The oracles rest on the code intersection problem, plus codes with very strong list-recovery traits. The paper thus sharpens the line between quantum and classical help in proof-checking and advice.
arxiv-2602-09585:
Aryan Sanghi and two co-authors study iterated line graphs. Each edge of a graph becomes a vertex, linked when edges share an endpoint, and the operation repeats. Their 2026 paper asks two questions for a graph on n vertices. For which iteration counts does the iterated line graph admit an Euler path? How does its maximum degree grow? Since iterated line graphs can dwarf the original, both answers need efficient methods.

For Euler paths, the largest iteration count admitting one grows at most like vertices times edges. An algorithm lists all such counts in polynomial time. For degree growth, paths, cycles, and claws are easy. All other connected graphs, called prolific, follow a formula. Beyond some iteration, degree equals a graph constant times a power of two plus two. The smallest such constants are three, four, five and a half, six, and seven, with full characterizations for the first four.
arxiv-2602-09785:
Seydou Diallo and five co-authors offer the first standard benchmark for testing auto speech hearing in the Bambara language, using one hour of pro taped Malian charter text. Their 2026 paper designs the set as a set model under near-optimal sound and language settings, then tests thirty-seven models ranging from Bambara-trained systems to large-scale store models.

Current scores remain far below use standards even in this narrow formal domain. The top system misses nearly half of words, while the best letter error rate, set by another model, sits near an eighth. Several known multi-tongue models exceed a hundred percent word error rate. Multi-tongue pre-training and scaling alone prove too little for rare tongues, and these best-case figures stay new against real settings. The benchmark and a board support open future tests.
arxiv-2602-10085:
General intelligence should expand its own skill set, yet most agent frameworks lean heavily on human engineering. A 2026 paper led by Richard Bornemann, with two co-authors, introduces CODE-SHARP, a framework that grows an archive of Python programs encoding skills. It trains a generalist agent from scratch by reinforcement learning, directly from source code. Each skill program carries a local success condition plus prerequisites delegated to earlier skills.

At runtime, skills route the agent through prerequisite chains, rewarding each completion, so the agent learns only the marginal behavior each new skill adds. On two game benchmarks, autonomous agents beat prior work sixfold and about two and a half times in median performance, uniquely crafting iron tools and mining diamonds. Extended runs discovered over ninety skills and solved long-horizon tasks zero-shot.
arxiv-2602-10385:
Most trajectory learning works at group level, smoothing away single-patient complexity. Patient subtyping stays difficult, and single-patient modeling stays largely out of reach. A 2026 paper led by Jia Li, with two co-authors, proposes a data-driven approach around a dedicated patient-level time variable. The variable captures Timing Attention: how tightly an event's timing clusters across the patient group, turning timing into a workable dimension. The authors embody the idea as the Level-of-Individual Time Transformation, applied to health records from more than three thousand two hundred breast cancer patients.

The authors report two firsts, to their knowledge: finding clinically meaningful patient paths on their own, and what-if timing deduction. Both results come purely from the data, needing no prior domain knowledge. The method also does well at timing prediction and survival analysis, suggesting a practical path toward patient-level trajectory learning in medicine.
arxiv-2602-10685:
Alejandro Mendoza Barrionuevo and three co-authors measure cooperation itself, not just task success, in a 2026 paper. Heterogeneous multi-agent systems working under partial observability and time role dependence need richer testing than completion rates. Speed alone hides coordination failures, unfair burdens, and fragile dependencies.

The paper proposes a general-purpose suite of cooperation metrics organized into three levels: primary metrics, inter-team metrics, and intra-team metrics. Jointly they portray speed, coordination, dependency, fairness, and sensitivity across teams and agents. Checked in a realistic destructive foraging setting, the metrics transfer to other sequential multi-agent domains. They give teams a shared language for how well agents work jointly.
arxiv-2602-11185:
Training signals in language models pile into a few dominant directions. Zhendong Huang and sixteen co-authors show that this spike-tail split persists through training, with a tiny share of directions dominating optimizer statistics. That dominance throttles tail learning through second-moment scaling and tightens the safe learning rate.

Their optimizer, Spectra, suppresses the low-rank spike subspace without amplifying the noise-sensitive tail. Cached, warm-started power iteration tracks the spike with little overhead and far less optimizer memory. On a large LLaMA model, Spectra reaches target loss faster than AdamW, cuts overhead and memory, and lifts downstream scores. Against Muon it runs far faster in optimizer time with lower loss.
arxiv-2602-11285:
Integer straight programming is NP-complete, yet central to scheduling and logistics. Gabriel Escrig and two co-authors present a fully quantum Metropolis-Hastings recipe that walks the feasible region with reversible circuits alone, without quantum RAM or classic pre- and post-processing. Each step prepares candidate moves, checks objective and constraints reversibly, and encodes acceptance amplitudes.

Resource scaling is straight in logical qubit count, with explicit adder constructions supporting straight objectives and mixed constraints. Circuit-level simulations on random instances confirm straight scaling and show progressive thermalization toward low-cost feasible solutions under annealing. The method offers a coherent, resource-characterized rival for fully quantum constraint solving, ready for future speedups.
arxiv-2602-11585:
Wireless researchers often cannot get hands-on time with distant radio testbeds, and setting up remote access takes heavy local infrastructure. Annoy Dey and eight co-authors present C-POD, a cloud-native framework that automates deploying and managing edge pods so testbeds can be shared and reached remotely. Containerized edge environments, persistent secure-shell tunnels, and stable graphical interfaces let experimenters run flexible workflows without building the plumbing themselves.

The team prototyped C-POD on the Amazon Web Services cloud and linked two testbeds, one for radio signal generation and one for fifth-generation communications. The demo shows cloud-assisted deployment, elastic computing resources, and clear experiment monitoring. By lowering the barrier to over-the-air experiments, C-POD aims to make shared wireless research routine rather than exceptional.
arxiv-2602-12285:
Language models now act as agents, not just chatbots, so biases in their personas can change real outcomes. Linbo Cao led this work with two co-authors, running the first systematic case study of demographic persona effects on agent performance. Persona bias in plain text is well known, but its effect on task work was largely untested.

Across benchmarks spanning strategy, planning, and technical operations, persona cues shifted performance by up to 26.2 percent, even though those cues were irrelevant to the tasks. The shifts held across task types and model designs, showing that persona prompts and simple injections can warp decision reliability. The finding flags a direct operational risk for deploying agent systems safely.
arxiv-2602-12385:
Robots working in the wild take damage, and that damage changes how they move in consistent, notable ways. Anuj Pokhrel led this work with four co-authors, asking whether plain language can capture the variety of structural failures well enough to inform motion models. Their system, ZLIK, grounds damage descriptions in kinodynamic behaviour through self-supervised learning, learning a forward motion model from data.

Data come from the high-fidelity soft-body simulator BeamNG.tech, across a range of structurally compromised vehicles. The learned model adapts to unseen damage types with no extra training, cutting kinodynamics error by up to 81 percent. It also generalises across sim-to-real gaps and from full size to tenth scale, pointing toward robots that adjust on the fly when their bodies change.
arxiv-2602-12485:
Firms win by turning shoppers into loyal buyers, yet broad campaigns can erode brand value while economic methods misread highly engaged buyers as ideal targets. Keerthi Gopalakrishnan led this work with seven co-authors, giving a two-stage multi-model design with Self-Paced Loss for intent-aware buyer grouping. The first stage uses a multi-class neural network to split campaign-swayed, organically engaged, and low-engagement buyers.

The second stage applies a binary label fix model to find true campaign-driven intent under a missing-label frame, tuning grouping during training. By splitting prompted visits from organic behaviour, the system enables sharper campaign aiming, lower reach costs, and better sales gains. A/B testing shows over 100 basis points gain in key success metrics, showing the value of intent-aware grouping for value-driven selling.
arxiv-2602-12685:
Quantum computers need codes that protect fragile quantum data from errors, and Floquet codes do this cheaply by building their checks on the fly from simple two-part measurements. Higher-dimensional versions promise extra toughness, but they have barely been studied. Yoshito Watanabe and two co-authors construct a three-dimensional Floquet code whose checks at each instant form a fermionic toric code, while keeping all three logical qubits safe through the whole measurement run.

The key is a lattice shape where removing any one edge colour leaves only short closed loops, so no logical data leaks away during the schedule. A plain three-round cycle misses some error signs, but the authors add a further sequence that recovers them without disturbing the stored qubits. The same lattice shapes also yield a family of monitored quantum models with rich, topologically ordered phases.
arxiv-2602-12785:
Factory workers' views of robot collaboration depend on how risks and benefits weigh up, and news framing may tilt that balance. Philipp Brauner and three co-authors ran a pre-registered study with 1,150 participants, each reading a positive or negative newspaper story about robot collaboration in autonomy, employment, or safety contexts. They then measured perceived risk, benefit, and overall value with standard scales.

Framing shifted absolute ratings, and in both frames risks and benefits predicted value. Under positive framing the effects simply added up, but under negative framing the effects grew stronger and interacted: higher risk weakened the pull of benefits. Positive framing also explained more variance in value. The study shows that how robot collaboration is communicated shapes not just opinions, but how people combine pros and cons.
arxiv-2602-12885:
Fluorine's origin in the early Universe is still debated, with Wolf-Rayet stars proposed as early producers. Akiyoshi Tsujita and twelve co-authors test that idea with ALMA Band 5 spectroscopy of hydrogen fluoride absorption toward a dusty star-forming galaxy at redshift 6.024. The galaxy is young enough that low-mass asymptotic giant branch stars cannot yet have contributed much, isolating massive-star yields.

No significant absorption was found, at about two sigma, yielding a conservative five-sigma upper limit on the HF-to-H2 ratio below 2.2 times ten to the minus nine. That is roughly ten times below typical local values, pointing to inefficient fluorine enrichment about 0.9 billion years after the Big Bang. The limit fits models without Wolf-Rayet yields at that epoch, and more high-redshift measurements will pin down when such enrichment began.
arxiv-2602-13185:
Video making control often relies on ambiguous or task-given signals, but separating appearance from motion offers a cleaner path. Mingzhi Sheng and six co-authors propose FlexAM, a unified system built on a novel 3D control signal that represents video motion as a point cloud. Three enhancements distinguish it: multi-frequency positional coding for fine motion, depth-aware coding, and a flexible signal balancing sharpness against generalisation.

That picture disentangles appearance and motion, enabling image-to-video and video-to-video editing, camera control, and spatial object editing within one system. Wide tests show FlexAM achieving superior scores across all evaluated tasks. For video making, the point-cloud control signal provides a general, robust other to the patchwork of task-given controls used today.
arxiv-2602-13385:
Stellar streams torn from globular clusters trace galaxy formation and may expose dark matter. Modeling them forces a trade-off: particle-spray methods simplify escape physics, while direct N-body runs are too costly for realistic systems above a hundred thousand particles. KRIOS, a new basis-expansion N-body code for collisional stellar dynamics, aims to bridge that gap for stream modeling.

KRIOS reproduced NBODY6++GPU cluster models and their streams more accurately than particle spray, in a fraction of the wall-clock time. On ten orbits like known Milky Way streams, KRIOS and spray methods disagreed most for tightly bound progenitors under strong tides, and the paper weighs which progenitor physics matters most. Brian T. Cook leads the work with eight co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13485:
Industrial sensor networks watch many linked subsystems at once. But raw readings cannot be shared across sites, each client runs a fixed proprietary model, and nonlinear dynamics hide cross-client links inside state-transition functions. This paper offers a vertical federated learning framework for one-step-ahead cross-client temporal links under those constraints. Each client compresses local high-dimensional readings into low-dimensional latent states with a nonlinear state-space model.

A central server then learns a state-transition model over those states with a graph attention network, given a candidate graph skeleton. Attention coefficients are tied analytically to the Jacobian of the learned dynamics. Synthetic tests validate the theory on known graphs, and real data tests show superior federated root cause analysis over baselines. Ayse Tursucular leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14785:
Fengyuan Cao and others build a speech quality system that rates multi-rate speech, from 16 to 48 kilohertz. Labelled data are scarce there, and standard self-supervised models, pretrained at 16 kilohertz, discard higher-frequency information. Their spectrogram-augmented approach adds a parallel branch carrying high-frequency features up to 48 kilohertz into the quality estimate.

The system, SA-SSL-MOS, predicts mean opinion scores across sampling rates without forcing all speech down to one narrow band. By keeping the top frequencies in play, it judges wideband speech more fairly. Speech assessment gains a model that listens across the full range it claims to rate.
arxiv-2602-14885:
Ramon Nartallo-Kaluarachchi and others give drift-diffusion matching, a drill for teaching loop nets to act out any set random rate law in a small hidden room. Old Hopfield-style nets lean on twin-way links and slide-like flows, while live brain nets use one-way links to back rich, time-bound acts.

With one-way links let in, the team shows loop nets can hold true both the drift and the spread of a set law, in that small room. Brain-like nets thus gain a drill that honours one-way wiring. Time-bound net acts turn from chance to craft.
arxiv-2602-14985:
Esmaeilbeig and colleagues build fast, real-time localization for multi-static backscatter networks, a candidate technology for joint communication and sensing in ambient 6G Internet of Things settings. Large deployments with thousands of tags need cheap ways to estimate range and angle of arrival and to fuse those estimates into positions. The team proposes two low-complexity estimators, JRAC and SRAE, matching FFT and subspace baselines at far lower cost.

For localization they add a maximum-likelihood method solved by gradient search and an iterative re-weighted least squares method. Tests on a real testbed use 4 illuminators, one multi-antenna receiver, and 100 tags. JRAC and SRAE cut runtime by up to 40 times, and the least squares method runs up to 500 times faster than brute force search. Median error across all tags is 3 metres.
arxiv-2602-15185:
Jacobus measures complexity in 2D Ising phase transitions through image compression. Measuring it in dynamical systems remains an open problem with broad uses. The 2D ferromagnetic Ising model, a classic system with a second-order phase shift at a key temperature, is often cited for complex shape. Jacobus defines a structural score through code-based information theory, gauging Kolmogorov complexity of lattice layouts with standard lossless image compression.

The metric is tuned by matching a layout's compressibility with that of its pixel-wise sorted and randomly shuffled twins. The score is a product of two parts capturing drift from perfect order and from disorder. Plotted against temperature, runs show a clear peak exactly at the known critical point. Information-theoretic measures of this kind, the paper argues, can serve as sensitive signs of tipping points, directly measuring complex structure at the order-chaos boundary.
arxiv-2602-15285:
Khoruzhii and colleagues develop algebra methods for cutting non-Clifford gates in fault-tolerant quantum work. Non-Clifford gates, built via magic state making, drive costs. While T-count cuts are well-studied, special CCZ plants shift the natural target to direct Toffoli cuts. Building on a connection between Toffoli count and tensor decomposition over F2, their methods match or improve all known results for both Toffoli and T-count. The connection itself drives the method.

Most loops finish in under a minute on a single CPU, instead of many TPUs used by older work.
arxiv-2602-15385:
Richman and Wüthrich offer a new method for finding chain-ladder funds based on a deep rework of data use for the forecast steps. The chain-ladder tool is the most far used claims saving technique in non-life cover. Instead of pushing forward total claims with set chain-ladder factors, they set multi-period factors that carry the newest readings straight to the final claims.

This other view on chain-ladder saving opens a plain path for using ML tools to single claims saving. As a proof of idea, they show a small-scale real data trial using brain nets for single claims saving.
arxiv-2602-15685:
Simms works alone to bound a class of curve-counting invariants: the genus zero logarithmic Gromov-Witten invariants of projective space relative to its toric boundary. Such invariants count curves with prescribed tangency to the boundary, and sharp bounds on them help organise enumerative geometry. The paper gives an upper bound that is polynomial in the contact orders, with degree set by the number of marked points.

The proof hinges on positivity of intersections for projective spaces, a classical feature that keeps intersection numbers on the right side of zero. Readers of enumerative geometry gain a clean, explicit growth control: as contact orders rise, the invariants grow at most polynomially, with the exponent tracking how many points are marked. The result is a useful yardstick for future exact computations.
arxiv-2602-15785:
Hullman and colleagues ask when large language models used as fake subjects can support a valid read about human conduct. Such runs offer cheap, near-instant answers for social science tests, but guidance on when they support valid reads remains thin. The paper contrasts two routes for valid causal figures and spells out the rules under which each suits early versus final research.

Heuristic routes try to show fake and real human conduct as the same through prompt tuning, fine-tuning, and other repairs that cut model-induced errors. Useful for early work, they lack formal stats guarantees needed for final work. Stats tuning instead joins extra human data with fixes for gaps between real and fake answers. Under stated rules, tuning keeps validity and gives sharper causal figures at lower cost than human-only tests. Both routes hinge on how well models match the key groups.
arxiv-2602-16085:
Sean Trott leads a team of five researchers testing whether language statistics can explain false belief reasoning in language models. Most prior work used a small set of closed models, which limits tests of theories about human social cognition. The team replicates and extends false belief studies across forty-one open-weight models from distinct families, checking sensitivity to implied knowledge states.

Only about a third of the models show such sensitivity, and none fully explains away the effect seen in humans. Larger models show more sensitivity and stronger power to predict human responses. A new test finds that both humans and models lean toward attributing false beliefs when knowledge is cued with a non-factive verb rather than indirectly. The size of that cue effect in humans falls within the model range, suggesting language statistics could account for it, though not for the main knowledge effect.
arxiv-2602-16485:
Jeffrey Wong leads three coauthors on Team-of-Thoughts, a framework for multi-agent systems that treats varied models as specialist tools. Most multi-agent systems use one model setup for every role, missing the varied strengths of different trained models. Team-of-Thoughts instead uses an orchestrator to pick and combine agents for each task.

Two new parts drive the design. Orchestrator Calibration finds models best at coordination and synthesis, while Agent Self-Assessment lets tool agents report their own domain strengths to guide selection. At run time, the orchestrator activates the most compatible agents to cover the task. Across five math and code benchmarks, the system beats single models and prior multi-agent baselines, reaching ninety-six percent on AIME24 and about seventy-eight percent on LiveCodeBench.
arxiv-2602-16585:
Dimitri Yatsenko and Thinh Nguyen argue that rigorous operations decide whether human-agent science collaboration succeeds. Data pipelines need a SciOps discipline like DevOps, yet common tools scatter provenance with no transactional guarantees. DataJoint 2.0 answers with a relational workflow model. Tables stand for workflow steps, rows for artifacts, and foreign keys set execution order.

The schema states both what data exists and how it was derived, in one queryable, enforceable system. Four additions extend it: object-augmented schemas, semantic matching from attribute lineage, an extensible type system, and distributed job coordination. Agents can thus join scientific workflows without risking data corruption, and labs get a shared substrate for reproducible, machine-readable science.
arxiv-2602-16685:
A. El Mazouni, D. S. Nagaraj, and Supravat Sarkar widen a classic idea in algebra and geometry. The idea is the determinantal form of a hypersurface. Here it is stretched to cover sections of a line bundle tied to a vector bundle. A few cases are shown. Rules that must hold for such a form to exist are proved. The move takes a classic tool into a wider geometric world.

As a payoff, take any whole degree above one. There is a rank-two bundle on the flat projective plane that cannot be split. Almost all curves of that degree come from a pair of its smooth sections, up to a change of coords. A linear algebra payoff stems from that fact. Geometers get a wider toolkit with a striking payoff for curves.
arxiv-2602-17085:
Shogo Sato led a seven-author team building a better way to pinpoint faint gamma-ray bursts with Compton cameras. These bursts rank among the most energetic flashes in the universe. They can open a window on early star formation. Yet faint, distant ones hide in noise, with few photons to work from. Prior machine learning tools tend to trade statistical robustness against noise suppression instead of getting both.

ComptonUNet joins both strengths in one hybrid framework, processing raw data and reconstructed images together. In realistic simulations of low-Earth-orbit missions, with burst-like events buried in background, it beat existing methods on localization accuracy across low-photon and high-background cases alike. The tool gives astronomers a sharper fix on weak bursts that older methods would blur or miss.
arxiv-2602-17185:
Uğur Genç led a six-author team testing whether a chatbot's projected persona sways charitable giving. Language-model chat agents now project nuanced personas through words alone, but the effects on users were unclear. In a crowdsourced study, hundreds of people each talked with one of eight agents, whose personas mixed attitude, authority, and reasoning styles.

Overall persona did not change gift decisions directly, yet it shifted views and feelings. People meeting gloomy agents felt worse, liked the cause less, and rated the agent less trustworthy and less competent, but still tended to give more. Trust, competence, and situational empathy predicted giving. The authors warn that chat agents can subtly steer views and choice, a manipulation risk worth naming.
arxiv-2602-17285:
Erika Hausenblas led a three-author paper extending a classic existence tool to random equations. One standard route to existence for deterministic, highly nonlinear partial differential equations runs through the Schauder-Tychonoff fixed-point theorem. The paper presents and verifies a random variant of that theorem.

The new result is then applied to nonlinear diffusion problems with non-Lipschitz perturbations, a class where standard Lipschitz-based arguments fail. The random Schauder-Tychonoff theorem thus gives analysts a fixed-point route to existence for noisy, strongly nonlinear diffusion problems, stretching the classic deterministic toolkit to the random setting.
arxiv-2602-17685:
Agni Bandyopadhyay and Gunther Waxenegger-Wilfing tackle multi-target active debris removal in low Earth orbit. They introduce a unified coelliptic maneuver frame that joins Hohmann transfers, safety ellipse proximity operations and explicit refueling logic. The setting is a realistic orbital simulation with randomized debris fields, keep-out zones and delta-V limits.

Three planners are benchmarked: a greedy heuristic, Monte Carlo tree search, and deep reinforcement learning with masked proximal policy optimization. Over one hundred test scenarios, masked PPO wins on mission efficiency and runtime, visiting up to twice as many debris items as greedy and beating tree search clearly on speed. The findings support modern reinforcement learning as a scalable, safe and resource-efficient route to debris removal autonomy.
arxiv-2602-17785:
Xinwei Ju and team propose PRISM, a self-supervised frame for monocular endoscopic depth and pose estimation in colonoscopy. Depth and pose estimates improve screening by cutting blind spots and lowering the risk of missed lesions and incomplete exams. The task is hard given texture-less surfaces, complex lighting, deformation, and a lack of in-vivo sets with reliable ground truth.

PRISM uses anatomical and lighting priors to guide geometric learning, combining edge detection with luminance decoupling for structural guidance. Edge maps come from a learning-based edge detector built for thin, high-frequency edges, while intrinsic decomposition separates shading from reflectance so shading cues aid depth. Tests on real and synthetic sets reach state-of-the-art performance. Ablations yield two practical insights: self-supervised training on real data beats supervised training on realistic phantom data, and video frame rate strongly shapes performance.
arxiv-2602-17885:
Christina Frederick and Haomin Zhou present a finite dimensional variational model for multi-agent path-planning in a moving medium. A group of agents travels from initial positions to a target distribution through a moving medium. The model derives from the agent-based formulation of Wasserstein Hamiltonian flows that transport between probability distributions while optimizing a running cost.

The goal is the mismatch between final positions and the target distribution. Agent trajectories come from a system of Hamiltonian equations imposed as constraints, while the problem rests on a finite vector of initial velocities for the agents. Numerically, the model is tackled through L-BFGS with a shooting strategy. Simulation examples, including a time-dependent moving medium, illustrate the model's performance, giving readers a tractable variational tool for coordinated motion in flowing environments.
arxiv-2602-18085:
K G Smith and colleagues examine AD Leo, an active M dwarf whose field has weakened from strongly to mildly negative over two decades, raising fears of a polarity reversal. Solar reversals occur every eleven years, but M dwarf reversals are poorly understood, with none observed for fast-rotating M dwarfs. The team studies its space weather.

From ESPaDOnS and SPIRou data, the authors measure the longitudinal field and reconstruct the large-scale field with Zeeman-Doppler imaging. Five magnetograms from twenty nineteen to twenty twenty-three feed 3D stellar wind simulations. They find no polarity reversal. Instead the field restores to a simpler, axisymmetric, poloidal-dipolar form with consistently negative values and greater mean strength. Simulated mass loss averages ten times solar. The habitable zone sits beyond the Alfven surface, likely shielding magnetized planets above zero point three four gauss from wind erosion. Conditions vary by epoch.
arxiv-2602-18185:
Xuan Chen and eight co-authors compute, for the first time at this precision, how often electron-positron collisions spray four jets. Their 2026 paper works at next-to-next-to-leading order, the highest jet count yet treated at that accuracy. Handling the infinities takes an antenna subtraction scheme with generalized antenna functions.

New two-loop corrections rest on a fresh basis of special functions built for four-particle decays. Against data from the LEP collider, the new numbers agree better than the previous order's, and where theory is most trusted, its uncertainty now falls below the lab's own error bars. The calculation gives collider physicists a sharper yardstick for strong-force predictions in multi-jet events.
arxiv-2602-18385:
Aman Awasthi revisits whether the LISA gravitational-wave observatory could hear the Sun ring. His 2026 paper builds on Polnarev's finding that low-frequency solar modes might in principle register in a LISA-type interferometer. Using current solar models, new detector sensitivities, and tighter limits on mode amplitudes, Awasthi recomputes the gravitational response of solar oscillation modes.

Solar models come from MESA, with mode frequencies and shapes from GYRE, focusing on g-modes of degree two and azimuthal orders zero and two. Both earlier and current LISA sensitivity curves are tested, plus a comparison with the TianQin mission in the low-frequency band. Responses from two standard solar models, built on GS98 and AGSS09 abundance sets, come out nearly identical. Solar metallicity uncertainty thus barely affects whether LISA-class detectors could spot solar g-modes.
arxiv-2602-18785:
A liquid in a sealed container at fixed volume can sit as a uniform liquid, or it can hold a vapour bubble, and the bubble may be stable, fleeting, or doomed. Frédéric Caupin, with three co-authors, studies in 2026 how long a metastable bubble lasts before it collapses, and how long the uniform liquid lasts alongside it.

Lifetime here means the average waiting time until collapse is observed. For the smallest systems the authors predict a stranger behaviour, phase flipping, in which the fluid oscillates back and forth between states with and without a bubble. A simulation of a Lennard-Jones fluid provides a concrete example, showing how external constraints reshape phase equilibrium in confined fluids.
arxiv-2602-18885:
Predicting how genes respond to a perturbation is hard. Signals are sparse and noise is severe. Yinhua Piao, with nine co-authors, tackles a common failure in 2026. Many methods collapse to the mean. They predict average expression and look good on correlation, while missing perturbation-specific responses. That yields false positives and poor interpretation.

Their method, AdaPert, extracts a sparse subgraph for each perturbation. It uses differentiable node selection on a knowledge graph. It then quiets spurious variation in non-responsive genes. It emphasises genes that truly change. Across several benchmarks, AdaPert beats existing baselines. Its largest gains come on metrics that care about differentially expressed genes.
arxiv-2602-19085:
Online ads run on auto-bidding, so buyers chase value under money limits, not simple profit. Xiaodong Liu, with two co-authors, designs mechanisms in 2026 for buyers whose budgets and return-on-spend limits stay private, while valuations are public, a setting shaped by machine-learned prediction.

The work extends the Eisenberg-Gale program, a convex optimization framework, to cover return-on-spend constraints. Its solution is unique and pins down the market's competitive equilibrium. That analysis yields a market-clearing mechanism with two proven traits. Truth about money limits is best. Revenue hits a tight one-half approximation of the first-best benchmark, the most any feasible mechanism could earn. A decentralized online algorithm makes the scheme usable. Log factors aside, seller revenue and buyer utility move toward equilibrium benchmarks, with regret at a tilde O(sqrt(m)) rate over many auctions.
arxiv-2602-19185: Louis Garrigue, writing alone in 2026, provides precise effective operators for single-layer graphene at Fermi energy. A lattice creates the tiny-scale potential. A large-scale field with the same repeat, varying at a much larger scale, creates a super-grid. Energy-based guesses, small-change theory, and a multi-scale method combine in the approach. At the working level, the usual massless Dirac operator gives way to other tools. Tests for graphene illustrate the results.
arxiv-2602-19385:
Spotting implicit visual and textual patterns matters across modern AI uses, yet long-tail patterns challenge pretrained base models. Minxue Tang and five co-authors propose ADAMAB, a lean framework for tuning embeddings in few-shot pattern recognition. It trains lightweight, embedder-agnostic tuners above frozen embedding nets without touching their parameters, keeping compute cost low.

To reduce the need for large training sets, ADAMAB adds adaptive data boosts driven by a multi-armed bandit method. Using an adjusted upper confidence bound rule, it cuts gradient shifting and offers a theory-backed guarantee of convergence in few-shot training. Multimodal tests show up to 40 percent accuracy gain when training with fewer than five initial samples per class.
arxiv-2602-19685:
Virtual cells that predict how cells answer perturbations are a long-standing systems-biology goal, yet single-cell sequencing destroys the cell, so no cell is seen before and after. Xinyu Yuan and five co-authors note that current models map control and perturbed populations but assume one fixed response distribution per context. Real responses vary with hidden factors like microenvironment shifts and batch effects, forming a spread of possible distributions for the same conditions.

PerturbDiff shifts modeling from single cells to whole distributions, placing distributions as points in a Hilbert space and running diffusion over probability distributions. That design captures population-level shifts across hidden factors. Benchmarks show state-of-the-art single-cell response prediction and much better generalization to unseen perturbations, with code and data promised public.
arxiv-2602-20085:
Optomechanics couples light to motion. Reaching the regime where single photons matter has been hard. A 2026 arXiv paper by Lei Du and three co-authors studies a Fano-mirror optomechanical setup in the quantum nonlinear regime.

Two strongly lossy optical modes merge through coherent and dissipative couplings. They form one working mode with a sharply reduced linewidth. That reduction lets the system reach single-photon strong coupling and sideband resolution at the same time. The authors model the dynamics with an effective master equation. They check it against two other accounts: quantum Langevin and dressed-state master equations. With parameters experiments can reach, they predict clear quantum signs: photon blockade plus cat states of motion. The paper presents the Fano-mirror architecture as a strong candidate for using single-photon optomechanical nonlinear effects in quantum state engineering under conditions experiments can reach.
arxiv-2602-20185:
Step responses are a popular test for whether a smoothing operator keeps signals within bounds. For example, does it map signals in the unit cube back into the unit cube? A 2026 arXiv paper by Justin Grieshop, working alone, shows step-based tests can mislead for cyclic convolution maps on finite cyclic groups.

The paper studies shift-invariant smoothing operators written as periodic convolutions and analyzed with the discrete Fourier transform. Its sharp criterion says a constant-preserving periodic convolution keeps the unit cube inside itself exactly when its convolution kernel never goes negative. In other words, each row of the linked matrix sums to one with no negative entries. The proof builds worst-case binary examples and proven lower bounds on how badly the bound can fail. Three standard Fourier-domain averaging methods, including Fejér averaging and sharp spectral cutoff, are then measured against that criterion.
arxiv-2602-20285:
Amisha Srivastava and two co-authors design a processor that runs cryptography fast while resisting power side-channel attacks. Such attacks infer secrets from changes in power use, and common defenses either slow software down or lock hardware to one algorithm. Their 2026 paper presents CryptRISC, the first RISC-V processor to combine cryptographic acceleration with hardware-level masking against power leaks, built by extending the CVA6 core.

Two new components drive the design. A field detection layer identifies the dominant algebraic field of each cryptographic instruction, and a masking control unit then randomizes operands at run time. The masking style, Boolean, affine, or arithmetic, is chosen from the instruction meaning, covering algorithms from AES to SHA and the SM family. Masking happens inside the pipeline without changing instruction encoding. Tests show speedups of up to nearly seven times over baseline software, with hardware overhead under two percent.
arxiv-2602-20385:
Junghyun Koo and eight co-authors demonstrate top-gated transistors built from the ultra-wide bandgap oxide SrSnO3. Channels were grown by hybrid molecular beam epitaxy, with hafnium oxide gate dielectrics deposited by atomic layer deposition. The devices show field-effect mobility above sixty-five square centimetres per volt-second and an on-off current ratio above one hundred million. A near-ideal subthreshold slope of sixty-eight millivolts per decade and negligible hysteresis point to a clean interface.

On-state current reaches one hundred ninety-four milliamps per millimetre, with contact resistance at sixty-six hundredths of an ohm-millimetre. Strontium stannate thus joins ultra-wide bandgap semiconductors aimed at power electronics. The demonstration matters for power devices, which need materials blocking high voltages while switching cleanly. With a top-gated design, teams can test the platform and push it toward power use.
arxiv-2602-20485:
Flexomagnetism couples magnetism to strain gradients, a useful effect. Swarnava Ghosh presents a theory of elastic wave travel in a linear elastic flexo solid with fine structure and strain-gradient elastic interactions. The paper derives rate, phase speed, and group speed for head-on and transverse waves, showing all depend on the flexo factor and fine structure.

Unlike older linear stretch, where waves do not disperse, flexo solids with fine structure show both normal and odd spread. Transverse wave phase speeds can even exceed head-on ones, odd for older stretch. Waves also fade over certain wavelength ranges set by the flexo factor and fine-structure settings. Finally, the theory admits zero group speed modes with strong local energy trapping, and minus group speed modes moving against travel. It also admits wave freezing, where a wave stops in space without spreading.
arxiv-2602-21185:
Uniform-state discrete diffusion models generate well in few steps but stall as sampling steps grow. Justin Deschenaux, Caglar Gulcehre, and Subham Sekhar Sahoo break that plateau in this 2026 arXiv paper with predictor-corrector samplers for discrete diffusion, generalizing prior methods to arbitrary noise processes. Paired with uniform-state diffusion, the samplers beat ancestral sampling on language and image modeling.

Unlike conventional samplers, the new methods keep improving with more steps, challenging the assumption that masked diffusion is the inevitable future for diffusion language models. Beyond sampling, a memory-efficient curriculum for the Gaussian relaxation training phase cuts training time by a quarter and memory by a third against a prior method, with comparable perplexity. Code, checkpoints, and a video tutorial are released.
arxiv-2602-21285:
Quantum gravity in the far-out safety program raises a natural hope: a fixed point should tame bounce sizes. Benjamin Knorr tests that hope in this 2026 arXiv paper, working out leading quantum-gravity parts to a simple scalar size in a model that admits hand treatment. Four findings tangle the simple picture.

A fixed point alone does not imply bounded sizes. Gravity log terms can rule the low-energy zone of massless theories, slope series fail in numbers for Wilson numbers there, and standard polish tricks fail in kind for push tie. Only push-tied math resolves these issues. Massive theories mostly escape, except for edge and purely gravity couplings, and the author guesses about a no-pattern form.
arxiv-2602-21585:
Sweta Karlekar and seven co-authors present Duel-Evolve, a reward-free test-time tuning method driven by language-model self-preferences. Many apps tune language-model outputs at test time by proposing, scoring, and refining options. But tuned scalar judges for the goal are often missing, too sparse, or shaky.

Pairwise matchups prove easier to elicit, still signal better paths, and come from the model itself with no outside help. Duel-Evolve pools these noisy option matchups with a Bayesian Bradley-Terry model, yielding doubt-aware quality scores. Those scores guide matchup spending toward likely optima with Double Thompson Sampling and pick strong parents for better options. On MathBench it gains 20 points over older methods and baselines. On LiveCodeBench it improves over similar round-based methods by over 12 points. The method needs no reward model, no ground-truth labels in search, and no hand-made scoring function.
arxiv-2602-21885:
Andrei Shumilin and four co-authors give a minimal model that can be solved for low-frequency magnon relaxation in magnetic insulators. It covers magnon-phonon and magnon-magnon links. The model ties small-scale relaxation steps to Gilbert damping. It also shows how magnon decay shifts from bulk systems to the monolayer limit.

Magnon-phonon links give Gilbert damping of like size in three- and two-dimensional magnets. Flexural phonons in free-standing monolayers differ in kind from three-dimensional phonons in substrate-supported layers. Non-Gilbert damping from four-magnon scattering, by contrast, grows much stronger in two dimensions. There it no longer depends on spin-orbit coupling. To test the model on real matter, the team adds a numeric route to work out magnon damping from ab initio spin Hamiltonians. Core results hold for bulk YIG and van der Waals magnets CrSBr, CrI3, and CrPS4.
arxiv-2602-21985:
The curve given by a squared term equal to a sixth power plus one has a large symmetry group. That symmetry opens up twist families that do not come from the usual hyperelliptic route. Keunyoung Jeong and Junyeong Park study one such family, asking how its average analytic rank behaves. Rank here measures, in loose terms, how many independent rational solutions the curves in the family tend to carry.

Assuming a broad version of the Riemann hypothesis for the family's L-functions, the authors prove an explicit upper bound on that average rank. They also propose an analogue of the Goldfeld conjecture for this family, following the philosophy of Katz and Sarnak about how ranks should spread. The paper thus extends a famous rank guess into new, non-hyperelliptic territory.
arxiv-2602-22185:
When strong electron ties meet symmetry and topology, new gapless phases of matter can appear, but only a few examples are known. Kuan-Sen Lin and nine co-authors hunt for more in hexagonal heavy-fermion systems, a family rich in chiral nonsymmorphic crystal structures. Those structures promote Weyl nodes, while geometric frustration shapes the magnetism of f-electrons.

Their work finds Weyl-Kondo semimetals with chiral or achiral Weyl nodes across the classes studied. The work also builds tools for the wider search, attacking the shortage of test materials from both sides. For physicists, it widens the map of correlated phases that need no free-standing counterpart.
arxiv-2602-22285:
Dosing errors in clinical trials endanger patients, yet trials at high risk are usually spotted only after errors accumulate. Félicien Hêche and four co-authors build a machine-learning framework that stratifies trials by dosing-error risk before they start, using only information available at initiation. Their dataset spans over forty-two thousand trials from a public registry, with structured, semi-structured, and free-text protocol data.

Labels marking elevated dosing-error rates come from adverse-event reports, medical terminology, and confidence intervals. Three models are tested, and a late-fusion model combining structured and textual signals achieves the strongest discrimination, with calibrated probabilities for interpretable trial-level risk. Trial overseers gain an early-warning tool for steering monitoring where it matters most.
arxiv-2602-22685:
Fabian Muşat and one co-author forecast intermittent demand, the retail pattern of long zero-sale stretches broken by sudden orders. Classic tools like ARIMA, exponential smoothing, and Croston variants, plus modern DeepAR and transformer models, all stumble here. They treat demand as one smooth process or grow too costly across many sparse series.

Switch-Hurdle splits the job in two. A mixture-of-experts encoder routes each input to one expert going forward, while staying nearly dense going backward through a straight-through estimator. A hurdle decoder then separates the sale-or-no-sale call from the how-many call, using cross-attention autoregression with a shared hurdle head. On the M5 benchmark and a large retail dataset, it reached leading accuracy while staying scalable.
arxiv-2602-22785:
Ling Wang and eleven co-authors build 3D scenes with clear structure from a single image. Past methods produce part-level 3D objects but fail to sort parts into distinct items in open-world scenes. A bias-free grouping probe traces the failure to missing shape constraints inside the model's matching works.

SceneTransporter recasts scene building as a global linkage matching problem, solved with an entropy-based optimal transport goal inside the cleanup loop of a part-based spread model. The transport plan gates cross-focus into sole one-to-one routing of image patches to part latents, blocking mixing, while rivalry grouping plus an edge-based cost assembles tidy objects without splitting. Tests show clear gains in instance tidiness and shape truth.
arxiv-2602-23485:
Daniel R. Kattnig examines whether pigeons could sense Earth's magnetic field through electromagnetic induction in the semicircular canals of the inner ear. A recent study proposed that motion through the geomagnetic field induces a voltage, redistributing ions in the endolymph, opening voltage-gated calcium channels, and engaging downstream neural circuits.

Using a toy model of induction plus an information-theoretic analysis, Kattnig finds that, even under idealized assumptions, Faraday induction in the canals would not carry enough information to extract directional field data. The model does, however, allow tiny radio-frequency waves to support inferences, offering a possible account of their disruptive effect on avian compass navigation. The analysis does not dispute evidence for magnetically responsive vestibular pathways; it narrows which physical mechanisms remain viable.
arxiv-2602-23685:
Manbir Sodhi and two co-authors introduce the Vehicle Routing Problem with Resource-Constrained Pickup and Delivery. Units carry same goods to client sites for self-run work before pickup and reuse. Unlike older pickup-and-delivery problems, where one unit must do both jobs per client, this variant lets other units handle dropoff and pickup at the same site, creating links between routes.

That splitting fits self-run robot use, portable medical gear sharing, crisis relief, building tool rental, and farm sensor nets, where transport units are scarce and need not wait during work. The goal is to cut finish time, when the last unit returns after all goods are deployed, done, and picked up. Exact methods fail past 16 clients. The team builds a two-step search line starting with a GPU-sped-up tunable large-area search (ALNS).
arxiv-2602-23785:
Zhiwei Han and two co-authors study nonlinear canonical correlation analysis across several views of the same hidden factors. The 2026 paper treats each view as an unknown nonlinear mix of shared latent variables plus view-only noise, a setting where exact unmixing is known to be ill-posed.

Rather than chase exact recovery, the authors reframe the task as finding the shared signal subspaces, up to rotation within each view. Under latent priors and spectral separation, they prove that pairwise correlation goals recover those subspaces. With three or more views, pooling the views isolates the jointly shared part and drops view-only variation. They also give finite-sample error bounds, and tests on synthetic and rendered images back the theory and show why the assumed conditions matter.
arxiv-2602-23885:
Andrea Bizzotto and two co-authors bound the basic reproduction number and final epidemic size when the next-generation matrix is only partly known. The 2026 paper studies a multitype SIR model, where people fall into types and spread is encoded in a matrix of cross-type infections together with type shares.

When only row sums or column sums of the matrix are known, the authors derive sharp upper and lower bounds for both the reproduction number and the final sizes by type. For the special case where the matrix follows a contact pattern with detailed balance, bounds on the reproduction number narrow but are not sharp. Final-size bounds are obtained only for two types. The results tell epidemiologists what can still be concluded about an outbreak when contact data are incomplete, and where extra data would matter most.
arxiv-2602-24085:
Gilad Sadeh and two co-authors present an analytic framework for the hydrodynamics of stratified ultra-relativistic outflows, aimed at explaining the X-ray plateau phase seen in many gamma-ray burst afterglows. The 2026 paper accounts for a continuous distribution of Lorentz factors within the ejecta, rather than treating the outflow as a single shell.

That structure yields a long-lived, mildly relativistic reverse shock and an analytic crossing time. Synchrotron emission from the forward shock then naturally produces a shallow, long-lasting X-ray decay matching plateau properties, including a known luminosity-time relation, without prolonged central-engine activity or an extra high-energy component. Matching observed plateau durations requires a broad Lorentz-factor distribution reaching down to modest values. The reverse shock also predicts long-lived millimeter emission that outshines the forward shock there, with both components ending smoothly once the slowest ejecta are processed.
arxiv-2602-24185:
Meiqi Wang and six co-authors present a multi-messenger study of a solar energetic electron event driven by a solar jet, asking why so few accelerated electrons escape into space. The 2026 paper focuses on a November 2022 event linked to recurrent jets and interplanetary radio bursts. It combines microwave and X-ray analysis with in situ measurements from spacecraft at several distances and longitudes.

Consistent with earlier work, results show that only a tiny fraction of energetic electrons escape into interplanetary space. New microwave spectral imaging suggests that energetic electrons concentrate in a compact region just above a mini-flare arcade at the base of the jet spire. Number density falls sharply away from it. That confinement helps explain the severe deficit of upward-propagating electrons: most accelerated electrons stay trapped near the Sun rather than escaping along open field lines.
arxiv-2603-00285: Yuan and colleagues introduce TraderBench, a benchmark testing AI agents in adversarial capital markets without relying on language-model judges. It pairs expert-checked static tasks with live trading simulations scored only on realised results such as Sharpe ratio, returns and drawdown. Tracks cover crypto trading under four market-manipulation shifts and options work scored on profit, Greeks and risk control. Across 13 models on about 50 tasks, most crypto scores cluster near 33, and extra thinking lifts retrieval but leaves trading flat.
arxiv-2603-00485: Gu, Palani, and Setlur study how data workers revisit long analytical chat transcripts that run linear while real analysis loops back on itself. A design probe adds structured navigation aids such as filtering, multi level browsing, and detail on demand to standard scrolling and search. In a ten person study, workers met recall, reorientation, and prioritisation needs through visual recall, sequential reading, and abstractive moves, plus summaries enriched with process detail. The team draws design lessons for revisiting and sharing past analyses.
arxiv-2603-00985: Tang and four colleagues diagnose boundary aliasing, a clash in synthetic training for medical transformers where added textures corrupt the gradient signals that teach shape edges. Their spatially decoupled synthesis first builds a gradient-shielded buffer around boundaries for stable shape learning, then injects physics-driven textures into object cores. The split reconciles shape learning with noise invariance and beats prior formula-driven and self-supervised methods on two benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-01085: Li and Ruan predict the rebound of Chinese outbound tourism after COVID-19 with RISE, a three-stage plan splitting figures into initial levels, final levels, and the rebound curve joining them. Method blending and many information sources run through all stages, blending model output with expert judgment under sudden breaks and high uncertainty. Against standard methods, this plan lifts hit rate and toughness, giving a handy tool for post-crisis rebound paths.
arxiv-2603-01285: Zade and three colleagues propose Attention Smoothing Unlearning, a plan casting unlearning as self-teaching from a forget-teacher drawn from the model's own focus. Raising the softmax heat flattens focus spreads and straight kills lexical-level and meaning-level links that rebuild kept knowledge. The result is a bounded tuning goal erasing factual information while keeping answers to forget prompts sane. Tests on TOFU, MUSE, and WMDP, plus real-world and ongoing forgetting cases, assess the approach.
arxiv-2603-01485:
Self-driving cars use laser scans to track other cars and people over time, but one tracking style misses too many objects. Brian Cheong, Letian Wang, Sandro Papais, and Steven Waslander tackle that miss rate in this 2026 study. In tracking by attention, a query tied to a known track can block fresh queries from spotting new objects.

Their model, SCATR, adds two training tricks that work with many designs. One gives blocked track queries a second chance to match a real object during training. The other drops some track queries at random, so the model learns to cope with gaps and new arrivals. On the nuScenes test set, SCATR led its class and closed much of the gap to the older detect-first style.
arxiv-2603-01985:
Giacomo Canevari, Federico Dipasquale, and Bianca Stroffolini bound the cost of lifting maps into curved target spaces. Their 2026 work studies Sobolev maps from a planar domain into a closed Riemannian manifold. A lifting rewrites such a map through a double covering of the target, at the price of jump lines.

They prove a sharp lower bound on the jump length of any such bounded-variation lifting. The bound uses a geometric quantity: the minimal connection of the non-orientable singularities, relative to the domain. Minimal connection measures the cheapest way to pair up those singular points. As an application, minimizers of a ferronematics model are analyzed under mixed boundary conditions. Dirichlet data fix the liquid crystal order, while Neumann data govern the magnetization vector in that model.
arxiv-2603-02385:
Henrik Jeldtoft Jensen, Petr Jizba, and Piergiulio Tempesta unify generalized entropies in this 2026 paper. Classic theory assumes the number of states grows in an exponential way with system size. Strongly linked systems break that assumption, and many patch entropies exist. No patch had yet tied cleanly to the classic laws of heat and energy.

Their group entropies sort entropies into classes by how state counts grow. Each class still yields an entropy that scales in the right way with size. Written in state variables, these entropies match classic theory in the large limit. A notion of temperature emerges from the zeroth law, and absolute temperature from the second. Applied to black holes with stretched state growth, negative heat capacity appears in a natural way. The entropy framework stays consistent throughout.
arxiv-2603-02585:
Wen-Han Zhou, Eiichiro Kokubo, Harrison Agrusa, and colleagues study thermal forces on planetary rings in this 2026 paper. Saturn's rings show sharp inner edges that standard viscous models leave unexplained. The team introduces the Eclipse-Yarkovsky effect, a thermal torque from uneven heat emission during eclipses. It acts on ring particles larger than about a millimeter.

They cast the effect in a continuum model with viscous diffusion included. Particle spin data from N-body simulations constrain its strength. The effect pushes angular momentum outward and can overcome viscous drag. Long-term flow then moves ring material outward, a decretion pattern. Three regimes follow from optical depth: dense, transitional, and tenuous. In dense regimes the torque can carve a sharp inner edge like Saturn's A ring. Planetary heat pushes back with an opposing torque.
arxiv-2603-02985:
Reuben Docea, Rayan Younis, Yonghao Long, and colleagues release a dataset for rebuilding moving surgical scenes in four dimensions. The Dresden dataset pairs endoscopic video with precise structured-light geometry of deforming abdominal tissue. It comes from six pig cadaver sessions filmed with a surgical robot's stereo camera.

Three clip types stress different skills: whole deformations, step-by-step deformations, and moved-camera shots. Each release includes corrected stereo images, tool masks, depth maps, and point clouds at the start and end, plus camera details. The full set holds over three hundred thousand frames and hundreds of point clouds across nearly one hundred recordings. It benchmarks non-rigid tracking, depth estimation, and scene reconstruction in realistic surgical conditions.
arxiv-2603-03185:
Jan Provazník, Šimon Bräuer, Vojtěch Kala, and colleagues turn easy lab measurements into hard guarantees about quantum light. Truly non-Gaussian states of light power quantum computing and precision sensing beyond classical limits. The stellar rank grades that non-Gaussian character, but measuring it directly is impractical.

Witnesses, by contrast, use simple averages and spreads of measurable quantities to certify non-Gaussian behavior. The team proves those witnesses set rigorous lower bounds on stellar rank, and arranges them into a hierarchy of thresholds matching the rank ladder. Normalized versions of the expectation and variance quantifiers make the tests comparable across setups. The bridge lets experimentalists certify how deep a state's non-Gaussianity runs with scalable, routine measurements.
arxiv-2603-03585:
Angana Borah, Zohaib Khan, Rada Mihalcea, and Verónica Pérez-Rosas ask whether language models can predict who falls for false claims, and what drives the prediction. Susceptibility differs across demographic groups, largely through basic beliefs. Their 2026 approach, Belief-Sim, builds group belief profiles from psychology-based classes and survey data, then sets simulated people on those profiles.

Two modeling plans are studied: conditioning through prompts alone, and adapting models after training. Evaluation runs on two axes, plain accuracy at gauging who falls for false claims, and counterfactual care, checking whether swapping demographics changes predictions the right way. Across data sets and plans, beliefs prove a strong prior for simulating susceptibility. Scores reach above nine in ten in the best configuration. The study suggests belief profiles, not surface traits, carry the signal.
arxiv-2603-03785:
Erdun Gao and colleagues propose using observational data to design randomized trials instead of discarding it. Trials are the gold standard for causal inference but scarce, while large observational datasets are usually used only after the fact because of bias concerns. The authors argue that starting experiments from a blank slate is wasteful. Their Active Residual Learning paradigm treats the observational model as a prior and focuses the experiment on estimating the residuals needed to correct its bias, through a framework called R-Design.

They prove that estimating smooth residual contrasts converges strictly faster than reconstructing full outcomes, and that standard acquisition rules waste budget on nuisance uncertainty. Their R-EPIG criterion targets the causal quantity directly. On synthetic and semi-synthetic benchmarks, R-Design beats baselines, suggesting that repairing a biased model is far cheaper than learning one from scratch.
arxiv-2603-03985: Yansong Shi and others present RIVER Bench, a real-time contact benchmark for video language models evaluating online video comprehension. Nearly all multimodal large language models operate offline, hindering real-time interactivity despite impressive capabilities. Its tasks cover Retrospective Memory, Live-Perception, and Proactive Anticipation, echoing live conversation instead of answering after a full video. Evaluations across model kinds reveal offline models perform well on single question-answering tasks but struggle with real-time processing.
arxiv-2603-04285: McClure and colleagues treat solar vortices as interacting networks, not isolated swirls. Small swirls cover only a small share of the photosphere at any moment, yet their cross scale links are little explored. The team networks the vortices, applies community detection, and assigns peripheral, connector, and hub roles in each group. Role vortices reach higher in the chromosphere and live longer than unclassified ones, on average. Between 32 percent and 58.6 percent of communities show global periodic motion on a helical path, suggesting stronger wave excitation.
arxiv-2603-04385: Jin and colleagues rebuild 3D scenes in linear time with ZipMap. Top transformer methods grow quadratically with image count, while sequential methods lose quality. ZipMap folds a whole collection into one compact scene state in a single pass, using test time training. It handles 700 plus frames in under 10 seconds on one H100, over 20 times faster than VGGT. That state also supports live scene queries and streaming rebuilds.
arxiv-2603-04685: Liu and Song analyze sequential testing. Sequential testing with independent streams seeks signals while controlling familywise, false discovery, and non-discovery rates. First-order procedures are known, with sample ratios to the minimal size tending to one. This work builds a unified second-order theory. Conditions show second-order Bayesian optimality implies frequentist optimality for procedure classes. Several first-order procedures thus prove second-order optimal, with ESS gaps staying bounded. A second-order expansion of the minimal ESS, refined by a boundary-crossing correction, is derived for error metrics.
arxiv-2603-05585: Flower and Schönherr combine MC@NLO parton shower matching with QED summing-up via the electron function, obtaining an NLO-matched QED parton shower that runs alone for any process. The electron-positron case challenges the method through a tameable spike point in the lepton function, unlike QCD PDFs. New methods let a dipole shower operate despite it. Checks cover ties to low-energy settings, NLO-rightness, and summing-up traits. Higgs making at two FCC-ee levels with an on-shell Z boson is first this exact.
arxiv-2603-05685: Boudourides puts forth a class framework joining counting graph structure with topos meaning for knowledge graphs. Knowledge graphs appear as labelled one-way multi-graphs, studied with meeting tables plus line knowledge digraph builds. Its graph gives a free class with maps as linking paths. For context-set meaning, a Grothendieck shape on the graph's free class leads to a topos of sheaves holding local-to-global meaning work. The framework joins graph structure with class joining and sheaf meaning in one unified math model for context-set thinking.
arxiv-2603-06185: Drmota and Salvy study critical recursive composition schemes, where composing two combinatorial classes yields counting generating functions composed in turn. A composition counts as critical when the inner function's value at its radius of convergence equals the outer function's radius, so both singular behaviors shape the result. Such schemes arise often in map enumeration, for instance through block decomposition of rooted planar maps into two connected blocks. The paper makes precise, at the level of singular structure, how statistical properties transfer between two connected maps and all maps.
arxiv-2603-06285: Kostana studies all Boolean algebras below a strongly inaccessible cardinal as a Fraïssé class, together with regular embeddings. He proves the class qualifies as a Fraïssé class, with a limit sharing its completion with the Lévy collapse. He also shows directly that the collapsing algebra of density kappa is not the union of a kappa chain of regular subalgebras of smaller density.
arxiv-2603-06385: Semane and his team use MeerKAT radio dish sharpness to hunt synchrotron emission from WIMP death or decay in the nearby Reticulum II dwarf spheroidal galaxy. Radio work now offers a strong method for finding weakly acting massive particle signs. Dwarf galaxies are good targets due to dark matter rule and minimal normal background glow. Careful data reduction and self tuning yield limits on WIMP properties beating previous radio studies. This shows the promise of MeerKAT and next age telescopes for probing the WIMP parameter space.
arxiv-2603-06485: Vineis and team present PONTE, a human-in-the-loop method for explainable AI stories, fixing notes missing user differences. PONTE models tuning as closed-loop validation and tuning, not prompt craft. It joins a small preference model, a tuned generator grounded in set AI items, and verification modules keeping stylistic alignment, numerical truth, and full completeness. User feedback updates the taste state for quick tuning, and tests in healthcare and finance show the check loop lifts depth and style fit beyond free making.
arxiv-2603-06585: Iwashita and team present an open, sport-free platform turning tracking into spatial measures comparable across pro Ultimate, basketball, and soccer. It answers where usable space lies and when an off-ball run should start. The workflow unifies inputs, and gives timing-aware spatial scores. It allows reuse of the same analysis across sports, shown with it as a focused testbed and transfer tested between hoops and soccer. All the results show a practical route to consistent, matching evaluation across various invasion sports.
arxiv-2603-06685: Ren and team address gauge error in later-sampling guidance for random differential equation models, giving wrong gradients and uneven generation. They propose a backward cleaning step with Monte-Carlo sampling, ABMS, a plug-and-play tweak for guided spread. Theory supports the method, with a dual-focus framework showing cross-condition clash in existing approaches. Tests span handwritten trajectory making, image inverse problems with fill-in and sharpening, and molecular inverse design. Results show ABMS works with higher-order samplers and improves sample quality across scenarios.
arxiv-2603-06785: White and colleagues introduce CEREAL, a low-redshift reference sample of galaxy clusters for evolutionary studies. Comparing distant clusters with local ones depends on trustworthy local samples, yet most X-ray-selected samples skew toward relaxed, cool-core systems. CEREAL draws on Chandra X-ray observations of clusters selected from the Planck Sunyaev-Zel'dovich catalog, with a simple, well-understood selection function and uniform high-resolution follow-up. Its surface brightness results find far more non-cool-core systems than X-ray-selected samples show.
arxiv-2603-07085: Pozzi and colleagues design a low-fuel, low-thrust tour of Saturn's five inner large moons: Rhea, Dione, Tethys, Enceladus, and Mimas. The tour starts at Rhea and ends at Mimas, alternating long observation phases at each moon with low-thrust spiral arcs centered on Saturn. Halo orbits serve as staging points for loops that allow repeated, full surface coverage. The design fits current power and propulsion tech, including radioisotope generators and Hall thrusters.
arxiv-2603-07285: Sharma builds a single-network tool that restores missing high frequencies to narrowband audio. Input clips are resampled to a common rate and run through a neural vocoder backbone, so one model covers many upsampling ratios. A light refiner then blends the kept low band with the new high band across a smooth crossover. Validation shows strong spectral scores at extreme speed on both a graphics card and a plain multi-core processor.
arxiv-2603-07485: Dixit unifies network coordination problems, from traffic signals to communication slots, under a Fourier-sparse structure. He introduces Fourier Network Coordination across eight application domains. With abelian and dihedral groups, classical sparse transforms match quantum methods, capping the edge at polynomial. The genuine separation appears for the symmetric group, where a conditional super-exponential speedup is claimed for class-function costs. A three-regime trichotomy then maps the quantum-classical gap to group structure.
arxiv-2603-07685: Yan and colleagues scale mixture-of-experts training with Megatron Core, tackling coupled memory, communication and compute limits. Sparse firing lets total parameters outgrow per-token compute, so tuning one dimension squeezes another. Joined tricks span redoing, offloads, routers, overlap, grouped matrix math, fusions and CUDA graphs, plus parallel folds and light training. The system hits top throughput on flagship graphics hardware and serves models up to trillions of weights.
arxiv-2603-08185: Park and colleagues present SERQ, a saliency-aware error reconstruction method for low-bit large language model inference. Quantization shrinks models for edge and server use, but accuracy drops sharply under W4A4 settings, and older low-rank fixes need two sequential factors with extra quantization during inference. SERQ instead uses a single low-rank compensation matrix, keeping 4-bit matrix multiplication in linear layers. It jointly cuts quantization errors from activation and weight saliency through static activation flattening, error reconstruction, and offline weight permutation.
arxiv-2603-08385: Huisman and colleagues investigate AI-driven follow-up brain MRI for brain tumor patients. Brain tumors cost 20 years of lost life on average, and standard therapies induce complex shape changes monitored through MRI. Using the public SAILOR dataset of 25 patients, the authors build a 2D rectified flow model conditioned on axial slices of pre-treatment MRI and dose maps. Cross-attention adds temporal and chemotherapy data. The model generates realistic follow-up MRI for any time point, and comparisons of real versus predicted images give a structural similarity score of 0.88.
arxiv-2603-09085: Alvaro Paredes Amorin and colleagues ask when news tone helps foresee aluminum prices, building monthly scores from English and Chinese headlines with a tuned Qwen3 model. They mix those scores with metal indices, exchange rates, inflation, and energy prices in long-short tests on a Shanghai exchange. In wild, high-swing periods the tone-fed model clearly beats plain data-only rivals. The gain also shifts with news source, topic, and event kind.
arxiv-2603-09285: Yuezhi Yang and colleagues recast convex decomposition of 3D shapes as feature field learning, where a continuous field over a shape can later be clustered. Splitting shapes into unions of convex bodies speeds collision checks in physical simulation and more. Their self-supervised aim comes straight from the classical definition of convexity, so no labeled parts are needed. The result is the first learned model of its kind that works feed-forward on open-world shapes, giving higher-quality splits that carry across meshes, CAD models, and Gaussian splats.
arxiv-2603-09385: Yinrui Ren and colleagues present EventVGGT, a framework for event-based monocular depth estimation that treats the event stream as a coherent video rather than lone frames. Dense depth labels are scarce, and past annotation-free methods distilled knowledge from vision foundation models frame by frame, losing temporal consistency. EventVGGT pulls spatio-temporal, multi-view priors from the Visual Geometry Grounded Transformer into the event domain. A tri-level strategy, starting with cross-modal feature mixing, bridges the modality gap.
arxiv-2603-09685: Jacopo Vitale and colleagues automate cardiac risk classification from large-context electronic health records, to replace manual coding in care of older patients. On Dutch narratives from 3,482 patients they benchmark classical machine learning, deep learning built for long records, and generative LLMs used zero-shot. A late fusion adds medication embeddings and body data to the text. The custom Transformer wins on F1 and correlation scores, thanks to hierarchical attention over long text.
arxiv-2603-09785: Maria Kunilovskaya and Christina Pollkläsener release an updated pair of English German corpora from the European Parliament. One part holds spoken speeches with their interpretations, the other written speeches with translations. This version fixes metadata and text errors, refreshes annotations and adds word alignment plus surprisal scores. A sample study checks the rebuilt speech data by predicting filler words in interpreting.
arxiv-2603-10085: Sun and coauthors present KernelClaw, a multi agent framework that optimises GPU kernels with explicit expert knowledge. Language model pipelines for kernel tuning usually rely on hidden heuristics, causing wasteful trial and error. KernelClaw instead coordinates agents whose long term memory holds reusable expert rules, plus short term memory that blocks repeated backtracking. On KernelBench it succeeds on every task and speeds code up several fold over Torch Eager.
arxiv-2603-10185: Abhijit Saha and coauthors establish a set of faint DA white dwarfs across the whole sky as spectrophotometric standards. Pure hydrogen model fluxes for hot DA stars predict observed broadband fluxes from near ultraviolet to near infrared within a few parts per thousand. Fitting reddening alongside the models leaves residuals near half a percent, showing dust effects are handled. The stars extend the CALSPEC scale to brightness levels suited for large telescopes.
arxiv-2603-10385: Avi Bagchi, Michael Tesfaye, and Om Shastri test a conditional diffusion model that predicts asset returns and builds portfolios from large equity data. The model learns the full spread of future returns given firm traits, and portfolios come from the resulting moments. A clear bias-variance trade-off shows up: too few factors underfit and over-diversify, while too many overfit into unstable, concentrated bets that fail out of sample. An ablation over factor count finds a middle range that generalizes best and beats baseline strategies.
arxiv-2603-10485: Reza Ghane, Danil Akhtiamov, and Babak Hassibi study dual space preconditioned gradient descent, a family that includes normalized gradient descent and gradient clipping, in the overparameterized regime.
