For a linear model with convex loss, they prove full-batch iterates converge exponentially fast to a point that fits the data exactly. That limit point depends on step size for general preconditioners, blurring any neat implicit bias story. They give an approximate bias bound there, and exact convergence to the plain descent limit for isotropic preconditioners, in batch and stochastic forms.
arxiv-2603-10585: Ludvig Lindström and co-authors plan paths for an autonomous underwater vehicle that estimates the sound speed profile of a region. That profile shapes how sound travels, so sonar, communication, and navigation depend on knowing it. The vehicle carries a CTD sensor and an acoustic receiver, and an unscented Kalman filter fuses local readings with transmission loss data. A receding-horizon planner picks future positions to cut predicted variance. In Bellhop simulations, the two data kinds proved complementary, and planned paths beat constant motion on uncertainty.
arxiv-2603-10685: Huayu Zheng and co-authors propose A2-Edit, an inpainting framework that replaces any target region with a reference object from only a coarse mask. The user marks where the swap should happen, and the model does the rest. To fight homogenization and thin coverage in older data, they built UniEdit-500K, a large multi-category dataset. A Mixture of Transformer module models categories differently through dynamic expert selection. A mask annealing strategy relaxes mask precision during training. On VITON-HD and AnyInsertion, it beat existing approaches across all metrics.
arxiv-2603-10885: Jonathan Liu and Kia Ghods build a diffusion transformer. It designs short synthetic regulatory DNA sequences that are tailored to a cell type. They swap the usual U-Net backbone for a transformer. They add a small convolutional encoder. Their model trains far faster than the usual design. It also memorizes less of its training data. Fine-tuning then uses a learned activity predictor as reward. That step raises predicted regulatory activity sharply. An independent check suggests the gains reflect real signal. They do not reflect reward gaming.
arxiv-2603-10985: Peter Balogh argues that transformer feed-forward layers route signals in a binary way. They decide whether a token needs nonlinear processing. They decide through on-off neuron activations. The signals being routed are continuous by contrast. In GPT-2 Small, he finds a consensus architecture. It has default-on neurons plus one exception handler. Early layers use single gateways. Late layers crystallize larger consensus quorums. Causal tests confirm the routing is functional. Binarizing the decision loses essentially no information. That loss is compared with continuous activations.
arxiv-2603-11185: Jiahui Chen and David Cory present a step-by-step method for building higher-order effective Hamiltonians, the strong control layer that quantum tools need. It reaches effects that zeroth-order control cannot produce. They identify the minimal subspace of effective Hamiltonians that can be reached at each order. They provide universal cost functions for hitting wanted targets. Worked examples cover robust decoupling sequences and three-body interactions. They also cover links between detuning and interaction terms.
arxiv-2603-11285: George Umbrarescu, Oscar Higgott, and Dan Browne merge quantum error mitigation with error correction by treating a code's distance as the noise knob in a zero-noise extrapolation. Lower physical noise and larger code distance both cut the logical error rate. Extrapolating to infinite distance therefore mimics extrapolating to zero noise, with correction as a subroutine inside mitigation. Tests on the rotated surface code under realistic circuit noise show the method reduces errors across expectation values, even for non-stabilizer input states.
arxiv-2603-11385: Debangan Dey, Rahul Ghosal, Kathleen Merikangas, and Vadim Zipunnikov build a functional principal component method for mobile health data that mixes scales within day curves. The streams yield activity, truncated pain, ordinal mood, and binary life events, all by time of day across domains. Their semiparametric copula method gets latent components through a rank-based bridge, with two covariance estimators: one fully multivariate, one using partial separability. In a mood-disorders family study, it finds shared patterns across mood, anxiety, energy, and activity. These mark subtypes.
arxiv-2603-11785: Jiang and Liu derive a recursion formula for Weil-Petersson volumes of moduli spaces of hyperbolic surfaces with cone points. The surfaces have genus g, m geodesic boundary parts of given lengths, and n cone points of given angles. Using generalized McShane identities, they show the volume is a polynomial in the lengths and the cone angles. The formula extends Mirzakhani's classic recursion to this wider setting.
arxiv-2603-11885: Ackerman and Keszegh sharpen bounds on tangencies among families of plane arcs. Pach conjectured only linearly many tangent pairs when every pair of arcs meets exactly once and no three share a point. The best general bound stood at order n to the 7/4. For the relaxed case, where pairs meet at most once, they improve the bound to order n to the 5/3, and to order n to the 3/2 for Pach's case. They also settle monotone variants and prove a graph theory result along the way.
arxiv-2603-11985: Kozlov studies a quiet source of error in high-accuracy calculations of polyvalent atoms. Such work needs long basis sets, and adding high partial waves improves results only slowly. That slow pace makes the runs costly and leaves truncation error hard to judge. Kozlov uses valence perturbation theory to estimate what the high partial waves add. These estimates help physicists judge how much trust to place in a stated theoretical error.
arxiv-2603-12185: Borse, Xie, Huang, and Jin present ComFree-Sim, a GPU physics engine for contact-rich robot tasks. Mainstream engines solve contact through costly repeated optimization at each step. ComFree-Sim instead computes contact impulses in closed form, with no extra constraints to solve. Each contact pair decouples, so the work maps cleanly onto GPU kernels. A unified 6D model covers tangential, torsional, and rolling friction. Tests show near-linear scaling and higher throughput than MuJoCo Warp in dense scenes, plus real-time control on a multi-fingered hand.
arxiv-2603-12285: Farmer, Kochar, and Lee study short-lived dynamics in Fisher-regularized Wasserstein gradient flows. A cross-dissipation term from the coupling of transport loss and Fisher geometry can change sign mid-flow. The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Fokker-Planck system gives a tractable test case with exact reduced variance dynamics. Below a critical scale the Fisher curvature speeds the fall of free energy. Above it, the same term fights the pullback and creates transient overshoot. The cooperative phase provably lasts a bounded time, and simulations back the analysis.
arxiv-2603-12485: Ibn Ziad and Kozyrakis hunt CUDA bugs at scale with cuFuzz, the first CUDA-oriented fuzzer. GPU programs mix host and device code, breeding memory-safety and concurrency bugs. Prior GPU fuzzing hit false positives, missing device coverage, and clashes between coverage and sanitizers. It fuzzes whole programs, merges NVBit device coverage with host coverage, and splits sanitizers into separate processes. It found 43 unknown bugs in 14 CUDA programs, 19 in commercial libraries. Gains in covered edges and unique inputs beat baselines, above all on closed-source targets.
arxiv-2603-13085: Jose Marie Antonio Miñoza and co-authors show that linearized attention cannot reach the kernel regime at any practical width. Softmax attention resists exact kernel study, so linearized forms serve as the tractable stand-in. Even that stand-in fails to settle to its NTK limit at sane widths. The attention step cubes the condition number of the data Gram matrix, they show. Needed width then grows past any feasible size for image data. They name the effect influence malleability, which also raises data attack risk.
arxiv-2603-13185: Rohith Peddi and co-authors move video scene graphs from frame-bound views to a persistent world frame. Older methods drop objects when they leave sight and work only in 2D. Their ActionGenome4D dataset lifts Action Genome videos into 4D scenes with boxes for hidden objects too. The new task asks for a full world graph at each time step. Three methods test unlike biases: a permanence buffer, masked completion, and temporal attention. Strong vision-language baselines are also set for the task.
arxiv-2603-13285: Angelika Romanou and co-authors present Brittlebench, a way to measure LLM robustness via prompt sensitivity. Clean, static benchmarks can overstate real skill, since user inputs carry typos and varied phrasing. Their framework splits data-driven difficulty from prompt-driven variability in model scores. They apply meaning-preserving changes to a suite of popular benchmarks. Scores fell by as much as 12 percent, and model rankings shifted in most cases after one change. Prompt variation drove up to half of the score variance for some models.
arxiv-2603-13385: Youting Wang and co-authors introduce VisualLeakBench to audit vision-language models for privacy leaks. Alignment tests stress explicit harmful content, yet privacy-critical multimodal cases stay under-tested. Their suite uses 1,000 synthetic adversarial images with 8 PII types, plus 50 real screenshots. Four frontier systems were tested with OCR injection and contextual PII leakage attacks. One model had the lowest OCR attack rate but the highest PII leak rate, with disclosure before any warning. A defensive prompt cut leaks sharply for some models but not for others.
arxiv-2603-13885: Kaczorowski and Perelli extend the theory of standard twists of L-functions to several functions at once. A single twist is already well understood, with poles tied to a spectrum of the function. Here they define a multiple twist for a set of L-functions and describe its meromorphic continuation to the whole space. Much of the one-variable picture carries over, and the pole set links to a joint spectrum. The shape of the singularities, though, differs in real ways.
arxiv-2603-13985: Jiang and co-authors survey supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning as the two main ways to post-train large language models. The study compares their goals, algorithms, and data needs in one frame. It then maps how the two methods interact, from hybrid pipelines to schemes that use each method's strengths. Application studies from 2023 to 2025 show a clear shift toward hybrid post-training. The authors close with lessons on when each method works best and open directions.
arxiv-2603-14085: Clayton rebuilds the historical light curve of the R Coronae Borealis star V854 Cen from 1890 to 2026. The star was found only in the 1980s, though it shines at seventh magnitude at peak. Thick dust clouds kept it faint for nearly a century. Old plates from Harvard College Observatory and other sites fill the early record. They show the star sat far below peak from 1890 to 1980, often near sixteenth or seventeenth magnitude.
arxiv-2603-14385: The CMS Collaboration studies jet peak shapes in two-particle correlations from lead-lead collisions at 5.02 TeV. Data from 2018 at the CMS detector cover pairs split by angle in pseudorapidity and azimuth. Jets appear as a sharp peak at small angles, and its shape probes how jets interact with the medium. Low-momentum peaks widen as collisions overlap more, most strongly along pseudorapidity. Peak asymmetry also grows with mean pseudorapidity. Proton-proton data at the same energy serve as the comparison.
arxiv-2603-14585: Jablonowski studies where the Jones polynomial of knots and links takes the value one. Double-twist knots form the first test family. For each root of unity except minus one, some double-twist knot hits the value one there. The solution set for that family is thus dense in the unit circle. A second family of links pushes the point further. Its solutions spread densely across the whole complex plane. The proof adapts a density trick known from work on Jones polynomial zeros.
arxiv-2603-15085: Samanta and Saha review low-cost edge AI and TinyML systems for precision farming in resource-poor settings. Most farm AI still runs in the cloud, which needs steady connectivity that smallholders lack. Surveying work from 2023 to 2026, they find microcontroller boards like ESP32 dominate local inference. Quantization is the main compression trick, used in about half the studies. Reporting of energy and memory use is patchy, which hurts comparison. They close with a layered, privacy-preserving edge design drawn from the literature.
arxiv-2603-15285: Kruse and co-authors present Matcha, a fast method for aligning three-dimensional volumes by pose. Classic matched filtering searches a huge grid of rotations and shifts. Matcha instead treats rotation as continuous optimization on SO(3), using a bandlimited Wigner-D expansion for fast values, gradients, and Hessians. A coarse low-bandwidth search seeds candidates, which Newton steps refine as bandwidth grows. On synthetic tests it reached sub-degree accuracy much faster than exhaustive search. Inside a RELION-5 workflow, pose refinement ran over ten times faster at equal quality.
arxiv-2603-15685: Li and Huang trim token load in models that read audio and video together. Long mixed token streams make such omnimodal models costly to run. Fixed windows and attention pruning miss the segment shape of sound and image. Their DASH method uses audio as a semantic anchor. Cosine gaps mark segment borders, which then guide video tokens. A three-signal score picks which tokens survive inside each segment. Tests on three benchmarks keep accuracy while cutting more tokens.
arxiv-2603-15785: Talbut, McCormack, and Monod study when sample Fréchet means are unique. Fréchet means average data by minimizing mean squared distance. Most theory covers smooth spaces or bounded curvature spaces. Polytope-normed spaces sit outside that coverage. The team maps the geometry of the mean set there. They characterize the sample size where uniqueness gains positive probability. That threshold sits at most one past the space dimension. Exact thresholds follow for the l-infinity and l-one norms.
arxiv-2603-15885: Sharma and Pursiainen argue that embodied AI in vital systems needs bounded autonomy. Power, water, and transport networks now host AI for monitoring and upkeep. Such systems falter when failures cascade past their training range. The pair outline four oversight modes for operators. Modes map to sectors by task complexity, risk, and harm size. EU AI Act rules, ISO standards, and crisis research inform the map. Sound governance splits judgment between machines and people by design.
arxiv-2603-15985: Golterman and Shamir test where a no-go theorem still binds interacting lattice fermions. Symmetric mass generation seeks chiral lattice theories through interactions alone. Mirror fermions gain mass with no symmetry breaking in the plan. Two-point zeros in such phases may be mere kinematical artifacts. The pair builds a one-particle lattice Hamiltonian for the spectrum. They state when the Nielsen-Ninomiya theorem applies to that Hamiltonian. Where its conditions hold, the light spectrum must stay vector-like. Chiral hopes then fail even at strong coupling.
arxiv-2603-16185: Jimenez, Lalanda, and Vega study how drug-response models can adapt to patient tumors. Models trained on cell lines often fail on real tumors. Their fix splits learning into stages. First, cell and drug features are learned from unlabeled data with autoencoders. Next, the features are matched to drug response in cell lines. A few labeled patient cases then tune the model. Gains were clearest when patient labels were scarce.
arxiv-2603-16385: Tong and co-authors align two generations of nighttime light satellite data. DMSP and VIIRS sensors disagree, which blocks long-term urban studies. Their CUT network turns DMSP images into VIIRS-like ones. Patch-wise contrastive learning keeps content consistent across the swap. Training used the overlap years 2012 and 2013. The network then enhanced DMSP images back to 1992. Generated data matched real VIIRS readings closely, with R-squared above 0.87.
arxiv-2603-16885: Shabanpour and co-authors present DECODE, a diffusion framework that forecasts EEG signals during thinking tasks. Brain signals are hard to forecast because they are noisy and shaped by context. DECODE guides the diffusion process with plain language descriptions of each event. It also uses past signals to keep the forecast coherent over time. On a driving dataset with five behaviors, the authors report a mean error of 0.626 microvolts across 75 steps. Its uncertainty estimates stayed well calibrated. The design also points toward use on new behaviors with no retraining.
arxiv-2603-17385: Wu, Xie, and Li set limits on counterfactual moves in continuous generative models. They define a Counterfactual Event Horizon and prove a Manifold Tearing result. Strong interventions force deterministic flows into finite-time singularities, they show. A trade-off follows between intervention strength and keeping identity intact. Their Geometry-Aware Causal Flow uses a topological radar to steer around tearing, tested on single-cell RNA data.
arxiv-2603-17485: Hashizume works in complex analytic geometry, where spaces are built from complex numbers and maps between them. He proves a generalized canonical bundle formula for generalized lc-trivial fibrations. The bases in his setup need not be compact, and the coefficients need not be rational. He shows two objects, the discriminant b-divisor and the moduli b-divisor, behave well when cut down to open subsets. That match lets local and global steps line up. He also treats when complements stay bounded in this setting.
arxiv-2603-17785: Del Grande, Brune, and Carioni prove sparsity for infinite-width shallow ReLU network training. The training problem is convex over measures on the unit sphere, with total variation control. Duality gives a certificate that is piecewise linear in weight space. Each linear region holds at most one extreme point of that certificate, they show. Minimizers thus use finitely many neurons, with a data-driven cap. Low noise keeps the same sparse pattern stable.
arxiv-2603-17885: DiIorio, Fonseca, Tsung, Winjum, and Thomas add deterministic collisional ionization to the OSIRIS plasma code. Particle-in-cell runs often miss this electron source in laser-plasma work. Their extension swaps random sampling for a fixed-rate algorithm. Ionization rate errors fall by up to a hundredfold, they report. Cost grows only linearly with particles per cell. Benchmarks against other codes check the physics across plasma regimes.
arxiv-2603-17985: Soloviev and Spaliński study late-time Bjorken flow in an expanding superfluid. Their model joins Mueller-Israel-Stewart theory with a complex scalar field that breaks a U(1) symmetry. They find late-time solutions written as a transseries of a new form. That form shows how early data fades as the flow spreads and loses energy. Two end states appear: a plain damped fall or damped waves, set by how fast the condensate relaxes.
arxiv-2603-18085: Chia, Wong, and Pan build a steering framework that reveals harmful patterns in human-AI interaction. Real harmful chats grow over long contact and are hard to simulate in controlled settings. Their Multi-Trait Subspace Steering uses crisis-linked traits to make Dark models with cumulative harmful behavior. Single-turn and multi-turn tests show these models produce harmful outcomes in a steady way. They also propose protective steps to cut such outcomes.
arxiv-2603-18185: Bertoli, Goddard, and Pavliotis find critical coupling thresholds for tilted Kuramoto-Vicsek models with confinement. Without confinement, the uniform density is steady and the first instability is spatially uniform. They compute that threshold for four kernel normalization variants. With confinement, they build the new steady state by perturbation and derive an explicit threshold formula. The threshold grows quadratically with field strength, and tilt enters through the steady-state fix.
arxiv-2603-18485: Song, Wu, and Wang propose augmented reverberant-target training for unsupervised monaural speech dereverberation. No clean reference or spatial cues exist, making the task an ill-posed inverse problem. Stage one reverberates the observed mixture further, then trains a network to recover the original mixture. The resulting network still cuts reverberation in practice. Stage two adds online self-distillation with a mean-teacher method, and tests beat past unsupervised baselines clearly.
arxiv-2603-18785: Blumenstein and co-authors model how foliage shapes wireless channels at 60 and 80 gigahertz. A stochastic method builds a 3D tree model from traits like crown shape, leaf size, and leaf density. Ray tracing on that model gives deterministic channel estimates. A measurement campaign with 2 gigahertz bandwidth checks the approach. Receivers sat on a half-circle around the tree. Path loss and delay spread both depend on angle, the team finds. Material properties join the shape traits as model inputs.
arxiv-2603-18985: Alves and co-authors revisit a known deep model for spotting faults in multi-channel data. Past gains for such models often rest on mixed test rules, which blocks fair checks. They compare the model with a simple linear method on server machine data. Both face the same thresholds and scoring across many runs. Scores vary a lot by machine. The simple method matches the deep model and beats it when a lenient scoring tweak is dropped. They question the worth of added complexity.
arxiv-2603-19085: Sabatucci and Sedrakian study hybrid stars whose cores may melt into quark matter when neutrinos are trapped. Star mergers and newborn neutron stars give hot, lepton-rich settings for such a shift. Their hadronic part uses a covariant density model. Their quark part uses a Nambu-Jona-Lasinio model with pairing and extra terms. A mixed phase joins the two while baryon and lepton counts hold. Trapped neutrinos shift the melt point to higher densities. They compute star shapes and mass-radius links for hot and cold cases.
arxiv-2603-19185: Shafieinejad and co-authors report on MIDST, a challenge that tested the privacy of synthetic tables made by diffusion models. Such data should keep the stats of real records while hiding who was in them. Teams built black-box and white-box membership attacks for single tables and linked multi-table cases. The attacks try to tell if a known record helped train the model. The event gave a shared way to grade privacy claims. Its code and tasks are public on GitHub.
arxiv-2603-19385: Wu and co-authors model heat from subhalos dragging through the gas of early dark matter halos. They take the subhalo mass spread from the TNG50 simulation. Drag turns gravity energy into heat across halo sizes and cosmic times. In the early universe, this heat can rival molecular hydrogen cooling in small halos. That raises the gas share needed for the first stars by up to ten times. With Lyman-Werner light, it also favors direct-collapse black hole seeds. Heat rates vary widely with subhalo counts.
arxiv-2603-19485: Hainzl gives a shorter proof of a central limit theorem for pattern counts in random planar maps. An earlier proof reduced the count to a face count problem. Hainzl skips that step and works from a functional equation with one catalytic variable. Bivariate coefficient asymptotics do the heavy lifting. The result also extends to patterns with any boundary shape. New classes of maps are covered as well.
arxiv-2603-19585: Zhou and co-authors present SaFRO, a fusion framework that ranks short videos by user satisfaction, not just clicks. Search fusion blends many prediction signals into one score. Optimising for instant engagement can miss long-term satisfaction. SaFRO first builds a reward model from query-level behaviour proxies. A dual-relative policy optimisation step then learns the fusion policy by group comparisons. A task-relation module adapts weights to context. On Kuaishou search, offline tests and large A/B tests beat prior baselines on ranking and retention.
arxiv-2603-19685: Wang and co-authors present a subgoal-driven framework that improves long-horizon language model agents. Agents on web and app tasks often lose track as new information arrives. Their online planner uses strong proprietary models to split goals into subgoals. A second piece, MiRA, trains agents with dense milestone-based rewards. On WebArena-Lite, the planner lifts Gemini success by about ten points. MiRA raises an open Gemma model from about 6 percent to 43 percent success. That beats several proprietary systems and the prior open-model best.
arxiv-2603-19785: Liu, Long, and He study genuine tripartite nonlocality in a three-qubit W state near a dilaton black hole. Most past work in this setting used GHZ-like states, not W states. The authors use numerical methods to track two quantities. One is genuine tripartite nonlocality, the other genuine tripartite entanglement. They vary both decoherence and the dilaton parameter. Nonlocality in the reachable region shows sudden death under strong decoherence. Entanglement instead holds steady, then decays at large dilaton values. Entanglement also appears in the region beyond the horizon.
arxiv-2603-19985: Jacqmin and Liénardy break four arbitrated quantum signature schemes from recent literature. Such schemes use an arbitrator to vouch for a message's origin. They also aim to stop senders and receivers from denying their roles. The authors study schemes based on chained CNOT encryption, GHZ states, and controlled teleportation, among others. For each scheme they find concrete attacks. Senders can repudiate messages or falsely claim reception in several cases. Dishonest receivers can also forge signatures in some of the schemes.
arxiv-2603-20285: Bansal and Gangwani introduce AgentComm-Bench, a test suite for cooperative embodied AI under bad network conditions. Most such systems are judged with perfect links, which real robots never have. Their suite stresses six flaws, from latency and packet loss to stale memory. It covers three task families and five communication strategies. Stale memory and bandwidth collapse cut navigation scores by over 96%. Their redundant coding method more than doubled navigation scores under heavy packet loss.
arxiv-2603-20485: Zaar and co-authors derive a simple test for when a disrupted tokamak makes large runaway electron currents. Such currents can hit the wall and cause grave damage in ITER or SPARC. In deuterium-tritium plasmas, seed runaways can come from tritium beta decay. Compton scattering can add more seeds. Their criterion counts both sources in the avalanche gain factor. It also counts partial screening by injected noble gases. Fluid simulations with the DREAM code support the model. The aim is a fast map of safe operation zones.
arxiv-2603-20585: Sethuraman and Fekri propose RECLAIM, a method to learn causal graphs with cycles and noisy measures. Most tools assume no cycles and clean access to system variables. Real fields like genomics break both rules. RECLAIM fits the graph by maximum likelihood with an EM loop. Residual normalizing flows keep the math workable. They prove consistency for two noise setups. Tests on synthetic data and protein signaling data support the method.
arxiv-2603-20985: Sadanandan and Behzadan warn that steady answers can hide false reliability in medical vision-language models. A model can answer the same way across reworded prompts by leaning on text patterns, not the image. They sort samples into four groups by consistency and image reliance: Ideal, Fragile, Dangerous, and Worst. On two chest X-ray data sets, fine tuning cut answer flips but pushed most samples into the Dangerous group. Those samples still scored high accuracy, so standard screening missed them.
arxiv-2603-21085: Li and co-authors make latent diffusion models more robust to sampling noise. Latent diffusion generates images in a compact latent space, which is efficient and high quality. They find that common tokenizers make the latent space too compact, so small sampling perturbations degrade the output. Their Variance Expansion loss fights this variance collapse while reconstruction fidelity stays strong. Tests across several latent diffusion designs show steady gains in generation quality.
arxiv-2603-21485: Tanaka and co-authors tackle off-policy evaluation for ranking systems, where a new ranking policy must be judged from logged data only. Standard estimators need the logging policy to be random enough, and they fail badly when logging is fully deterministic. Their Click-based Inverse Propensity Score instead leans on the randomness in user clicks as the importance weight. Theory covers the bias and variance of the new estimators. In synthetic and real-world tests, bias dropped sharply versus strong baselines under deterministic logging.
arxiv-2603-21685: Ishihara reviews Cherenkov neutrino telescopes, huge detectors that watch for flashes from high-energy neutrinos. These tools open a view of cosmic accelerators and extreme places that other messengers cannot reach. The review covers why finding astrophysical neutrinos matters. It also lays out how telescope designs change with the medium and site used. A further theme is how these observatories differ from particle physics neutrino experiments, though both rest on Cherenkov light. Their role in multimessenger astronomy, above all for tracing cosmic ray origins, closes the survey.
arxiv-2603-22785: Gabriel and co-authors measure bed and chair fall rates with continuous AI monitoring. Rates are scaled by exposure hours, not occupied bed-days. The study covers 3,980 monitoring units from August 2024 to December 2025. Weighted rates come to 17.8 falls per 1,000 chair hours and 4.3 per 1,000 bed hours. The adjusted chair-versus-bed rate ratio is 2.35, with wide uncertainty. Most direct chair falls in a side cohort involved footrest faults. The authors call the findings early and suggest testing safer chair setups.
arxiv-2603-22885: Chen and co-authors present a cascading system for general aviation health management. Their Long-Micro Scale Diagnostician splits the work in two. A global stage scans full sequences for anomalies. A micro stage then classifies faults with narrow receptive fields. A distillation module adds explanations that trace back to physics. Tests use a public flight database with 36 classes. Safety metrics improve by four to eight percent over end-to-end baselines. Training also runs far faster.
arxiv-2603-23185: Ziggaf, Torlo, and Ricchiuto develop high-order finite element methods that preserve steady states. The target is multidimensional nonlinear hyperbolic balance laws on Cartesian grids. Their methods aim to capture all steady states at accuracy above the scheme's nominal order. A local preprocessing step recasts the fluxes into a Raviart-Thomas type space. Both Galerkin and SUPG forms fit this frame. Tests use the compressible Euler equations with gravity. A source term rewrite preserves hydrostatic balance to machine precision. Benchmarks beat standard methods on robustness and accuracy.
arxiv-2603-23285: Andriyash and Thaury review numerical methods for tracking shaped laser pulses through plasma. The methods live in Axiprop, an open-source toolkit used to design laser plasma acceleration studies. Two worked examples show the tools in action. One builds an optical plasma waveguide and tracks where the pulse energy lands. The other studies a phase-locked flying-focus setup and its wakefield shape. Both cases show how pulse travel details set the traits of the accelerated electron bunches. The toolkit now serves design work at high-power laser sites.
arxiv-2603-23385: Ortega and three co-authors study how envy spreads in random matching markets. They focus on the Deferred Acceptance algorithm that assigns proposing agents. They count two groups: agents nobody envies, and agents who envy nobody. An exact formula covers the first group in finite markets, via the coupon collector problem. Bounds cover the second group as markets grow. Under Random Serial Dictatorship, a fixed share of agents get their top choice. Yet both rules leave the same expected count of unenvied agents, the harmonic number H n.
arxiv-2603-23685: Catovic argues that cheap AI building tools will crowd digital markets, not enrich most builders. His Builder Saturation model pairs elastic output with a fixed pool of human attention. With near-zero costs and open entry, more makers split the same gaze. Average pay per maker falls even as total output climbs. Adding quality spread and rich-get-richer dynamics bends outcomes toward a few winners. The math points to winner-take-most markets, not broad success for all.
arxiv-2603-24285: Sapozhnikova and co-authors grow perovskite microwire lasers from colloidal nanocrystals. Their route uses a hot-injection synthesis in diphenyl ether. The solvent binds lead strongly and lets them cut the usual ligand excess, which blocks regrowth. Early crystals release material slowly, then join into nanowires and grow into laser microwires. Ion exchange with YCl3 tunes emission across 485 to 540 nanometers. They wire one laser to a waveguide and a photodetector, making a device with a nonlinear response fit for on-chip computing.
arxiv-2603-24385: Xu and co-authors present ArrayDPS-Refine, a training-free method that cleans up the output of multi-channel speech enhancement models. Regression-trained models can distort speech, above all in hard noise. Their method first estimates the noise spatial covariance from the enhanced speech. It then uses a clean speech diffusion prior for posterior sampling, guided by that covariance. The method works with any array layout and needs no retraining. Tests show steady gains for both waveform and STFT domain models.
arxiv-2603-24485: Metchev and co-authors outline POET, a planned Canadian micro-satellite mission to study exoplanet transits. POET is a top priority in Canada's astronomy long-range plan, with launch possible in late 2029. It carries a 20 centimetre telescope and observes in three bands at once, from near-UV to short-wave IR. That coverage helps split star spot effects from the spectra of exoplanet air. The design builds on Canada's earlier MOST and NEOSSat missions, and its IR band suits work on ultracool dwarf stars.
arxiv-2603-24585: Niraula and co-authors analyse Hubble spectra of the active star HAT-P-11 to find calm windows for exoplanet transmission spectroscopy. The star hosts an eccentric, misaligned sub-Neptune and has a spotted surface that can distort transit spectra. Using out-of-transit spectra across several instruments and bandpasses, they fit the surface with two-component photosphere models. The infrared data favour a cool component near 3,400 kelvin covering 26 to 33 percent of the disk. Optical fits fail, which they attribute to limits of current stellar atmosphere models at that precision.
arxiv-2603-24685: Koutroulis proposes a UV-complete, stable version of Quintom dark energy. Quintom models cross the cosmological-constant boundary, but lack a UV completion. The proposal embeds Quintom in a five-dimensional anisotropic orbifold lattice gauge-Higgs unification model. A bulk gauge field projects onto the boundary as the dark energy sector, while the Standard Model and dark matter stay in four dimensions. Late-time higher-derivative terms yield physical and phantom degrees of freedom. A massive gauge ghost gives an excellent fit to DESI data with negligible fine-tuning.
arxiv-2603-24785: Kumar and Kim present a cost-aware design framework for cyber-physical systems in precision agriculture. High system cost and weak design methods slow adoption on farms. Their framework explores multimodal drone-rover platforms under budget, energy, sensing, payload, computation, and communication limits. Integer linear programming with SAT-based verification trades off cost, coverage, and payload while keeping designs valid. Case studies on small and large farms reach full coverage within budget. The method also maximises payload efficiency and beats prior design exploration approaches, the authors report.
arxiv-2603-25085: Miao and co-authors test flight-ready detector ladders for the AMS-02 upgrade on the Space Station. The new top layer chains silicon strips into long ladders, tripling the cosmic ray catch. The team ran the ladders through a 350 GeV mixed hadron beam at CERN. They compared ladders built from 8 to 12 sensors. Position sharpness at straight incidence ran from 9.5 to 11.4 microns. They also checked response at the head and tail of each ladder. Angled hits were tested as well, since real cosmic rays arrive at many tilts.
arxiv-2603-25185: Lee and co-authors verify that the East Asia VLBI Network can measure light polarization well. The network of radio dishes recently gained dual-polarization modes at 22 and 43 gigahertz. They observed four bright radio sources, including M87, and checked the results against near-in-time VLBA images. Most stations show steady leakage of five to ten percent over months. Some phase wobbles trace to field-rotator offsets, and a math fix restores stability. Polarization shapes and angles match the VLBA within error, which certifies the network for such studies.
arxiv-2603-25285: Lacava asks how trade policy doubt moves the link between stocks and Treasury bills. That link guides how investors balance risk, and trade shocks may bend it. He stretches the Dynamic Conditional Correlation model with outside drivers. One version uses a trade policy uncertainty index. One adds a presidential-cycle marker, and one mixes both. Daily data cover big US stock indices and the three-month bill. Trade doubt shifts the correlation a lot, and more so under some political settings. Forecasts gain real economic value too.
arxiv-2603-25385: An, Suh, and Kim trim the cost of fixing errors in squeezed language models. Low-bit quantization saves memory but hurts accuracy, and past patches repair every layer at a price. GlowQ shares one low-rank factor across each group of layers that share an input. It restores only the groups that repay the cost most. A selective variant narrows that further. First-token delay drops and speed rises against strong rivals. The selective form cuts delay by near a quarter while accuracy barely moves.
arxiv-2603-25485: Collins and co-authors show that webs of quantum reference frames can scramble the bookkeeping of conserved quantities. One frame can mint several others, and those can ready systems that later meet. Following a conserved charge through such a web turns subtle fast. Odd features emerge that clash with naive counting. The team also offers a fresh way to analyze quantum frames. They expect it to help future debates about what frames really are.
arxiv-2603-25685: Bardhan and co-authors improve robot world models so their video rollouts stay stable for longer. Such models predict future frames from a robot's action sequence. When each clip feeds the next, errors pile up and quality drops fast. Their fix trains the model on its own rollouts with reinforcement learning. The training compares several candidate futures from one state and rewards the sharper ones. Rewards blend perceptual metrics from multiple camera views. On the DROID dataset, the authors report the best rollout scores to date.
arxiv-2603-26185: Hamanaka reviews the multifractal side of the non-Hermitian skin effect. The skin effect piles states at a system's edge under nonreciprocal loss. In many-body systems, this pile-up spreads through Hilbert space with a fractal pattern. That differs from the plain occupation seen for single particles on lattices. The many-body effect can also live alongside random-matrix spectral statistics. This sets it apart from many-body localization, which pairs fractality with broken ergodicity. A solvable model on a Cayley tree yields the fractal dimensions in closed form.
arxiv-2603-26285: Pathak, Arani, Pechenizkiy, and Zonooz present PhysVid, a way to make generated videos obey basic physics. Video models often look sharp yet break simple physical rules. PhysVid adds local notes on states, contacts, and limits for short chunks of frames, fused with the main prompt. At run time, negative prompts name local law breaches to steer away from them. On VideoPhy, commonsense physics scores rise by about 33% over base models.
arxiv-2603-26385: Chen and co-authors present RAR, a framework that restores images by looping through repair and review. Restoration must cope with mixed damage from weather, blur, and low light, often of unknown type. RAR joins quality assessment and restoration in one model that works in the latent domain. Each pass spots the damage, repairs it, and checks the result, then repeats if needed. Tests show steady gains on single, unknown, and mixed damage, with less delay than split pipelines.
arxiv-2603-26485: Lan and co-authors show that one quarter-wave plate can reshape light inside a simple confocal microscope. Spin-orbit effects link the polarisation and spatial shape of light, but their role in paraxial confocal setups was unclear. Placed between polarisers, the plate boosts the polarisation extinction ratio by over a hundredfold. It also turns a Gaussian beam into a two-lobe Hermite-Gaussian-like profile. Turning the plate steers the pattern, and an extended Jones matrix model with complex terms matches the measurements.
arxiv-2603-26585: Agarwal, Katz, and Sharir design a dynamic data structure for nearest-neighbour search under general metrics in three dimensions. The stored shapes are scaled copies of one fixed convex body that defines the metric. Their structure answers intersection and nearest-neighbour queries fast, and lists every shape a query shape touches. It also supports insertions and deletions at low amortised cost. A second set of results uses the structure on the intersection graph of the stored shapes, widening where the method applies.
arxiv-2603-26885: Djoumessi and Berens introduce TTE-CAM, a test-time way to make black-box image networks explain themselves. Medical image networks perform well but stay opaque, which blocks clinical trust. TTE-CAM swaps the network's classification head for a convolution-based one. The new head starts from the original weights, so accuracy is preserved. The converted model then produces its own class activation maps. Its explanations rival post-hoc methods in both look and measured quality. The code is public for reuse.
arxiv-2603-26985: Joseph and Schaich test holography with lattice simulations of three-dimensional supersymmetric Yang-Mills theory. Their lattice keeps part of the supersymmetry exact at finite spacing. They study the spatial deconfinement transition with eight colors and several lattice shapes. Holography maps that transition to one between localized and uniform black branes. The measured transition temperatures scale with aspect ratio cubed. That matches the holographic low-temperature, large-N prediction. The match adds evidence for the gauge-gravity correspondence in this setting.
arxiv-2603-27185: Tan and co-authors present MotionRFT, a unified reinforcement fine-tuning framework for text-to-motion generation. Supervised training alone misses high-level goals like realism and human preference. Earlier post-training targeted one motion format or one quality aspect at a time. Their MotionReward model maps varied motion formats into one text-anchored semantic space. That enables rewards across several quality dimensions at once. EasyTune then updates step by step instead of over full denoising paths. The framework cut memory sharply while improving FID and text alignment scores.
arxiv-2603-27285: Hardy and co-authors show how surfactant orientation under shear changes surface tension and droplet shape. Surfactant molecules are elongated, so flow can rotate them against thermal diffusion. A phase-field model tracks both concentration and local average orientation. Perturbation theory gives an effective surface tension that depends on shear rate. Hybrid simulations then deform a surfactant-covered droplet in imposed shear. Weak flow matches modified classical droplet theories well. Strong flow scrambles the polarization field across the surface. The droplet then deforms almost like a surfactant-free one.
arxiv-2603-27385: Treerath and Pittorino ask how to pick the best samples to label for table data. Their method works with TabPFN, a model that learns from examples in context. No retraining is needed. They test four rules for choosing samples. The rules use doubt, spread, a mix of both, and a fast two-stage screen. Across twenty test sets, their method beats boosted-tree baselines. Gains are strongest at the cold start, with at most one hundred labels.
arxiv-2603-27485: Bagchi asks why some collapsed polymers form helices while most do not. Plain collapse tends to yield globules, rings, or rods. Two simple routes can still favor a helix. One route uses tube-like packing with broad attractions. Left and right helices then tie in energy. Handedness emerges on its own. The second route uses sticker bonds at a fixed spacing. That spacing locks twist and pitch in step. Both routes need no special chemistry.
arxiv-2603-27785: Kestin and Soares survey views on AI extinction risk around a Harvard event. The event featured the book If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies. Matched surveys ran before and after the session. Eighty-nine attendees completed both rounds. The post-event median risk estimate hit 70 percent. Ninety-six percent called mitigation a global priority. Prior views were already high at 50 percent and 93 percent. Newer attendees shifted upward the most.
arxiv-2603-27885: Loftus links weight spectra to label noise in neural networks. The tail index of bottleneck eigenvalues predicts test accuracy. Under label noise sweeps, fit reaches R squared of 0.984. Classic metrics lag far behind that mark. Results hold on MLP, CNN, and ResNet-18 models. MNIST and CIFAR-10 both show the pattern. Under tuning changes at fixed data quality, prediction fades. The index thus serves as a data quality diagnostic.
arxiv-2603-28085: Bluhm, Koßmann, and Schwonnek show how to ground device-independent quantum key distribution in local self-tests. The device-independent model avoids detailed device assumptions but leans on trust in the lab setup. Their approach has each party run routed Bell tests on its own gear, turning the protocol into a device-dependent one with proof. They build a strict math framework for that transfer. A routed BB84 protocol serves as the worked example.
arxiv-2603-28285: Penitente, Foryś, and Gürbüz analyze an epidemic model that spreads both by contact and through dirty surfaces. Their SVEIR model adds vaccination, births and deaths, and a saturating dose response for the surface route. They derive threshold conditions based on a control reproduction number. Below the threshold, the disease-free state is globally stable, with a sharp classic limit when vaccination is absent. Above it, the infection persists and an endemic state exists.
arxiv-2603-28485: Alkan and five co-authors widen two classic recipes for bent Boolean functions, the Maiorana-McFarland and partial spread classes. Bent functions matter in cryptography for their extreme nonlinearity. The team builds generalized versions that provably sit outside both completed classes. They also show that generalized partial spread functions of low degree rarely split into bent or semibent parts. A new concatenation construction rounds out the work, which leans on curve theory and second derivatives.
arxiv-2603-28585: Ignace reviews how linear polarization can reveal structured winds around massive stars. Polarization adds a diagnostic tool for dense stellar settings and for stars that are not spherical. After a short overview for hot massive stars, Ignace turns to Wolf-Rayet winds. Examples cover clumpy wind flow, co-rotating interaction regions, and colliding wind interactions. Each case shows how polarized light traces shape and structure that plain light may hide. Ignace also notes the promise of UV spectropolarimetry with the Polstar mission concept for future massive star studies.
arxiv-2603-28685: Dimitrova presents the PADME experiment's search for the dark photon at Frascati. The dark photon is a hypothetical boson that could link visible matter to a hidden sector. PADME fires positrons at a fixed target and looks for annihilation events. If a visible photon and a dark photon are produced together, the calorimeter records the visible one. The dark photon mass can then be rebuilt from the beam energy by the missing mass method. Dimitrova describes the analysis techniques and background rejection in use.
arxiv-2603-28885: Maan and co-authors report first results from SCOPE, a survey that seeks pulsars in compact radio sources. Image based searches have found pulsars before, including the first millisecond pulsar. SCOPE uses radio images and time domain data to seek pulsations and classify sources. The first stage followed 31 compact, steep spectrum sources with the GMRT and GBT telescopes. They found two millisecond pulsars. One is a 1.6 millisecond pulsar, and the other is the match of a gamma ray pulsar once thought radio quiet. Both have very steep radio spectra.
arxiv-2603-28985: Hassanin benchmarks Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks for cyber threat detection in IoT networks. These networks replace linear weights with spline based univariate functions that learn activation patterns. A KAN-LSTM model joins spatial and temporal encoding. Tests used UNSW-NB15, NSL-KDD, and CICIDS2017, plus a new combined dataset with diverse traffic patterns. KAN models beat traditional multilayer perceptrons with far fewer learnable parameters, Hassanin reports. The combined KAN-LSTM model performed best of all. The work points to adaptive defensive models for network security as a next direction.
arxiv-2603-29085: Li and co-authors present a retrieval system for multi-hop questions. Such questions need facts combined from several documents. Their method first searches broadly to build a wide pool of evidence. It then digs deeper in rounds, checking whether the evidence is enough. This split keeps the search from locking onto a weak early path. On four benchmarks, the authors report up to 23.5 percent higher accuracy than a leading rival method.
arxiv-2603-29385: Jorjani and co-authors model signal loss for terahertz aerial links in 3D. Aerial radios can sit at mixed heights and spots. Older models cover only flat or vertical layouts. Their model takes any 3D layout of the two radios. It also counts how the air absorbs each frequency band. A regression in two dimensions shapes the model. They check it against data from an atmospheric tool. Link types range from drone pairs to high-altitude craft.
arxiv-2603-29885: Birindelli, Galise, and Leoni study a fully nonlinear logistic equation with a sanctuary term. The equation sits in a bounded domain with Dirichlet boundary values. A growth term with power p above one shapes the solutions. A nonnegative weight function modulates that growth. They pin down, in terms of the parameter mu, when a positive solution exists. They also settle when it is unique or absent. They trace solution behavior as mu nears the range edges.
arxiv-2604-00185: Hubard and Schulte study two-orbit polytopes, abstract polytopes whose symmetry groups split flags into exactly two orbits. Such shapes fall into classes numbering one less than a power of two, set by their local flag configuration. The authors build a structural theory for any rank, pinning down face- and section-transitivity and describing symmetry groups through distinguished generating sets and face stabilizer subgroups. Their results characterize the shape's partial order through its symmetry group, extending the group-theoretic framework of regular and chiral polytopes.
arxiv-2604-00385: Khamesian and colleagues propose GUIDE, a reinforcement-learning aid for type 1 diabetes care that complements automated insulin pumps. Pumps have improved blood-sugar control, but many patients still miss clinical targets, and current learning systems focus on insulin alone. GUIDE instead recommends behaviour: what action to take, how large, and when, covering extra insulin doses and carbohydrate intake. A glucose predictor fitted to each patient, trained on real monitoring data, powers offline and online learning.
arxiv-2604-00685: Xia, Xie, and Zhang build one framework that joins differential equations with probability theory. It bounds slopes and curvatures of Markov semigroups from random differential equations with rough, unbounded coefficients. Under mild local rules, they get sharp short-time smoothing bounds and long-time decay bounds with no need for global smoothness, boundedness, or uniform ellipticity. The same framework also solves Poisson equations on the whole space and bounds slopes for equations with spread-out drifts.
arxiv-2604-00785: Vooturi and colleagues pretrain language models from scratch on Aurora, an exascale machine with 127,488 Intel Ponte Vecchio GPU tiles. They use their Optimus training library for the work. They first train 1-billion dense and 7-billion mixture-of-experts models on 3072 tiles for 4 trillion tokens, then scale to 220-billion-parameter models. On the largest model, scaling efficiency reaches around 90 percent at 12288 tiles, aided by custom kernels and a sharded optimizer.
arxiv-2604-00885: Zhong, Wold, and Windmann show the common assumption behind Java static-analysis comparisons is wrong at its core. Studying Soot, SootUp, WALA, and Doop with precision rankings, they find precision orders break within frameworks over lambdas, reflection, and native modeling, while configuration choices interact together with algorithms. Cross-framework comparisons expose clashing ideas of what a true call graph is, challenging usual ways of judging tools.
arxiv-2604-00985: Yi and team study T2-only prostate cancer finding, using diffusion-weighted images in training only, then finding cancers from T2-weighted images alone. They treat those images as a latent channel. A flow-matching maker estimates the hidden image in E-steps, while a cancer finder raises the mean score in M-steps. The T2-only methods match or beat multi-sequence standards, lifting patient-level F1 by 14.4 percent over the T2-plus-diffusion standard, in tests on 4,133 patients with tissue-checked labels.
arxiv-2604-01185:
Lea Delance and five co-authors study how charged chain molecules stick to a solid in a liquid. Their 2026 paper links that sticking to a flaw in how drops pull back. Drop control matters for inkjet printing, health care tools, and food work.

Drops that spring and stretch slide more slowly on tilted water-shedding surfaces. They also stretch out more than plain drops do as they slide. Why this happens at the small scale is still not well known. The team works at the surface where a drop meets the solid. What they find there should help explain the slow, stretched slide. The work fits fields that must place small drops with care.
arxiv-2604-01485: Krishna and colleagues investigate how gamma-ray bursts would be localized by the LVK network in run O5. They ask whether counterparts could be found from localizations alone, without gamma-ray instruments. They find events localized to sky regions, often a few to tens of square degrees. Counterparts are detectable by one telescope during O5. Detectability depends on depth: counterparts are fainter than 22 mag within a day. Facilities reaching at least 23 mag play a role. Depth and finding the counterpart among other transients form the challenge.
arxiv-2604-01585: Gao, Wang and Zou work out wavefront sets for genuine representations of two cover families of p-adic general linear groups. A wavefront set tracks the sharpest local behavior of a representation. They build on Brylinski-Deligne covers and Bernstein-Zelevinsky derivatives, and recall the classification of the irreducible genuine spectrum for Kazhdan-Patterson and Savin covers. For both families they express the sets through repeated degrees of the highest derivatives. For Kazhdan-Patterson covers they restate the result through the local Langlands correspondence and covering Barbasch-Vogan duality.
arxiv-2604-02085: Goychuk builds one nonlinear mean field theory for active polymers pushed by uneven kicks and linked flows. He uses a Gaussian closure on pair correlations to get a self consistent diffusion equation for chain shapes. In the continuum limit the theory recovers coiled, globular and self avoiding scalings. For chromatin like chains it predicts crossovers between coiled, swollen and hyper compacted fractal states.
arxiv-2604-02285: Kontogiannis, Panageas and Pollatos settle how hard it is to find second-order stationary points, the stable resting points sought in non-convex optimization, when constraints apply. They prove that computing an approximate such point under the tractable definition is PLS-complete, even inside the two-dimensional unit square. The result bars any efficient deterministic iterative method with a continuous update rule, unless PLS sits inside PPAD.
arxiv-2604-02485: Jhaveri and three colleagues test whether large language models show confirmation bias, the habit of seeking proof for a guess instead of trying to disprove it. In a number-triple guessing game borrowed from human psychology, eleven models often proposed triples that confirmed their hypothesis, slowing discovery of the hidden rule. Prompts urging counterexamples cut the bias and lifted rule discovery from 42 to 56 percent on average.
arxiv-2604-02685: Levinson builds a method to hunt for belief geometries inside transformer inner states. These are simplex-shaped structures that encode beliefs about hidden states. He mixes sparse autoencoders, subspace clustering, and simplex fitting, and checks the method on a hidden Markov model with known geometry. On Gemma-2-9B it finds 13 priority clusters with candidate simplex geometry. The hunt starts from a known case, then moves to a real model. He warns that simplex-shaped latents need not carry predictive signal beyond single features.
arxiv-2604-02785: Jian and six colleagues present CANDLE, a method for restoring true object colors under multi-colored ambient lighting. Severe color shifts, highlight saturation, and material-dependent reflectance defeat geometric and low-level priors. The team observes that DINOv3 self-supervised features agree across colored-light inputs and ambient-lit truth, and uses them as illumination-robust semantic priors, gaining 1.22 decibels in PSNR on CL3AN.
arxiv-2604-03285: Lara-Martínez and colleagues measure national peace levels from the style and structure of news text, rather than from economic indicators or conflict counts alone. Using articles from 20 countries, they compare word embeddings and a one-dimensional convolutional network against a nearest-neighbor baseline. The network wins on classification and preserves peace rankings, tracking the Positive Peace Index even for unseen countries.
arxiv-2604-03385: Nagarajan and colleagues use deep Keck adaptive-optics imaging to test whether the millisecond pulsar PSR J1928+1815 has a helium star companion. No source appears at the pulsar position down to a faint detection limit, ruling out any plausible helium star under standard models. A massive white dwarf remains consistent with the non-detection, with eclipse explanations ranging from a white-dwarf wind to ablated material.
arxiv-2604-03985: Momoka Iida and colleagues built an autoencoder method to estimate parameters of superposed damped sinusoidal signals. Such signals decay fast, stack several components, and carry noise, making standard estimation hard. Their latent-space method recovers frequency, phase, decay time, and amplitude per component, even for weak or nearly opposite-phase parts. Tests under Gaussian and uniform training showed high accuracy and fair robustness when training data grew less informative.
arxiv-2604-04185: Yildirim, Coley and López ask whether a black hole can survive a cosmic bounce. A bounce is the turnaround from contraction to expansion in a non-singular universe. They embed the hole in a bouncing, positively curved cosmological model built on teleparallel new general relativity. Near its minimum, the bounce closely mirrors the general-relativity case, except that the curvature term is re-normalized. At higher orders the local horizon's evolution turns on the perturbation signs, breaking symmetry across the bounce.
arxiv-2604-04485: Scagnetto evaluates an ArcFace-trained 1D Inception-v1 model for ECG biometrics under large galleries, domain shift and multi-year gaps. The model trains on 164,440 12-lead ECGs from 53,079 patients. It is tested on MIMIC-IV-ECG and HEEDB cohorts. Under general comparability it reaches Rank@1 near 0.95 on ASUGI-DB, lower on MIMIC-GC and HEEDB-GC. In a temporal stress test at constant gallery size, Rank@1 falls from 1 to 5 years. ECG identity stays measurable at large scale, but quality hinges on domain shift, drift, gallery size and score processing.
arxiv-2604-04585: Priya and three colleagues test a non-holomorphic modular symmetry framework giving Yukawa couplings negative and zero modular weight as functions of a modulus driving CP asymmetry during leptogenesis. The team pins the modulus to symmetry fixed points rather than its domain, freezing the Yukawa couplings, and adopts a type III seesaw mechanism. The model faces neutrino oscillation data in a chi-squared analysis with NuFIT. Nearby regions are checked by shifts of fixed points. Certain fixed points and nearby regions yield viable neutrino phenomenology and baryon asymmetry.
arxiv-2604-04785: Feng studies bootstrap inference for the kth largest coordinate of a normalized sum of high-dimensional random vectors. Standard theory for maxima does not carry over, since the key event is not a rectangle and its local shape follows exceedance counts. He builds an approach from factorial moments and weighted inclusion-exclusion, reducing the problem to rare-orthant probabilities. That reduction lets Edgeworth and Cornish-Fisher expansions transfer to order statistics, and a third-moment matching wild bootstrap reaches coverage error of order one over n.
arxiv-2604-04885: Bose, Sarkar, and Majumdar study metallic nanohybrids, where joins inside the material create unusually strong electron-phonon effects. That strength surprises, since coupling in the bulk parts is weak. Modeling a system where strong coupling lives only at interfaces inside a weakly coupled metal, they compute electronic and lattice spectra. They use a real-space Holstein model plus Langevin dynamics. More interfacial sites broaden electronic features through scattering while leaving band dispersion largely intact, and they soften and damp the phonon spectrum.
arxiv-2604-05085: Menon, Hu, and Krawczynski report a signature for testing Einstein's gravity close to rapidly spinning black holes. Penrose processes involve particles decaying or interacting close to a spinning black hole. Some enter negative energy trajectories and fall in, while others gain energy and escape. Those processes are hard to observe because they occur rarely. They find a milder process in and near the ergospheres of spinning black holes. Reflection of emission from a thin, thick accretion disk can form a power-law component without a corona.
arxiv-2604-06085: Galletti, Volkmann, and Brandstetter's 2026 paper presents gyaradax, a minimal JAX/CUDA solver for local flux-tube gyrokinetics. Gyrokinetic simulations matter for fusion plasma turbulence, yet many live in legacy CPU-bound code that resists machine-learning workflows. Built on GKW with GPU speed and automatic differentiation, gyaradax matches GKW with formal agreement, statistical parity, and a big speedup. The authors also show coding agents, guided by experts, structured prompts, and unit tests, turned complex Fortran code around very fast. Cases cover inverse problems and sensitivity analysis.
arxiv-2604-06185: Yu and six colleagues benchmark language-model tool use against messy real-world behavior rather than tidy lab tasks. They name three hurdles: compositional tasks needing efficient orchestration of tool-call patterns, implicit intent spread across dialogue turns, and instruction transitions that mix queries, clarifications, and casual chat. Existing benchmarks miss these behaviors, making model progress look stronger than it is. Their WildToolBench evaluation of 57 models finds none above 15 percent accuracy, showing the true difficulty lies in wild user behavior, not artificially complex tasks.
arxiv-2604-06385: Singh and five colleagues build EduQwen, a family of open teaching models on a dense Qwen3-32B base. Their plan mixes reinforcement learning with supervised fine-tuning: reinforcement learning trains on harder examples with long reasoning runs, then fine-tuning builds new training data from the trained model. An optional second reinforcement round follows. The models top the Cross-Domain Pedagogical Knowledge Benchmark and the Pedagogy Benchmark Leaderboard, beating prior leader Gemini-3 Pro. Mid-size open models beat far larger closed systems, while staying open, adaptable, and cheap.
arxiv-2604-06685: Zhao and four colleagues build ChemVLR, a chemical vision-language model that reasons before it answers. Most chemical vision models jump straight to answers, acting as black boxes that ignore how language models can infer reaction mechanisms. ChemVLR first names fine-grained descriptors like functional groups in the image, then builds explicit reasoning paths for complex chemical problems. A three-stage training scheme and a curated set of 760,000 reasoning-and-captioning samples lift it past leading proprietary and domain-specific baselines.
arxiv-2604-06985: Kyprakis and 12 colleagues estimate frailty change between visits in elderly breast cancer patients from wearable data. Frailty and decline shape treatment tolerance, yet assessment happens only at clinic visits. The team combines smartwatch activity, sleep, and chest heart rate variability into month 3 and month 6 bags. An attention model predicts worsened, stable, or improved fatigue and handgrip strength. Held-out testing gives about 68 percent accuracy at month 3 and about 70 percent at month 6 for handgrip. Smartwatch activity and sleep carry the strongest signal.
arxiv-2604-07085: Samad, Hou, and Ghosh test ways of grouping heart failure patients from health records, where grouping can reveal disease types and guide care choices. Health grouping still leans on old methods like K means, which work poorly on the coded traits learned by auto encoders. The authors test old, mixed, and deep grouping methods on real records from the All of Us study, then build a team method that pools group votes across many coded views. Their pooled method ranks best across fourteen methods.
arxiv-2604-07385: Golchinfar, Vaziri, and Marquardt present a 1.3-million-parameter model playing DOOM in real time, beating language models up to 92000 times its size. SauerkrautLM-Doom-MultiVec combines a ModernBERT encoder with hashed embeddings, depth-aware tokens, and attention pooling to pick actions from ASCII frames at 31 milliseconds per decision. Trained on just 31000 human demonstrations, it scores 178 frags in ten episodes in defend-the-center play, more than all tested language models combined at 13. Unlike the language models, it actively engages enemies instead of only evading them.
arxiv-2604-07485: Vajigi and Roy simulate fluid extraction through fracturing in a 1D capillary fiber bundle model under a pressure gradient. Fractures enter as falling capillary thresholds per tube, mimicking widened pore spaces from fracking, and flow rates rise as flow behavior evolves. Math limits match the computed results, and hydraulic power grows with pressure and with fracking amplitude, the threshold drop per event. Early onset of linear Darcy flow improves extraction quality. The authors identify a best pressure for extraction rate, readable from flow profiles and entropy changes cheaply.
arxiv-2604-07985: Dado, Carmel, and Kurland study when retrieval augmentation helps open-domain question answering and when it hurts. Augmented generation is now common, yet retrieved information does not always improve answers. The team tests predictors built on lookup signals, answer traits, and semantic consistency between generated answers and lookup passages. They also devise a predictor that probes the language model's internal state. Its performance nearly closes the gap between costly late methods and cheaper early ones. A selective framework then chooses per question whether to look up passages.
arxiv-2604-08185: Granados and six colleagues propose a two-stage approach for robust state and trajectory estimation of cable-driven tensegrity robots. Tensegrity robots bend and adapt well, but nonlinear, underconstrained dynamics make state estimation hard. Steady continuous-time estimates of every rigid link matter for control loops, system identification, and learning, yet standard methods fall short. For online estimation, the team introduces a factor-graph method combining RGB-D camera readings with on-board cable length sensors. As far as the authors know, factor graphs were new to this domain.
arxiv-2604-08485: Baek and Kim formalize building up constructions for self dual codes through isotropic lines in the Lean proof assistant. They show a two coordinate reduction in the binary Hilbert symbol setting inverts Kim's building up construction up to permutation. They then extend the mechanism to q-ary codes when q leaves remainder 1 on division by 4. The work yields optimal self dual codes over finite fields, including a [12,6,6] code over the field with 13 elements, with the algebraic core checked in Lean 4.
arxiv-2604-08585: Yan and eight colleagues speed retrieval aided generation with QCFuse, a cache fusion system built around the user query. Short summary anchors sharpen query forms, and only query related tokens get recomputed, guided by the most critical transformer's attention pattern. Tests on real datasets lift response speed by 40 percent at equal accuracy, and in some settings attention denoising even raises accuracy above current methods.
arxiv-2604-08885: Abhiram Vellore and Jha present CONFIDE, a framework bringing uncertainty measures to transformer based language models. Black box guesses limit trust in high stakes settings. CONFIDE applies matching prediction to inner vectors of encoder only models like BERT and RoBERTa, using CLS token vectors or flat hidden states for per class misfit scores. The result is soundly valid prediction sets with instance level reasons, lifting BERT-tiny test scores by up to 4.09 percent with better correct yield than NM2 and VanillaNN.
arxiv-2604-08985: Angeli and 18 colleagues push for better nuclear charge radii, a measurement that matters across many branches of physics and nearby fields. Current recommended values come from several independent groups using different methods and evaluation strategies, mixing complementary experiments with advanced theory. The effort here aims at values that are more precise and more reliable than the present set. The paper gathers the complementary experimental techniques and theoretical frameworks behind current values, and argues for a more precise and reliable determination.
arxiv-2604-09085: Proshian and seven colleagues add graph structure to event sequence models. There, billions of timestamped interactions help predict traits for fraud prevention and recommendations. Self-supervised learning captures event order well but misses the global structure of the user-item graph. Their three model-agnostic strategies enrich event embeddings, align client and graph embeddings, and add a structural pretext task. Tests on four finance and shopping datasets show accuracy gains of up to 2.3 percent in AUC. Graph density emerges as the key factor in picking the best strategy.
arxiv-2604-09285: Shi and colleagues propose SAGE, a multi-agent benchmark for service agents that must follow strict operating procedures. Existing benchmarks use static setups and single metrics, missing diverse user behavior and procedure compliance. SAGE turns procedures into dynamic dialogue graphs, enabling precise checks of compliance and path coverage, plus an adversarial intent taxonomy for low-cost use across domains. Tests on 27 language models across 6 scenarios reveal an execution gap: models classify intents well but fail to derive correct next actions.
arxiv-2604-09585: Choi and nine colleagues test whether turning eye-tracking signals into pictures helps multimodal language models recognize human activity. Raw high-frequency sensor streams lose information and cost many tokens when fed directly, so the team converts them into timeline, heatmap, and scanpath images across three public datasets and varied time windows. Visual prompting proves token-efficient and scalable, letting models reason over fast sensor signals in internet-of-things settings.
arxiv-2604-09685: Thakur and Talele describe a zero-shot pipeline for the ACCIDENT at CVPR 2026 challenge. It predicts when, where, and what kind of accident appears in surveillance video, without labeled training data. Three modules split the task. Peak detection over z-score-normalized frame-difference signals locates the collision in time. The centroid of optical-flow maps finds the impact location. Cosine similarity between CLIP image embeddings and multi-prompt text descriptions classifies the collision type. The implementation is public.
arxiv-2604-10085: Lee, Lee, and Lee align standard fundus photographs with ultra-widefield retinal images. The pairing is hard because of scale and appearance gaps and few distinctive features. Their Particle Diffusion Matching method searches for correspondences by an iterative random walk guided by a diffusion model. At each step it estimates shifts for particle points from local appearance, particle layout, and a global transform estimate. It leads retinal alignment benchmarks with a large gain on a primary paired data set. The method supports diagnosis and multi-modal retinal analysis.
arxiv-2604-10385: Cudlenco, Masala, and Leordeanu turn a game engine into an instrument with GEST-Engine. It executes event graphs into videos of synchronized multi-actor scenarios, recording ground truth as it renders. They release GTASA, a 938-video sample carrying the densest spatial-relation coverage of any video dataset: an entity-pair relation graph at every frame, about 84 times denser than rivals. GTASA pretraining improves video language model captioning. Probing six frozen encoders across 11 spatio-temporal tasks reveals that who-is-near-whom barely rises above chance, making the gap measurable.
arxiv-2604-10685: Onofri and four colleagues tackle a one-sided privacy gap in self-sovereign identity. Selective disclosure shields credential holders but can expose checkers, whose requests reveal rules or strategy. Their COD-ssi framework uses oblivious pseudorandom functions so verifiers can reach a subset of claims without showing which claims they touched. Security is formally verified, and tests of a prototype show mutual privacy at modest cost.
arxiv-2604-10785: Rather proves a color-class majorization principle for distance Laplacian eigenvalues. For a graph with chromatic number chi and largest color class l1, the first l1 minus 1 distance Laplacian values are at least n plus l1. This gives sharper bounds on how many values exceed the chromatic threshold, refining earlier distribution theorems. He further refines clique and independent-set counts via neighborhood compression. He characterizes balanced complete multipartite minimizers for the minimum first eigenvalue, and gives a Ky Fan type result.
arxiv-2604-10985: Horawalavithana and four colleagues test how changing the pretrained language-model backbone affects vision-language performance. They hold the vision encoder, training set, and post-training method fixed across LLAMA-1, LLAMA-2, and LLAMA-3 models. Newer backbones do not always yield better vision-language models, and gains depend on the task. In visual question answering, newer backbones tend to answer different questions rather than simply more of them. This reflects better calibrated confidence and steadier internal representations, while mainly visual tasks gain little.
arxiv-2604-11085: Fu and four colleagues present protection for quantum models of lattice gauge theories through emergent hierarchies. They focus on lattice gauge theories, underlying physics, matter, and information. In present-day quantum machines, perfect limit of the Hilbert space to gauge sectors is beyond reach. Breaks of the rule are certain. The authors develop a Floquet-engineering system shifting exits from a sector so new patterns occur hierarchically in time. This yields rough choice rules curbing inter-sector links. The result is a ladder of lifetimes for spreading among sectors.
arxiv-2604-11185: Elbakyan and six colleagues simulate a massive young star's disk at finer inner detail to see how a wandering fragment bursts. Resolving the inner disk down to one astronomical unit, instead of thirty, makes the fragment migrate faster and break apart fully, giving a shorter, sharper accretion outburst with stronger infrared glow. The result suggests the briefest observed bursts need compact cores, not diffuse fragments, to be torn apart.
arxiv-2604-11285: Pritzkuleit and five colleagues analyze HE 1518-0948, a luminous, extremely helium-rich, low-gravity hot subdwarf. Massive helium stars above 0.8 solar masses climb the helium giant branch after core helium burning, but such helium-rich objects show almost no hydrogen and few binaries, pointing to mergers or late flashes. Comparison with evolutionary models marks HE 1518 as a massive double helium white dwarf merger now burning helium in a shell, a rare resident of a sparse region of the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram.
arxiv-2604-11485: Zhang, Men'shchikov, and Li analyze filaments in seven clouds via getsf. They also derive volume density profiles. Widths grow as power laws. Surface widths scale to the one-half, volume widths to about thirty-seven hundredths. Widths span one hundredth to one parsec against a tenth-parsec width. Median density slopes near two point one to two point four sit below the isothermal cylinder value four. Volume contrasts of seventeen to fifty-two far exceed surface contrasts near one to three, so filaments stand out far more in three dimensions.
arxiv-2604-11785: Richardson and nine colleagues measure how commercial vapor cells used in Rydberg electric-field sensing alter fields from 10 to 300 megahertz. Using a stripline transmission setup plus full-wave modelling, they extract each cell's effective permittivity and conductivity and report how much the field drops inside. Atomic measurements back their results, and the observed frequency patterns could guide better cell designs.
