arxiv-2604-11885: Zenati, Beniamini, and Hotokezaka model how yttrium and strontium abundances relative to europium evolved, finding the pattern needs three neutron-capture sources on different timescales. A delayed r-process channel, most likely binary neutron-star mergers, supplies at least 95 percent. A prompt channel makes first-peak elements with little europium, while delayed AGB stars add s-process enrichment with minimum delays of 0.3 to 0.6 billion years. The prompt-to-delayed first-to-second peak yield ratio is at least 3.4, ruling out models where the two ratios match.
arxiv-2604-11985: Bordenave, Dong, and Šarić prove geodesic flow on an infinite Riemann surface with a bounded pants decomposition is ergodic exactly when its dual-graph random walk recurs. Dual vertices are pants pairs; edges are cuffs with length weights. That yields cuff-length ergodicity tests and new families with recurrence phase transitions. Rough surface isometry need not preserve ergodic flow, while dual graphs keep it. The proof turns measured layer conditions, from straightened flat layers of finite-area quadratic differentials, into a square summed flow on the graph.
arxiv-2604-12185: Wu and eight colleagues note most retrieval systems treat evidence as an unordered set, though real reasoning often turns on the order in which steps unfold. Their OKH-RAG stores knowledge as higher-order links in a hypergraph with precedence structure and recasts retrieval as finding paths over hyperedges. A learned transition model infers precedence from data alone. On order-sensitive tasks it beats baselines that ignore order, with ablations tracing the gains to order.
arxiv-2604-12485: Andreu Queralt McBride and three colleagues simulate liquid metal flow in a rectangular duct under a magnetic field. Side walls are heated evenly, and a transverse field runs across the flow. The team varies wall conductivity, from highly conducting to fully insulating. Buoyancy acts in horizontal and vertical ducts, sometimes with the flow and sometimes against it. Vortex promoters at the inlet stir the flow. Four distinct flow types emerge across the parameter range. Heat transfer for each type is scored with the Nusselt number, a heat transfer measure.
arxiv-2604-12785: Zirui Wang proves global decay estimates for the multi-phase Muskat problem. Density takes exactly n plus one distinct constant values across phases. The proof linearizes around a flat stable setup and studies the linearized operator. Low-frequency eigenvalues yield decay like one plus t to the power minus s over two minus one quarter. Bounding the nonlinear term then closes the argument.
arxiv-2604-13085: Khanda, Baqar, Chakrabarti, and Changdar present Adaptive Memory Crystallization, a memory architecture that lets autonomous agents learn continually without erasing prior knowledge. Inspired by synaptic tagging and capture theory, it moves experiences through Liquid, Glass, and Crystal stability phases under a utility signal. Tests on Meta-World, Atari, and MuJoCo show forward transfer gains of 34 to 43 percent, forgetting cuts of 67 to 80 percent, and a 62 percent smaller memory footprint.
arxiv-2604-13185: Peña and seven colleagues show that flat-band engineering can tune quantum heat engines built from noninteracting bosons on a rhombic chain lattice. A magnetic flux reshapes the single-particle spectrum. Driving toward full Aharonov-Bohm caging flattens the bands, suppressing heat dumped to the cold reservoir and boosting Otto-cycle work and efficiency. The Stirling cycle instead gains work over a wider parameter range at lower efficiency, governed by entropy changes in flux-driven isothermal steps.
arxiv-2604-13285: Kondadadi and Ortega introduce Learning to Defer for clinical text. The framework learns when a BERT classifier should hand cases to a large language model based on uncertainty signals and text traits. On adverse drug event detection, BioBERT beats it, yet selective deferral of 7 percent of cases lifts F1 to 0.928, a gain of 1.7 points over the BioBERT baseline. On treatment outcome sorting, deferring 16.8 percent of cases lifts F1 to 0.980, a gain of 9.3 points over the ClinicalBERT baseline, showing adaptive deferral uses its strengths while limiting API costs.
arxiv-2604-13585: Li, Jiang, and Luo ask when the Sun's surface magnetic field can actually forecast the next solar cycle. Applying Stokes' theorem to the induction equation, they link the surface field directly to the dynamo process below and derive a quantitative test for predictive power, applied to five dynamo models. The surface field forecasts well when flux-transport processes feed it back into the dynamo loop, or when it mirrors the interior poloidal field's radial part.
arxiv-2604-13985: McLemore and colleagues show the accepted limit on real-time path-length noise suppression in optical fibers is not fundamental. By exploiting temporal correlations between round-trip and one-way signals, they optimize the feedback correction for any noise distribution along the path. A deployed urban fiber beats the standard limit by about 6 decibels, and a lab testbed exceeds it by well over 10 decibels for some noise layouts, with no new hardware.
arxiv-2604-14385: Pedroni and sixty-one colleagues measure helicity-dependent cross sections for proton and deuteron targets under photon energies from 200 to 1400 MeV at the Mainz Microtron's A2 facility. A circularly polarized beam on longitudinally polarized targets feeds a Crystal Ball/TAPS calorimeter covering 97 percent of the full solid angle, with fine energy steps. Combining deuteron and proton results also yields neutron information. With models filling unmeasured energy regions, the data confirm the Gerasimov-Drell-Hearn sum rule for proton, neutron, and deuteron alike.
arxiv-2604-14885: Zhang, Li, Zhang, Wang, and Zhao propose RACER, a lightweight training-free speculative decoding method joining retrieved exact patterns with logit-driven future cues. Retrieval-based drafts fail without exact matches, while logits-based drafts lack structural guidance; RACER supplies reliable anchors plus flexible extrapolation for richer drafts. Tests on Spec-Bench, HumanEval, and MGSM-ZH show consistent acceleration above two times over autoregressive decoding, beating prior training-free methods. The method offers a scalable plug-and-play route to efficient language-model decoding, with code public.
arxiv-2604-14985: Thim, Ekström, and Forssén predict ground states of hydrogen-3, helium-4, and lithium-6 in chiral effective field theory up to N3LO. Subleading two-nucleon interactions are treated perturbatively, with helium-4 and lithium-6 corrections from numerical derivatives of Lanczos-diagonalized levels. Including the hydrogen-3 binding energy in calibration proves essential for robust helium-4 and lithium-6 results. The work shows the power counting can build predictive nuclear interactions for light nuclei, moving nuclear theory closer to a quantum chromodynamics foundation.
arxiv-2604-15485: Bedell, Siavash, and Moin build LLM4C2Rust, a retrieval-assisted scheme that turns C and C++ code into memory-safe Rust. It splits code into balanced blocks and guides a large language model with Rust docs and compiler error notes, paired with a small language model. Tests on three OpenAI models show gains in correctness and security, with several Coreutils programs shedding all raw pointer dereferences and unsafe casts.
arxiv-2604-15685: Ying and seven colleagues probe shake modes in light-matter blends hit by short light bursts, using the field-driven Holstein-Tavis-Cummings model. Burst hits spread drive across charge, light, and shake parts, with plain and mixed parts rising as the square and fourth power of field strength. The mixed part comes from a burst-time Raman-like kick steered by the blends, tying in one view how such fast tests read and steer.
arxiv-2604-15785: Perez, Doster, Menke, ElSheikh, and Busch build a chance-based flow ladder for cracked rock, joining crack shapes from images to doubt-aware forecasts across scales. Bayes fixes bridge-gap misses, a deep net stand-in predicts flow stats, and Darcy-scale lift carries doubt to flow rates. Tests on Utah shear cracks show stock gap-flow links lean wrong for wild cracks. The new ladder gives doubt-aware flow guesses that match physics, catching channel runs, links, and knotty voids.
arxiv-2604-16285: Bradshaw, Gouveia, and Hance show how to map between any two pure quantum states with a single closed-form exponential. Older methods needed two explicit bases, one for the start state and one for the target, so their complexity grew with the dimension of the Hilbert space. Their construction uses novel algebraic methods and only one unitary generator. It needs no bases and does not depend on dimension. The tool suits studying relations among pure states, quantum circuits, and unitary operators.
arxiv-2604-16385: Bai and colleagues built StressWeb, a stress test for web agents that act through browsers on realistic tasks. The test first sets clean, stable tasks as base cases. It then adds controlled shocks such as shifting layouts, changed click meanings and breaks in running. Checking agents across the clean and shocked settings exposes failure modes that calm tests hide. Top agents showed big weak spots, so high scores in calm tests flatter agents for the real web.
arxiv-2604-16585: Kermiche offers the Global Neural World Model, a frame for action-based planning. It maps worlds onto a set 2D grid with shift symmetry and no pixel work. Grid snapping acts as an error fix, stopping shape drift during rollouts. Training by maximum entropy search through random walks teaches broad change motion. It learns change motion rather than copied expert paths. Tested across passive watching, active control and abstract series, it serves as a causal finding model. It sorts smooth concepts into ordered shape maps, beyond a mere physics model.
arxiv-2604-16785: Yi and colleagues propose HyMOR, a hybrid framework pairing a multimodal language model with CLIP for open-ended object recognition. The language model handles coarse-grained recognition while CLIP specializes in fine-grained identification of animals, plants and similar objects. A new dataset, TBO, holds 20,942 textbook images annotated with 8,816 object categories. HyMOR narrows the fine-grained gap with CLIP to zero point two percent and improves general recognition by two point five percent over a baseline model. Overall average similarity improves by about 23 percent across all evaluated datasets.
arxiv-2604-17085: De Santis and three colleagues study how humans and language models read implicit meaning, the unsaid content woven into talk. Their Implicit Information Extraction pipeline builds a knowledge graph from a context sentence by extracting relational triplets, validating inferred readings, and analyzing temporal relations. Humans agree with most model triplets but keep adding their own, showing limited model coverage, and models prove more cautious than people about implicit inferences in socially rich settings.
arxiv-2604-17285: Bund, Leshem, and Medina ask what happens to Turing machines when some input bits never settle to a stable value. This hardware fault is called metastability. They prove the full closure over all possibilities is generally uncomputable. Yet they pin down tractable corners: one uncertain bit makes EXPTIME problems EXPTIME-complete, while polynomial-time problems stay tractable for a logarithmic number of uncertain bits. They also sketch a realizable universal machine that computes the closure for bounded-time machines at exponential time cost.
arxiv-2604-17785: Koh and three colleagues propose Entropy-guided Token Weighting, a token-level erasing control using forecast entropy for token value. Uniform erasing loss harms utility by skipping token weight, while older controls rely on ground-truth scores or outside parsers, missing context and forecast state. Function words like 'the' serve grammar roles and are easy, but rich words admit multiple options with greater doubt. Rich tokens show higher entropy, frame tokens lower, so ETW erases better while keeping utility better than older token-level methods.
arxiv-2604-17885: Allison asks how far lazy evaluation and recursive data structures can carry an efficient implementation of Conway's surreal numbers. The system, named by Knuth, extends the reals with infinities and infinitesimals. The note tests surreal arithmetic built this way. It reports a considerable speedup over more direct approaches. Delaying computation until values are actually needed, Allison shows, pays off for this unusual number system.
arxiv-2604-17985: Zemánková and seven colleagues build a platform from a levitated particle with full control over coupling between its modes, including non-reciprocal interactions. Tuning the trapping beam's shape and polarization moves the system from reciprocal to strongly non-reciprocal behavior, revealing parity-time symmetry phase transitions. In a unidirectional regime one mode stays decoupled while driving the other, and beam settings spanning both regimes move energy one way. That move cools one mode on its own, with no outside help.
arxiv-2604-18185: Plugers and Kaneko develop a theory for how noisy gene expression still yields reliable cell differentiation. Weakly stable intermediate states, called frustrated states, get nudged by random fluctuations and then locked in by slow epigenetic feedback. Removing the fast expression dynamics shows the slow epigenetic variable is driven by gene-expression noise, amplified by regulation. The theory predicts a logarithmic link between noise strength and differentiation onset time, plus input-dependent odds for each fate.
arxiv-2604-18285: Ma, Fang, Xie, Wang, and Hanzo propose EQE-QAOA, a qubit-saving version of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm for large combinatorial problems. Qubit counts bottleneck the method, and past cuts lose information and hurt performance. By exploiting symmetries and conserved quantities, the authors confine dynamics to an invariant subspace exactly matching the full system. An isometric map then re-encodes that subspace with fewer qubits, and Max-Cut simulations confirm equal solution quality at lower cost.
arxiv-2604-18885: Korichi, Hiekkamaki, and Fickler show multi plane light conversion written into fused silica glass. Multi plane conversion uses phase modulations plus free space propagation for unitary transforms. Usual builds are bulky, scalar only, or need advanced nanofabrication. Laser written nanogratings shape the glass birefringence. Their device, only a few cubic millimeters in size, controls full vectorial light structures. It shows multi mode transforms, mode conversions, beam splitting, and a telecom multiplexer.
arxiv-2604-18985: Sun and 23 colleagues describe the Gamma-Ray Monitor aboard the SVOM satellite, built to detect and study gamma-ray bursts. Launched into a 625 km low Earth orbit in June 2024, it watches hard X-rays and soft gamma rays from 15 keV to 5 MeV. It triggers and localizes bursts promptly, measures their spectra and timing, and tracks charged particle fluxes. It caught its first burst days after launch and now detects more than 100 bursts per year. Cross checks against GECAM and Fermi/GBM confirm its performance and data quality.
arxiv-2604-19185: Wang, Lin, and Kao introduce SCURank, a framework ranking summaries by the richness and semantic importance of their content, using Summary Content Units. Small models such as BART can match large models via distillation, but ranking strategies are unstable and classical metrics such as ROUGE rank high-quality summaries poorly. SCURank beats traditional metrics and model ranking methods across measures and datasets. Diverse model summaries also enhance abstractiveness and distilled model performance, showing the value of content ranking in multi-model distillation.
arxiv-2604-19385: Sten and Ghosh study the Josephson diode effect, which allows one-way dissipationless supercurrents, in multichannel Rashba nanowire junctions. Hybrid semiconductor-superconductor nanowires offer an accessible platform for this effect and for hosting Majorana bound states. Most theory assumes a single channel, yet real devices are inherently multichannel because of transverse confinement. The authors show that coupling between subbands changes both the topological phase diagram and the diode response in a qualitative way, unlike the single-channel case.
arxiv-2604-19885: Ben Zeev and three colleagues link the generalized Schur index of four-dimensional superconformal theories to the non-relativistic limit of the elliptic Ruijsenaars-Schneider model. They express class S indices through Jack functions, with Lamé equation eigenfunctions in the simplest case. The same expressions check a recent mapping between Deligne-Cvitanović series theories, implying new identities for related models. Slow limits of other integrable models then yield Schur-like limits of one-supersymmetry theories, shown for the Inozemtsev model and rank Q E-string compactifications.
arxiv-2604-19985: Mukherjee compares electoral rules by geometry under feedback, where voters and candidates adapt to repeated results. He defines the winner radius, the distance from winner to farthest voter, and the supporter centroid radius, the largest candidate-to-support gap. The first bounds how fast voter disagreement shrinks, the second does likewise for candidate spread, and the goals pull against each other. Simulations over seven standard rules plus a combination benchmark confirm the tradeoff: winner-take-all rules cluster candidates but leave voters polarized, while combination rules reverse it.
arxiv-2604-20085: Arnaud and three colleagues build, for the first time, a physics-informed neural network for the time-dependent quasi-static magnetohydrodynamic equations in tokamak geometry. Trained without any experimental or synthetic data, the network learns an ITER-like tokamak plasma solution after careful treatment. It predicts a vertically displacing plasma in general agreement with ground truth simulation. The proof-of-principle case shows physics-constrained deep learning can capture complex plasma behavior.
arxiv-2604-20185: Sarker and Dahlin present a risk aware plan for sizing bendy load links, like cars that plug in and AI data hubs, on power grids. Their plan pairs load cutback leeway with grid trust, using a Conditional Value at Risk cap to bound the tail risk of too much cutback. A weighted plan caps grid run cutbacks, with a dial setting the cutback budget. The convex form solves fast, and tests show it lifts host room a lot while holding risk pledges and cutback counts in check.
arxiv-2604-20285: Bauer, Fuchs, and Schamberger model football fever as a latent process in Arminia Bielefeld fans wearing smartwatches through the 2025 DFB Cup final. Watches logged heart rate, stress, and related signs in short bursts, feeding a time-dependent structural equation model with growth and carry-over parts. Results pool across many imputations of missing measures, with fit judged under high data dimensionality. Fever runs high at kick-off, falls steadily, then rises anew in the second half, varying widely across fans in baseline level and time pattern.
arxiv-2604-20385: Voronchikhin and Kirpichnikov study the reach of the ILC beam-dump experiment for inelastic fermion dark matter tied to the photon by an off-diagonal magnetic dipole. Dark matter forms when high-energy electrons strike target nuclei, yielding two dark states. Boosted dark fluxes then reach the detector, where signals come from electron scattering or monophoton decay of the heavier state. With two benchmark mass splittings, five hundredths and one thousandth, the experiment can probe a viable slice of parameter space over one and ten years.
arxiv-2604-20485: Surya Ratna Prakash D and Raha develop a co-state fusion method for spacecraft navigation that watches for model errors during landing. A co-state, used as a Lagrange multiplier, checks whether measurements fit the motion model and flags geometric mismatch. Over longer spans, co-state and innovation paths feed a Markov generator that forecasts risk through mode chances and mean first-passage time. Tested on lunar descent telemetry, it spots internal inconsistency well before physical drift or a Kalman filter shows trouble, giving warning for autonomous landing.
arxiv-2604-20985: Yin, Zaheer, and Li address privacy needs that shift after deployment. How, they ask, can any target differential-privacy level be met without retraining? From models trained on the same data at varied tradeoffs, they offer two post-processing routes. Random selection and linear combination each yield a final private model at the desired level. Privacy accounting with Rényi differential privacy and loss distributions characterizes each route's tradeoff. Exact analysis for private mean estimation backs the accounting, and tests on synthetic and real data confirm it.
arxiv-2604-21085: Shuochen Wang and three colleagues build a transformer model that remembers past weather states to mimic convection, the small-scale rising and sinking air that climate models struggle to resolve. Unlike memory-free rivals, their emulator tracks how conditions evolve over time, works best with about 100 minutes of history, and stays stable across a decade of linked simulation. The result argues for giving climate emulators an explicit sense of time.
arxiv-2604-21385: Ruifeng Shi and seven colleagues optimize photometric filters for measuring metallicities of very metal-poor stars from Gaia XP spectra, a cornerstone task for Galactic archaeology. The best filters center near 3960 angstroms for giants and 3920 angstroms for dwarfs, both 80 angstroms wide. Applied to synthetic photometry, they reach precision of about 0.2 dex in the higher metallicity band, worsening for more metal-poor stars but reaching down to about -4 for giants and about -3 for dwarfs. The resulting catalog holds more than 14 million metal-poor stars with robust measurements.
arxiv-2604-21485: Bereneice Sephton and 10 colleagues design custom interferometers inside a single optical beam using structured light, dodging the stability-versus-complexity trade-offs of usual setups. Their common-path setups need no complex post-processing and fit into existing setups. A range of interferometers, each shaped by its structured mode and built with active and passive modal conversion optics, proves adaptability. Applied to precise phase imaging across varied samples, results match atomic force microscopy benchmarks, and mapping phase objects to amplitude or polarization opens real-time phase retrieval.
arxiv-2604-21685: Ortega and Zografopoulos propose a Multidimensional Resilience Index for power grids facing coordinated cyber-physical attacks as inverter-based resources spread. It scores damage in five areas: physical, operational, cyber-digital, climatic, and regulatory. It then adds the extra loss caused by their interaction. The team tested it on the IEEE 39-bus system, using scenarios rebuilt from a December 2025 attack on the Polish grid. Coupled attacks raise resilience loss nearly fifteen times over the baseline.
arxiv-2604-21985: Khoroshiy and six colleagues measure spin waves in iron-doped manganese silicide deep within its field-polarized state, using high-resolution neutron scattering. Non-reciprocal spin waves show parabolic dispersion that shifts with field. Spin-wave stiffness is very anisotropic: 17.2 meV square angstroms parallel to the applied field and about 9 meV square angstroms across it. While the applied field lowers symmetry from cubic to one-axis, the anisotropy is large, not captured by simple theories.
arxiv-2604-22085: Abtahi and five colleagues present Memanto, a memory layer for agent AI that drops the idea that graph complexity is needed for true-to-life agent memory. Memanto combines a typed meaning store with thirteen set groups, auto clash fixing, and time versions. On LongMemEval and LoCoMo, Memanto achieves top accuracy of 89.8 percent and about 87 percent. It beats all tested hybrid graph and vector systems with one search, no intake cost, and much lower running complexity.
arxiv-2604-22285: Zhou and five colleagues speed formal checks of hardware made by high-level synthesis. Such synthesis turns C-like code into register-level circuits. Machine-made circuits can hide bugs or flaws, yet model checks often run too long on large designs. Their AutoINV tool builds helper claims from high-level traits to guide the checker. A proof loop reuses past proof data to pick the most useful helpers. It ran up to 6.05 times faster than plain checks, and more than twice as fast on average.
arxiv-2604-22385: Erraqabi, Valko, Carpentier and Maillard present pliable rejection sampling, a new way to sample hard laws. Rejection draws from a target by trying candidates and keeping or dropping them, but high rejection rates limit its use. Past adaptive methods either work only for set laws or lack guarantees. Their method learns the proposal using a kernel estimator. Since it builds on rejection, obtained samples are with high odds independent and identically distributed from the target. It also guarantees accepted samples.
arxiv-2604-22585: Jouttijärvi, Kroencke, and Yudowitz prove stability and instability results for static vacuum spacetimes with negative cosmological constant, viewed as self-similar solutions of Ricci-harmonic flow. Static metrics turn out stable exactly when a positive-mass type theorem holds nearby. Their main tool is a new variant of expander entropy adapted to this flow.
arxiv-2604-22685: Basak, Pal, and Bhattacherjee introduce CosmicDancePro, an open-source tool for LEO solar-storm resilience. The May 2024 superstorm showed the weakness of fast-growing low Earth orbit networks against severe space weather. The tool joins space weather measurements, upper-air density states from data-physics models, and path and network traces, to gauge orbital decay from added density and link loss. The authors use it on Starlink during two major solar storms. They pin down Starlink's fleet plans during the May 2024 superstorm and contrast them with routine operations.
arxiv-2604-22785: Ben-Gal and Tong argue that shared rewards mislead training in multi-agent language-model systems. One reward cannot tell which agent truly caused it, and no single score per agent can capture joint performance once agents interact. They define a background-dependent marginal contribution measure and derive training signals from it, identified through filtered feedback plus a limited budget of exact counterfactual checks. Built into GRPO, their signal lifts routed GSM8K accuracy over winner-take-all training without extra generation cost.
arxiv-2604-22885: Zhou and nine colleagues present RCSR, a federated framework for cross-modal retrieval when client data differ widely and some modalities are missing. Built on a frozen CLIP backbone, it pairs lightweight shared adapters for global knowledge with local adapters for each client. Prototype anchoring aligns unimodal clients with global cross-modal meaning, and a server-side router weights updates by retrieval consistency to limit drift. Tests on MS-COCO, Flickr30K, and other benchmarks show steadier training and better retrieval, above all for clients missing a modality.
arxiv-2604-22985: Ye and seven colleagues present the first evaluation of uncertainty quantification methods for LLM function calling, where wrong calls can have irreversible effects like moving money or deleting data. Multi-sample methods like Semantic Entropy, strong for question answering, show no clear advantage over simple single-sample methods in this setting. The particularities of function-call outputs can still improve existing methods. Multi-sample methods gain from clustering outputs by abstract syntax tree parsing, while single-sample methods gain from using only meaningful tokens in logit-based uncertainty scores.
arxiv-2604-23085: Anyaso-Samuel and six colleagues build an importance-sampling algorithm for p-values in all-subset meta-analysis for single-cell eQTL mapping. Pooling studies of related traits boosts power for pleiotropic variants, and ASSET searches all subsets for signals. Its analytic p-value approximation under normality was tested only to one thousandth. The new algorithm gives accurate estimates for independent and overlapping studies, beating naive Monte Carlo, especially for tiny p-values. When normality fails, ASSET p-values can shift hugely, while importance sampling holds.
arxiv-2604-23185: Hakamata and 15 colleagues track iron, calcium, argon, and sulfur lines around Cygnus X-3, a Wolf-Rayet binary. With XRISM Resolve, they measure Doppler shifts of hydrogen-like lines for all four elements, with amplitudes of 500 km per second. Iron follows the compact object's motion most closely, with widths from 400 to 1000 km per second and strengths peaking near phase 0.5 of the orbit. Wind models place iron near the compact object and sulfur across the system, with mass loss between five millionths and one hundred-thousandth of a solar mass per year.
arxiv-2604-23385: Do and sixteen colleagues test whether open ECG foundation models can support echo-confirmed heart disease spotting on EchoNext. Targets span reduced ejection fraction, wall thickening, aortic stenosis, valve leaks, and right heart dysfunction. Comparing hand-made features, waveform learning, and foundation transfer, they add in-domain adaptation plus chosen fine-tuning. Adapted models perform best with peak macro-AUROC of 0.8509, and an efficient variant nearly matches it with the best F1. Target-domain adaptation plus chosen updating is thus the strongest transfer strategy.
arxiv-2604-23485: Sun extends the anabelian study of pointed virtual curves, objects that encode Galois sections through fundamental groups, from genus zero to curves of any genus. To make the jump he introduces two new group- and category-theoretic notions, then proves a criterion for when a section genuinely comes from a rational point. The paper thus carries the central results of the genus-zero case into full generality.
arxiv-2604-23585: Guo, Wu, and Yiu build ComplianceNLP, a system that watches regulatory change for banks and flags gaps against their internal policies. A knowledge-graph-augmented retrieval pipeline grounds answers in nearly 13,000 provisions across three major rulebooks, while obligation extraction and severity-aware gap scoring complete the chain. It beats a strong GPT-4o retrieval baseline on gap detection and held up well in a four-month live deployment.
arxiv-2604-23685: Fu and colleagues tackle text recognition in the dark, where dim light and noise defeat ordinary reading systems. They release LSTR, a dataset of over 11,000 low-light images derived from well-lit collections, plus a small set of real night street scenes for testing only. Jointly training an enhancement module with a text reader beats either part alone, and the team asks how bright is bright enough for reliable reading.
arxiv-2604-23785: Becker, Koutentakis, and Schmelcher study core-hole excited states in a 1D Fermi gas. A spin-aligned bath couples to one heavy mobile defect. A sudden switch-on of their coupling triggers quench motion, solved with two exact methods. The response hinges on coupling strength, trap shape, mass mismatch, and hole place. Deep core holes prove far more robust against refill than bulk or edge holes.
arxiv-2604-23985: King, Fedorenko, and Hosseini connect a geometric feature of language models to their uncertainty about the next word. As a model's internal path through recent context bends more sharply, its next-word guesses grow less certain, a link that appears during training in two models. Bending the path on purpose shifts uncertainty, while off-direction nudges do nothing, and training models toward straighter paths modestly lowers uncertainty without hurting validation loss.
arxiv-2604-24085: Andersson and Monperrus present the first broad study of cryptographic API misuse detection in Go. They survey four leading tools and build a taxonomy of 14 misuse classes, then evaluate 328 security-critical open-source projects. The scan finds 7,473 misuses, mapping how often each class appears. Tool coverage varies widely, giving security engineers a practical guide to tool choice and researchers a baseline for future detectors.
arxiv-2604-24285: Nguyen and three colleagues give a polynomial-time method for cardinality-constrained 2-anticlustering. k-Maximum Dispersion asks for a split into k limited groups maximizing within-group spread. The problem is NP-hard for k of 3 or more, but whether the 2-group case admits polynomial time was open. They solve the 2-group case via a square number of limited 2-color cases, turned into a narrow subset sum class, where pseudopolynomial methods run in polynomial time. Open-source code beats the method many times, handling 10,000 items in under a second.
arxiv-2604-24385: Deng and Zhang build a perfectly secure 1-private distributed point function with shorter secret keys. A point function converts to shares such that each server computes an additive share from its key, while any single server learns nothing about the function. Their share conversion builds on the private information retrieval method of Ghasemi, Kopparty, and Sudan. With output group Z_p for any prime p, the new function beats existing perfectly secure versions with asymptotically shorter keys.
arxiv-2604-24585: Dadkhah and Lambrecht study single layers of arsenic in flat honeycomb and puckered forms, computing electronic and optical properties with density-functional and quasi-particle methods, with and without spin-orbit coupling. They use the Bethe-Salpeter equation for optical response and trace low-lying excitons to their band origins. Under biaxial strain, the puckered phase gradually flattens, and band inversions explain how the structure and optics evolve.
arxiv-2604-24785: Renney, Trad, Mattarock, Evetts and Wood propose a multi-dimensional test method for language-model inference on hardware-accelerated single-board computers. Cloud-first deployment raises privacy, latency and cost worries, acute in factory and defense settings, while distillation, quantization and cheap edge accelerators now make local inference feasible. Existing edge benchmarks often rely on CPU-only inference and generic tasks. The authors jointly test inference speed and hardware efficiency on four IoT-suitable edge platforms with current accelerators.
arxiv-2604-24885: Patel and four colleagues launch VibeToken, a 1D image token system for autoregressive making. It encodes images into a user-set sequence of 32 to 256 tokens. Building on it, VibeToken-Gen is a class-based maker for any resolution with far less compute. It synthesizes 1024 by 1024 images using only 64 tokens, beating a diffusion rival that needs 1,024 tokens. Unlike fixed-resolution models whose cost grows quadratically with resolution, VibeToken-Gen keeps flat cost at any size. The authors hope VibeToken unlocks wider use of such visual models in real products.
arxiv-2604-25185: Zheng, Zhao and Liu study Whittaker modules over a Cartan type Lie algebra of polynomial vector fields with constant divergence. They show each block of the category of Whittaker modules with finite-dimensional Whittaker vector spaces is equivalent to modules over a parabolic subalgebra. Then they classify all simple Whittaker modules in every block. Finally, they link one block to modules over an algebra whose generators they also determine.
arxiv-2604-25385: Pietroni and Schmidt build a field-level posterior for data, with initial states and noise folded in. While aimed at large-scale structure data, results apply to weakly non-Gaussian measures. Opening it around its Gaussian limit, they derive a Fisher matrix formula and recast information as correlation terms. This shows which terms power-spectrum, bispectrum, or sums capture, and which shrinking loses. They recover the Gaussian power-spectrum result, and the Gaussian bispectrum likelihood matching its contribution. For the BAO scale, the field holds all information for optimal rebuild.
arxiv-2604-25585: Jabal Ameli and three colleagues give new algorithms for the Strongly Connected Steiner Subgraph problem: finding a smallest subgraph strongly connecting a set of terminals. Their main result runs in time exponential in treewidth times a polynomial factor, given a tree decomposition of that width. That is the first such time for strong connectivity. They also give an exact exponential-time algorithm in vertex count for general directed graphs. Finally, no polynomial kernel exists for vertex cover size unless the polynomial hierarchy collapses. The spanning variant does admit one.
arxiv-2604-25785: Shapiro studies level crossings of random matrix pencils across several ensembles, from complex and real independent-entry matrices to Gaussian and Hermitian cases. He writes the scaled log-discriminant via pairwise eigenvalue interactions and states conditions for a deterministic potential limit. Given a uniform circular law, log tail control, and small-spacing estimates, crossing measures converge to an explicit fixed limit. The complex Gaussian case is verified up to one uniform step. In the real case, no limit sits on the real projective line.
arxiv-2604-25885: Patel and Ganguly compare three explainability methods for jet tagging at the Large Hadron Collider: GNNExplainer, GNNShap, and GradCAM. Graph and transformer taggers lead jet-tagging benchmarks, yet their physical reasoning stays opaque. The authors adapt all three methods to LundNet's Lund-plane graph, where each node marks a meaningful parton splitting. Monte Carlo truth masks and a physics-informed framework judge explanations beyond standard fidelity. Results across transverse-momentum bins show explanation quality shifts between non-perturbative and perturbative regimes, with learned features tracking known QCD structure.
arxiv-2604-26285: Mastropasqua and four colleagues tested event cameras for face liveness checks, the task of telling a live face from a replayed one. Event cameras record only brightness changes, catching fast eye flicks with microsecond precision that replay attacks cannot faithfully copy. The team extended an eye-tracking set with replay recordings and studied motion features from the eye region. Their spiking network told genuine from replayed clips with about 95 percent top accuracy.
arxiv-2604-26385: Chen, Jianxi Li, and Yongtao Li settled a conjecture on graphs with minimum distance spectral radius among connected graphs with a given edge count. Earlier work by Lin and Zhou covered part of the range. A harder stretch remained, where the conjectured minimizer complements a balanced disjoint union of paths. Using matrix analysis, a comparison principle, and walk enumeration, the authors proved that minimizer unique and supplied a unified proof across the whole range.
arxiv-2604-26685: Yilmaz and fifteen colleagues report a sharp surface state in 1T-TiSe2 that emerges when charge density wave symmetry breaking reshapes the low-energy range. Fine angle-resolved scans resolve the two-dimensional state, whose signal strength collapses around 160 kelvin even though the charge density wave transition sits near 202 kelvin. Slab calculations reproduce the surface state when wave folding brings valence and conduction states to near-equal energies. The work suggests a route to build low-dimensional quantum states in layered materials through broken symmetry.
arxiv-2604-26885: Dutta and five colleagues tackle cable-reflection flaws in 21-centimetre radio hunts for the Epoch of Reionisation, when early stars ionized hydrogen. Reflections make dim copies of bright foregrounds leak outside the wedge where foregrounds should stay. Building on the hydra-pspec Gibbs sampler, they model the flaws as a multiplicative effect in delay-fringe rate space and fold it into inference. The flaw term can then be marginalized rather than filtered out, avoiding signal loss. Simulated tests recover the delay power spectrum well wherever the flaws sit.
arxiv-2604-27285: Al Sayem and six colleagues show stable use of a thin-film lithium tantalate device at very high temperatures. Signal control and bandwidth of such devices are not affected by high-temperature use. Both waveguide and ring-type devices stay DC-bias stable even at 120 degrees Celsius. At higher temperatures the device's Vpi even falls by 10 percent. Those results position thin-film lithium tantalate devices as a strong candidate for uncooled use in co-packaged optics.
arxiv-2604-27685: Gouvêa and Rignanese introduce VibroML, an open-source toolkit for automated crystal checks and shape repair using learned potentials. Learned potentials speed phonon calculations, but spotting flaws is not enough; automated fixes are needed. VibroML uses a genetic method that beats soft-mode following, uncovering diverse, stable forms. A dynamics workflow checks whether structures hold under heat, and ProtoCSP link fixes stuck shapes by targeted alloying, saving perovskite networks.
arxiv-2604-28185: Wu's team argues visual generation must move beyond photorealistic appearance toward intelligent image-making grounded in structure, motion, knowledge and cause and effect. They propose a five-level ladder from atomic generation through conditional and in-context generation to agentic and world-model generation. Looking at benchmarks, stress tests and expert cases, they find current tests prize looks-based quality while missing failures of shape, timing and cause.
arxiv-2605-00185:
Mohammad Hossein Moslemi and 4 co-authors study a fairness problem in dataset distillation, which squeezes a large dataset into a small synthetic one for training. Because social groups follow distinct predictive patterns, the squeezing can keep the signal for some groups and lose it for others. The resulting models then perform much worse for the shortchanged groups.

Simply balancing group sizes does not fix the gap, since the cause is mismatched patterns, not counts. The authors analyze how the two sources of bias interact, then aim the distillation at a shared center of the groups' predictive information. Training toward that center gives alike representations across groups. The approach works alongside existing distillation methods and cut the added bias sharply in experiments.
arxiv-2605-00285:
Mauricio Corrêa, Pablo Perrella, and Sebastián Velazquez study foliations, sets of surfaces that fill a space like pages, on rough spaces that arise as limits of smooth ones. Their setting is normal crossings spaces, a standard way shapes break down at an edge. The question is when such a space can be smoothed back out.

Working with logarithmic structures, the authors develop a notion of foliated d-semistability suited to this setting. They find local and global obstructions that can block it. To study smoothings, they build a deformation theory for foliations in that language, moving the foliation and the space together. They show the moduli problem behind this has a versal hull, one local model that organizes all small deformations.
arxiv-2605-00685:
David C. Dunbar examines the color structure of two-loop gluon amplitudes in Yang-Mills theory, the gauge theory underlying the strong interaction. Scattering amplitudes in such theories factor into a color part, tracking the charges of the interacting gluons, and a kinematic part. At two loops the color structure grows intricate, and organizing it cleanly is a prerequisite for any precise calculation.

Dunbar studies the color decomposition from two directions at once: an expansion in a basis of color traces, and an alternative built from the theory's structure constants. Using the comparison as a vehicle, he systematizes the relations among the partial amplitudes of the trace formalism, the individually simpler pieces into which a full amplitude splits. The paper is a work of theoretical organization: no new scattering process is computed, but the bookkeeping that future two-loop calculations rely on is made more transparent and consistent.
arxiv-2605-01185:
M. Berk Sahin, Dilek Yalcinkaya, Abolfazl Hashemi, and Behzad Sharif propose synthesizing MRI phase maps from magnitude-only images so those images can train accelerated reconstruction models. Deep learning reconstruction needs large raw k-space datasets, but clinical practice usually discards raw data for storage and privacy reasons, saving only magnitude images. Their generative approach uses a conditional score-based diffusion model to produce a realistic phase map for a given magnitude image.

Combining synthesized phase with magnitude images creates a large k-space training set. A reconstruction model trained that way beats models trained with naive smooth phase or with phase from a generative adversarial network, and is compared against ground truth training as well. Gains appear in quantitative metrics and in avoiding hallucinated features.
arxiv-2605-01585:
Levy teaches graduate quantum mechanics through two-state systems first. Rather than opening with wave mechanics and the Schrodinger equation, his course builds the whole theory from spin one-half systems, where superposition, measurement, collapse, and unitary evolution appear in their clearest form. A physical Bloch cube, a six-faced object like a die with one quantum state per face, lets students handle states with their hands before meeting abstract formalism. A notation called dot-vec bridges familiar vectors and Dirac notation.

Starting finite-dimensional keeps the mathematics transparent and the physical meaning unambiguous, and the foundation extends naturally to infinite-dimensional spaces later. The course text walks from foundations through measurement and dynamics, using the cubes to make superposition and collapse tangible rather than merely asserted. For students meeting quantum theory at graduate level, it offers a concrete route into ideas that usually arrive as pure algebra.
arxiv-2605-01985:
Shahzad Ahmad, Stefan Rass, and Zahra Seyedi propose a way to run private computations on an untrusted cloud while also denying what was computed under pressure. Fully homomorphic methods already hide the data from a curious provider. The new goal adds plausible deniability against a coercive adversary who demands to see what the user did.

Their framework defines a deniable computation medium and scheme in general terms, then builds one from colour images and Fredkin-gate circuits. One real circuit and several decoys share the same wiring, with control bits at each pixel choosing the true function. Under coercion, the user reveals a decoy with checkable results, while the real circuit stays hidden in the same pass.
arxiv-2605-02085:
Irene Aldridge proposes a faster Monte Carlo method based on eigenvalues, aiming to keep the same steady-state distribution as Markov chain Monte Carlo. Classic Monte Carlo can need up to a million paths for stable results, which is costly. Aldridge's small-sample approximation claims comparable results with as few as ten paths, depending on the time horizon.

Accuracy is judged by Wasserstein distance to the traditional result, a measure of how far two distributions sit apart. The method also reports a large drop in variance for the steady-state distribution. If the claims hold broadly, such a shortcut could cut simulation cost sharply in finance and other fields that rely on Monte Carlo sampling.
arxiv-2605-02285:
Pacome Simon Mbonimpa proposes choosing the smallest compressed language model that can still handle a circuit analysis task, based on where its knowledge stops. Deploying large models for engineering faces a trade-off between reasoning accuracy and compute cost. Flat performance scores hide the layered structure of electronics knowledge, where later concepts rest on earlier ones.

The framework arranges circuit concepts as a directed acyclic graph of prerequisites. An agentic pipeline builds prerequisite-based data sets, and an evaluation engine cascades each query across compressed model variants by tier. That reveals each tier's complexity horizon, the level where it begins to fail. The smallest model whose horizon covers a query can then be selected, saving compute without needless loss.
arxiv-2605-02385:
Gustav Jäger, Krzysztof Bieniasz, Martin Plenio, and Hans-Martin Rieser argue that entanglement is only half the story when tensor networks run as quantum machine learning models. Tensor networks began as tools to simulate quantum systems and later became learning models. The authors combine both fields to derive how quantum constraints on a network change what it can do.

They define a hybrid architecture by running classical tensor network inference on a quantum computer. The interpolation between classical and quantum cases hinges on post-selection, and its amount sets how strongly quantum constraints are enforced. They propose a new hyperparameter for that transition, complementing bond dimension. In their comparison, post-selection, not entanglement alone, marks the quantum advantage boundary.
arxiv-2605-02585:
Stephen Cantrell, Dídac Martínez-Granado, and Eduardo Reyes build a bridge between two ways of describing motion in negatively curved settings. One side holds the metrics on a hyperbolic group that stay comparable to a word metric. The other side holds continuous reparameterizations, or time changes, of a canonical flow space built for the group.

From that correspondence, the authors produce the first examples of time-changed geodesic flows on negatively curved manifolds where every closed orbit has whole-number length. For surface and free groups, they also get isometric actions where the fast-moving elements are exactly the non-simple ones. Key tools include the metric-Anosov property of the flow space and the density of Green metrics among symmetric metrics on the group. The result links group geometry with flow dynamics.
arxiv-2605-02685:
Viren Tyagi, Geert Brocks, and Shuxia Tao model how ions move inside a halide perovskite, a material used in solar cells whose lifetime depends on keeping defects still. Using molecular dynamics driven by neural network potentials trained on quantum data, they track motion triggered by missing or extra ions of iodine and of the organic methylammonium part.

Most of these species diffuse fast at room temperature, with low barriers to motion. Methylammonium interstitials move quickly despite being molecules, because several of them shift together in a concerted way. No motion of methylammonium vacancies was found. Iodine defect motion depends on charge state, while methylammonium motion does not. The results revise the standard picture of ion transport in these hybrid materials.
arxiv-2605-03285:
Tsubasa Ito and Shonosuke Sugasawa develop causal small area estimation for surveys where treatment and outcome are seen only for sampled units. Policy work often needs effects for small regions or groups, but past methods assumed treatment status was known for the whole population, which surveys rarely provide.

Combining survey-only covariates with population-level auxiliary data, they give a new identification strategy for area effects. Their doubly robust estimator stays consistent if either the outcome model or the assignment models are right, and it reaches the efficiency bound under stated conditions. Simulations favor it at small area sample sizes.
arxiv-2605-03385:
Morris Ang and Deven Mithal construct quantum natural time versions of quantum Loewner evolution for a new range of parameters. These growth processes on random quantum gravity surfaces are candidate limits for discrete growth models, and their natural time version encodes distance in the random geometry.

They prove the process shows three phases mirroring Schramm-Loewner evolution, answering a question of Miller and Sheffield for this setting. The unexplored surface stays stationary, and in the relevant phases the regions cut out are identified as quantum disks. The construction builds on recent radial coupling results between quantum gravity and Loewner evolution.
arxiv-2605-03485:
Kangkang Wang, Qinting Jiang, Wanping Zhang, Bowen Ren, and Shengzhao Wen introduce MHPR, a benchmark for joint human perception and reasoning by large vision-language models. Film analysis and digital humans need fine-grained human understanding, yet current benchmarks test single tasks and miss layered human detail.

MHPR spans individual, multi-person, and human-object scenes, with tiered data for captioning, fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and testing, built by an automated pipeline with multi-model voting. Findings show aligned fine-tuning data steadies instruction following, while hard-case reinforcement data lifts hard-instance skill. A mid-size model trained on MHPR nearly matched far larger rivals.
arxiv-2605-03985:
Sudipta Mukherjee classifies irreducible Harish-Chandra modules over an extended divergence-zero Lie algebra. The algebra is built from the divergence-zero derivations of a Laurent polynomial algebra in several variables. It is extended by the algebra itself acting as a module. Harish-Chandra modules are representations with finite-dimensional weight spaces, the natural class for classification results in this area. Mukherjee requires the action of the nonzero part of the Laurent algebra to be nontrivial.

He proves every such module is either cuspidal or a generalized highest weight module. He further proves every irreducible generalized highest weight module is in fact an irreducible highest weight module with respect to a suitable triangular decomposition of the algebra. Together these results give a classification of the irreducible Harish-Chandra modules in the stated regime.
arxiv-2605-04185:
Qijun Liao, Zhaoxin Yu, and Jue Yang address a safety limit for robots that learn by trial and error. Each joint can only change speed or position by a set amount at each step. Those limits differ a lot from joint to joint, so a single round limit wastes much of the space a robot could safely use.

Their method gives each joint its own changing radius, matched to where the robot now stands. In simulated robot tests it kept every step within the hard limits, earned the highest task scores, and needed no extra solver while the robot was running.
arxiv-2605-04385:
John C. Howell and Andrew N. Jordan design a measurement system for finding the position of a faint light source by triangulation, aiming to approach the limit set by photon shot noise. Their point is not new physics, but that existing systems throw away information as signals move through the measurement chain.

They keep signals in analog form and cancel shared noise at several processing layers, using a combined camera and balanced detector. The setup reached nanometre-scale depth precision at a distance of well over a metre, with a short baseline. That is far better than camera-only systems. It is still about a hundred times above the shot noise limit.
arxiv-2605-04585:
Yen-Ting Liu and seven co-authors build a robot interaction system that accepts the casual, imprecise way people naturally communicate. Saying a vague phrase while glancing or pointing at an object is clear to a human partner, but robots usually demand exact, explicit commands.

Their system, designed for extended reality settings, combines voice, gaze, and finger-pointing, and uses a language model to filter out irrelevant channels and noisy readings. It then generates candidate instructions for the user to confirm, rather than acting on a guess. The flexible input is meant to cut the time, effort, and attention that human-like robot interaction normally demands.
arxiv-2605-04885:
Tanty Widiyastuti and five co-authors compare two approaches to detecting hate speech in Indonesian posts on Twitter, now called X. One approach uses PyCaret, an automated machine learning tool, with word counts and a list-based count of abusive words. The other is a neural network that reads phrases and context in both directions.

Both approaches used the same data preparation on a corpus of more than thirteen thousand labelled posts. The neural model won, reaching accuracy in the mid-eighties, while random forest was the best conventional model in the high seventies. The authors still call the task hard, since many posts turn on short local word cues.
arxiv-2605-04985:
Joao Batista Florindo and Amanda Pontes de Oliveira Ornelas propose a new way to pretrain image models for medical classification without large labelled datasets. Standard self-supervised methods hide random patches of an image, which can destroy the fine detail diagnosis depends on. Their Chaotic Denoising Autoencoder instead scrambles an image with a chaotic transformation and trains the model to undo it.

An attention-based fusion then merges features from this chaos-trained encoder with a standard encoder, combining general and domain-specific strengths. On skin lesion and diabetic eye disease datasets, the fused model reached accuracy above ninety and eighty-six percent respectively. The results support chaos-based pretraining for medical imaging.
arxiv-2605-05285:
Yazheng Liu and five co-authors reduce catastrophic forgetting in large language models by working out which parameters actually store earlier knowledge. Models learning tasks one after another degrade on the old ones, and existing fixes replay data, freeze parameters, or regularise blindly. None of those can tell knowledge-bearing parameters from free ones inside the model.

Their attribution-guided fine-tuning uses layer-wise relevance propagation to estimate each parameter's importance for previous tasks, following the model's own computation. Important parameters then receive smaller updates, while less relevant ones stay open for new learning. Experiments show less forgetting than baseline methods while keeping adaptability to new tasks, highlighting the value of mechanistic attribution.
arxiv-2605-05385:
Chapter 2 of a larger work on evolution models, by A. S. Bratus, S. Drozhzhin, and T. Yakushkina, studies the shape of the fitness surface in replicator systems. Replicator dynamics describe how strategies or types grow and shrink according to their payoffs. The fitness surface maps each state to the population's mean fitness.

The authors derive how fast mean fitness changes along a path, and when that change is always upward. Surprisingly, paths usually miss the surface's peak, even near a stable resting point. They give exact conditions for a resting point to be a peak, and link peaks to evolutionarily stable states.
arxiv-2605-05485:
Atharva Naik, Yash Mathur Prakam, Carolyn Rose, and David Mortensen present ReaComp, a way to turn language model reasoning into reusable solvers. Language models can synthesize programs, but hard cases demand huge searches and repeated model calls. ReaComp instead uses coding agents to compile a few reasoning traces into symbolic synthesizers that need no model at test time.

The compiled solvers reached about ninety-one percent accuracy on a lite benchmark and eighty-five percent on a hard one. Paired with model search, they raised hard-set accuracy while cutting token use sharply. They even transferred to a historical linguistics task, predicting sound changes in real languages.
arxiv-2605-05685:
Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks replace fixed activations with learnable curves on every connection, which should make them explainable. Naveen Mysore builds Temporal Functional Circuits to turn those curves into faithful explanations for forecasting. The framework sits on a gated residual network that splits each forecast into a linear base and a sparse learned correction.

Each connection is mapped to the input lags it reads and ranked by its activation range. Faithfulness is then tested by intervention: zeroing edges or removing the spline parts and watching the forecast change. Explanations that survive those tests earn trust; the rest are exposed as decoration.
arxiv-2605-06085:
Maxim Lyutikov simulates what happens inside electrically charged current layers in astrophysical plasmas. Such layers occur in pulsar winds, where the plasma holds equal numbers of electrons and positrons. While the plasma as a whole is charge symmetric, the layers themselves can carry charge, and that changes their stability.

Using particle in cell simulations, Lyutikov follows tearing and plasmoid formation in two layer types. Charged layers prove electrostatically unstable, and Bernstein waves arise fast inside them. Those waves shuffle charge early on but do not greatly change overall plasmoid growth, and the plasmoids end up mildly charged. In rotating layers, even layers that start uncharged develop large charge swings, and in some settings the tearing rate grows strongly.
arxiv-2605-06285:
Yijia Zheng and Marcel Worring move the reasoning of agentic retrieval systems out of written language and into latent space. Agentic retrieval answers hard questions through many rounds of thought and subqueries, but writing each step token by token makes the process slow. Single step retrieval is fast yet fails on complex questions, leaving a wide latency gap between the two styles.

LatentRAG produces latent tokens for thoughts and subqueries directly from hidden states in one forward pass. The language model is aligned with dense retrieval models in that latent space, so retrieval runs over latent subqueries and the whole system trains jointly. A parallel decoder translates latent tokens back into language for transparency. Across seven benchmarks it matched explicit agentic systems while cutting inference latency by about ninety percent.
arxiv-2605-06385:
Ana Leticia Garcez Vicente, Gijs van Seeventer, and Saber Salehkaleybar tackle covariate selection for causal effect estimation from observational data. Choosing a valid adjustment set is hard when hidden confounding and feedback loops are present. Most existing methods assume no cycles or require learning the whole causal structure first.

The authors study a local, data-driven method based on conditional independence tests. Known to be sound and complete without cycles, they prove its guarantees also hold in cyclic models, using invariance under a form of acyclification. Tests on synthetic data support the theory, giving one unified method for both settings.
arxiv-2605-06485:
Nii Osae Osae Dade and four co-authors present Litespark, a CPU inference framework for ternary language models whose weights take only the values minus one, zero, and plus one. Such models could remove the need for costly floating-point multiplication. Existing frameworks ignore that structure and treat the models as ordinary dense networks, wasting the advantage.

Custom SIMD kernels replace matrix multiplication with additions and subtractions using integer instructions on modern CPUs. The package installs with pip and plugs into Hugging Face tools. On Apple Silicon it reports much higher throughput, faster first tokens, and lower memory use than standard PyTorch, with larger gains on Intel and AMD chips.
arxiv-2605-06585:
Vinit Ranjan, Jisun Park, and Bartolomeo Stellato learn first-order optimization methods that stay reliable when problem data shift. Learning-to-optimize tunes step sizes and speeds on a set of problems, but tuned methods can fail on new instances. Their approach minimizes a robust version of the performance estimation problem, built for shifted data over a Wasserstein ball of distributions.

The framework blends between ordinary learned optimization and worst-case algorithm design as the robustness radius grows. Training uses stochastic gradients through an inner matrix program. Theory bounds the true risk by the training optimum plus a shrinking slack. On logistic regression, LASSO, and linear programming, the learned methods beat both extremes out of sample.
arxiv-2605-06685:
Jalbert-Desforges builds a pipeline that turns raw piano recordings into composer profiles based on information theory, the maths of surprise in patterns. It first transcribes audio into notes with a layer whose accuracy is certified on a standard benchmark. It covers 1,238 pieces by 15 composers with at least ten attributed pieces each, from the Baroque era into the early twentieth century.

From the counts the author derives Shannon entropy, a measure of unpredictability, and asymmetric Kullback Leibler divergence, which measures how far one style sits from another. He also fits Zipfian rank frequency models of pattern recurrence. The profiles order composers by harmonic predictability within a narrow entropy band, and recover lineages such as Haydn to Beethoven through the smallest divergences. They separate modern neoclassical artists from historical composers, with a clearly stronger mean Zipfian fit for the neoclassical group.
arxiv-2605-06885:
Fred Zhangzhi Peng, Alexis Fox, Anru R. Zhang, and Alexander Tong convert autoregressive language models into diffusion language models by matching their internal representations instead of training again from scratch. Diffusion models write in parallel and edit both ways, suiting left-to-right models. Earlier conversions leaned on more denoising training with changed goals and attention.

Their REPR-ALIGN loss matches the diffusion model's hidden states to a frozen autoregressive teacher's at every layer, beside the usual denoising loss, with no adapters or design changes beyond the attention mask. The switch trains up to four times faster in their setting and works most of all well with little data. The results suggest language representations carry across generation orders.
arxiv-2605-07085:
Sana Nakamichi and ten co-authors study a pressured Dirac semimetal near a quantum phase change. The material can shift toward a charge-ordered insulating state as pressure varies. The team measured how long electrons stay in phase when cold, using weak antilocalization in current flow.

At high pressure, the effect followed the usual pattern expected for flat conductors. Near the critical pressure, the temperature pattern weakened, yet coherence length stayed large. The authors read that odd scaling as a sign of unusual scattering among Dirac electrons near the critical point. Persistence of the effect also supports a transition without a full energy gap.
arxiv-2605-07185:
JaeWon Kim and Alexis Hiniker examine how metaphors shape the way young people think about digital privacy. Drawing on three earlier studies with participants aged 13 to 24, they look beyond settings panels. Different metaphor families led youth to reason about permissions, presence, and disclosure in markedly different ways.

Spatial metaphors made permission structures feel like moving through rooms, while embodied ones framed norms around access and intrusion. Fantastical metaphors made privacy playful and sparked detailed design ideas. Relational metaphors carried a risk: a system framed as a loyal companion may invite over-sharing. Choosing a metaphor, the authors argue, is an ethical design choice.
arxiv-2605-07285:
Harrison H Li transports a treatment effect from a small trial to a large observational population, even when the big dataset's outcome measures are biased. His method first scales a treatment-control contrast from the survey data against the trial using least squares, producing an estimated effect for each case. Averaging those figures over the survey data gives the final number.

Li shows the target is a weighted transported average effect even if the scaling model is off. The method's error bars stay valid and sharp when the trial grows more slowly than the survey set, with no overlap need between them. Test runs and a crop rotation study using satellite yield figures show stable results.
arxiv-2605-07385:
Hao Liu and six co-authors edit 3D assets locally by intervening inside the generator's sampling process itself. Other methods impose locality from outside with masks, merging, or multi-view lifting, leaving the corruption source untouched. For a flow-based generator, the velocity field should push hard on the edit region and stay silent elsewhere, which one field struggles to do.

Their VS3D framework, needing no training, inversion, or masks, adds three modules aimed at three failure modes. One anchors identity per step, and one amplifies genuine edit signals. A third lets the sampler decide, token by token, what to preserve during generation.
arxiv-2605-07585:
The ATLAS Collaboration describes the algorithms that reconstruct charged-particle tracks and collision vertices in the ATLAS Inner Detector at the Large Hadron Collider. Track reconstruction is a foundation of the experiment: nearly every measurement starts from knowing which particles passed through the detector and where they came from.

The paper documents the most recent software configuration used for data-taking and reports its measured performance. Results cover Run 2 data from 2015 to 2018, a subset of Run 3 data from 2022, and matching simulations. Even with up to eighty proton-proton interactions at once in one crossing, the software keeps high efficiency, good resolution on key parameters, and low rates of fake tracks.
arxiv-2605-07785:
Amy Rafferty and two co-authors make chest X-ray models reason the way radiologists do. Concept bottleneck models predict clinical concepts before a diagnosis, which aids reading, but most treat concepts as mere clues. Real clinical reasoning runs the other way: diseases produce the visible findings on the film.

Their model, XpertCausal, encodes that direction with a noisy-OR structure linking diseases to concepts, then runs it backward, Bayesian-style, to score diseases from predicted concepts. Expert-curated links constrain the model to plausible clinical pathways. On the MIMIC-CXR dataset it beat a non-causal baseline and a freer causal ablation on accuracy, calibration, and explanation quality. Its learned links also aligned more closely with expert knowledge.
arxiv-2605-07985:
Joon Ha Kim and three co-authors cut the cost of profiling language model serving, the measurements that feed inference simulators used to pick optimal configurations. Simulators normally hardcode their operation set to one configuration and re-profile everything from scratch, which makes exploring hardware, engines, and model variants prohibitively expensive.

Their system, Dooly, exploits structure: every operation's input dimensions are fixed either by the model configuration or by the incoming request, and configuration values recur across models. A single pass with taint propagation labels each dimension's origin, and only operations missing from the latency database get profiled. Across two GPU platforms and many architectures, Dooly matched simulator accuracy within a few percent while cutting profiling GPU-hours by more than half across twelve models.
arxiv-2605-08085:
Giorgos Eleftheriou, Ziming Ji, and Sameer Murthy study trace relations in matrix models that mix bosonic and fermionic variables. Such invariants underlie supersymmetric indices of gauge theories, and the fermionic versions behave in ways the bosonic ones do not.

Two differences drive the study. A Grassmann matrix raised to a high enough power vanishes, which creates many new trace relations. Fermionic trace relations can also make the index grow as the matrix size shrinks, the opposite of bosonic intuition. Focusing on one simple model tied to a quarter-BPS index in a well-known gauge theory, the authors prove the index is independent of matrix size and examine the cancellations behind it.
arxiv-2605-08185:
Aomar Osmani argues that a service robot ontology needs more than tidy terms. The Robotic Service Ontology gives typed terms for services, functions, interactions, and deployment limits. Its revision trail raises a harder question. After a service is rebound, repaired, or redeployed, when is the result still the same protected service?

Osmani embeds the ontology into the Structural Model of General Intelligence. That model adds a structural interface. It also adds rules for how a service may change and what its conduct means. The embedding yields an adequacy result. Service descriptions become objects that can be governed, not just well-formed labels. Their identity holds across change.
arxiv-2605-08385:
ElMouatez Billah Karbab presents MAGMA, a malware detector built to say how unsure it is. Deep learning detectors dominate the field, yet the author argues their blind spot is epistemic: they cannot express doubt, which leaves them open to structural evasion tricks.

MAGMA splits analysis into retrieval and verification. A dual-stream embedding over assembly and pseudo-code isolates decision-critical functions from dead code, and a stochastic consistency ensemble has several copies of one reasoning agent judge the retrieved evidence independently. Two metrics, including function evidence strength, aggregate those judgments into a quantified confidence. The design targets robust detection that knows when its evidence is thin.
arxiv-2605-08485:
Medha Agarwal and Alex Luedtke introduce a treatment effect measure that compares whole outcome distributions instead of averages alone. Built from smoothed optimal transport, the Sinkhorn treatment effect registers differences anywhere in the counterfactual distributions. The authors show it equals a smooth transformation of average embedded outcomes under a suitable kernel.

That smoothness yields valid debiased estimators and tests for distributional effects at fixed smoothing, with matching smoothness under the null of no difference. Because power depends on the unknown smoothing level, an aggregated test pools evidence across a grid of choices. Simulations and image data show practical gains. Causal inference gains a rigorous way to detect effects that averages wash out.
arxiv-2605-08685:
Li Na, Yuanyun Zhang, and Shi Li treat body signals as events, not as strings of small patches. Heart and blood waveforms gain meaning from long, linked events. The edges of those events are not marked in the signal. Their model learns by staying the same across random cuts of one signal. It also stays the same across time and pitch views. This guards event shape while it drops surface noise.

One part of the model codes each event. One part tracks how events link to each other. Shared event views also line up unlike signal types. On rhythm sorting, blood flow tasks, and waveform search, the model beats string based rivals. It wins on score, strength, and label thrift.
arxiv-2605-08785:
Pragun Jaswal, L. Hemanth Krishna, and B. Srinivasu build a reconfigurable multiplier inside a RISC-V processor for neural network inference on tight energy budgets. Their design switches at runtime between exact and approximate multiplication at several accuracy levels through a dedicated instruction, giving fine grained control of the energy versus accuracy trade within a normal pipeline.

Power falls by roughly half in exact mode and by about two thirds in approximate mode, while standard speed scores hold steady. On error tolerant workloads like convolution and matrix multiplication, total energy drops by up to about two thirds. Edge AI gains arithmetic that can spend precision only where the task actually needs it.
arxiv-2605-08885:
Chen Wang, Siyu Hu, Guangming Tan, and Weile Jia shrink atomistic foundation models that respect three dimensional rotation symmetry, without breaking the symmetry that makes them accurate. These equivariant networks pay heavily for higher order tensor operations. Their structural pruning cuts whole blocks along channel and order dimensions, keeping or removing each symmetry unit entire so rotational equivariance survives intact.

Starting from a large trained checkpoint beats training a small model from scratch: the pruned flagship wins on most leaderboard metrics, carries far fewer parameters, and needs far less pretraining compute. Fine tuned, it slashes energy and force errors versus task specific training, and the method transfers to other equivariant architectures and stacks with quantization.
arxiv-2605-08985:
Kechen Fang and six coauthors rethink how multi mode models code high grade shots. That stage rules the compute bill. The stock way codes the whole shot at once. It floods the model with visual marks. It then press cuts the marks, at full cost paid. Set tests flip the stock way twice. Slice views beat whole codes on test sets. They keep fine traits that whole views lose. Cuts made soon, in the sight net's thin layers, save a lot with downstream worth kept.

Their LLaVA-UHD v4 joins both gains in one scheme with a compute dial. On doc work, text reads, and broad asks, sight code cost falls by more than half. Scores match or top the base.
arxiv-2605-09085:
Zhijun Zeng and three co-authors seek one method for estimating probability patterns across very different kinds of data. Continuous values, discrete choices, and mixes of the two are usually handled by separate tools, even though the underlying task is the same.

Their framework, called Constant-Target Energy Matching, learns an energy score for each possible state. Instead of chasing density ratios, which can blow up for rare outcomes, it trains toward a fixed target of one using a bounded transformation. The learned score recovers the log-probability without extra normalization steps. Across tests on continuous, discrete, and mixed data, the method beat strong rivals at density estimation and produced better samples under standard sampling routines.
arxiv-2605-09185:
Zhiwei Liu leads ten co-authors in building AutoRedTrader, a system that attacks financial trading agents with subtle false information. Their 2026 study notes that language-model trading agents read both market numbers and text, and that financial misinformation often arrives as small textual nudges rather than plain falsehoods. The framework generates such material through bias manipulation, minor wording changes, and rewriting, using agent feedback to strengthen attacks over time.

Tests run in a simulated trading environment, with an added setting that grounds agents in historical market series to probe robustness. On Bitcoin transaction data, the authors report the strongest attack results among the methods compared, measured by how often false material is retrieved and how often it changes decisions. Removing any module weakens the attacks, showing each part contributes. The work gives defenders a systematic way to test whether market evidence can steady an agent fed misleading text.
arxiv-2605-09385:
Dziarmaga tackles the compression of loopy tensor networks, whose internal correlations often make compression inefficient. He shows that even local bond optimisation can use nearby information about relevant loop correlations. Cutting a bond defines a set of states whose linear links show up through a zero mode of the states' metric tensor and can be used to truncate the bond dimension.

Where no exact zero mode exists, a mix of a few of the lowest modes can instead be optimised to give the best approximation to a zero mode. The truncation needs no prior gauge fixing. The method is tried on two-dimensional finite-temperature Z 2 lattice gauge theory, with a thermal-state purification taking the form of an infinite projected entangled-pair state.
arxiv-2605-09885:
