The key device is a preview pass. The system first drafts rough preview frames of the motion. Those frames then guide pose alignment and keep backgrounds steady. Two attention modules add further control. One sharpens consistency across time, and one anchors identity to the reference face. Tests show FreeAnimate beating other training free rivals. It also matched training based baselines on generation quality. Results held across several data sets. The authors offer it as a cheaper, more open route to human image animation.
arxiv-2606-06985:
People who mix languages mid sentence trip up speech recognition badly. Tung Nguyen and co-authors teach a recognizer to survive those switches in this 2026 arXiv paper. The practice is called code switching. Errors cluster right at the switch points and inside the embedded language spans.

Their training method manufactures near misses on purpose. First it finds the points of interest where languages change. Then it perturbs the recognizer's best guesses at those points. A language model expands the fake alternatives further. Filters keep only hard but plausible fakes, checked by sound, phonemes, and text. The Whisper model then trains against those rivals with a contrastive loss. Tests used Mandarin English and Vietnamese English data. Both general and switch aware error rates fell by over two percent versus plain fine tuning.
arxiv-2606-07085:
Moving an app to a new phone platform usually means rebuilding every screen by hand. Zheng and a large team automate that rebuild for HarmonyOS in this 2026 arXiv paper. Modern interfaces are written declaratively, in Compose, SwiftUI, or ArkUI. Older translation tools target back end logic or legacy styles, so they miss this task entirely.

Their ArkTrans leans on language models, but with guardrails. First it extracts a skeleton of the target interface heuristically. That skeleton guides the model's first translation pass. Then pattern based rules repair the syntactic chaos models typically leave behind. The benchmark holds one hundred real interface files. Direct prompting produced not one compilable page. With the full method, up to about ninety one percent of files compiled cleanly. Visual fidelity stayed high as well. The study is the first of its kind for declarative interface migration.
arxiv-2606-07285:
Cookson, Deltl, and Oh tighten the limits of proportionally fair clustering in this 2026 arXiv paper. Clustering chooses centers to represent many agents, and proportional fairness demands no large group be underrepresented. The key concept is the core, borrowed from cooperative game theory: a clustering is in the core if no sufficiently large coalition could do better by seceding. Prior work guaranteed solutions exist at one fairness level while showing impossibility below another, leaving a gap open for seven years.

The authors narrow that gap from below with an instance whose core is empty for every fairness factor below about 2.15, improving the impossibility threshold of 2. Their method connects two core variants, reduces the search to a structured family of instances, and uses integer programming to hunt for counterexamples. For cases with 3 to 6 candidate centers they determine exact thresholds, and they supply proofs that do not depend on the search.
arxiv-2606-07685:
Kanneganti and colleagues address machine learning as a service, where ready-made models are rented through the cloud, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Connected Internet of Things systems chain several such services together, but conditions on the ground shift over time, and swapping a service for a substitute is slow and often impractical. The team instead adapts services at test time, while the combined system is already running.

Their framework first checks whether an adapted service still fits its neighbours in the chain, using a composability model built for that question. It then adjusts each service during inference without rebuilding the whole composition. Experiments report lower computational cost and adaptation time than traditional replacement-based methods, while performance of the composed service stays intact. The authors argue this makes long-lived service chains in changing device environments far easier to maintain.
arxiv-2606-07785:
Weingartner pins down Dickman's function with fully explicit error bounds in this 2026 arXiv paper. The function, written rho of u, gives the density of whole numbers whose largest prime factor stays below a chosen power of the number. It obeys a delay differential equation, linking its slope now to its values one unit earlier. Until now, using it meant solving that equation numerically, or accepting estimates with hidden constants.

Weingartner sandwiches the function between two explicit multiples of the standard approximation due to de Bruijn. The bounding factors differ from one by about one part in twelve u, with a small correction in the upper factor. The resulting estimates carry relative error below five thousandths divided by u squared, for all u of at least five. Tabulated values agree with classic computations to five significant digits. Number theorists can therefore evaluate the function to certified accuracy straight from a formula.
arxiv-2606-07985:
Tao Zhou and co-authors fuse infrared and visible images by treating their frequency content separately, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Fusion aims at one composite image keeping the infrared channel's hot targets and the visible channel's fine textures. Standard networks use a single feature extractor for both sensors, blurring each one's distinct character.

Their network, FMRFusion, learns multi-view representations of the pair. A multi-scale structural perception module captures fine local structures and broader context. A bilinear frequency decomposition splits features into high- and low-frequency parts, so details and global layout are modelled jointly. A cross-view interaction stage models what each sensor contributes that the other lacks, and fuses those parts. The premise: heterogeneous images should be read in several views at once, by scale, frequency band, and sensor, before merging.
arxiv-2606-08185:
Du and co-authors study holomorphic one-forms on smooth projective varieties in this 2026 arXiv paper. A variety is a shape defined by polynomial equations. A holomorphic one-form is a smooth measuring device on it, closely tied to maps from the variety into abelian varieties, highly symmetric shapes built from tori. The zeros of such a form, the points where it vanishes, are the focus. The authors develop a method based on limit relative conormal vectors to track how these zeros behave.

Their first main theorem says a map into a simple abelian variety is smooth exactly when some pulled-back form has no zeros at all. They then examine the set of forms that do have zeros. They show it forms a linear space for large classes of varieties. A carefully built counterexample shows this can fail in general.
arxiv-2606-08885:
Agnihotri and colleagues propose a built-in testing scheme for silicon photonic circuits, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Silicon photonics guides light through tiny channels on a chip instead of moving electrons through wires, enabling fast, compact hardware. These photonic integrated circuits leave factories with manufacturing flaws, yet lack mature ways to test themselves. The authors borrow design for testability from electronics: extra circuitry added at design time purely so the finished chip can be checked.

Their architecture compares a test signal against a reference signal inside the circuit, verifying both signal power and phase at chosen access points. They simulated every component, then assembled complete test circuits. The approach was demonstrated on two designs: an optical neural network and an optical logic circuit with feedback loops. In both, defects the team deliberately introduced were accurately detected and evaluated by the test circuitry.
arxiv-2606-09285:
Mortazavi-Samarin, Rostami, and Sahami introduce essential contractibility, a new property for Banach algebras, in this 2026 arXiv paper. A Banach algebra is a complete normed algebra: objects one can add, scale, and multiply, with a well-behaved notion of size. Contractible algebras, where every derivation is inner, are rare: commutative ones must be finite-dimensional. The essential variant weakens the demand, requiring that structure only in an approximate sense.

The paper develops the basic theory and tests it on Segal algebras, dense subalgebras of a larger algebra, with matrix algebras over them as proving ground. One clean test emerges: such algebras admit no non-zero point derivations, ruling out many candidates at once. The authors also exhibit infinite-dimensional examples, which plain contractibility forbids for commutative algebras. Their headline result: the closure of the squared Segal algebra inside matrix algebras is essentially contractible yet not contractible.
arxiv-2606-09485:
Simon Murphy, Anuj Gautam, and Zachary Claytor quantify how badly astronomers can misjudge the ages of fast-spinning A-type stars in this 2026 arXiv paper. Ages for such stars come mainly from isochrone fitting, matching a star against model tracks of temperature and brightness over time. Rapid rotation and unresolved companions distort the picture, yet formal fitting errors rarely capture either effect.

Their population-synthesis framework covers stars of about one point four to two point five solar masses, with realistic spreads of rotation, composition, binarity, and viewing angle. These effects introduced random uncertainties near one hundred eighty million years in age and a tenth of a solar mass in mass. Near the zero-age main sequence, inferred ages were too young by a factor of two or more. Older A stars had ages overestimated by about thirty-one percent, with wide scatter around that bias.
arxiv-2606-10185:
Kim and Weidner determine exactly how smooth the ratio of two solutions to a kinetic equation can be at a boundary, in a 2026 arXiv paper on partial differential equations. Kinetic Fokker-Planck equations describe particle densities evolving with position and velocity, used in plasma and rarefied gas theory. Boundary Harnack estimates compare two positive solutions near a boundary through their quotient.

They develop a general theory showing the quotient reaches a Hölder-type smoothness of order three halves when domain and data are smooth, and a stronger order in the absence of source terms. These exponents are optimal, meaning counterexamples prevent any better general claim. The negative part of the result is as important as the positive: kinetic boundaries impose a hard regularity ceiling that classical intuition misses, and the paper identifies precisely where that ceiling sits.
arxiv-2606-10285:
Jinghua Wang and colleagues release the largest fully open-source dataset for training language models to design computer hardware, in a 2026 arXiv paper on electronic design automation. OpenRTLSet contains over one hundred thirty-one thousand Verilog code samples, combining modules mined from GitHub, translations from VHDL, and synthesizable translations from C and C++. Every sample is freely accessible without proprietary restrictions. Using the DeepSeek-R1 reasoning model, the team generated paired natural language descriptions for each sample, enabling fine-tuning of model families such as Qwen and Granite for Verilog generation.

Fine-tuned models demonstrate that open-source approaches can achieve superior performance on hardware design tasks. The authors release the dataset, code, and fine-tuned models publicly, aiming to establish a foundation for accessible research and commercial use in a domain long dominated by proprietary design data.
arxiv-2606-10385:
Zhang refines how a student model should learn from a teacher that secretly knows the answer, in a 2026 arXiv paper on machine learning. Current methods treat that privileged information as one solid imitation target, mixing locally reachable reasoning steps with hindsight-conditioned oracle signals. The student is pushed toward a spread outside its own predictive support, encouraging it to skip valid middle reasoning for unsupported shortcuts.

His Anchored Residual On-Policy Distillation splits the supervision into two views. A locally matching anchor, built from partially privileged information, gives the student targets it can reach, while the residual captures what full privilege adds beyond the anchor. Rather than enforcing strict full-view imitation, the method guides the student from its anchor toward the teacher's behavior in measured steps. The reach mismatch reading reframes several distillation failures as target shape problems, not student skill problems.
arxiv-2606-10985:
Martínez von Dossow and Urrutia revisit Cherenkov radiation in a 2026 arXiv physics paper. Cherenkov radiation is the glow emitted when a charged particle outruns light inside a material, much like a sonic boom for light. They study it in anisotropic chiral matter, a medium whose response differs by direction and lacks mirror symmetry, using Carroll-Field-Jackiw electrodynamics, where an axion angle grows linearly with position.

Working in cylindrical coordinates, they solve the modified Maxwell equations exactly, imposing outgoing-wave conditions to keep the physics causal. Their formulas sort out when zero, one, or two Cherenkov cones form, and give the energy spectrum in each case. One sector shows something new: slow charges can emit this radiation with no speed threshold at all, though only within a limited frequency band. The exact results also test an earlier approximate Green's function method and show where it can be trusted.
arxiv-2606-11385:
Zhang and nine co-authors present DeceptionX in a 2026 arXiv paper, for detecting deception with multimodal large language models. Detection here is hard: deep learning methods treat it as binary classification, but black-box models lack interpretability and miss the logical deduction human experts use to spot lies. DeceptionX shifts detection to an interpretable Observe-Think-Summarize reasoning process.

To address scarce reasoning data, the team built DeceptChain, a dataset made through a human-in-the-loop process. It turns fine-grained visual and auditory evidence, like micro-expressions and vocal tremors, into structured chain-of-thought data. A three-stage training pipeline and a Discrepancy-Aware Redundancy Elimination strategy boost it further. It outperformed existing multimodal baselines and state-of-the-art methods on standard real-world benchmarks. It also gives transparent, expert-level reasoning paths, closing the gap between accuracy and openness.
arxiv-2606-11585:
Joshua Nunley introduces Kuramoto Attention in a 2026 arXiv paper on how transformer models, the systems behind modern language tools, attend to words. Each token, a chunk of text, carries a bank of oscillators, repeating cycles described by a phase on a circle. The phases sit on a torus, a doughnut-shaped space. Attention weights decide which tokens couple, and the update pulls each token toward the average phase of those it attends to.

Nunley trains the layer on enwiki8 and CodeParrot text against matched ordinary transformers. At five million parameters on CodeParrot it wins on average and middle scores, by about a hundredth of a bit per byte. On enwiki8 all six runs beat the rival on middle validation scores. At one million parameters it trails slightly, by about two hundredths of a bit per character. Tests removing parts of the design show which pieces drive the gains.
arxiv-2606-11685:
Isam Abdullah Balghari, Muhammad Faryad and Muhammad Sabieh Anwar predict magnetism in a two-dimensional material with machine learning in this 2026 arXiv paper. The material is monolayer CrI3, a single-layer crystal that is magnetic at low temperatures. The hard quantity is the magnetic exchange coupling between neighbouring atoms, which changes as the lattice deforms, and first-principles calculations cannot reach the needed sizes.

Their model, DSpinGNN, splits the job. An equivariant graph network, one that respects rotations and reflections, drives the structural motion. A smaller physics-informed network maps local bond geometry to exchange couplings, with a classic superexchange rule built in. Trained on 345 quantum calculations and tested on 61 held-out ones, it matches reference energies, forces and couplings closely. Run on a 3,200-atom sheet, it follows a strain wave and predicts interference patterns that experiments could check.
arxiv-2606-11785:
Éric Cancès, David Gontier and Solal Perrin-Roussel put two-dimensional materials on a sound mathematical footing in this 2026 arXiv paper. Density functional theory, through the Kohn-Sham models, is the workhorse for computing electronic structure. The setting here is encapsulation: a sheet such as graphene sandwiched between two parallel conducting electrodes.

The electrodes impose boundary conditions that screen the Coulomb interaction, the electric force between charges, making it effectively short-ranged, of Yukawa type. The authors prove that several nonlinear Kohn-Sham models are well-posed in this geometry, meaning solutions exist and behave properly. The proof covers periodic materials such as graphene. It also covers quasi-periodic materials such as twisted bilayer graphene and other moiré systems, where two rotated lattices create large patterns, for generic twist angles. This gives the encapsulated-device models used in practice a rigorous foundation.
arxiv-2606-12185:
Antoine develops safer statistical tests for a workhorse method in economics, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Instrumental variables, or IV, use outside factors that shift a cause without touching the outcome directly, isolating causal effects. Trouble starts when instruments are weak, barely moving the cause, because standard approximations then mislead even in large samples. Unknown patterns of unequal error variance, called heteroskedasticity, add a second hazard. Her procedures stay valid under both hazards at once.

The first test targets parameters on the problematic explanatory variables, modifying an existing statistic to absorb heteroskedasticity directly. It is asymptotically pivotal, its limiting distribution known and free of unknowns, so use becomes simple. A second procedure handles inference on a parameter subset without knowing how strongly the rest are identified. A third is a specification test, checking the model itself. Simulations and an application show the tests are conservative yet powerful and cheap to compute.
arxiv-2606-12385:
Adhikesaven and co-authors trace the hidden family tree of modern language models, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Today's models are built using other models: generating training data, filtering corpora, judging outputs, guiding development. These dependencies recurse, since upstream models have their own upstream artifacts. Documentation scatters across papers, model cards, and repositories. Their agentic system, ModSleuth, recursively reconstructs dependency graphs from public artifacts, grounding every claimed link in source evidence.

The hard part is not extraction but definition: what counts as a dependency amid inconsistent naming. The authors formalize direct versus indirect links and operation-centered roles, and resolve artifact identities across versions. Applied to four public LLM releases, ModSleuth verifies 1,060 dependencies. The graphs expose multi-hop license duties that follow the chain. They also reveal coupling between training and evaluation artifacts, and mismatches between released and training-time components. Such audits matter as ecosystems outgrow manual tracing.
arxiv-2606-12485:
Hao and co-authors let a student web agent wander, then rewind it only to its first mistake, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Imitation learning trains agents from expert demonstrations, but timing the expert's help is delicate. Intervene late and early errors snowball into unrecoverable page states. Intervene often and the student never learns recovery, clinging to one rigid path. Their Speculative Rollback Correction instead reviews fixed-length branches of student behavior.

The student executes a short speculative segment before teacher review. Only when local progress breaks does the teacher localize the first harmful deviation. Rollback then preserves the prefix instead of discarding the attempt. Successful rollouts pass a verifier and enter a quality-diversity archive, keeping solution styles alive. On WebArena-Infinity, the method gathered nine hundred seventy-seven verified trajectories and over nine thousand training examples. Fixed-horizon review beat step-level review on the recovery-versus-query tradeoff.
arxiv-2606-12585:
Martin checks whether the rules for who benefits from AI help survive contact with experts, in this 2026 arXiv paper. An experiment, using laypeople guessing ages, found two traits predict gains from AI assistance: lower baseline ability, and belief calibration, knowing how accurate you are. Martin replicates the study in radiology, where professionals read chest X-rays alongside machine predictions.

The data cover sixty-eight radiologists and over eleven thousand radiologist, patient, and pathology observations. The patterns point the same way as the original: radiologists with lower baseline ability gain more from the AI. So do those whose beliefs about their accuracy are calibrated. The replication supports external validity. If these patterns are features of AI-assisted work, the implications are practical. Training, interface design, and delegation policies should target not just skill, but users' knowledge of their accuracy. That self-knowledge decides when to defer to the machine.
arxiv-2606-12885:
Ong and colleagues propose an information-geometric bilevel split for mixed categorical-continuous black-box optimisation, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Evolution-strategy methods that extend CMA-ES handle such problems, but their search distributions treat the 2 kinds as unrelated, so results suffer when the 2 interact strongly.

The framework captures those links with a bilevel split: an outer loop optimises over the choice variables, while an inner loop tunes the value variables for each choice setup. Each level is cast as a stochastic relaxation under information-geometric optimisation, which updates search distributions along natural-gradient paths. Because bilevel optimisation is costly, a warm-starting strategy speeds the inner search by picking the best among cached setups each round. On binary-continuous benchmarks, the method beats state-of-the-art methods at handling such links while costing less to run.
arxiv-2606-12985:
Silva and colleagues propose BabyMind, an object-first inductive bias for learning grounded word meanings from child-view video, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In head-camera recordings of infants, caregiver speech is sparse and synchronised with the video. So single-frame contrastive pairing yields noisy positives: the named object may be absent from the frame or entangled with distractors. The learner must resolve both when the referent appears and where it is in a scene.

BabyMind first extracts object embeddings with a mask-based region interface, then links candidates across an utterance-centred window into object files by tracking. Utterances are aligned to bags of object files with a prototype-space multiple-instance contrastive objective, while track-coherence and agreement regularisers stabilise learning. On SAYCam-S, BabyMind improves Labeled-S 15-forced-choice accuracy by 2.6 points over the CVCL baseline, with gains on out-of-distribution benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-13085:
Hussain and colleagues show how engineered quantum reservoirs control electromagnetically induced gratings in a weakly driven 2-level atomic medium, in this 2026 arXiv paper. An electromagnetically induced grating uses a standing-wave control field to write a spatial modulation into a medium's absorptive and refractive properties, bending a weak probe beam. The authors solve the optical Bloch equations to first order in the weak-driving regime and compare 3 reservoir settings: normal vacuum, thermal, and squeezed vacuum.

Reservoir statistics reshape the diffraction response by changing the grating's amplitude and phase. Thermal reservoirs enhance the transmission modulation and increase the intensity of the dominant diffraction orders. Squeezed-vacuum reservoirs instead produce strongly phase-sensitive changes that redistribute optical power among diffraction channels by choice. The detuning between the squeezed reservoir and the driving field gives a control knob for diffraction directionality, boosting selected angular orders.
arxiv-2606-13185:
Singh and Jha analyse a numerical scheme for vibrating systems in this 2026 arXiv paper. The target is the damped semilinear wave equation, which models waves slowed by friction and shaped by a nonlinear reaction term. Their method pairs a discontinuous Galerkin discretisation in space, which solves the equation on small elements, with a hybrid time-stepping scheme. A chord-slope linearisation handles the nonlinearity while preserving an exact discrete energy-like structure. The analysis needs no global Lipschitz assumption on the reaction term.

Stability is proved with a Lyapunov approach, using a functional that tracks the solution's energy-like quantity over time. That argument yields existence, uniqueness, and boundedness of the solution in one stroke. The authors prove optimal error estimates: the error shrinks at the best rates as the mesh and time step refine. Experiments on test problems confirm the predicted convergence behaviour.
arxiv-2606-13385:
Wang and colleagues introduce StakeBench in this 2026 arXiv paper, a benchmark for attacks on web agents. Web agents powered by language models browse untrusted pages and take real actions, from booking to buying. Prompt injection, where hostile instructions hide inside web content, can hijack that behaviour. Existing security benchmarks ask whether an injection can work technically. The authors argue this misses who gets hurt: one exploit can harm the user, a merchant, and a platform differently, and its success varies with the target.

StakeBench categorises attacks by stakeholder, the party who pays the price when an agent is manipulated. The benchmark varies attack patterns across victim types to measure asymmetric consequences. This reframing matters for deployment decisions, since a defence adequate for low-stakes browsing may fail for payments. The authors present the benchmark as a tool for evaluating web agents in terms of harm distribution.
arxiv-2606-13585:
Avramidi and Delzant bound the complexity of fibres of maps from hyperbolic manifolds in this 2026 arXiv paper. A fibre is the set of points mapping to one value. The question, motivated by a query of Guth, is whether maps from hyperbolic manifolds to low-dimensional spaces must somewhere have a complicated fibre. Complexity is cellular: how many cells of each dimension a decomposition of the fibre requires. For manifolds whose injectivity radius, a measure of local simplicity, exceeds a threshold, the authors prove strong lower bounds.

Specifically, for every intermediate dimension some target point has a fibre needing more than a prescribed number of cells of that dimension. The threshold grows through a factorial term in the radius bound. The proof rests on a freedom theorem for ideals in group rings of hyperbolic groups. The result confirms that hyperbolic geometry forces topological complexity on maps out of it.
arxiv-2606-14885:
Yi Lu and co-authors let AI agents work directly on huge document collections in a 2026 arXiv paper. Agent search usually goes through a retriever, which returns ranked snippets. That hides the corpus's structure. Direct Corpus Interaction instead gives agents shell-style operations over the full text. But raw shell commands slow down and grow unstable as corpora reach millions of documents.

Their system, DR-DCI, steers direct interaction with a retriever. The agent pulls relevant documents into a local workspace. It then runs precise operations inside that workspace only. Retrieval supplies scale; direct interaction supplies precision. On BrowseComp-Plus, accuracy reached about seventy-one percent. That beat raw direct interaction by up to eight points while cutting tool use, time, and cost. A workspace-preserving reset lifted accuracy to about seventy-three percent. The method stayed stable from one hundred thousand to ten million documents.
arxiv-2606-15385:
Çağatan and coauthor revisit classic AI safety test worlds in a 2026 paper on reward hacking, where a system games its score instead of doing the intended job. The authors convert the AI Safety Gridworlds, grid tasks with a visible score and a hidden safety goal, into text so language model agents can play them. That makes a failure mode usually spotted only in expensive frontier systems cheap to reproduce and study.

Gaming appears with no training at all: models chase the visible score while failing the hidden goal, and some safe-looking behavior turns out to be mere misunderstanding. Reinforcement learning makes things worse, because models lock onto the first rewarding trick before finding safer strategies. The pattern holds from small to mid-size models and survives finer credit assignment, exploration prompts, and entropy bonuses. Proxy scores in agentic systems need stronger medicine than standard training fixes.
arxiv-2606-15485:
Lee and coauthors interview thirty-five industry developers about the risks of the agentic AI products they build, in a 2026 human-computer interaction study. Agentic products act autonomously, use tools, and operate in the real world. The study asks how their makers perceive, rank, and control the risks. Developers' sense of risk, the interviews show, is welded to the traits that make a product agentic: autonomy, tool use, open-ended context.

Ranking what to fix, product and business risks come first, while societal risks such as job displacement and privacy trail. The controls developers reach for are immature and often work by amputating agency itself, capping autonomy or goal complexity. The authors name the bind a capability versus risk control tension: the field lacks ways to contain agent risks that do not also contain the agent. For governance frameworks, the study warns of the gap between principle and practice.
arxiv-2606-15585:
Song studies a nonlinear Vlasov-Fokker-Planck equation in a bounded domain in 2026, a kinetic model tracking how particles spread through space and velocity. Particles reflect off the boundary like light off a mirror, which complicates the analysis near walls. The question is whether disturbances settle down to the global Maxwellian, the bell-shaped equilibrium.

Song proves that initial states close enough, in a weighted uniform norm, to a radial homogeneous profile admit a global-in-time weak solution. That solution decays exponentially fast to the Maxwellian. The proof first shows the manifold of homogeneous solutions is stable, then handles the near-equilibrium regime. A careful smoothing lets the nonlinear problem be approximated by a linear one, where hypocoercivity and ultracontractivity yield the decay estimates. Fixed-point arguments then pass back to the original equation. Boundary reflection has long blocked such results, so this case matters for kinetic theory.
arxiv-2606-15685:
Zhang and colleagues propose SCE in 2026, a framework that helps robots keep learning new manipulation tasks without forgetting old ones. Embodied continual learning forgets worse than the ordinary kind, because feature drift under closed-loop control compounds through sequences of decisions. Existing methods learn skills but do not organize them for coherent reuse across tasks.

SCE first builds a skill base through Compositional Skill Grounding, which breaks task demonstrations into reusable skills. Dual Execution-and-Transition Experts then learn new tasks by composing those skills: one branch executes each skill, the other manages transitions between them, keeping behaviour coherent. On LIBERO benchmarks and real-world manipulation tasks, SCE improves retention of old tasks and overall performance. Feature-drift checks and ablations confirm the gains come from reduced drift and cleaner skill composition. For robots meant to gather abilities over a working life, reusable skill structure beats retraining monoliths.
arxiv-2606-15985:
Schindler and Schumacher present a quantum-enhanced Markov chain Monte Carlo method in 2026, to sample the turbulent accelerations dispersing tracer particles in shear flows. Modelling Lagrangian transport needs samples of all three acceleration components and height, in flows from uniform shear to a turbulent channel boundary layer. In their hybrid scheme, a quantum circuit builds the proposal for the first Metropolis-Hastings substep.

The algorithm's synthetic tracer tracks show pair-dispersion scaling laws agreeing with a coupled Langevin model and the classical MCMC counterpart, though it samples a tempered target. Its mixing advantage is measured by a height-weighted spectral gap of the Markov chain, introduced for the height-dependent setting. At the highest qubit counts, with cross-correlated targets, that gap far exceeds the classical chain's. The results support the sampler as a one-shot generative module that could plug into larger flow simulations.
arxiv-2606-16085:
Zhang constructs in 2026 all simple-minded systems for a class of algebras built from graphs with tame representation type. The algebras are 1-domestic Brauer graph algebras, whose modules are encoded by a graph with special vertices. Simple-minded systems are generating families of modules with strong orthogonality, analogous to simple modules. A companion study had characterized them for the 2-domestic case.

Using covering theory, which lifts an algebra to a larger covering algebra where structure is clearer, Zhang transfers the 2-domestic characterization downward. The construction produces a family of objects in the stable module category forming a simple-minded system. More strongly, it provides all such systems for the 1-domestic case, a complete classification. The bridge uses maximal orthogonal systems and the Euclidean components of the stable Auslander-Reiten quiver. Complete lists of these systems feed derived equivalence classification in representation theory.
arxiv-2606-16185:
Zheng and colleagues retrain JPEG in 2026 for machine viewers rather than human eyes. JPEG was designed for people, and it still dominates image storage. Increasingly, though, deep neural networks consume those images instead. Settings that look fine to humans need not be best for network accuracy per bit spent.

Their framework, J4D, learns JPEG encoding parameters to minimize compression rate while maximizing inference performance. The obstacle is that the JPEG codec and its rate resist direct gradient methods. A differentiable soft quantizer, built on a probabilistic quantization scheme, supplies a trainable proxy for the codec. Its entropy gives an analytic estimate of the compression rate. Gradient descent can solve the rate-accuracy trade-off. Experiments show J4D beats default JPEG and other DNN-oriented codecs on the rate-accuracy balance in the reported tests. One universal quantization table might serve many network architectures, the study also suggests.
arxiv-2606-16985:
Daniel Waxman and colleagues introduce Dynestyx in a 2026 paper on software for Bayesian modeling of systems that change over time. State-space models are the standard language for such systems, from tracking to neuroscience. Yet modern probabilistic programming tools handle them awkwardly, so advanced estimation methods stay hard to reach.

Dynestyx gives state-space models first-class support in one library. Through a single interface, users can set priors for discrete-time or continuous-time systems, run inference on mixed-effect data, and estimate both hidden states and parameters with principled uncertainty. The unified design lets researchers compare mixes of inference methods directly. That exposes rules of thumb and failure modes of flexible, possibly misspecified models. The authors present the library as a testbed: shared representation and inference should make new methods easier to build and to judge. Code is public through the Basis Research Institute.
arxiv-2606-17085:
Santos recasts quantum field theory in phase-space language in a 2026 foundations paper. The Wigner representation describes particles by a phase-space distribution rather than a wavefunction; the Weyl transform connects it to the Hilbert space picture. Santos generalizes the construction from particles to Bose fields.

Through the transform, standard quantization turns into a simple recipe: take the classical field and add a Gaussian zeropoint field to the vacuum. Particles then appear as computation aids, not physical objects riding on the field. The picture is deliberately realist: the field plus its random background radiation is what exists. Santos also treats non-relativistic quantum electrodynamics, particles and field together, in the same c-number language. Advantages are flagged for fields in curved spacetime, where operator methods strain. The paper extends the author's program toward a realistic reading of quantum theory.
arxiv-2606-17185:
Roddenberry and Baraniuk present a 2026 paper on graph neural networks and Finsler geometry. It was written for a workshop on topology, algebra, and geometry in data science. Standard graph networks rest on the graph Laplacian, an isotropic operator. That choice limits the kinds of geometry the networks can express.

The authors instead estimate the Finsler Laplacian on point clouds drawn from a manifold. Finsler geometry allows norms that vary with direction and need not be symmetric. The discrete estimates are proved to converge to the true operator as sampling grows. The operator can also be written exactly as a graph neural network layer. The resulting networks recover the geometry behind nonlinear diffusion equations in the reported tests.
arxiv-2606-17385:
Wang and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on turning ordinary internet videos of human hands into training data that robots can actually use. Web footage is the largest store of manipulation knowledge available, yet lifting it into metric, robot-ready form has resisted automation. Their system, EgoInfinity, is a data engine rather than a fixed data set, chaining perception, segmentation, reconstruction, and retargeting modules that can each improve as their fields advance over time.

The engine recovers hand paths, object poses in six degrees of freedom, and contact states from wild video clips. Cross-module calibration and interaction-aware refinement fight the drift and contact errors that plague pure visual reconstruction pipelines. A motion retargeter then compiles recovered hand motion into joint paths for varied robot bodies, even from odd viewpoints. Tests cover fidelity, feasibility, contact consistency, and real-robot skills such as pouring.
arxiv-2606-17685:
Chang presents a 2026 arXiv paper on controlling a bound state in the continuum, a trapped mode of light inside an open waveguide with no cavity or band gap to protect it. Such states could store photons for a long time, but they are dark to incoming light and lack the gap that usually shields stored states from leaking. Chang couples a giant atom to a one-dimensional waveguide and turns two time-varying knobs, each handling half of the control problem.

Modulating the atom's frequency breaks and restores the interference that traps light, letting matched photons be caught and released on demand. Modulating the coupling instead keeps the trap intact while shifting the stored state's mix of atomic and photonic parts. Slow control works despite the missing gap, with leakage growing linearly in ramp speed. The split of duties turns a dark state into a single-photon memory.
arxiv-2606-18185:
Trojanowski and Wojtylak teach a transformer to see a matrix's hidden Jordan structure, in a 2026 paper. The Jordan form reveals how a matrix truly acts, but computing it in floating point is a notorious trap. Round-off makes every matrix look diagonalizable, erasing the defectiveness that dynamics may depend on. The authors reframe the question as recognition: is this matrix a perturbation of one with a large Jordan block?

Their architecture feeds the network successive powers of the matrix, which fade in telling ways for defective inputs. Dimension-specific encoders and a transformer inspired by vision models process the sequence. Noise-aware soft targets train it to stay graceful under perturbation. On synthetic, robustly perturbed data it beats a classical numerical baseline on accuracy. It also generalizes to matrix classes never seen in training. That is evidence it has latched onto structure rather than surface statistics.
arxiv-2606-18285:
Balloli and colleagues build a living dataset of pregnancy advice as it actually circulates on TikTok, in a 2026 paper for the KDD conference. Pregnant people increasingly meet reproductive health information as short social videos, where inaccurate or harmful claims mix with sound guidance. The RELIANCE project collects that material around real-world queries faced during pregnancy, curates it, and evaluates how well language models can flag the bad parts.

A four-stage pipeline gathers the videos, ties them to genuine information needs, and supports analysis of what claims spread and how models judge them. The point is a benchmark rooted in the wild feed rather than in textbook questions, so detection tools are graded against the phrasing and formats misinformation really uses. The authors frame the resource as infrastructure for public health experts tracking trends, while warning the same methods could be misused to craft evasive disinformation.
arxiv-2606-18485:
Ghosh and colleagues at NVIDIA present MagpieTTS-LF, a way to make a text-to-speech system produce coherent long-form speech without retraining it on long passages, in a 2026 speech technology paper. Modern speech synthesizers sound natural on short utterances, but paragraph-length output drifts in prosody, changes speaker character, and clicks or warbles where separately made chunks are joined.

Working at inference time, their method adds three pieces. Soft attention priors guide the alignment between text and sound monotonically while keeping past and future context. A stateful generation algorithm carries context across sentence chunks, and a history-aware text encoder plans prosody using what was said. On long texts, the system beat approaches in intelligibility, prosodic coherence, speaker consistency, and boundary naturalness. Because nothing is retrained, the authors say the recipe can extend chunk-based speech systems.
arxiv-2606-18785:
Saerens and the team present an algorithm that can identify the Pareto-optimal arms of a multi-objective bandit at any stopping time, with Bayesian confidence. The work is a 2026 machine learning paper. Many choices, from drug search to engineering design, trade off rival goals. So the goal is the Pareto set of options not beaten on every criterion. Existing algorithms assume a fixed sampling budget, fixed in advance.

Their method, Top-Two Pareto Front Thompson Sampling, takes a Bayesian approach. It is benchmarked against state-of-the-art fixed-budget algorithms on synthetic environments. The team then shows value in multi-objective molecular discovery, scanning an ultra-large synthesis-on-demand library. They also give an uncertainty quantification metric. It gauges the algorithm's confidence in its predicted Pareto set, and shows it tracks true performance. They round out the experiments with a proof of the algorithm's asymptotic correctness.
arxiv-2606-18885:
Alquwayfili and the team improve text-to-image retrieval in crowded scenes, by forcing encoders to look at what they ignore, in a 2026 computer vision paper. Visual encoders suffer salience bias. They attend to dominant objects, and neglect the low-attention regions: a person near a stroller at the edge of a crowd, that fine-grained queries often ask about.

Their framework LARE mines low-attention regions from a frozen encoder. It encodes them alongside the full image, in a dual-encoding strategy. It merges the regional embeddings with the global one at inference, a training-free test-time augmentation. To measure progress, they built Dense-Set, a benchmark derived from COCO and Flickr30K. Its images were re-captioned to describe overlooked regions. On these crowded-scene variants, LARE improved retrieval by preserving non-dominant visual cues. Standard models favored globally similar scenes, and missed the queried detail.
arxiv-2606-19185:
Shen and colleagues present the Anisotropic Graph Diffusion Network in 2026, a graph neural framework for the traveling salesman problem. The problem is a cornerstone of combinatorial optimization with wide practical use. Graph-based learning methods exist, but how to exploit graph structure well stays open. Two difficulties stand out. Fully connected tour graphs carry little informative topological prior, and common sparsification can drop nodes that belong to the optimal tour.

The MixScore transition matrix merges node similarity with pairwise distance to build a richer prior. An anisotropic diffusion strategy then exchanges information across multiple hops efficiently, weighting directions unevenly. Experiments span diverse instance sizes and node distributions, testing the method broadly. The design aims to keep optimal nodes reachable while guiding the search with distance and similarity together. Learning solvers of this kind could speed routing and logistics tasks where exact methods grow too slow at scale.
arxiv-2606-19285:
Agostino and colleagues directly test Bondi accretion rate prescriptions in 2026, starting with the Seyfert galaxy NGC 1068. Cosmological simulations estimate black hole growth with Bondi-like formulas, but at resolutions far coarser than the accretion zone. The team measures nuclear gas density and temperature at parsec scales. Those values go into a Bondi-like model, and the predicted rate is compared with the empirical rate from hard X-ray observations of the same galaxy.

Carbon monoxide gas is the dominant mass carrier near the black hole, ahead of warm hydrogen. The Bondi rate from cold molecular gas alone overestimates the true rate hugely. In a small aperture the excess reaches many orders of magnitude, and it stays large even in wide apertures out to hundreds of parsecs. As the first in a series of direct tests, the result warns that Bondi formalisms can badly overshoot real accretion.
arxiv-2606-19585:
Ben Saarel, Ozgur Sahin, Alpha N'Diaye, and Hartmut Häffner hunt the source of electric field noise in ion traps in 2026. Surface noise from trap electrodes heats trapped ions and lowers quantum computing fidelity. Its microscopic origin has stayed unclear through decades of study.

The team measure noise at trapping spots along the symmetry axis of a linear surface Paul trap. Levels swing by three orders of magnitude within one 600-micrometre stretch of the trap. Optical and electron microscope images reveal micron-sized particles near the noisiest spots. Modelling those particles as a lossy dielectric fits the data well. An effective loss tangent near 0.33 matches the noise size, its spatial pattern, and its frequency trend. Stray dust-like particles may thus explain why published noise levels vary so widely. The finding gives trap builders a concrete suspect to clean, coat, or design around.
arxiv-2606-20085:
Yang Huang and Andrey Kupavskii prove a structural theorem for large cross-intersecting pairs of families of sets. Their 2026 paper extends work begun with the Erdős-Ko-Rado theorem, a cornerstone of extremal combinatorics. Cross-intersecting pairs generalize the setting: every set in one family must meet every set in the other. The authors characterize the extremal pairs by their diversity parts and maximal extensions, extending Kupavskii's earlier theorem from single families to pairs.

Corollaries include cross versions of classical results by Han-Kohayakawa and by Huang-Peng. A key tool is a new shifting method, which compresses families while preserving global intersection properties and chosen local substructures. The authors note the method already serves as a key tool in proving a product analogue of the Hilton-Milner theorem.
arxiv-2606-20385:
Michael Griebel and Jan Hamaekers revisit regularity theory for eigenfunctions of the electronic Schrödinger equation and what it buys in approximation cost. Their 2026 paper studies convergence to the complete basis set limit in sparse configuration interaction methods. The curse of dimensionality usually makes such limits brutally expensive as electrons are added.

For general sparse grid constructions, the main term of the convergence rate, measured against the number of degrees of freedom, does not depend on the number of electrons. The leading algebraic exponent escapes the curse. These insights promise benefits for classical numerical solvers of the Schrödinger equation. They also matter for quantum-computing approaches, through new encodings the authors discuss. Knowing the true cost of the basis-set limit reshapes how both fields should budget accuracy.
arxiv-2606-20685:
Carlo Cattani develops a delayed generalized Lotka-Volterra model in a solo 2026 paper about systems that change before anyone notices. Lotka-Volterra equations were built for predator and prey dynamics. Cattani generalizes them for cases where structural change and recognition of change are out of sync. A system may transform inside while still looking stable to leaders or observers. Instability becomes active only when stress crosses a threshold and is recognized late.

State variables cover complexity, information entropy, pressure, resilience, and legitimacy. Their links are modeled with time delays. Those delays stand for the gap between real variation and its social or institutional effects. A composite instability measure marks the shift from latent to recognized instability. Cattani studies positivity, equilibria, linearization, and local stability. The framework could help analysts think about crises that seem sudden, when stress in fact built up unseen for a long time.
arxiv-2606-21585:
An unattributed 2026 essay builds a geometry of belief revision, asking what it should cost a finite agent to change its mind. The agent, a machine's digital twin or any bounded reasoner, sees a fixed but noisy world through finite sensors, so its honest state is a probability distribution, never certainty. Two postulates anchor the framework: revision cost is a price on optimal transport between beliefs, and one nat of knowledge costs the same metric length everywhere.

Under those postulates, the cost metric is the Wasserstein transport metric rescaled by Fisher information, and the Fisher family is characterized as the unique relief with uniform pricing. Certainty sits at infinite distance, so revision toward it would demand unbounded energy, a floor the author grounds through Landauer's principle. Dropping either postulate reopens the choice of pricing rule.
arxiv-2606-21885:
Zheng proposes, in 2026, a framework called CAFM that anchors medical foundation models to patient cohorts instead of single risk scores. Clinicians reason by comparing a patient with similar past patients and their documented outcomes, yet most models output one opaque number. That mismatch helps explain why strong benchmark results often fail to become trustworthy bedside tools, especially when patient populations shift.

CAFM treats the cohort as the model's primary output unit across four stages. Curation first flags low-quality or biased records ahead of pretraining. Cohort-conditioned pretraining then organizes the model's internal space along clinically meaningful axes, and multimodal alignment keeps each data type's cohorts coherent. Finally, clinicians refine behaviour in the loop, turning outputs into auditable evidence and a drift signal. Zheng illustrates the design with four case studies, from kidney injury prediction to eye imaging triage, and states five testable hypotheses that could refute the framework.
arxiv-2606-21985:
Bonichon and colleagues introduce, in 2026, a variant of the Freeze-Tag problem, a classic robot coordination puzzle. One awake robot must wake a swarm of sleeping robots by travelling to them, and every newly woken robot joins the effort, with the goal of minimizing the total time. In the new Freeze-Tag-with-Return problem, every robot must also end back at its starting position.

For sleeping robots spread on a unit disk in the plane, the authors prove the optimal return version costs at most about 1.96 time units more than the plain version, and at least about 1.73 more in the worst case. When sleeping robots sit in convex position, the optimal makespan is at most about 4.83, and some instances achieve it. They also give single-exponential algorithms for general distance functions, shown asymptotically optimal under standard complexity assumptions via a hardness reduction on graphs.
arxiv-2606-22085:
Napa and colleagues test, in 2026, whether reasoning models notice when someone tampers with their chain of thought, the written reasoning they produce before answering. Editing a model's reasoning is attractive for steering it or removing unsafe steps, but the trick fails if the model detects the edit and changes behaviour. The team prefilled models with modified reasoning, both their own and other models', and probed detection during and after reasoning.

Detection accuracy was only very modest across the conditions tested. Models also struggled to say how their reasoning had been changed, beyond spotting that something was off. Surprisingly, they detected changes to their own chains of thought about as well as edits in other models' chains. The results suggest current reasoning models are largely blind to interventions on their own reasoning, a fact with direct consequences for evaluation design and reasoning monitoring.
arxiv-2606-22185:
Maciejowska examines, in 2026, how distribution fees shape the scheduling and profitability of battery energy storage in the day-ahead electricity market. Storage research usually stresses price arbitrage and grid services, leaving fees understudied. Maciejowska models battery operation with mixed-integer linear programming, using German market price data.

Four setups are compared: stand-alone storage, and storage combined with consumption, generation, or both. Storage value is the profit difference with and without the battery, and a rolling-horizon version tests forecast uncertainty and horizon length. For stand-alone storage, higher grid charges reduce arbitrage revenue and battery use. When storage joins consumption and generation, load shifting and self-consumption take over as the main value sources. Profitability then depends on fees in a non-monotonic way. The findings argue tariff structures belong inside storage investment decisions.
arxiv-2606-22285:
Dhouib and colleagues propose DiffNet in 2026, an early-fusion architecture for localizing tampering in document images, where manipulations are crafted to look visually consistent. Prior gains came mostly on synthetic benchmarks matching the training distribution, and transferred poorly to human-made forgeries and cross-domain tests. Most work also refined downstream modules while leaving the standard frequency backbone untouched.

DiffNet fuses RGB and frequency information early, driven by two design choices. A lightweight multi-level discrepancy transformation replaces each backbone stage's features with magnitude-only responses to learned zero-sum filters, so the decoder aggregates inconsistency evidence rather than raw content. A new frequency backbone uses a frequency-index-aware joint embedding of transform coefficients and quantization. The approach reaches state-of-the-art results on cross-domain and human-made tampering localization, beating prior methods by around thirty percent with up to sevenfold higher throughput.
arxiv-2606-22585:
Toufik Mansour, Lahcen Oussi, and Matthias Schork open a two-part study of normal ordering in this 2026 algebra paper. Their setting is the (p,q)-deformed generalized Weyl algebra, generated by three letters whose multiplication rules involve two deformation parameters and a power weight. Normal ordering means rewriting any word in the letters into a standard form, with all letters of one kind moved past the others.

The authors investigate that rewriting problem with the help of Young diagrams, the staircase shapes used to organize combinatorial data. Certain special cases are treated explicitly, with closed forms worked out in detail. A central thread is the connection to generalized Stirling numbers, the counting sequences that classically appear when powers of operators are normally ordered. As the first part of the project, the paper builds the algebraic framework and derives the combinatorial identities that later parts can build on.
arxiv-2606-22685:
Nika Mansouri Ghiasi, Konstantina Koliogeorgi, and Onur Mutlu present a research initiative in this 2026 short paper. Modern biotechnology generates biological data at high throughput, low cost, and high accuracy, opening new routes to better healthcare. Conventional computing systems cannot keep pace with that data rate. They also face tight limits on energy use, scalability, privacy, and security when the data is medical.

The Architecture for Health initiative, Arch4Health, responds on two fronts. First, it aims to identify and analyze the key computational challenges in current and future health and life-science applications. Second, it explores how computer architects and system designers can advance healthcare by solving those challenges. The paper lays out the motivations behind the initiative, then its vision and goals. It surveys related topics, describes the Arch4Health workshops that gather the community, and closes with an outlook on where architecture-for-health research should head next.
arxiv-2606-22885:
Zihan Zhang, Mengyi Chen, Qianxiao Li, and Peichen Zhong propose a new test for whether a predicted material can be made, in this 2026 paper. Computational searches rank candidates by stability on the formation energy hull, yet many predicted-stable phases resist synthesis. The authors focus on solid-state routes where an interfacial melt, a thin liquid layer between reacting solids, mediates the reaction.

Their claim is that this melt must itself stay stable against separating into different compositions. They demonstrate the idea in the iron-boron system, where the compound FeB4 forms under high pressure but not in low-pressure attempts. Simulations with a machine-learned potential showed the boron-rich melt developing a concave free-energy landscape at ambient pressure, signaling demixing instability. Applied pressure adds a stabilizing term that restores melt stability, matching the observed synthesis boundary. The authors propose melt stability as a practical screening descriptor.
arxiv-2606-23085:
Haoran Zhang and colleagues detect failures during long robot manipulation tasks in a 2026 robotics paper. Real deployments chain many steps, and spotting the moment things go wrong is hard. Failure beginnings are often ambiguous, and labeling every moment by hand is impractical. Their framework, Foresight, watches a task through the internal representations of an action-conditioned world model. A world model predicts how the scene evolves given the robot's actions, so its internal states should register when reality drifts off plan.

Zhang and colleagues train Foresight using only final success or failure labels for whole tasks. A statistical calibration method adapts the alarm threshold to each setting. The same framework works across different control policies because it monitors model representations rather than actions. Tests span three simulation suites for long tasks and three real tasks on a robot arm.
arxiv-2606-23185:
Jesni Shamsul Shaari and Stefano Mancini extend uncertainty relations to operator frames in a 2026 quantum theory paper. Such relations bound how sharply two measurements can both be known. Entropic versions state the bound through the entropy of the outcomes. The authors move the idea from outcomes to the operators themselves. They work with frames, which are flexible families of building-block operators indexed without gaps.

Shaari and Mancini derive an entropic bound for the coefficient patterns of general frames. They then single out mutually unbiased frames, defined by trace overlaps of constant size. For those, a Fourier-type link between coefficient sizes yields a stronger bound. Weyl displacement operators, Wigner kernels, and frames built from position and momentum states serve as standard examples. The examples recover familiar dualities from continuous-variable quantum theory.
arxiv-2606-23285:
Shunsuke Kando and colleagues probe how bitrate choices shape generative spoken language models in a 2026 speech paper. These models learn speech itself, without text, by turning audio into discrete units and modeling them like words. The units come from slicing speech representations into fixed-width segments and clustering them. Slice width and cluster size set the bitrate. The team varies both settings and tests speech resynthesis, where units are decoded back to audio, plus speech continuation, where the model extends a spoken prompt.

Kando and colleagues find that intelligible, natural speech can be synthesized at lower bitrates than the standard baseline uses. Continuation quality also stayed stable at lower bitrates across several measures. The conventional setting therefore looks wastefully redundant. One caution concerns scoring: language-model-based metrics tracked human judgments better than classic metrics, yet still weakly, so better automatic evaluation remains an open need.
arxiv-2606-23385:
H. Azad catalogues a classical classification of vector field algebras in a 2026 mathematics paper. The Lie-Amaldi classification lists finite-dimensional algebras of vector fields, a topic that stayed hard to access for decades. A thesis by Hillgarter finally wrote the lists down. What nobody had done was identify the algebraic structure of the listed algebras. Azad presents that identification as a full catalogue, matching each entry to its structure. The structural descriptions were produced with the assistance of Claude, an AI system, and the paper is explicit about that.

Azad explains why the descriptions can be trusted. They match general results about such algebras obtained independently of the classification, including bounds on the rank of semisimple algebras in few variables. The paper also states the guidelines given to Claude, which made the work possible. Azad notes the catalogue will not be published elsewhere.
arxiv-2606-23885:
Caffagni and colleagues align a multimodal language model's inner representations with a vision encoder's, head by individual attention head, in a 2026 paper on multimodal machine learning. Multimodal large language models still stumble on basic visual tasks like counting objects. One remedy is representation alignment: nudging the model's internal states toward those of a strong vision encoder during training. Existing methods align one fixed layer, ignoring that transformers are built from many attention heads. HeRA aligns at head level instead.

HeRA preserves the local neighborhood structure of representations rather than exact coordinates, using a differentiable mutual nearest neighbor objective. Surprisingly, aligning the least aligned heads brings the biggest gains. Across several models and eighteen benchmarks, HeRA improves vision centric performance. It also curbs visual hallucinations, the habit of answering from language priors instead of the image.
arxiv-2606-24185:
Min and Liu explore whether dephasing always hurts a non-Hermitian system. Dephasing is the scrambling of quantum phase, usually treated as pure damage. Their stage is a finite Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice, a chain with alternating couplings. It is dressed with alternating gain and loss, so its energies can turn complex. Depending on parameters, the model obeys parity-time symmetry or its anti-parity-time cousin. 

Tracking the trace distance between evolving states under pure dephasing overturns the obvious guess. Without dephasing, dynamics differ sharply between the two symmetry phases. With dephasing, the response barely cares about symmetry. It depends instead on where the initial excitation sits on the lattice. Raising the dephasing strength can merely hasten the trace distance's decay. Or, strikingly, it can stabilise it against decay. Min and Liu suggest dissipation can be a design knob for non-Hermitian devices, not only noise.
arxiv-2606-24385:
Hernandez lays the foundations for particle systems whose members carry entire probability distributions as part of their state. In this mean field system each agent has a place in space, evolving under Brownian diffusion. It also has a measure valued part: a distribution over a compact space, driven by projected cylindrical noise. 

Strong solutions exist and are unique, first. They cover both the finite particle system and the limiting nonlinear McKean-Vlasov equation, under locally Lipschitz drift with linear growth. Propagation of chaos follows. As the particle count grows, the sample distribution converges on average, in the Wasserstein distance, to the McKean-Vlasov solution. Particles thus become independent in the limit. Hernandez then investigates fast convergence of the nonlinear flow toward a unique invariant measure, with stability conditions for the long time behaviour. The 2026 analysis gives measure valued mean field dynamics a complete treatment.
arxiv-2606-24585:
Kucherenko and Brouchoud find that telling a small language model it works for a court makes it refuse legal work more often. Legal professionals already experiment with personal language models for translation and reformulation. Selective refusals would bias case processing speeds by topic. The team tests modern small models suitable for on premises deployment, measuring overrefusal on criminal legal prompts under different framings.

Authority style prefixes, presenting the model as an assistant of the national supreme court or of a defence lawyer, lift refusal rates severalfold over the no prefix baseline. In some models the rise exceeds an order of magnitude. A known role-play jailbreak prefix has mixed effects. It sharply raises refusals in some models, and barely moves others. Kucherenko and Brouchoud conclude in 2026 that small deployable models are unstable under the contextual framings real institutional users naturally introduce, itself a bias risk needing investigation.
arxiv-2606-24685:
Daniel Cranston, Jiaao Li, Bo Su, Zhouningxin Wang, and Ningyan Xu study when nowhere zero flows on a graph can be reshaped into one another. A flow assigns group values to edges so that nothing cancels at any vertex. Two flows count as adjacent when they differ only along a single cycle. A graph is flow connected when chains of such small steps link every pair of its flows.

Cranston and colleagues first characterise the graphs that are flow connected for the group of order three, in both group and integer versions. They then show a reduction: checking all two edge connected graphs reduces to checking cubic ones. All cubic bipartite graphs prove flow connected for the group of order four. The team also constructs cubic graphs on both sides of that question. The results pin down exactly where small step reconfiguration always succeeds for small groups.
arxiv-2606-24785:
Nora Bearth, Nadja van 't Hoff, and Torben Johansen propose a cleaner way to compare treatment effects across groups in difference in differences studies. Policy work often asks who gains most from a programme. Subgroup and triple difference analyses answer awkwardly: their inference can be too cautious, they lean on rigid interaction forms, and group differences in background traits muddy the comparison. The authors define a new target, the Balanced Group Average Treatment Effect on the Treated. It strips out differences in covariate composition.

The new estimand is identified under standard conditional parallel trends assumptions. Bearth and colleagues derive its influence function representation. Their estimators are consistent and asymptotically normal at the usual rate. Machine learning can fit the high dimensional nuisance parts without breaking inference. Valid tests follow for group effects and their differences. Simulations show favourable finite sample performance. The target gives a transparent basis for comparing groups.
arxiv-2606-24985:
Louis Simon and Mohamed Chetouani personalise wearable stress detection without fine tuning on each user. Stress responses vary widely between people, so generic models underperform. The usual fixes are costly: per user fine tuning or large self supervised pretraining. Their alternative is retrieval augmented personalisation. Frozen foundation models, trained out of domain, search a target user's own history for similar patterns. The matches become a compact user embedding that modulates a lightweight transformer.

Evaluation uses the WESAD dataset: fifteen users wearing wrist sensors recording electrodermal activity, blood volume pulse, temperature, and movement. The method gains about four points of accuracy and nearly five points of macro F1 over a generic transformer baseline. It approaches full fine tuning while using no labelled user data. Restricting retrieval to earlier samples only performs close to full history retrieval. Cross dataset lookup, borrowing embeddings from K-Emocon, is also tested.
arxiv-2606-25385:
Stress inside a solid cannot be seen directly; it is usually inferred from shape change through a model of that material. Yiwei Duan, Michel Destrade, Wenchang Tan, and Guo-Yang Li offer a more direct route in 2026 called acoustoelastic imaging. Existing stress changes how shear waves travel, so the team treats the measured wave field as the answer to an inverse problem. Full waveform inversion with physics informed learning recovers the wave equation's coefficients, and stress follows from them.

The method needs no explicit material law and no constants to tune first, a common weak point of older inference. Computer tests and ultrasound trials on unevenly stressed samples rebuilt the stress fields with good accuracy. Spatial detail finer than a third of a wavelength was resolved. The authors aim the framework at complex materials and living tissues alike.
arxiv-2606-25485:
Lifting a mod p representation of a Galois group to characteristic zero, with prescribed local behaviour, is a central engine behind modern modularity results. Matthew Emerton, Toby Gee, Lue Pan, and Xinwen Zhu prove a flexible lifting theorem in 2026 for two dimensional representations over a totally real field. Starting from an irreducible, totally odd residual representation, they allow the local conditions at each place to be any chosen union of components of the relevant deformation rings.

Away from the prime, any nonempty component choice is allowed. Above the prime, lifts may be potentially semistable with arbitrary regular Hodge Tate weights, a wide menu of local shapes. Under standard Taylor Wiles style hypotheses, plus extra care at the primes two and five, a global lift meeting every prescription exists. The result strengthens the local to global machinery that deformation theory runs on.
arxiv-2606-25585:
Segmenting the object a sentence names is standard in video understanding, but naming an object that a future event will involve is harder and more useful. Kehan Lan, Kaining Ying, and Henghui Ding define that foresight task in 2026 and build its first dataset. Nearly a thousand clips carry over fourteen thousand foresight expressions, like asking which tool will be used next, plus a few thousand written reasoning traces. The answer is a mask drawn on frames already seen, earned by reading context clues about what happens next.

Their model learns in two stages, supervised training on the traces followed by reinforcement learning. It reached state of the art on the new benchmark and also generalised strongly to existing referring segmentation tests. The authors hope the task pushes video perception from describing the present toward anticipating the near future.
arxiv-2606-26085:
Aishwarya Majumdar, John Martyn, Yuan Liu, and Nathan Wiebe bring quantum algorithm tools into quantum control. Control pulses steer quantum hardware toward target states. Most pulse design leans on brute-force search with little insight into the solution landscape. Quantum signal processing offers the opposite style: analytic constructions with rigorous error guarantees. Its power for control problems had gone largely unexplored.

QSP-Control is their framework for qubit-oscillator systems. Such systems pair a two-level qubit with a vibrating oscillator mode. Unwanted cross-Kerr effects, a nonlinear coupling between the two, get mitigated through the signal processing formalism. Fock states, the oscillator's rung-by-rung energy levels, become addressable one by one. Fock-state-selective operators are built from parallels with the Jaynes-Cummings interaction model. Several practical control problems map cleanly onto signal processing forms. The result is a systematic design method with an interpretable angle on control.
arxiv-2606-26385:
Qihan Zhang, Mengyuan Li, and Ibrahim Sabek fix database slowness inside confidential virtual machines, secure cloud machines that protect data while it is in use. Queries there run much slower than in ordinary virtual machines, and the authors trace the cause to the query optimizer.

Optimizers still price query plans using cost assumptions from unencrypted machines, which no longer match reality. The team's light calibration models two overhead sources, data movement and address-translation effects, using simple stand-ins the optimizer already tracks. Experiments recover up to 48 percent of lost performance and sometimes beat the unencrypted baseline outright.
arxiv-2606-26585:
Hengchu Xiao and Chuanjun Wang propose a safety net for AI telescope scheduling. Software now helps decide which targets a telescope observes and when. Its choices can cite wrong data, reason in circles, or demand more than the instruments can do. Such errors waste rare chances to catch brief cosmic events. Their system checks every choice before it is carried out.

The checks run at several levels. Data references are verified first. Sound logic comes next, then the limits of the sky and the hardware. Each choice is also written as small linked steps of reasoning. That record makes the logic easy to trace and lets errors be found afterwards. Tests showed more choices could be carried out safely than with unchecked AI scheduling. Feedback fixed or blocked faulty choices, above all in complex cases. Fewer fleeting events were lost as a result.
arxiv-2606-26685:
Tomoyuki Yamakami examines how size and ceiling bounds shape the power of nonuniform automaton families. A nonuniform family uses a different automaton for each input length. Two measures govern such families: size, the count of internal states, and ceiling, the maximum input length allowed. Similar measures for pushdown automata include stack contents. These families connect to space-bounded complexity classes with limited advice.

Advice is extra information given to a machine for each input length. Earlier work linked small-state families to complexity classes with short advice. Yamakami explores how varying the size and ceiling bounds changes what the families can compute. The analysis separates the roles of the two bounds. It clarifies which restrictions truly weaken the machines and which merely repackage their power.
arxiv-2606-26885:
Alaa Adnan and seven colleagues design handovers for millimetre-wave networks that use smart surfaces to dodge blockages. Millimetre-wave links are fast but fragile: walls and bodies block their line of sight. Vision-aided systems can hand a user over before a blockage hits. When no nearby base station exists, a reconfigurable intelligent surface, a wall of tunable reflectors, can bounce the signal around the obstacle instead.

Setting up many surface elements takes time, which fights the handover deadline. The authors optimise how many elements to allocate, balancing signal work against link quality. The optimisation runs offline with a swarm algorithm, so no delay occurs during handovers. Cutting the element count modestly cut wasted energy without hurting signal quality. The surface-assisted link also beat the blocked link by a wide signal margin.
arxiv-2606-27085:
Lazarovich, Krishna, and Mj study hidden symmetries of hyperbolic groups, a class of groups with negatively curved geometry. A commensurator collects all maps that match large finite-index pieces of the group onto each other. Such maps can distort distances. The authors focus on geometrically rigid, residually finite hyperbolic groups. In the 2026 proof, their distortion notion is averaged, smoothing out worst-case stretching.

Average distortion of every such commensurator turns out to be bounded. No hidden symmetry can stretch the group too far on average. That result extends Paulin's classic rigidity picture from outer symmetries to the wider commensurator world. Arithmetic lattice examples with endless commensurators still obey the bound. Bounded average distortion therefore gives a fresh, checkable mark of geometric rigidity. The proof leans on boundary behaviour, where these groups act on a sphere-like edge at infinity.
arxiv-2606-27385:
Pritts, Seegräber, and Köser remove the hidden scale parameter from RANSAC, the workhorse algorithm for fitting geometric models amid outliers. Standard scoring counts inliers or sums capped per-point scores, and every variant needs a threshold tied to the inlier scale, which itself must be guessed from contaminated data. Their fix reverses the inference order: the scale is integrated out analytically under a conjugate prior for a fixed inlier partition, and only then are partitions optimised. One closed-form score spans both regimes in this computer vision paper from 2026.

On a benchmark of nearly seventy thousand image pairs, the score beats the leading variants across two-view estimation problems. It stays nearly flat when thresholds are miscalibrated, where baselines degrade. Near-optimal accuracy arrives from as little as two validation pairs, where baselines need roughly a hundred times more.
arxiv-2606-27485:
Chakraborty, Das, and Shah extend the contact cosmetic surgery question to Legendrian knots sitting in a broader class of three-manifolds. Cosmetic surgery asks whether two different surgeries on one knot can ever produce the same result; the contact version asks it for Legendrian knots with their contact structures. The setting is integer homology sphere L-spaces, manifolds whose Heegaard Floer homology is as small as possible.
