The drug shifted the abundance of about a third of bacterial taxa and cut the community's richness and diversity, though the size of the effect differed between people. By four weeks after treatment ended, each community looked close to its starting state again. Yet several taxa had still not recovered six months later. The authors note participants reported normal gut function throughout, suggesting backup species cover lost functions.
europmc-pmc2726785:
Colijn and co-authors presented E-Flux in 2009. The method turns gene expression data into predictions of metabolic flux. Flux is the rate at which chemicals flow through a cell network. Genome sequences list which reactions are possible but not how active each one is. They applied the method to Mycobacterium tuberculosis, the tuberculosis bacterium, focusing on mycolic acids, key wall fats targeted by first-line drugs.

Using over four hundred expression arrays covering seventy-five drugs, drug pairs, and nutrient states, E-Flux forecast changes in mycolic acid making capacity. It correctly picked seven of the eight known fatty acid blockers in the set and matched their specificity. It also flagged new candidate modulators, which offers a way to screen drug effects from expression data alone.
europmc-pmc2748685:
Ooi and co-authors mapped in 2009 which oncogenic pathways are active in gastric cancer, the second leading cause of cancer death worldwide, and whether pathway patterns predict survival. Gastric tumors vary widely in which growth pathways they deregulate, and single-marker studies miss interactions between pathways. They used gene expression signatures to infer pathway activity in three hundred one primary tumors.

Three pathways were deregulated in over seventy percent of tumors: proliferation and stem cell signaling, NF-kappaB, and Wnt/beta-catenin. Cell line tests validated the predictions. Grouping patients by combinations of pathway activity gave reproducible, significant survival differences across several cohorts. Tumors can thus be classified into biologically and clinically meaningful subgroups by pathway activity alone.
europmc-pmc2764385:
Bohn and co-authors built in 2008 the Clinical Impairment Assessment, a short self-report measure of the harm eating disorders do to everyday functioning. Eating disorders hit personal life, thinking, and social life in specific ways that generic quality-of-life scales can miss. Their sixteen-item questionnaire scores impairment overall and in three domains: personal, cognitive, and social.

They tested the instrument with data from a transdiagnostic treatment trial, a therapy tested across eating disorder types. The scale showed high internal consistency, sound construct and discriminant validity, and good test-retest reliability. It also proved sensitive to change as patients improved. They propose it for clinic use when assessing patients and their response to treatment, and for research on how common such impairment is.
europmc-pmc2788585:
Hong and co-authors showed in 2009 that microvesicles shed by colorectal cancer cells are packed with cell-cycle messenger RNAs that make blood vessel cells multiply. Cancer cells release these tiny membrane bubbles into nearby tissue and the blood, where they carry messages between cells. The team compared the full RNA content of vesicles from a human colorectal cancer line against the RNA of the cells themselves.

They catalogued over eleven thousand vesicle RNAs tied to tumor processes. Two hundred forty-one RNAs sat in vesicles at levels above the parent cells. Twenty-seven of those drove cell-cycle work, mostly the division phase. Across patient samples these division RNAs varied in step with disease. Adding the vesicles to endothelial cells, the cells lining blood vessels, significantly raised their growth. Tumor vesicles, they conclude, may feed growth and spread by encouraging new blood vessels.
europmc-pmc2808385:
Corti and a large team mined memory B cells from people infected with HIV-1 in 2010 to find antibodies that block many virus strains at once. Such broad blockers are rare and prized, since they show vaccine designers which virus spots stay exposed across strains. Donors were picked for blood that already neutralized many HIV types.

The team froze the B cells so they kept making antibodies, then screened the output against virus coat proteins. They pulled out fifty-eight antibodies, most of which blocked the virus. Three stood out for breadth. One hit a new spot near the CD4 binding site, one hit a conserved crown region, and one hit a steady stretch of the gp41 stalk.
europmc-pmc2914085:
Ganann, Ciliska, and Thomas examined in 2010 how rapid reviews are conducted and what their shortcuts cost. Policy makers often need research evidence gathered within six months or less. A traditional systematic review typically takes at least twelve months, so rapid reviews streamline the process to deliver answers faster.

The team searched five electronic databases plus grey literature, hand-searched journals, and contacted key informants. Two reviewers independently screened 1,989 titles and abstracts, and the team extracted data from 45 methodological articles and 25 examples of rapid reviews. Rapid reviews took from three weeks to six months. Common shortcuts included limiting searches by year, database, or language, and using one reviewer where traditional reviews use two. The authors warn that faster extraction can miss relevant information and that shortened searching and appraisal can introduce bias. They urge rapid reviewers to describe their methods in detail and discuss what the streamlining might have changed.
europmc-pmc2919785:
Boyko and colleagues ran in 2010 the largest genetic study yet of dog shape, genotyping nine hundred fifteen dogs from eighty breeds plus wild relatives. Dogs vary in body size more than any other land mammal, alongside huge variety in legs, skulls, and coats. A dense map of canine DNA variation let the team hunt the genes behind nearly one hundred measured traits.

The striking result was simplicity: most traits trace to a handful of genes with large effects, not the hundreds of tiny nudges typical in humans. A few master loci set body size across breeds, and similar hotspots govern leg length and head shape. Breeders shuffling a small deck of powerful variants produced the species' dramatic variety, which makes dogs an unusually clean system for finding trait genes.
europmc-pmc3004885:
Jolley and Maiden introduced BIGSdb, a database system for bacterial population genomics, in a 2010 article. Fast sequencing was flooding labs with bacterial genomes, and older typing databases could not hold whole genomes linked to sample details.

Built on software long used for multi-locus typing, the new system stores anything from a single read to a full genome alongside specimen data. Users can define any loci and variants, group them into schemes for typing or evolution studies, and cross-reference names across projects. Access controls and lab sample tracking are built in, and the code is open source for any group to run.
europmc-pmc3044685:
Zhernakova and a large consortium combined in 2011 the gene hunting data for two autoimmune diseases, celiac disease and rheumatoid arthritis, to find risk genes they share. Each disease already had dozens of known risk spots outside the main immune gene region, and a few overlapped. Pooling the two datasets boosted power to catch weaker shared effects.

Follow up testing in thousands more patients confirmed eight new shared signals, including four never firmly tied to either disease before. Four spots known from one disease were also confirmed in the other, bringing the shared total to fourteen. Several shared spots change how nearby genes are expressed in immune cells. The pattern points to antigen presentation and T cell activation as common drivers. The authors show that cross disease pooling is a cheap way to find real risk genes.
europmc-pmc3045385:
Hedlund and coauthors found in 2011 that stressed leukemia and lymphoma cells release tiny parcels that blunt the immune attack on them. The parcels, called exosomes, carry stress signal proteins that normally mark cells for killing by natural killer immune cells. On parcels, the same proteins act as decoys, soaking up the killer signal away from the tumor cell.

Two blood cancer cell lines made these signals constantly and shed them on parcels, which measurably weakened killer cell action in lab tests. Heat stress and oxidative stress, the kind caused by some cancer treatments, made the cells shed even more parcels and deepened the immune block. The authors warn this may help explain weak killer cell function in patients. They also urge care when heat based therapies are planned, since treatment itself could raise the decoy shield.
europmc-pmc3074985:
Rentz and colleagues reported in 2010 that brain amyloid, the protein deposit of Alzheimer disease, already tracks with weaker thinking in healthy older adults. They also found that mental reserve can blunt the link. Reserve is the idea that education and lifelong mental activity let brains cope with damage. The team scanned older adults, some healthy and some with Alzheimer disease, with a tracer that sticks to amyloid, and gave them thorough thinking tests.

Across the whole group, more amyloid in a key hub region meant worse scores, above all on memory, but also on language and spatial tasks. At higher reserve levels, the same amyloid load cost far less performance, and at the top it cost nothing measurable. The pattern held in healthy adults alone on a hard memory test. The authors read this as evidence that reserve protects against amyloid's early effects.
europmc-pmc3079585:
The ENCODE Project Consortium published in 2011 a user's guide to its encyclopedia of the working parts of the human genome. The genome's letter sequence alone does not say which stretches are genes, switches, or structural marks. The project set out to map all of those functional elements, along with their chemical states, using many technologies under shared quality standards.

Since its pilot phase on one percent of the genome, the project had expanded to the whole sequence, releasing data freely as it was produced. The guide explains what kinds of data exist, how to reach them through the project database, and how to use them to interpret a genome stretch of interest. Worked illustrations show researchers answering real questions with the resource. The authors present it as shared infrastructure for biology and medicine, much like the genome sequence itself.
europmc-pmc3146885:
David Alexander and Kenneth Lange upgraded a popular ancestry-estimation program in a 2011 paper in BMC Bioinformatics. Estimating what share of a person's DNA comes from each ancestral population is now basic in genetics. Their program already ran thousands of times faster than the older standard tool; this paper adds four capabilities.

The program can now pick the number of ancestral populations itself by cross-checking. It can learn from people of known ancestry for sharper estimates, and trim tiny ancestry shares to keep results readable on small datasets. It also splits work across several processors for very large files. Together the changes make the tool more accurate, faster, and easier to apply to modern genome collections.
europmc-pmc3153485:
Gemma Atkinson, Tanel Tenson, and Vasili Hauryliuk classified a family of bacterial alarm enzymes across the tree of life in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. These enzymes make and destroy a small alarm molecule that switches bacteria into survival mode under stress. Names and groupings had grown confused as members turned up in odd places, from plant chloroplasts to animals.

Searching more than a thousand genomes, the team sorted the family into thirty subgroups under three headings: long multi-part enzymes, small makers, and small breakers. Nineteen subgroups were new, including the first found in archaea, extending the alarm system to that whole branch of life. Patterns of which members coexist in a genome, plus exposed surface patches unique to the long forms, suggest how regulation signals travel.
europmc-pmc3161885:
Deirdre O'Hanlon, Thomas Moench, and Richard Cone challenged a textbook belief about vaginal protection in a 2011 paper in BMC Infectious Diseases. Helpful vaginal bacteria make hydrogen peroxide, long credited with killing the bacteria that overgrow in a common vaginal condition. Much of that evidence came from oxygen-rich lab setups unlike the body, so the team retested under body-like, oxygen-free conditions.

At levels found in the body, peroxide failed to kill any of the seventeen overgrowth species tested, and a splash of vaginal fluid blocked even extreme peroxide doses. Lactic acid at natural levels and acidity, by contrast, killed all the overgrowth species while sparing the helpful bacteria. The authors conclude acid, not peroxide, does the protective work, reshaping how probiotic strains should be chosen.
europmc-pmc3198985:
Simone Patergnani and a large group of co-authors reviewed calcium signaling at mitochondria-associated membranes in this 2011 article. These membranes are zones where the endoplasmic reticulum, the cell's main calcium store, sits in close contact with mitochondria. Calcium controls metabolism, growth, and cell death, and mitochondria help shape each calcium signal in strength and timing.

The review gathers what was known about how calcium leaves the endoplasmic reticulum and enters mitochondria across these contact zones. It describes the structure and molecular makeup of the contact sites and the close interplay between the two organelles. That exchange lets healthy signals pass through, but it can also carry harmful calcium loads that push a cell toward death.
europmc-pmc3217985:
Enrique Zudaire and colleagues presented AngioTool, software for measuring blood vessel networks, in this 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Studying angiogenesis, the growth of new vessels, depends on images of networks in tissues such as the embryonic hindbrain, the young retina, and the allantois. Quantifying those images by hand is slow, laborious, and error-prone.

AngioTool automates the job, computing the area a network covers, the number and total length of vessels, vessel density, and a measure of the gaps within the network. It also calculates a branching index, the number of branch points per unit area, which reflects sprouting activity. The team validated the tool on mouse hindbrain, retina, and allantois images. The software is open source and free to download.
europmc-pmc3247885:
Henrik Husted and colleagues asked what actually keeps joint-replacement patients in hospital under a fast-track program, in this 2011 study in Acta Orthopaedica. Their unit had already cut stays after hip and knee replacement to a median of two days, using spinal anesthesia and strong non-opioid pain regimens. The team tracked nearly two hundred consecutive patients against functional discharge criteria, checking twice daily.

In the first day or two, pain, dizziness, and general weakness caused most of the delay. Nausea, vomiting, and confusion played only minor roles. Logistics mattered too: waiting for transfusion, physiotherapy, or X-rays delayed about a fifth of patients. The authors advise that further gains should target better pain control, prevention of dizziness on standing, faster recovery of muscle strength, and tighter organization.
europmc-pmc3278385:
Simone Mader and colleagues searched for the missing antibody target in neuromyelitis optica patients who lack the known marker, in this 2011 paper in the Journal of Neuroinflammation. The disease attacks the optic nerves and spinal cord, and most patients carry antibodies against the water channel aquaporin-4, but a substantial minority do not. Animal work hinted that antibodies to myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein, MOG, might fill the gap.

The team tested several hundred patients and controls. Aquaporin-4 antibodies appeared in nearly all definite cases. High-titer MOG antibodies clustered in a childhood demyelinating disease. They also appeared in a slice of the marker-negative optic and spinal patients. Two of the three MOG-positive neuromyelitis patients, and all such high-risk patients, lacked the aquaporin antibody entirely, marking a distinct subgroup. Both antibody types could trigger complement-driven cell killing at high levels.
europmc-pmc3286485:
Heusinkveld and van der Burg published a review in 2011 about macrophages that gather inside human tumors. These white blood cells show up in most cancers and often point to a poor outlook for the patient. The authors sort out what was known about the different forms these cells take and why findings from mouse studies do not transfer cleanly to people.

Inside a tumor, macrophages can lean toward attacking cancer or toward shielding it and helping it grow. The review covers the signals in tumor tissue that push cells one way or the other. It closes by weighing treatments that try to block, remove, or retrain these cells as a form of immune therapy.
europmc-pmc3296185:
Bendas and Borsig reviewed how sticky molecules on cancer cells help tumors spread, in an article from 2012. To form new growths elsewhere, cancer cells must grip blood vessel walls, slip out of the bloodstream, and settle in fresh tissue. Along the way they also interact with platelets and white blood cells that help them travel.

The review gives special attention to heparin, a blood thinner long given to cancer patients to treat clots. Studies in animals show heparin also slows spread, and patients on it tend to live longer. The authors argue it blocks one family of grip molecules, the selectins, and may also interfere with another family, the integrins, opening a path toward new anti spread treatments.
europmc-pmc3312285:
Ahmad and colleagues reviewed a miniaturized kind of antibody used in research and medicine, in a 2012 article. Normal antibodies are large Y shaped proteins, but scientists can build just the gripping tip as a single chain fragment. These small fragments, called scFv, can be produced inside bacteria, which makes them cheap and quick to manufacture.

Fragments can be fused to glowing or color producing marker proteins, giving a tool that finds a target and signals its presence in one step. They can also be hitched to toxins, used to deliver genes, or sent inside cells as blockers against cancer related proteins. The review covers how the fragments are designed and made, and closes with their growing use in breast cancer research.
europmc-pmc3349985:
De la Monte examined the evidence that Alzheimer's disease involves a failure of insulin signalling within the brain itself. Drawing on post-mortem studies and experimental work, the review develops the idea that the condition behaves partly like a metabolic disorder confined to the nervous system.

Human brain tissue from Alzheimer's cases showed reduced insulin and insulin-like growth factor signalling, alongside the familiar plaques and tangles. In experimental models, impairing brain insulin pathways reproduced features of the disease, including memory problems and abnormal tau. The author argues that this brain insulin resistance helps explain why diabetes raises Alzheimer's risk and points toward metabolic therapies.
europmc-pmc3358085:
Tadesse and colleagues traced how Escherichia coli in the United States grew resistant to antimicrobial drugs across half a century, from 1950 to 2002. They drew together isolates from people and from food animals, treating this common gut bacterium as a sentinel for resistance trends in both populations.

Resistance proved consistently highest against the drugs that had been in use the longest in human and veterinary medicine. More recent decades brought major increases in multidrug-resistant strains and in resistance to newer drug classes such as fluoroquinolones. The authors argue that tracking these long trends is essential for choosing treatments and shaping public health responses.
europmc-pmc3362085:
Altman and colleagues wrote the explanation volume for REMARK, the checklist for studies of tumour markers and prognosis. The first REMARK paper named what such studies should report. This companion guide explains the thinking behind each item, so authors can see what good practice looks like on the page.

Each item is spelled out in depth and paired with published examples of clear write-ups. The authors also show how choices in specimen picking, assay methods, and study design can sway results, which is why full reporting matters. They mean the guide to serve as a reference for planning, running, and writing up this kind of study.
europmc-pmc3526785:
Bile acids loop between gut and liver on dedicated carrier proteins, and Emina Halilbasic, Thierry Claudel, and Michael Trauner review that transport system in 2013. Bile acids drive bile flow, help the gut take up fats, clear cholesterol, and shape metabolism, so their levels need tight control.

Nuclear receptors tune the carriers that keep bile acids in balance. Faults in the carriers, whether inherited or acquired, feed bile blockage, gallstones, fatty liver, and liver cancer, plus gut and metabolic disorders past the liver. Since the receptors can be drugged, tuning transport has become a treatment path. The review maps the machinery, its faults, and the openings for therapy.
europmc-pmc3531285:
Genome-wide association studies reshaped human genetics in a decade, and William S. Bush, Jason H. Moore, Fran Lewitter, and Maricel Kann teach the method in this 2012 textbook chapter. Part of the Translational Bioinformatics collection, it reviews how scanning hundreds of thousands of markers across many genomes links variants to disease.

The chapter covers the architecture of common disease, the structure of human variation, genotyping technologies, and study designs. Statistical analysis, replication, and interpretation of hits get full treatment, including what follow-up an association needs before it means biology. A closing look reaches beyond GWAS to what comes next. Written as a primer, it assumes a reader new to the field and builds from basic genetic concepts.
europmc-pmc3596785:
Gopi Patel and Robert Bonomo surveyed a rising class of drug-destroying enzymes in Frontiers in Microbiology in 2013, under the warning title of stormy waters ahead. Carbapenem antibiotics were the last reliable line against serious infections by gut bacteria. Enzymes called carbapenemases chew them up, and only five years earlier resistant cases were rare reports from intensive care units and outbreak wards. By the time of this review, that picture had collapsed.

Named enzymes, including KPC, the New Delhi metallo-beta-lactamase, and OXA-48, were turning up across continents, carried by travel and by patients with little hospital exposure. Alternatives are few and shaky, and none are coming soon. The authors chart where each enzyme has surfaced, how laboratories can detect them early, and why infection control now carries the weight that drug development no longer does. Clinicians, they warn, should expect the resistant cases at their own doors.
europmc-pmc3628085:
Se Jin Song and colleagues asked whether housemates swap microbes in eLife in 2013. People living together touch, eat together, and share air, so their bacterial communities might converge. The team sampled gut, mouth, and skin microbes from sixty families, mixing couples, children, and dogs in various combinations. They measured how much of each person's community was shared with each other member.

Household members, above all couples, resembled each other more than strangers did, with the strongest effect on skin. Dogs raised the sharing between adult partners, and owners matched their own dogs more than other people's dogs. Whether the shared microbes truly live on the body or only pass through after contact is left open. Contact, the authors conclude, is a real architect of our microbial makeup.
europmc-pmc3658985:
Blood and spinal fluid chemistry shift early in Alzheimer disease, Trushina, Dutta, Persson, Mielke and Petersen report in a 2013 PLoS ONE study. The disease affects over five million Americans, and its body changes start decades before memory fails. The team ran a broad chemical scan, called metabolomics in the text, on blood plasma and spinal fluid from the same people. Stages ran from normal thought to mild impairment to full disease.

The scan found 342 changed chemicals in plasma and 351 in spinal fluid, with about a fifth named. At the mild stage, 23 pathways were off in plasma and 20 in spinal fluid against normal levels, and counts grew with severity. Energy, fat transport and nerve signal pathways recur across the lists. Some plasma pathways split all three groups cleanly. Such scans may yield early markers and new drug targets.
europmc-pmc3686085:
Bernhoft reviews cadmium, a toxic metal with no useful role in the body, covering how people take it in, the harm it does, and the options for treatment. Cigarette smoke is the largest exposure source for most people, and the lungs absorb a far larger share of inhaled cadmium than the gut absorbs from food. Diet, drinking water, and industrial work add further exposure.

Once inside, cadmium builds up over years and damages the kidneys, bones, lungs, and other organs. Treatment rests mainly on avoiding further exposure. Chelating drugs such as EDTA, DMPS, and DMSA bind the metal for removal. Experts still disagree on when chelation helps, and whether it can stress the kidneys. Bernhoft also argues for screening people at high risk.
europmc-pmc3692085:
Zhou and colleagues present DNAshape, a method and web server that predicts the three-dimensional shape of DNA from sequence alone, at genome scale. Proteins read DNA partly through its shape, features like groove width and twisting, but measuring shape experimentally for millions of sites is impossible.

Their method slides a window along the sequence and looks up shape values mined from Monte Carlo simulations, returning minor groove width, roll, propeller twist, and helix twist almost instantly. Predictions held up against crystal and NMR structures, cleavage data, and molecular dynamics checks. The free server is meant to let genome researchers add shape to the sequence analyses they already run.
europmc-pmc3726785:
Pavan Kumar and ten co-authors reported a biomarker study in PLoS ONE in 2013 on Alzheimer's disease. A simple blood test for early Alzheimer's would help select patients for trials, track the disease, and plan care. The team focused on microRNAs, tiny RNA pieces that control gene activity and stay stable in blood.

They found a set of seven microRNAs in blood plasma that separated Alzheimer's patients from healthy controls with over 95 percent accuracy in their tests. Each of the seven differed more than twofold between the groups. Studying the genes those microRNAs target pointed to disturbed pathways in fat handling and other cell processes. The authors present the seven-piece signature as a candidate for a low-burden diagnostic test.
europmc-pmc3751685:
Ian Cameron and eight co-authors reported a randomized trial in BMC Medicine in 2013 on treating frailty in older people. The trial ran in Sydney, Australia, with frail older adults. One group got a program that targeted each person's own frailty traits, with input from several professions; the other group got usual care and support services.

Of those who entered, 216 people, about 90 percent, finished the study; most were women and the average age was about 83. At twelve months, the treated group showed about 15 percent less frailty than the control group. Mobility scores held steady in the treated group while the control group declined, a clear gap. Side effects were few and mild, mostly muscle and joint aches from exercise.
europmc-pmc3766985:
Shengxi Meng, Jianmei Cao, Qin Feng, Jinghua Peng, and Yiyang Hu wrote a review in Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine in 2013 on chlorogenic acid. It is a plant compound common in the diet and a major part of coffee. Disorders of sugar and fat handling underlie diabetes, obesity, fatty liver, heart disease, and cancer, so food compounds that help are of wide interest.

Chlorogenic acid also shows antibacterial, antioxidant, and anti-cancer activity in earlier work. This review gathers the studies on its roles in glucose and lipid metabolism specifically. It walks through how the compound affects sugar uptake, fat making and breakdown, and the enzymes and signals that govern them, and weighs what is known about its promise for metabolic disease.
europmc-pmc3798585:
Ritei Uehara and Ermias Belay wrote a review in the Journal of Epidemiology in 2012 on the epidemiology of Kawasaki disease. The disease is a body-wide inflammation of blood vessels that mainly strikes children under five. Dr. Tomisaku Kawasaki reported it over forty years earlier, but its cause is still unknown. It has now been diagnosed in more than 60 countries.

The review describes the disease's incidence, its seasonal pattern, and its most serious complication, coronary artery abnormalities, with focus on Japan and the United States plus Europe and other Asian countries. Such abnormalities develop in about a quarter of untreated patients, making Kawasaki disease a leading cause of acquired heart disease in children in developed countries. Incidence differs sharply by country, with Japan far ahead.
europmc-pmc3805485:
Kaforou and colleagues reported in PLoS Medicine in 2013 that patterns of gene activity in blood can flag active tuberculosis, even in people also living with HIV. Telling active disease from latent infection is a long-standing problem, because standard tests often fail exactly where HIV is common.

Using case-control samples from African adults with and without HIV, the team built a disease risk score from the blood RNA patterns. The score separated active tuberculosis from latent infection and also from other diseases that can look similar. The authors present the signature as a step toward a blood test that works in the clinics that need it most, while noting it still needs testing in wider groups.
europmc-pmc3828585:
Hannah Blencowe, Simon Cousens, Doris Chou, Mikkel Oestergaard, Lale Say, Ann-Beth Moller, Mary Kinney, and Joy Lawn review preterm birth rates in Reproductive Health in 2013. It is the second paper in the Born Too Soon supplement. Their aim is a clear global picture of how many babies arrive before full term.

About one in nine live births in 2010 came early, the review finds, and rates are climbing in most tracked countries. Direct harm from early birth kills about a million babies a year, and it plays a role in over half of all newborn deaths. Survivors face more long-term health needs, and care costs run high. The authors press for steady counting rules and better data so trends can be tracked and plans can be judged.
europmc-pmc3849585:
Neil A. Mabbott, J. Kenneth Baillie, Helen Brown, Tom C. Freeman, and David A. Hume build a human cell gene atlas in BMC Genomics in 2013. Genes that work in the same path tend to switch on together. By pooling many public gene data sets from real human cells, the team can spot those partnerships.

Network tools draw the links between genes that rise and fall as one. Key switch genes show up next to the genes they likely control, which hints at each gene's job. The atlas gives close care to the immune cell family that eats germs and shows cell debris. Some claimed marker genes for immune subtypes did not hold up in the data. The full set is posted free online for other labs to mine.
europmc-pmc3889685:
Paul J. Lucassen leads a team of co-authors in a review of stress and the brain in Acta Neuropathologica, with the record dated 2014. Stress is a daily fact of modern life, and stress hormones act powerfully on the brain. When stress helps and when it harms is still poorly mapped.

The review gathers proof on the lasting structural marks stress leaves in rodent, monkey, and human brains. It covers the stress control hub, the memory hub, the fear hub, and reward and planning areas. Cell shape changes, lost plasticity, and imaging signs of strain all feature. The authors sort which parts of stress exposure do the damage and which brain spots are most open to it. Their aim is a firmer base for judging stress-linked mental illness.
europmc-pmc3952085:
Viktoria Gudi, Stefan Gingele, Thomas Skripuletz, and Martin Stangel review what support cells do when myelin is stripped and rebuilt, in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience in 2014. Their evidence comes from the cuprizone model, in which a toxin kills the cells that make myelin in the mouse brain, without the autoimmune attack seen in multiple sclerosis. That purity makes the model ideal for studying damage and repair mechanics.

When myelin dies, astrocytes swell into their reactive state and microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, switch on in patterns that differ between brain regions. A central job for microglia is eating the myelin debris, because repair cannot start until the wreckage is cleared. The review draws lessons from this model on the timing and teamwork of glial responses during both breakdown and regrowth.
europmc-pmc4029785:
Paweł Maciejasz, Jörg Eschweiler, Kurt Gerlach-Hahn, Arne Jansen-Troy, and Steffen Leonhardt survey robots that help restore arm and hand function, in the Journal of NeuroEngineering and Rehabilitation in 2014. Therapists who guide such rehab are in short supply, and patient numbers keep rising. Robots could share the load of intense, repeated practice.

The survey covers devices in use and in development, and sets them side by side in a broad table. Each is judged by where it is used, whom it serves, and what kind of help it gives. Design choices, control plans, and clinical test results are compared too. Few devices have reached clinics so far, which leaves wide room for better designs. The authors aim to give builders a full reference on what exists, what works, and where new devices could improve on the current field.
europmc-pmc4043485:
Kirsten Ridder and a large team show that blood cells can post RNA packages straight to brain neurons during inflammation, in PLoS Biology in 2014. Immune signals were long thought to reach the brain only through loose messenger proteins. Cell fusion between blood cells and a class of brain neurons was another known route, but rare.

Using a genetic switch system in mice, the team tracked messages between the two systems. When inflammation struck, blood cells released tiny vesicles loaded with RNA. A special class of cerebellar neurons took the packages up. The cargo included small regulatory RNAs, and it stayed functional after arrival. That means blood cells can rewrite gene activity inside neurons without fusing or entering the brain. The route gives inflammation a direct line to brain cells. It may help explain how immune states shape brain function and disease.
europmc-pmc4045285:
Maria Kechagia and six colleagues review the health claims made for probiotic bacteria, in ISRN Nutrition in 2013. Probiotics are live bacteria sold as health aids, mostly in fermented dairy foods. Their use has grown fast over two decades on a rising stack of studies.

The idea is old. Over a century ago, breast-fed infants were found to carry gut rods missing in sick, formula-fed infants, seeding the notion that gut bacteria guard health. Later work, much of it weakly controlled at first, has grown more solid. Benefits are reported for gut disorders and immune outcomes, among others. Effects depend heavily on the exact strain, and growth in food bases can be slow. The authors sift the evidence food by food and claim by claim. Their verdict: promise is real, but stronger trials must catch up.
europmc-pmc4053985:
Kenneth Day and seven colleagues compare how DNA methylation ages in four human tissues, in Genome Biology in 2013. Methylation clocks tick in blood, but whether other tissues age by the same marks was unclear.

Arrays on close to three hundred samples of blood, brain, kidney, and muscle found two kinds of age-linked sites. Some shifted in all tissues; others were private to one. The shared sites tended to gain methylation and sit in CpG islands. The private sites more often lost it and sat outside islands. Muscle had its own flavour, with age sites near contraction genes and muscle-specific binding sites. Kidney leaned toward gains. Underlying chromatin states separated the shared, poised sites from the active private ones. A simple drift story cannot cover the pattern, the authors argue. Aging writes both a common script and tissue-specific notes into the methylome.
europmc-pmc4060385:
Glynn Dennis Jr. and a large team examined joint tissue from people with rheumatoid arthritis to see whether tissue types predict drug response. Their study appeared in Arthritis Research and Therapy in 2014. Rheumatoid arthritis varies a lot between patients, and how its tissue drivers relate to treatment success was poorly understood.

Combining gene activity, tissue, and cell studies in two patient groups, the team found four main synovial patterns: lymphoid, myeloid, low inflammatory, and fibroid. A myeloid signal at the start predicted the strongest response to anti-TNF drugs. Blood samples from a trial comparing two biologic drugs were also checked. The work points toward blood markers that could match patients to the therapy most likely to help them.
europmc-pmc4074385:
Hongshan Jiang, Rong Lei, Shou-Wei Ding, and Shuifang Zhu created Skewer, a tool that trims adapter sequences from next-generation sequencing reads. Their software paper appeared in BMC Bioinformatics in 2014. Adapters are short DNA pieces attached for sequencing; when a fragment is shorter than the read, adapter text leaks into the data and must be cut.

Existing trimmers rarely managed to be both fast and accurate, especially for paired reads and a newer mate-pair protocol that places junction adapters mid-fragment. The team's new matching algorithm lists every candidate site within a set error allowance, keeping run time low. In tests, Skewer reached accuracy the authors describe as unmatched, with a low time cost, making it a practical first step for sequencing analysis.
europmc-pmc4102485:
Luana Micallef and Peter Rodgers presented eulerAPE, the first software that draws accurate area-proportional Venn diagrams for three sets using ellipses. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. Such diagrams appear across medicine and science, and readers expect each region's area to match the size it stands for.

Circles look clean but cannot match most three-set data, so their areas mislead. Polygons can be exact but their jagged edges are hard to follow. Ellipses offer a middle path: smooth like circles, flexible like polygons. The authors describe their drawing method and an evaluation against existing tools. They argue ellipse-based diagrams keep the data honest while staying easy to read, filling a gap in automatic diagram generation.
europmc-pmc4132285:
Andrew R. Bassett, Chris P. Ponting, and colleagues set out the pitfalls of studying long noncoding RNA function in living organisms. Their guidance paper appeared in eLife in 2014. A few of these RNAs have proven effects in cell studies, but what most do across development and disease remains unclear.

Deleting a whole genomic stretch cannot prove the RNA itself mattered, since the cut also removes overlapping DNA control elements. Effects acting locally versus at a distance are also hard to separate. The authors weigh current techniques against different models of how these RNAs might work. They advise on designing mutations that isolate the RNA's own contribution. Their considerations aim to sharpen a field built on tricky, interwoven transcription.
europmc-pmc4139785:
Curtis M. Steyers and Francis J. Miller reviewed the failings of the lining of blood tubes in long-term ills marked by swelling of tissue. Their review came out in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences in 2014. Such ills, from joint swelling to lupus and psoriasis, bring faster clogging of the heart's tubes and more heart risk.

A weak tube lining is a key first step in that clogging and a sign of events to come. The sick show it early, often before clogging can be seen. Many things switch the lining to a bad state. They span swelling signals, harsh oxygen forms, worn fat bits in the blood, the body's own attack proteins, and the old risks of smoke and weight. The result is stiff tubes, sticky walls, leaks, and blood prone to clot. The team weighs drugs aimed at these paths.
europmc-pmc4147885:
Gregory G. Faust and Ira M. Hall presented SAMBLASTER, a tool that speeds genome analysis pipelines by cutting how often huge alignment files are read, sorted, and compressed. Their software note appeared in Bioinformatics in 2014. Illumina sequencing had become the main source of genomic data, and volumes were outgrowing the pipelines.

SAMBLASTER works as a piped after-step on aligner output, marking duplicate reads in sorted files before compression to the standard BAM format. In the same pass it can split out the discordant pairs and split reads used to call structural variants. Its own overhead is negligible while overall runtime and complexity drop sharply. Run alone, it beat established duplicate markers on speed and memory with nearly identical results. The code is open source.
europmc-pmc4169585:
V. Campana, G. Logroscino, and six co-authors reviewed bone substitutes in the Journal of Materials Science: Materials in Medicine in 2014. Surgeons carry out over two million bone grafting operations a year worldwide. A patient's own bone is still the best filler, but taking it causes harm and the supply is small.

The review weighs each class of substitute. Banked human bone works but raises cost and infection worries, and animal bone has given mixed results. Ceramic fillers based on hydroxyapatite and related minerals are widely used and break down safely in the body, though they are weaker than real bone. Growth proteins BMP2 and BMP7 are the only ones approved for human use, for spine work and stubborn leg fractures. Newer injectable cements allow smaller surgical cuts.
europmc-pmc4222885:
Antonia Trichopoulou, Dariush Mozaffarian, and six co-authors gathered expert views on the Mediterranean diet in BMC Medicine in 2014. The diet is praised worldwide for heart and health benefits, yet writers use the same name for somewhat different menus. A forum of specialists set out to pin down what the term means in different places.

The traditional pattern, from the olive-growing Mediterranean before the mid-1960s, rests on olive oil, vegetables, grains, legumes, and modest wine and animal foods. Experts from several regions describe their local versions and where they overlap with other healthy patterns. They also discuss how to study a whole diet rather than single nutrients, and which benefits have solid backing. The piece serves as a shared reference for a much-used but loosely defined term.
europmc-pmc4326185:
Stephen B Hladky and Margery A Barrand weigh the evidence on how fluids move into, through, and out of the brain. Their review appeared in Fluids and Barriers of the CNS in 2014. Brain cells sit in interstitial fluid, while cerebrospinal fluid fills the brain's larger spaces, and tight control of both keeps neurons working.

Barriers between blood and brain, the fluid making choroid plexuses, and drainage routes through the skull base all share the work. The authors question old estimates of fluid flow, many taken under deep anesthesia, and ask which movements are bulk flow and which are diffusion. The careful audit matters for drug delivery, which depends on knowing where fluid in the brain actually goes.
europmc-pmc4349985:
Michal Bassani-Sternberg, Sune Pletscher-Frankild, Lars Juhl Jensen, and Matthias Mann mapped the peptides that cells display on their surface to alert immune patrols. Their study appeared in Molecular and Cellular Proteomics in 2015. HLA class I molecules hold up fragments of the cell's own proteins; killer T cells read them to judge cell health, yet how the protein pool shapes the display was largely unknown.

Their high throughput mass spectrometry workflow identified over twenty two thousand distinct displayed peptides across seven cancer cell lines and primary cells. Comparing display with protein levels showed that abundant proteins and fast turned over proteins contribute disproportionately. The rules help predict which fragments a tumor will show, knowledge vaccine and cell therapy designers need.

Lawrence Mbuagbaw and six co-authors explain how to read treatment rankings in a 2017 paper in Systematic Reviews. Their topic is the network meta-analysis, a method that pools many trials of rival treatments for one health problem. It can compare treatments that never met in a single trial by using shared rivals. Yet its ranked lists can be hard for doctors to grasp and easy to misuse.

The authors walk through ranking tools, charts, and one common score that sums a treatment's rank chances. They weigh what each tool shows well and where each can mislead. A worked example shows how a ranked result should turn into a care choice, with care for weak proof and close calls. The paper serves readers who must act on pooled trial results.
europmc-pmc5408485:
Qinrui Li, Ying Han, Angel Belle C. Dy, and Randi J. Hagerman review gut germs and autism in a 2017 paper in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience. Gut symptoms are common in people with autism spectrum disorder, but the reason is not known. Many studies find changed gut germ mixes and changed germ products in such patients. Germs can sway brain growth and behavior through hormone, immune, and nerve routes between gut and brain.

The review lays out that two-way gut-brain traffic and the proof tying germ shifts to autism signs. A faulty germ mix also appears in bowel disease and mood disorders, which hints at shared paths. The authors weigh germ-based treatments, such as diet shifts or germ transfers, as a possibly safe and useful route. They stress that the causal chain is still being worked out.
europmc-pmc5440985:
Koliada and co-authors link body mass index to gut bacteria balance in Ukrainian adults. Their study appeared in BMC Microbiology. Obesity research often ties weight to gut microbes. Findings differ across populations, though. The team measured fecal bacteria in 61 adults. They tracked three phyla and one ratio. The ratio compares Firmicutes to Bacteroidetes. Actinobacteria stayed minor in every weight group. They made up only five to seven percent.

A clear gradient emerged with rising BMI. Firmicutes share climbed step by step. Bacteroidetes share fell in mirror image. The Firmicutes-to-Bacteroidetes ratio rose accordingly. Statistical models tied that ratio to BMI. The link held after adjusting for age and sex. Smoking and physical activity were also accounted for. Adjusted odds came to 1.33 per ratio unit. Obese Ukrainians thus carry more Firmicutes and fewer Bacteroidetes. The pattern matches several earlier population reports.
europmc-pmc5456285:
Lim and co-authors review how human coronaviruses interact with the cells they infect. Their review appeared in the journal Diseases. Six such viruses were known at the time. Four cause common colds around the world. Two, SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV, cause severe lung disease and drew wide alarm.

The review covers the host factors these viruses exploit to copy themselves. It then tracks the cell paths they disturb. Those paths include cell death, early immune defense, and stress replies inside the cell. Two signal chains, MAPK and NF-kB, get their own sections. Readers get a map of where drugs might block the virus.
europmc-pmc5572985:
McKelvey and co-authors present a review on exosome uptake. Exosomes are tiny vesicles, 30 to 100 nanometers wide. Cells release them with cargo of RNA, protein, and lipids. Much is known about how cells make and shed them. Far less is known about how other cells take them in.

That gap matters for medicine. Exosomes are eyed as treatments for cancer, infections, and immune disease. The review covers how exosomes reach target cells, bind, and enter them. It gives special attention to T cells and immune signaling. New tracking tools are starting to reveal the process live. Readers get a clear picture of a young field's key unknown.
europmc-pmc5666185:
The GBD 2015 LRI Collaborators present a systematic analysis in The Lancet Infectious Diseases. It estimates the burden of lower respiratory infections worldwide. The study spans 195 countries and 25 years of data. Cases, deaths, and causes were modeled by age and place. Two modeling platforms handled deaths and illness counts. Pathogen shares were estimated with counterfactual methods.

Infections caused about 2.74 million deaths in 2015. They also caused about 103 million lost healthy years. Children under five bore a heavy share of the toll. Their deaths fell by more than a third since 2005. Pneumococcal pneumonia caused over half of all infection deaths. Better air quality and child nutrition drove much of the decline.
europmc-pmc5702385:
Wang and co-authors sort out the tangled terms around social isolation in mental health. Their review notes that key terms lack clear and shared definitions. Researchers often use words like isolation and loneliness as if they meant the same thing. The team aimed to build a clear framework and find sound measures.

They searched the literature and drew on expert advice. Their model splits the field into five domains. Three cover social networks by amount, structure, and quality. Two cover how people judge their ties, in feelings and in resources. For each domain, they name well-tested measures. The model can help teams pick exact goals and the right tools.
europmc-pmc5753285:
Rawlings and co-authors report the state of MEROPS, a database of enzymes that cut proteins. MEROPS also covers what those enzymes cut and what blocks them. Its scheme sorts entries by protein, family, and clan. The site moved to EMBL-EBI in 2017, which forced a code rebuild.

Sequence search now runs through EMBL-EBI tools such as BLASTP and HMMER. Cross links with the PANTHER database were built at two levels. Future growth will focus on characterized proteins and key genomes. As an example, the team compared peptidases in Asgard archaea with other groups. That work hints at how proteasome parts grew with complexity.
europmc-pmc5797585:
Lu and co-authors review toll-like receptors in inflammatory bowel disease. These receptors sense microbes in the gut. They help trigger immune defense. When their signals go wrong, gut inflammation can persist and relapse.

The review traces the main signaling pathways, including MyD88 and TRIF routes. It explains how gene changes alter gut microbes and immune balance. It also covers treatment ideas that target these pathways. Readers get a compact account of how gut sensing, microbes, and immunity interact in this disease. Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis are the two main forms covered.
europmc-pmc5803285:
Bundschuh and co-authors review nanoparticles loose in nature. Factories now make vast amounts of tiny particles. They end up in water, soil, and living things. The authors ask where they go and what they do.

The review tracks sources, travel, and fate in water and land systems. Models now match field measures of particle levels. Particles can coat living surfaces and alter growth and behavior. They also bind other pollutants, for sink or harm. Gaps in detection still limit firm answers. Readers get a broad status report on a growing pollution question.
europmc-pmc5816785:
Cavalheiro and Teixeira review Candida biofilms and how to fight them. Candida yeasts cause surface and deep infections in people. They persist by building biofilms, slimy layers stuck to tissue or devices. Those layers shield them from drugs and immunity.

Four species get compared: albicans, glabrata, tropicalis, and parapsilosis. Each builds its film with its own mix of glue and cell shapes. Gene controls for sticking and growth differ widely among them. Film cells resist antifungals far better than free cells do. Mixed films with other species add more trouble. Promising attacks aim to block film growth or break mature films apart.
europmc-pmc5816885:
Voulodimos and co-authors review deep learning for computer vision. Deep methods now beat older machine learning on many visual tasks. Vision is among their clearest wins. The review keeps its scope brief and broad.

Four scheme families get short histories and structure notes. They are convolutional networks, deep Boltzmann machines, deep belief networks, and stacked denoising autoencoders. Each entry lists strengths and limits. Uses covered include object detection, face recognition, and pose estimation. The close looks at future design hurdles. Readers get a compact first map of the main deep vision methods.
europmc-pmc5833385:
Dai and co-authors review m6A, the commonest chemical mark on messenger RNA, and its hand in cancer. Their review appeared in Cell Death & Disease. Enzymes nicknamed writers add the mark, and erasers remove it. Reader proteins bind it and steer the RNA's fate.

The mark touches nearly every step of RNA life. It shapes splicing, export, translation, and decay. In cancer it feeds stem cell renewal and fast growth. It also helps tumors resist radiation and chemo. Early blockers of m6A factors slowed cancer in tests, marking the system as a drug target.
europmc-pmc5835085:
Winklewski and co-authors ask what two MRI measures really say about white matter damage. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Neurology. Diffusion tensor imaging tracks water movement along nerve fibers. Axial diffusivity runs along the fiber, and radial diffusivity runs across it.

Four early animal studies tied the pair to injury types. Axial drops marked axon damage, and radial shifts marked myelin loss. Later work muddies that clean split. Swelling, inflammation, and crossing fibers all distort the readings. The authors judge the pair useful in calm conditions, and they warn against reading them alone.
europmc-pmc5911985:
Campbell and Turner challenge the claim that hard exercise suppresses immunity. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Regular activity lowers infection and chronic disease risk in older age. Yet a single hard bout is often said to open a window of weakness. The authors call that idea a myth. They re-examine each pillar behind it.

Evidence for higher infection risk after hard exercise is thin, they argue. Saliva antibody shifts do not prove suppression either. Cell counts fall after exercise because cells move to tissues. That move raises surveillance, not weakness. Vaccine studies show exercise can boost responses. Regular activity may also slow immune ageing.
europmc-pmc5934485:
Solleiro-Villavicencio and Rivas-Arancibia review how chronic oxidative stress shapes the immune response in neurodegenerative disease. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience. They searched PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar for work from 1997 to 2017. The focus is neuroinflammation driven by CD4+ T cells. Microglia and astrocytes also play central roles.

Loss of redox balance shifts CD4+ T cell groups toward Th1 and Th17 responses, they conclude. That shift feeds inflammation in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and multiple sclerosis. Regulatory T cells and Th2 cells push the other way. The authors note that moving anti-inflammatory T cells into damaged brain regions could protect nerves. Such cell movement might become a therapy strategy.
europmc-pmc5934885:
Holeček reviews branched-chain amino acids in health and disease. His review appeared in Nutrition & Metabolism. The three branched-chain amino acids are valine, leucine, and isoleucine. They are essential amino acids that help build protein. They have been studied in muscle wasting disorders for over fifty years. Their value as therapy is still not settled.

The review explains how skeletal muscle starts the breakdown of these amino acids. It covers the roles of the BCKD enzyme and of branched-chain keto acids. Blood levels rise or fall in many conditions, from cirrhosis to diabetes. Maple syrup urine disease, kidney failure, burns, and sepsis also alter levels. Holeček weighs where supplements help and where more study is needed.
europmc-pmc5961885:
Young studies how cancer mortality varies across Glasgow districts and relates to social status. His paper appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal. The city health report for 1924 gave striking ward figures. Blythswood showed 1,748 cancer deaths per million people. Maryhill showed only 598 per million. A London newspaper read this as cancer striking the leisured classes harder. That reading clashes with the accepted view, Young notes.

Most earlier studies found cancer mortality falls as social rank rises. Crude rates can mislead, since age makeup differs by district. Young sets out to test the contrast with proper classification. His analysis weighs age and sex incidence by class.
europmc-pmc6004385:
Weber and co-authors review how myeloid-derived suppressor cells hinder the anti-cancer activity of immune checkpoint inhibitors. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Checkpoint drugs free T cells from tumour-imposed brakes. They have won approval for melanoma and other cancers. Many patients still fail to respond, though. Deep immune suppression is one likely reason. Suppressor cells block T and natural killer cell attacks. They also boost regulatory T cells that calm immunity.

Their levels may predict who will respond to therapy, the authors note. Combining suppressor-cell targeting with checkpoint drugs could help. The review analyses such pairing strategies in detail.
europmc-pmc6030385:
Hu and co-authors review light-based therapy against biofilm infections. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Microbiology. Biofilms are microbial communities stuck in a self-made matrix. They may cause up to 80 percent of human infections. Biofilm cells resist antibiotics far more than free cells.

The therapy uses harmless dyes plus visible light. Excited dye makes reactive oxygen species. These damage proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids nearby. Studies in labs and animals show strong biofilm cuts. Uses range from dental biofilms to chronic wounds. The review explains how the damage unfolds. It also covers ventilator pneumonia and sinus infections. Readers get a survey of a promising non-antibiotic approach.
europmc-pmc6053985:
O'Connor and Kirtley present a model of suicidal behaviour. Their article appeared in Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B. Suicide takes about 800,000 lives each year worldwide. Prediction has barely improved in fifty years. One gap was a full theory of the process.

Their model splits the path into three phases. Background factors set the stage first. Feelings of defeat and entrapment then spark suicidal thoughts. A separate set of factors governs action on those thoughts. Those factors include access to means and past behaviour. Planning, impulsivity, and pain tolerance also count. The article traces the model's origins and tests. It ends with directions for future research. Readers get a structured way to think about risk.
europmc-pmc6060985:
Abramowicz and Gos review splicing mutations in human genetic disorders. Their article appeared in the Journal of Applied Genetics. Splicing cuts introns from early RNA copies of genes. Guide sequences mark where the cuts must fall. Mutations at those marks can wreck the final message.

Such changes can skip exons or leave introns in place. Some quiet-looking variants also disturb splicing. Computer tools can predict a mutation's likely effect. Only lab tests can confirm it, though. The review gives examples drawn from inherited disease. It also covers detection methods used in diagnosis. Readers get a guide to a common but hidden class of mutation.
europmc-pmc6092785:
Tomiyama and co-authors argue that weight stigma itself harms health and drives weight gain. Their opinion article appeared in BMC Medicine. Weight discrimination is common worldwide. In some surveys it outruns racial discrimination. Health care settings show strong anti-fat bias.

Stigma predicts higher mortality beyond body mass index. Lab studies show it raises eating and stress responses. Those paths feed further weight gain. Patients with obesity often receive poorer care. Some medical students report coping through alcohol and drug use. The authors target the stigmatizers, not the stigmatized. Training compassionate providers is their first fix. Readers get a case for eradicating weight bias in medicine.
europmc-pmc6116485:
Clausen and co-authors present a methods article in BMC Bioinformatics on a fast tool for mapping DNA reads. Clinics now use DNA sequencing to find germs and drug resistance. That work needs reads matched against databases full of near-duplicate entries. Older tools can be slow or pick the wrong match.

The tool, called KMA, matches raw reads straight against such databases. It uses short word-like seeds to speed the search. A classic alignment method then refines each match. Tests used fake data and E. coli reads. The authors report that KMA beat six rival tools on speed and accuracy. Memory use stayed about the same.
europmc-pmc6133085:
Al-Mahmood and co-authors wrote a review in Drug Delivery and Translational Research on metastatic and triple-negative breast cancer. Triple-negative tumors lack three receptors that many drugs target. That leaves fewer treatment options. They make up about 10 to 20 percent of breast cancers. Spread to distant organs is the main danger.

The review covers standard care, from surgery and radiation to chemo and hormone drugs. It then turns to newer tactics. Targeted drugs, gene therapy, and immune therapy all feature. One nano-based plan pairs gene silencing with gefitinib against the EGFR pathway. The authors stress that combined treatments are usually needed.
europmc-pmc6177485:
Ormel and co-authors present a research article in Nature Communications on microglia growing inside brain organoids. Cerebral organoids are lab-grown brain models made from stem cells. They were thought to hold only nerve-lineage cells. That limits them, since microglia, the brain's immune cells, come from a different lineage.

The team shows microglia arise on their own within these organoids. The cells take their normal branched shape and carry the right markers. Their gene activity closely matches adult microglia taken from human brain tissue. They also respond to inflammatory triggers and can engulf particles. Organoids with built-in microglia open a new way to study brain development and disease in human tissue models.
europmc-pmc6193685:
Huang and co-authors report in Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report on HIV preexposure prophylaxis use in the United States, 2014 to 2016. PrEP is a daily pill of antiretroviral drugs that strongly prevents HIV infection. The approved drug combines tenofovir and emtricitabine. It is meant for people whose behavior puts them at high risk.

CDC analysts used a national prescription database to count PrEP users. The yearly number aged 16 and over rose 470 percent, from 13,748 in 2014 to 78,360 in 2016. The report describes users by sex and by race and ethnicity. It gives public health a baseline for judging whether PrEP reaches those who need it most.
europmc-pmc6199985:
Ge and co-authors report in Emerging Infectious Diseases on the virus behind China's first African swine fever outbreak in 2018. On August 3, 2018, an outbreak in pigs was reported in China. African swine fever causes high fever, bleeding, and severe depression in domestic pigs. Death rates can approach 100 percent.

The team took virus from a positive pig sample and placed it on the virus family tree. The strain belonged to p72 genotype II and CD2v serogroup 8. That matches the lineage then spreading in the region. Naming the strain precisely helps trackers follow the outbreak's origin and movement. The short report is an early genetic record of a major animal disease event.
europmc-pmc6262585:
Patel and co-authors review the causes and costs of physician burnout. Their review appeared in Behavioral Sciences. Burnout mixes deep exhaustion, detachment from patients, and a sense of failure. Rates reported across medical fields run from a quarter to three fifths of doctors. Daily care demands weigh on doctors, and record keeping adds more. Many doctors get little training for the clerical load.

Harm spreads in three directions when burnout takes hold. Doctor health suffers first. Patient outcomes then slip as focus fades. The wider care system loses skilled staff and money. The authors weigh fixes with proof behind them. Group sessions, mindfulness training, and discussion groups all show gains. A healthier work setting is also on the list. The review urges systems, not just doctors, to change.
europmc-pmc6264685:
Galdiero and co-authors review silver nanoparticles as possible antiviral agents. Their review appeared in Molecules. Virus infections remain a global health burden. Resistance and side effects limit many current antiviral drugs. Tiny silver particles offer a different attack route. They have shown action against several virus types. The list includes HIV, hepatitis B, herpes, and respiratory syncytial virus.

Silver particles can strike many targets in a virus at once. That breadth may make resistance less likely than with single target drugs. The review first covers how the particles are made. It then weighs results virus by virus. Safety and dosing questions are also raised. The authors see metal particles as a real option for new antiviral design. More work is needed before clinic use.
europmc-pmc6304785:
Chuo and co-authors review ways to image extracellular vesicles. The review appeared in the Journal of Biomedical Science. Vesicles are tiny sacs that cells release. They carry proteins, lipids, and RNA between cells. They play roles in development and in cancer. Their nanometer size makes them hard to picture.

The authors survey current labeling and imaging strategies. Each method has strengths and trade-offs. A wrong label choice can distort what researchers see. The review also covers newer emerging tools. It explains how vesicles move in space and time. Readers gain a guide to picking a method. That helps future vesicle studies stay accurate.
europmc-pmc6341685:
Outeiro and co-authors update what is known about dementia with Lewy bodies. Their review appeared in Molecular Neurodegeneration. This dementia grows with age and steadily erodes thinking. It hampers daily life as it advances. Brain tissue shows clumps of a protein, alpha-synuclein. Those clumps form Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites.

Movement problems like Parkinson's disease often appear too. They are common but not required for diagnosis. Many Parkinson's patients also develop dementia over time. That overlap has blurred the line between the two conditions. Guidelines now help clinicians separate them in practice. The review lays out current definitions and core concepts. It then lists open questions the field must answer. Better tests and care hinge on that clarity.
europmc-pmc6353785:
Butt and Volkoff review gut microbes and energy balance in fish. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Endocrinology. Gut microbes talk to the brain along the gut-brain axis. Hormones, immune signals, and nerves carry the messages. Those talks can shape feeding and digestion. Most research so far concerns mammals.

Fish offer a fresh window on the same system. The review covers feeding behavior and gut motility. It covers the gut barrier and nutrient uptake too. Growth and energy balance tie the pieces together. Brain and gut hormones receive special attention. Environment and species differences also matter. The authors argue fish studies can reveal shared rules. Those rules may apply across vertebrates, humans included.
europmc-pmc6360685:
Zhang and co-authors review the microRNA-34 family in the Journal of Experimental and Clinical Cancer Research. These small RNAs help hold back tumors, working with the well-known guard protein p53. Their levels drop in many human cancers.

The review explains how miR-34 blocks tumor growth and spread. It acts on shape-change programs in cancer cells and on key growth signals. A drug based on miR-34, called MRX34, reached an early clinical trial. Lab studies also test tiny delivery packages to carry miR-34 into tumors. The authors see miR-34 as both a tumor brake and a treatment lead.
europmc-pmc6417085:
Kuczek and co-authors report a study in the Journal for Immunotherapy of Cancer on collagen and immune cells. Tumors remodel their surrounding scaffold, making it rich in collagen and stiffer. The team asked whether that dense scaffold slows the T cells that kill cancer.

T cells grown in three-dimensional collagen at high density killed cancer cells less well. Low-density collagen let them act more freely. Confocal imaging tracked the cells' movement and contact with targets. The work suggests the tumor's physical setting can blunt immune therapy. Loosening the scaffold may help T cells do their job.
europmc-pmc6417285:
Zhang and co-authors report a lung cancer study in Molecular Cancer. Lung cancer spread kills most patients, and bone marrow stem cells sit in the tumor's neighborhood. Low oxygen in tumors changes how those stem cells act.

Stem cells in low oxygen packed small RNAs into exosomes and sent them to lung cancer cells. The RNAs switched on a shape-change program called EMT through STAT3. Cancer cells then moved and invaded more readily. Blood exosomes from patients carried the same small RNAs. The authors present these signals as both a warning marker and a drug target.
europmc-pmc6435685:
Formisano and co-authors uncover FGFR signaling as an escape route that ER-positive breast cancers use against CDK4/6 inhibitor drugs. A kinome screen in treated MCF-7 cells flagged FGFR1 first. Cells carrying extra FGFR1 copies resisted fulvestrant alone or combined with ribociclib or palbociclib.

FGFR-blocking drugs reversed the resistance, and adding erdafitinib to standard therapy produced complete responses in patient-derived tumors grown in animals. Blood tumor DNA from 34 patients who progressed on CDK4/6 therapy showed FGFR1 or FGFR2 changes in 41 percent of samples. Trial data also linked FGFR1 amplification to shorter progression-free survival, supporting combination trials that add FGFR blockade.
europmc-pmc6450685:
Corder and co-authors locate the unpleasantness of pain in a distinct ensemble of neurons in the mouse basolateral amygdala. Pain's sting and its suffering are separable, as rare human cases show detection without aversion, but the circuit for the aversive part was unknown. Calcium imaging in freely behaving mice picked out the ensemble as it fired to harmful stimuli.

Silencing that ensemble removed pain's affective and motivational behaviors while leaving detection, reflexes, anxiety, and reward untouched. After nerve injury, even light touch recruited the same ensemble, matching the aversion of neuropathic allodynia. A target that dulls suffering without numbing sensation is the therapeutic promise.
europmc-pmc6524685:
Gill, Catchpole and Forterre review the small membrane bubbles that cells of every kind shed, writing in FEMS Microbiology Reviews. Archaea, bacteria and eukaryotes all release these extracellular vesicles, sized roughly 20 to 500 nanometres. How cells make them is still poorly known, though shifts in membrane lipids seem to start the budding.

The vesicles carry proteins, lipids, sugars and nucleic acids between cells. Their jobs span stress response, rivalry, gene transfer, attack and detox, and they figure in human disease and aging. The review also covers the viral world: vesicles can act as decoys that soak up viruses, yet infected cells release vesicles that help viruses spread. Long dismissed as cell dust, the bubbles now look like a universal postal system.
europmc-pmc6645485:
Liljequist and co-authors rework the theory of the intraclass correlation coefficient. Their paper appears in PLoS ONE. The ICC measures reliability in repeated measurements. Choosing the right version confuses many researchers. Software often hides the logic behind menus. The team re-derived the single-score ICC theory. Monte Carlo simulations checked the probability distributions. Their practical recipe skips the upfront model choice.

Instead, analysts compute all three single-score formulas. Near-equal values signal no systematic bias. The classical one-way ICC then applies safely. A consistency value above the absolute agreement value signals bias. In that case both biased versions should be reported. An F-test can confirm the bias formally. A clinical example illustrates the workflow.
europmc-pmc6653385:
Zhou and co-authors review ways to trigger immunogenic cell death in cancer therapy. Their review appears in the Journal of Cellular and Molecular Medicine. Some dying cancer cells alert the immune system. They expose damage signals called DAMPs. Dendritic cells read those signals and mature. They then present tumour antigens to T cells. The result can be lasting protective immunity. Classic apoptosis was long thought silent or tolerogenic. Certain treatments break that rule.

The review surveys present and emerging inducers. Physical therapies feature among the newer options. Combination approaches are covered as well. Concepts and molecular mechanisms get brief treatment. The authors see inducer design as a growth area. Pairing cell death with immune activation is the goal.
europmc-pmc6658985:
Lee and Giuliani review the role of inflammation in depression and fatigue. Their review appears in Frontiers in Immunology. Both symptoms burden patients with chronic disease heavily. Sufferers rank them among their most disabling problems. Both track with raised immune activation. The signal appears in blood and in the brain. Autoimmune diseases like multiple sclerosis show the pairing clearly. So do infections such as sepsis. Treatment evidence points the same way.

Antidepressants tend to lower inflammation levels. High starting inflammation predicts weaker drug response. Yet those patients may answer better to immune-targeted therapy. Such treatments helped depression and fatigue in some cases. The authors call immune pathways a valid treatment target. They urge work on the exact mechanisms involved.
europmc-pmc6863385:
Zhang and co-authors report a study in Molecular Cell on why old B cells flag. Ageing weakens antibody responses, so vaccines protect the elderly less and infections hit harder. The team found that autophagy, the cell's recycling system, runs low in mature lymphocytes of older individuals. Memory B cell responses suffer as a result.

A natural compound, spermidine, restored the recycling. It modifies a translation factor, eIF5A, which is needed to build TFEB, a master regulator of autophagy. Spermidine levels fall with age in these cells. In blood cells from donors aged 65 years and older, TFEB protein was sharply reduced. Feeding the pathway back revived old B cell function in tests.
europmc-pmc6953885:
Kowalski and co-authors show that a large, diverse genome panel sharpens gene hunting in understudied populations. Their study appeared in PLoS Genetics. Most gene studies so far used people of European descent. African and Hispanic/Latino populations have more tangled patterns of inheritance, and far fewer data.

The team used more than 100,000 deep whole-genome sequences from the TOPMed program as a reference panel. Filling in genotypes for admixed African and Hispanic/Latino samples worked far better than with older panels. For rare variants, well-estimated variants rose 2.3- to 6.1-fold. Blood trait analyses in about 21,600 African-ancestry and 21,700 Hispanic/Latino people then found two rare variants in the HBB gene that older panels would have missed.
europmc-pmc6987885:
Thye and co-authors review how unusual sensory processing may feed social difficulties in autism. Their review appeared in Developmental Cognitive Neuroscience. Autism spectrum disorder centres on social communication problems and repetitive behaviour. Odd responses to sight, sound, touch, smell, and taste have featured in descriptions since the earliest reports.

Sensory trouble appears early and may cascade. A child who misreads sights and sounds can miss the raw material for learning social cues. The authors gather behaviour and brain evidence across all senses, including how senses combine. Theories of autism are judged on whether they link the two domains. Brain anatomy, function, and wiring differences underlie both sensory and social processing. Separating basic sensory faults from attention and thinking effects, they argue, is the key next step.
europmc-pmc6996285:
Blackmore and co-authors review ultrasound as a way to nudge brain activity without surgery. Their review appeared in Ultrasound in Medicine and Biology. Low-intensity ultrasound aimed at nervous tissue can briefly change how neurons fire. The field is growing fast.

Findings span cell cultures, animal work, and human cognitive studies, in both central and peripheral nerves. The authors explain how sound waves might physically interact with neurons to alter firing. A detailed safety review finds human study settings fall inside the envelope used for ultrasound imaging. Hard problems remain: aiming the beam precisely and monitoring the response. Even so, they conclude ultrasound offers a safe, non-invasive stimulation method. It localises better and reaches deeper than rival techniques, suiting both research and therapy.
europmc-pmc7045485:
Zhang and co-authors report how gastric tumours resist chemotherapy in Molecular Cancer. Ferroptosis is a form of cell death driven by iron and toxic lipid build-up. Cancer-associated fibroblasts, the support cells around a tumour, secrete many substances that help cancers grow and resist drugs. Whether they also control ferroptosis in cancer cells was unexplored.

The team linked the enzyme ALOX15 to lipid peroxide production in gastric cancer, then found a microRNA, miR-522, that blocks it. That microRNA travels in exosomes shed mainly by the fibroblasts. A packaging protein loads miR-522 into the exosomes, steadied by a de-ubiquitinating enzyme. Cisplatin and paclitaxel themselves prompt more miR-522 release, so treatment feeds its own resistance. Cancer cells receiving the microRNA suppress ferroptosis and survive chemotherapy. Interrupting this supply line could restore drug sensitivity.
europmc-pmc7062685:
Ratnatunga and co-authors chart the rise of non-tuberculous mycobacterial lung disease in Frontiers in Immunology. These bacteria are cousins of the tuberculosis bacillus that live freely in water, soil, and vegetation. Once dismissed as harmless except to damaged lungs or weak immune systems, they now infect seemingly healthy children and adults at growing rates, and deaths are climbing alongside.

Treating the disease is difficult because the bacteria resist many antibiotics. Highly resistant strains have even spread between people across continents.
