The review catalogues the global and economic burden, the populations at risk, current treatments, and how host and bacterium interact. Tropical regions carry particular concern: 40 percent of the world's people live in the tropics, and climate change is expanding that zone. The authors set out research priorities, arguing the field needs solutions before the map of infection widens further.
europmc-pmc7195385:
Kim and co-authors test how a diabetes drug class calms a harmful immune alarm called the NLRP3 inflammasome. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. SGLT2 inhibitors cut heart events in type 2 diabetes, but the reason was unclear. Inflammasome activity drives interleukin-1 beta release, which feeds artery disease and heart failure. The team treated high-risk patients for 30 days.

Patients received either empagliflozin or a sulfonylurea drug. Both lowered blood sugar about equally. Only the SGLT2 drug reduced inflammasome activation in patient macrophages. Ketone bodies and lower insulin seemed to mediate the effect. The authors propose this calming action helps explain the heart benefits. The work links a diabetes drug to immune control.
europmc-pmc7215485:
Setti and co-authors argue that the standard two-meter distance may not protect against airborne COVID-19. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Environmental Research and Public Health. Official guidance rested on droplets falling within about 2 meters, or 6 feet. Newer studies suggested the virus can travel farther in fine aerosols. SARS-CoV-2 also survives well in air and on surfaces.

Field studies inside Wuhan hospitals detected viral RNA in air samples. That supports airborne spread as a real pathway, the authors say. Small particles can linger and drift beyond the droplet range. Ventilation and crowding therefore matter as much as distance. The article urges officials to treat indoor air as a route of contagion. It questions rules built only on droplet thinking.
europmc-pmc7269385:
Nalla and co-authors compare how well different test recipes detect SARS-CoV-2. Their study appeared in the Journal of Clinical Microbiology. Many laboratories built their own PCR tests using published primer-probe sets, short DNA pieces that home in on the virus. With case numbers climbing, knowing which sets worked best was urgent.

The team ran seven different primer-probe sets plus one commercial assay kit against the same samples. Each set targets a different part of the viral genome, such as the E gene or the N2 region. Performance differed between sets, which matters when a missed positive can seed new infections. The comparison gave laboratories evidence for choosing and validating their own high-throughput testing setups during the first months of the pandemic.
europmc-pmc7281985:
Martens and co-authors review how vitamin D affects the immune system, beyond its classic role in bone health. Their review appeared in Nutrients. Interest grew after the vitamin D receptor was found on almost all immune cells. In laboratory dishes, high doses of the active form clearly change how immune cells behave.

Turning those dish results into clear clinical benefits has mostly failed, the authors admit. Yet evidence linking vitamin D deficiency to worse outcomes is strong, especially in early life. The review covers autoimmune and infectious diseases, including type 1 diabetes, multiple sclerosis, and rheumatoid arthritis. Their practical conclusion is plain: whatever the open questions, avoiding deficiency remains important for immune health.
europmc-pmc7359085:
Shi and co-authors present an overview article in Theranostics on cancer nanomedicine. It opens a special issue built around the EPR effect. That effect is the tendency of tiny drug carriers to gather in tumors. For 30 years it has guided tumor-targeted drug design.

The authors note that the effect is now hotly debated, above all in human patients. Results in animal tumors look far stronger than in people. The issue gathers 24 research and review articles on the topic. They cover how carriers enter tumors and how the tumor setting shapes them. Other pieces test priming treatments, active targeting, and pairing with immunotherapy. Imaging to sort patients gets attention too. Readers get a state-of-the-field guide to smarter cancer drug delivery.
europmc-pmc7384285:
Stein-Zamir and co-authors report a major COVID-19 outbreak in an Israeli high school in Eurosurveillance. Israel closed all schools on 13 March 2020 and fully reopened them on 17 May, with masks, hygiene rules, and distancing required. Ten days later the outbreak surfaced.

The first two cases, registered on 26 and 27 May, were not linked to each other. Testing the whole school community found 153 students positive, an attack rate of 13.2 percent, and 25 staff members, at 16.6 percent. Crowded classrooms and a heat wave that suspended mask use form part of the account. The report became an early warning on reopening schools at full capacity during active spread.
europmc-pmc7387485:
Sheller and co-authors demonstrate federated learning for medicine in Scientific Reports. Deep learning needs large, diverse datasets, but hospitals cannot freely pool patient data for privacy and ownership reasons. Federated learning instead sends the model to each hospital, trains locally, and merges only the learned updates.

Across 10 institutions, federated models reached 99 percent of the quality achieved by centralizing the data. The team also tested how models generalize to hospitals outside the federation, and how uneven data splits affect learning. The approach promises collaboration without surrendering records. Readers get a proof of concept for a privacy-preserving way to build medical AI at scale.
europmc-pmc7500085:
Grondin and co-authors review mucins, the gel proteins that guard the gut lining. A mucus layer coats the whole digestive tract. It eases food passage, joins cell signaling, and shields the wall from microbes and toxins.

Mucins split into secreted gel-forming types and membrane-bound types. Goblet cells among the gut lining cells make and release most mucins. Immune ties shape their output strongly. Bowel diseases, colon cancer, and gut infections all shift mucin amount and quality. Goblet cell faults and changed sugar coats on mucins show up in these states. The review covers mucin build, control, and immune ties. It links those basics to barrier strength and host defense in gut inflammation.
europmc-pmc7519685:
Rada and co-authors review lipotoxicity in fatty liver disease and ask if CD36 is a key driver. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease is the most common chronic liver disease worldwide. It ranges from simple fat buildup to hepatitis, cirrhosis, and liver cancer.

Lipotoxicity starts when fatty acid inflow swamps liver cells. Cells fail to store or export the fat as triglycerides. Stress in the ER, oxidative stress, and inflammation follow. The fatty acid carrier CD36 raises fatty acid uptake in the liver. It helps start fat buildup and may push progression to NASH. Patients show more CD36 in the liver and in blood. Its blood level tracks the grade of liver fat. Targeting CD36 or its regulators may prevent or treat the disease.
europmc-pmc7532385:
Alexander and co-authors compare office and telemedicine primary care visits in the US. They ask how COVID-19 changed visit volume and content. The data come from a national audit of practice.

The analysis covers more than 125.8 million primary care visits. It spans 10 quarters from 2018 into 2020. Visit volume fell by 21.4% in the second quarter of 2020. That drop was measured against prior second quarters. Blood pressure checks fell during the pandemic period. Cholesterol checks also fell. Telemedicine visits checked these measures less often than office visits. The results show a real shift in how primary care was delivered.
europmc-pmc7788585:
Teng and Fussenegger review how extracellular vesicles form and how they can be engineered. These vesicles are tiny sacs that cells release. They carry proteins, RNAs, DNAs, lipids, and metabolites. Cells that take them up can change behavior.

Vesicles cause little immune reaction. That trait makes them strong candidates for drug delivery. The authors sum up recent gains in vesicle biology. They then cover new engineering strategies. Vesicles can be loaded or tuned to carry cargo to chosen cells. The review weighs the path toward clinical use. It also names the hurdles that still block bioengineered vesicles in medicine.
europmc-pmc7816485:
Emami Nejad and co-authors review how low oxygen in tumors feeds cancer stem cells. Hypoxia is a shared trait of solid tumors. Fast growth outruns the oxygen supply. Abnormal vessels make blood flow worse.

Low oxygen wakes vessel growth and boosts invasion. It raises the risk of spread to new sites. It shields tumors from immune attack and blunts therapy. Gene switches and loss of genome stability play a part. The authors give cancer stem cells a central place in this story. Stem-like cells thrive in hypoxic pockets and seed regrowth. Managing the hypoxic setting is proposed as a treatment route.
europmc-pmc7905985:
Nooraei and co-authors present a review of virus-like particles and their uses in medicine. These particles are built from virus proteins that self-assemble into shells. They mimic a real virus in form and size. But they carry no genetic material, so they cannot infect cells. That mix makes them safe and strongly noticed by the immune system.

The review explains how the particles are made in living and cell-free systems. It covers both enveloped and non-enveloped types. Many vaccine candidates rest on this platform, including one against SARS-CoV-2. The particles trigger both antibody and cell-based defences. They are also being tested as carriers that deliver drugs to set tissues. Surface tweaks may stretch their life in the body and sharpen their aim. The authors map the hurdles that remain for wider use.
europmc-pmc7910485:
Fang and co-authors present a software package called SnapATAC for single-cell chromatin data. The data come from scATAC-seq, a method that reads which parts of the genome lie open in each cell. Open regions reveal the control switches that set a cell's type. But single-cell profiles are noisy, and datasets are huge.

SnapATAC sorts cells into groups without prior labels. It can also trace how cell states change along a path. A fast maths method lets it handle up to a million cells. The package bundles the full workflow, from raw data to results. As a test, the team analysed 55,592 profiles from a mouse brain region. They found about 370,000 candidate control elements across 31 cell groups. The tool also pointed to the regulators likely to run each group.
europmc-pmc8072585:
Silva Andrade and co-authors review the long tail of health problems that follow COVID-19. Survivors face months of care needs across the whole body. Earlier coronavirus diseases left the same kind of catalog. The team set out to map post-COVID and long-COVID outcomes in full. They grouped the damage by body system, eight in all.

Immune, blood, and lung damage lead the survey. Heart, gut, liver, and kidney problems follow close behind. Muscle, skin, and nerve complaints fill another large section. Mental health effects, from stress to anxiety, close the list. For each outcome, the authors propose molecular routes that might explain it. A shared thread runs through most of them. Cytokine storm, vessel inflammation, and tiny clots in small vessels do much of the harm.
europmc-pmc8074985:
Borghouts and co-authors sort what helps and what blocks engagement with digital mental health tools. These apps and programs widen access to care, and trials show they can ease symptoms. Yet many users drift away early. The team searched five major databases for studies of real use. A total of 208 articles met the bar for this systematic review.

Factors fell into three groups: the user, the program, and the tech setting. Severe symptoms often crushed the will to engage. Technical glitches and a lack of personal fit also drove users off. Social connection built into a tool pulled the other way. So did fresh insight into one's own health. A felt sense of control helped users stay. The authors offer the map to designers and evaluators. Engagement, they argue, is designed, not accidental.
europmc-pmc8108485:
WHO Immediate KMC Study Group ran a five-country trial of kangaroo mother care started right after birth. Skin-to-skin care after stabilization already saves low-birth-weight babies. Yet most deaths strike before babies stabilize. The trial enrolled 3,211 infants weighing 1.0 to under 1.8 kilograms at birth. Hospitals in Ghana, India, Malawi, Nigeria, and Tanzania took part. Half the mothers began continuous skin contact at once.

Mothers in the intervention arm logged a median of 16.9 hours of skin contact daily, against 1.5 hours in the control arm during those first days. Deaths in the first 28 days came to 12.0% with immediate care and 15.7% with standard care across the trial's five sites. The gap forced an early stop on safety advice. Deaths in the first 72 hours did not differ clearly. Starting skin contact at birth, not after stabilization, saved lives. The finding presses guidelines toward the earlier start.
europmc-pmc8224385:
Günther and co-authors screen thousands of compounds against the SARS-CoV-2 main protease. The protease, Mpro, cuts viral polyproteins into working parts. Without it, the virus cannot mature, so it is a prime drug target.

X-ray methods screened more than 5,000 approved or trial-stage compounds. Thirty-seven compounds bound the protease. Most bound the active site, but two side sites also appeared. Binding there shifted the active site's shape. Seven compounds fought the virus in cells without toxicity. The strongest, calpeptin, leads the follow-up list. Cell assays then sorted binders from true antivirals.
europmc-pmc8257585:
Wang and co-authors build a Z-scheme photocatalyst for efficient hydrogen evolution from water splitting. Pairing two light absorbers in a Z-scheme can keep strong charges apart. Steering that charge flow on purpose has stayed hard.

Their design joins sulphur-poor ZnIn2S4 with MoSe2. A molybdenum-sulphur bond at the interface and a built-in electric field guide the charges. Surface photovoltage and spin-trapping tests confirmed the Z-scheme path. Computer modelling backed the same picture. The catalyst produced hydrogen at a high rate under light. The work shows how interface design can sharpen solar fuel tools.
europmc-pmc8285185:
Samsu surveys diabetic nephropathy, its causes, diagnosis, and treatment. The disease is the leading cause of end-stage kidney failure worldwide. High blood sugar and high blood pressure drive it.

Screening checks urine protein each year. It starts 5 years after type 1 diabetes diagnosis. In type 2 diabetes it starts at diagnosis. Standard care targets A1c under 7% and pressure under 130/80 mmHg. Blocking the renin-angiotensin system anchors drug care. A form without protein in urine breaks the classic pattern. That form poses hard problems in detection and care. Cutting albumin loss remains a central treatment goal.
europmc-pmc8344985:
Gee and co-authors report the first month of COVID-19 vaccine safety monitoring in the United States. Two vaccines held emergency authorisation, Pfizer-BioNTech and Moderna. Monitoring ran from December 14, 2020 to January 13, 2021.

In that month, 13,794,904 doses were given. The VAERS system processed 6,994 adverse event reports. Of those, 90.8% were classed as nonserious. Headache, fatigue, and dizziness led the symptoms. Anaphylaxis came to 4.5 cases per million doses. Reviews of 113 reported deaths showed no causal link. The profile held no unexpected serious harms. V-safe text surveys supplied the active monitoring arm. The first month set the tone for how the rest of the roll out would be watched and judged by all.
europmc-pmc8398285:
Aitcheson and co-authors explain the role of macrophages in skin wound healing, and what goes wrong in diabetes. Early in repair, these cells stir inflammation and clear germs, debris, and dead cells. Later, they calm inflammation and send signals that guide new tissue growth.

In people with diabetes, macrophages react too strongly to inflammatory cues. They clear germs and dead cells too weakly. That failure blocks their switch into the repair mode. As a result, wounds stall and diabetic foot ulcers form. Such ulcers heal slowly, get infected often, and can lead to amputation. The review points to ways this cell fault might be treated.
europmc-pmc8426185:
Oberhardt and co-authors track CD8 T cells raised by the BNT162b2 mRNA vaccine. Protection from severe disease starts about ten days after the first dose. At that point, neutralizing antibodies are still hard to find. T cells may carry the early defense.

A strong, stable CD8 T cell response appeared one week after the first dose. That was before CD4 T cells and antibodies matured. The booster dose expanded the pool into highly developed effector cells. Memory precursor cells were not harmed by the boost. Vaccine-raised early memory cells worked as well as those from natural infection. Their subset mix, though, differed from infection.
europmc-pmc8497485:
Li and co-authors review myeloid-derived suppressor cells as cancer targets. These immature immune cells expand hugely as tumors grow. They help tumors escape immune attack in direct ways. They also aid invasion through non-immune routes.

Worse, the cells blunt chemotherapy, radiotherapy, and immunotherapy alike. That makes them a strong target for new treatment. Drugs aimed at these cells have shown promise in lab studies and in trials. Gains appear alone and in pairs with other cancer therapies. The review covers the cells' biology and suppressive tricks first. It then surveys the targeting strategies now in play.
europmc-pmc8533685:
Marinho and co-authors review hyaluronic acid as a key ingredient in inflammation therapy. This natural polymer is made by the human body itself. It is gentle on tissue and breaks down safely. Those traits drew wide study for use in inflammatory diseases.

Added hyaluronic acid cannot fully copy the body's own form. Still, it can give solid pain relief in practice. The review gathers progress made between 2017 and 2021. It covers the polymer's chemistry and how size changes its action. Uses across inflammatory conditions are weighed in turn. The authors close with what stands between lab promise and routine care.
europmc-pmc8716585:
Damiani and co-authors report the global burden of psoriasis from the Global Burden of Disease 2019 study. Psoriasis is a common, long-term inflammatory skin disease. New targeted therapies have reshaped its care. Updated burden counts were needed to judge past policy and plan new strategy.

The study counted 4,622,594 new cases worldwide in 2019. The age-standardized incidence rate was 57.8 per 100,000 people. That rate fell by 20.0 percent since 1990. Rates in men and women were near equal. Burden varied widely by region and by development level. The team also measured years lived with disability from the disease.
europmc-pmc8825285:
Johnson and co-authors map protein changes in the Alzheimer's disease brain at large scale. They analyzed proteins from more than 1,000 brain tissues. The goal was to find groups of proteins that rise and fall together. Such groups can reveal which processes break down in the disease. The team compared protein groups with RNA groups from the same cohorts.

Nearly half of the protein groups had no match at the RNA level. Two disease-linked groups stood out as protein-only finds. One tied to MAPK signaling and metabolism. The other tied to the matrisome, the tissue scaffold. The MAPK group tracked closely with the pace of mental decline. The authors offer both groups as leads for drugs and biomarkers. The study argues that Alzheimer's is, at heart, a protein disease.
europmc-pmc8844085:
Wang and co-authors review therapeutic peptides, from current uses to future directions. Peptides are short chains of amino acids. They sit between small drugs and large protein medicines. New production and testing methods revived the field. More than 80 peptide drugs now have approval worldwide. Their story began with insulin in 1921.

The review weighs the strengths and drawbacks of peptides. It follows their path from discovery to production to fine-tuning. Chemical and biological production routes are both covered. Modification tricks that extend a peptide's life get attention. The authors then survey disease areas where peptides serve. Diabetes and cancer feature among them. They close with the value and the hurdles ahead. Delivery and stability remain the chief problems to solve.
europmc-pmc8931585:
Liu and co-authors review cancer vaccines, their platforms, and their clinical progress. A cancer vaccine teaches the immune system to attack tumors. It delivers tumor antigens in some form. Whole cells, peptides, and nucleic acids all serve. An ideal vaccine would break the tumor's immune suppression. It would raise both antibody and cell responses. The field has moved fast in recent decades. Many candidates now sit in clinical trials.

The authors explain how the vaccines work first. They then summarize four development platforms. Each platform's strengths and limits are weighed. Clinical application gets the largest section. Trial results and real efficacy are the focus. The authors highlight where vaccines already help patients. They also note where results disappoint. Design lessons for the next generation close the piece. The review suits readers tracking immuno-oncology's front edge.
europmc-pmc9205785:
Rivellese and co-authors analyze joint tissue from the R4RA trial comparing rituximab and tocilizumab in rheumatoid arthritis. About 40% of patients fail any single biologic therapy. Tissue markers might predict who responds to which drug. The trial enrolled 164 patients and sampled their synovial tissue.

Deep tissue analysis found gene signatures tied to response for each drug. A stromal and fibroblast signature marked patients who resisted all drugs. After treatment, joint gene changes differed sharply between the two drugs. Machine learning models predicted response to each drug and to multidrug resistance. The authors argue that disease subtypes in tissue drive treatment response. Such signatures could steer drug choice in clinic.
europmc-pmc9380485:
Emmons-Bell and co-authors systematically review heart failure rates and survival across the world. Their search covered studies from 1990 to 2020 with clear diagnostic rules. From 42,360 candidate papers, 125 population studies qualified. The set feeds estimates for the Global Burden of Disease 2020.

Prevalence ranged from 0.2% in a Hong Kong hospital study to 17.7% among older US Medicare members. Yearly new-case rates ran from 0.1% to 4.3% across studies. One-year death after diagnosis averaged 33% across all studies. Definitions and case-finding methods varied widely between countries. The authors say heart failure stays common in older adults with a grim first year. Cleaner shared definitions would make future counts comparable.
europmc-pmc9646485:
Balood and co-authors show that pain sensing neurons weaken cancer immune watch in melanoma. Solid tumors draw in nerve fibers from the body. Whether pain neurons among them change immune control was unclear. Melanoma cells turned out to talk with these neurons directly.

Contact made the neurons sprout more branches and fire more readily. They also released more of the peptide CGRP. That peptide pushed killer CD8 T cells toward exhaustion. Worn T cells then cleared melanoma with less force. Cutting the pain neuron line had the reverse effect. Silencing the neurons or blocking the CGRP receptor also helped. Tumor growth fell and mouse survival nearly tripled in one model. Patient biopsies backed the pattern in human tissue. T cells bearing the CGRP receptor looked more exhausted than kin without it.
europmc-pmc9825485:
Seal and co-authors describe the HGNC gene naming resources as they stand in 2023. The committee assigns the official symbols for human genes. Unique, stable names keep science talking about the same genes. The database now holds over 43,000 approved symbols.

Of those, over 19,200 mark protein coding genes. Pseudogenes account for 14,000 of the approved entries. Nearly 9,000 symbols name non-coding RNA genes. Each gene gets a report page on the public site. Reports gather curated names plus links to other data. The committee has run for over 40 years now. This update improves the site's search facility. New download features were added for bulk users. Links to related resources were widened as well. The authors stress using approved symbols over aliases. Alias mix-ups can silently corrupt large studies.
europmc-pmc9883685:
Polański and co-authors introduce BBKNN, a fast graph method that aligns single-cell transcriptome batches. Large single-cell RNA sequencing projects now produce huge shared datasets. Batch effects between labs can distort combined analysis. Most correction methods are slow on very large data.

BBKNN uses a graph approach to remove batch effects with far lower run time. The authors tested it on large mouse atlas data. It compared well on speed against several rival methods. The tool runs in Python and can be installed from pip. Example notebooks and documentation are provided online. BBKNN aims to make atlas-scale data integration practical for routine work.
europmc-pmc9931585:
Sorin and co-authors map single-cell spatial landscapes of the lung tumor immune setting. Tumor subtypes are often classed by tissue type alone. The spatial layout of cell types inside those groups stays poorly known. The team applied imaging mass cytometry to lung adenocarcinoma samples.

Samples came from 416 patients across five histological patterns. The team resolved more than 1.6 million cells for spatial analysis. Immune lineages and activation states showed distinct links to outcomes, including survival. A deep learning model predicted post-surgery progression from a single 1-mm2 tumor core. It did so with high accuracy. The dataset is shared as a resource for lung cancer research. It shows how AI can read tumor layout for care.
europmc-pmc9977685:
Tintelnot and co-authors report that a gut microbe product shapes chemotherapy response in pancreatic cancer. Pancreatic cancer often spreads early and responds poorly to treatment. Fewer than half of patients respond to chemotherapy. Genes alone cannot explain that gap.

Shotgun metagenomic sequencing and metabolite screening flagged indole-3-acetic acid, called 3-IAA. This tryptophan product from gut microbes was enriched in patients who responded. Fecal transplants raised chemotherapy effect in humanized mouse models. Short-term diet changes in tryptophan did the same. Oral 3-IAA also boosted treatment effect in those models. Loss and gain tests traced how the effect works. The findings link diet, microbes, and drug response in this cancer.
four-books-concerning-the-secrets-of-the:
Weidenfeld's four books teach the use of Lully's spirit of wine, the great solvent of the adepts. Charles the Second granted him a royal licence for the sole printing of the work. The text gathers the ancient and modern fathers of adept philosophy into one practical system.

Its receipts turn on menstrums, solvents fitted to their designed uses. Mercury, the book declares, must first be reduced into the first matter with a vegetable or animal water. Otherwise its crudity corrupts the work and nothing good can be done with it. Johann Seger Weidenfeld published the treatise in 1685, in the old long-s type that marks this copy.
four-books-of-johannes-segerus-weidenfel:
Weidenfeld collected this practical work, in his title's words, with very great study out of the ancient and modern fathers. Where the old adepts disagreed, he reconciled them by comparing one with another. The subject is Lully's spirit of wine and the preparations drawn from it.

The Rosarium of Arnald of Villa Nova anchors one key teaching. Mercury reduced to its first matter, with the said vegetable or animal water, is the condition of all success. A compounded menstruum, the receipts add, improves the oftener its composition is repeated. Johannes Segerus Weidenfeld printed the four books in 1685 under royal licence.
fox-underhill-missing-link-1885:
Leah Fox, the eldest of the famed girls, tells her own tale in The Missing Link in Modern Spiritualism, out in 1885. As A. Leah Underhill she looks back on 1848, when raps in her kin's house in Hydesville sparked a world faith. She was there. She managed, taught, and at times fought her own young kin in the years of fame.

Her tale is part log, part plea for her place in the tale. Feuds, fraud claims, and fame crowd the pages. No past of the faith can skip her voice. She was in the room where it all began.
frus-1861-d185:
A second letter from the Acting Secretary of State to Carl Schurz bears the date 5 November 1861. It is document 185 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Two letters to Madrid in one day from the acting chief match the Secretary's own habit. Each takes its own point in the Spanish file. The pair falls days before the Trent seizure, in the last calm week of the autumn. Last calm weeks in this file are few, and this pair of letters marks one. Few calm weeks remained in 1861, and the file soon shows why.
frus-1861-d285:
By the date of 19 August 1861, Seward had new word ready for Mr. Haldeman. Congress received it as Document 285 in the papers printed with the President's message that year. The date falls in the first summer of the Civil War, when the Union fought to keep foreign powers from backing the South.

The text is Washington speaking: orders, guidance, and the facts the envoy was told to stress. Its worth grows in context, as one link in a chain of letters that kept the peace with Europe. The Foreign Relations series, kept by the State Department's Office of the Historian, preserves the full run.
frus-1861-d85:
Writing on 25 September 1861, William H. Seward counseled patience in a letter to Charles Francis Adams. The letter is document 85 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Late September found the war at a standstill in the East. Seward's letters abroad grew more plain and more patient. This one kept Adams to the long game in London: hold the line, make no threats, and let time work for the Union. Time, Seward judged, fought for the side that could feed and fund its armies. Letting time work was a plan that asked much of men's nerves, and Seward had them.
frus-1862-d185:
Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Charles Francis Adams in London on 10 November 1862. Opening a run of four same-day letters printed in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume as Documents 185 through 188.

Four letters in one mail marks a desk-clearing day at the State Department, with a steamer waiting. The topics would have ranged over the whole London brief, from British politics to ships building for the South. This first letter of the set starts a batch that, read whole, gives Washington's position in mid-November in unusual detail. The legation's clerks copied each dispatch into bound letter books before the mail sailed.
frus-1862-d285:
William H. Seward, the Secretary of State, wrote to William L. Dayton in Paris on 6 June 1862, in a dispatch printed as Document 285 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. The letter followed a Dayton report by one day in the file.

Early June brought the Union victory at Memphis on the Mississippi, news that traveled fast and impressed shipowners and bankers in Europe. Seward's dispatches often carried such facts to his envoys as arguments. A letter like this one let Dayton walk into the French foreign ministry with fresh proof that the Union was winning the river war. Edouard Thouvenel ran the French foreign ministry for most of 1862 and set Dayton's agenda there.
frus-1862-d385:
On 28 July 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward sent Simon Cameron a dispatch printed as Document 385 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Cameron was the American minister in Russia, at St. Petersburg.

Late July 1862 was a season of Union setbacks, and letters to St. Petersburg took the longest road in the Department's mail. Seward wrote knowing his words would be read a month later, in a different military world. Dispatches to Russia therefore favored lasting lines over daily news, a quality that marks this channel's papers. The czar's government had freed its own serfs in 1861 and watched America's struggle closely.
frus-1862-d485:
On 27 February 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote again to James Shepherd Pike in The Hague. The instruction is Document 485 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the official record for the year.

Three weeks had passed since Seward's last Dutch order, and the war news in them was good: Fort Donelson had fallen. Good news was a diplomatic asset, and Seward spent it promptly, sending his ministers the facts to use at court. Pike's work in the Netherlands also touched Dutch colonial ports in the Caribbean, where belligerent ships might seek entry. The letter shows Washington feeding a small post the material it needed to hold its ground.
frus-1862-d585:
On 28 March 1862 Thomas Corwin sent a further report from Mexico to Secretary of State William H. Seward. It is Document 585 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, printed with the President's annual message.

Three Corwin reports in eight days mark March 1862 as a turning point in Mexico. Spain and Britain were preparing to withdraw. France would be left to press on alone. Corwin's letters home caught that shift as it happened. They weighed what it meant for the United States. That country was then too busy with its own rebellion to do more than protest. The file is the nearest thing the volume offers to a front-line diplomatic diary, written by a veteran statesman in a capital under foreign threat.
frus-1862-d685:
On 8 April 1862, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to William Sydney Thayer, the American consul general in Egypt. The letter is document 685 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862. It answers the run of reports Thayer had sent from Alexandria.

Seward's outward mail told consuls what Washington wanted watched and how far they could go. For Egypt, trade and the safety of Americans on the Nile route sat high on the list. This letter shows the State Department guiding a lone post on a busy sea road. In the same weeks, it fought to keep Europe out of the Civil War.
frus-1862-d85:
Seward heard from Charles Francis Adams on 26 June 1862, in a dispatch sent from abroad. Congress received it as Document 85 in the foreign affairs volume that went with the President's message. It belongs to the summer of 1862, the war's second year, when keeping Europe out of the war was a core task for Washington.

Readers get the field report side of the exchange, sent home for Seward to weigh and answer. For students of the war, the value lies in the sequence: one dated step in a long exchange. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1863p1-d185:
An instruction dated 5 May 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward in Washington to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, in London. It appears as document 185 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It is one of the papers the State Department later printed in its Foreign Relations series for 1863. It was one of 5 letters between the same men dated that day.

For readers today, these instructions reveal the thinking inside the State Department as clearly as any memoir. They show choices being made in real time, with poor information and high stakes. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d285:
The State Department's mail for London dated 5 September 1863 carried this instruction from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. It is document 285 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. It appears in the Foreign Relations series, where the State Department printed the papers it sent with the President's yearly message to Congress. It was one of 4 letters between the same men dated that day.

Confederate agents were buying ships and arms in Britain, and Washington wanted the trade stopped. Orders to London often carried protests, evidence, and legal arguments for Adams to use. For a modern reader, it offers the war as working diplomats saw it: slow mail, sharp words, and constant risk.
frus-1863p1-d385:
A formal note dated 7 February 1863 passed from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, in Washington. It stands as document 385 of the 1863 diplomatic papers. It survives in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official record of its work abroad.

Canada, then a British colony, shared a long border with the Union. Worries about raids, plots, and smuggling across that line sit behind part of this correspondence. It is a small piece of a huge correspondence, but the whole picture only emerges from pieces like this one.
frus-1863p1-d485:
Dated 29 April 1863, document 485 is a letter from Britain's minister in Washington, Lord Lyons to Secretary of State William H. Seward. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Read with its neighbors, the note helps explain a fact of the war: Britain never stepped in, and the record shows the effort that took. Kept with the rest of the 1863 papers, it helps the full story of wartime diplomacy stay traceable, letter by letter.
frus-1863p1-d585:
William H. Seward, Secretary of State wrote this official letter to Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington on 14 July 1863. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail. The exchange belongs to the Civil War years, when Washington's first task abroad was keeping Europe out of the fight.

None of these letters worked alone. Read in sequence, they show two governments testing each other's limits while both, in the end, avoided a second war. For historians, the value lies in the run of the letters. Together they trace, almost day by day, how the Union kept its most dangerous foreign problem from boiling over. That is the use of such a page: not a famous text, but a firm rung in the ladder of the record.
frus-1863p1-d685:
On 10 November 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward wrote to Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington. The letter is printed as document 685 in the 1863 volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official set of American diplomatic papers.

Seward and Lyons dealt with each other often, and their calm tone helped keep a hard tie steady. Britain stayed out of the war, but strains over ships, ports, and seized goods kept coming up. A note like this one did the daily work of that tie. It shows how big aims, such as keeping peace with Britain, rested on short, clear, polite words.
frus-1863p1-d85:
A cluster of same-date letters opens with this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, dated 19 February 1863. Adams was the American minister in London, and Adams letters of the same date sit right after this one in the volume. The letter is document 85 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward wrote in a week when the two men's pens would cross once more. His letters fed Adams the facts and the tone for talks with the British foreign office. This one opens a same-date cluster in the file. Read with the Adams sheets that share its date, it shows both ends of the sea mail working at once. Each end was in the dark about the other's page.
frus-1885:
Cleveland's first message opens the 1885 volume in mourning. Vice-President Hendricks has died suddenly, he reports. The country files then spread wide. Central America takes the longest run. Colombia's Washington legation papers match its main file. Haiti and Spain both run long. A new name appears in the list. The Congo earns a short section of its own.

Britain's fisheries diplomacy gets a separate block. It prints the papers on the new fisheries agreement. Germany's file turns on one man's status. A young man in Alsace-Lorraine faced prison and expulsion. Berlin argued the army would lose recruits to emigration. Washington weighed his father's presence in his favor. Citizenship cases like his fill these years. The volume shows their human scale.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d185:
Ambassador Averell Harriman cabled President Roosevelt from Moscow on 2 November 1943 with news from the foreign ministers' conference just ended there. His long, urgent message reports the deal that Soviet foreign minister Molotov and Britain's Anthony Eden had initialed the night before about Turkey.

Under that deal, both governments wanted Turkey to join the war against Germany before the end of 1943, and to hand over air bases for Allied use at once. Harriman describes signing the conference papers at Molotov's office near midnight, then being pressed by Molotov at the ballet for a fast American answer. He warns that Moscow set great store by Turkey's entry, and he asks Roosevelt either to join the deal or to say when a decision would come.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d285:
President Roosevelt sent Marshal Stalin a secret telegram, marked operational priority, from Cairo on 22 November 1943, the day he arrived there. Carried by Navy channels through Ambassador Harriman, it is his first word to Stalin about the timing and lodging of their first meeting at Tehran.

Roosevelt says talks with Churchill have begun, the Chinese meetings will end the week. He could reach Tehran on the afternoon of 29 November. He would stay two to four days, as Stalin's duties allow. He asks Stalin to name the day and warn of weather delays. He also raises a security worry: the Soviet and British embassies in Tehran stand close together, while the American legation is far off, so driving between meetings would risk all three leaders. Where, he asks, should we live?
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d385: Harry Hopkins sent James Byrnes, director of war mobilization, a two-line telegram from Tehran on 28 November 1943. It answers Byrnes' telegrams of 24 and 27 November pressing for a bigger landing craft program. Extensive studies are required before a decision can be reached, Hopkins replies. In the meantime, Byrnes should proceed exactly as he did before the question of an increase in landing craft was raised. The terse message held Washington's shipbuilding plans in place while the conferences settled the operations those craft would serve.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d485:
A second report by the Combined Staff Planners bears the same date, December 5, 1943, showing how much staff work the Second Cairo Conference consumed in a single day. The planners served the Combined Chiefs of Staff, drafting and testing the schemes the chiefs debated. The State Department included the report in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Two planners' reports in one day point to parallel questions being worked at once, which was normal at a summit covering a world war. Each report turned a strategic idea into a practical judgment the chiefs could accept or reject. Together with the minutes, they let readers trace a decision from first sketch to final order.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d85: Churchill wrote to Roosevelt on November 2, 1943, as the president's departure for the East drew near. His message is Document 85 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. November's letters in this series carry a mounting sense of journey and decision. The catalog record supplies the date and the names and nothing more. The message rests in the Foreign Relations volume, among the last papers written before the leaders left home.
frus-1944-quebec-d185:
An editors' note introduces Lord Cherwell's two memoranda, the principal source for the September 14, 1944 meeting on Germany. It also preserves Morgenthau's later account to Treasury officials in Washington. The contrast between the two evenings is the point: Churchill had violently opposed the Treasury plan when it was presented raw on September 13.

Presented the next morning through Cherwell, much softened down, the program met a different reception. To Morgenthau's amazement, Churchill interrupted and said: "I will take it." White recorded more. Morgenthau said Churchill seemed to accept weakening Germany's economy. He had spoken of making Germany an agricultural state, as in the last quarter of the nineteenth century.
frus-1944-quebec-d285:
The memorandum initialed on September 15, 1944, creates the joint committee on lend-lease for the period after Germany's defeat. Roosevelt and Churchill had discussed the scope and scale of mutual aid during the war with Japan. The committee would agree and recommend the amounts of mutual aid in munitions, non-munitions, and services for the most effective prosecution of the war.

Its chairman's name was left blank; the American members named were Morgenthau, Stettinius, and Crowley. Pending the committee's recommendations, departments of both governments were instructed to make no major lend-lease decision for the period without its approval. The committee would be guided by the leaders' conversation of September 14, the figures discussion recorded by Cherwell.
frus-1944-quebec-d85:
Secretary of War Henry L. Stimson wrote to President Roosevelt on September 5, 1944. Stimson had run the War Department since 1940. His letter appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume. It came one week before the Quebec Conference.

Cabinet letters to the President carried department positions into summit planning. The War Department oversaw armies then advancing toward Germany. Its views mattered on occupation duties and future campaigns. For readers, Stimson's letter shows a senior cabinet voice in writing. He addressed the President directly while the Quebec briefings were assembled. The conference opened at Quebec City one week later.
frus-1945-50-intel-d185:
The meeting named in the title took place on 12 February 1947, and these minutes are its formal record. The Office of the Historian kept it as document 185 in the Foreign Relations intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. Central intelligence then sat with the National Intelligence Authority, a board of top officials served by the Central Intelligence Group.

Minutes are the formal record of a meeting: who sat in, what was put on the table, and what the group agreed to do. Read with the papers before and after it, the record shows a policy taking shape one meeting at a time. To read it in place is to watch the Cold War state being assembled at desk level.
frus-1945-50-intel-d285:
Dated 7 June 1948, this memorandum runs from the Assistant Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Lay) to Director of Central Intelligence Hillenkoetter. The State Department prints it as document 285 in Foreign Relations of the United States, in the intelligence volume for 1945 to 1950. The Cold War was turning harder that year, and the new Council and CIA were being tested by it week by week.

Memos like this one did the quiet work of the system. They carried facts, advice, and requests from one office to the desk that could act on them. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d385:
On 7 July 1949, staff wrote up the discussion at the 43d Meeting of the National Security Council for the President. The editors of Foreign Relations of the United States placed it as document 385 in the 1945 to 1950 intelligence volume. With the Dulles Report now public inside the government, agencies were sorting out what to change and what to defend.

A memcon lets later readers sit in on a talk they could not attend: who spoke, what was asked, what was left open. Later memos cite such notes the way lawyers cite a witness: as the best proof of words once spoken. The FRUS editors kept it because the chain of choices is not whole without it.
frus-1945-50-intel-d85:
Russell sent Secretary Byrnes a formal report on 12 February 1946. Reports from an administration chief sum up a period and recommend a course. The text comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States volume that looks back at American intelligence work from 1945 to 1950.

By February the new central group existed, and the State Department had to fix its own intelligence office's size and duties beside it. Russell's report belongs to that fixing. Readers can trace in it the department's retreat from its autumn ambition to house the nation's analysts. The report is the kind of paper on which offices are cut: measured, factual, and fatal. The volume's State thread bends here toward the office's transfer out of the department's heartland.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d185:
Roosevelt answered Churchill on the Italy row on 6 December 1944, from Warm Springs. His top secret telegram, number 669, is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. He tries to calm the prime minister without giving ground on the point of principle.

A letter to Berle, he explains, merely passed on Sforza's message to Badoglio and bound the United States in no way. Churchill may use that message as he sees fit. Roosevelt deplores any offense the press release gave. But Eden's prior speech in the Commons put Washington in an untenable place. Italy is an area of joint Anglo-American charge while the fighting runs on. Britain acted with no prior word to Washington, and American silence made it seem that Washington agreed.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d285:
Archibald MacLeish drafted words for the conference communiqué on 19 January 1945. His letter to James Dunn, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, discusses a draft the two assistant secretaries had gone over by phone at noon. It concerns how unconditional surrender should be explained to the world.

The communiqué, MacLeish suggests, might open with a restatement of allied war aims. The purpose is not the destruction of a nation or of a people. It is the destruction of the enemy's military might, and safeguards against its return. The measures follow. The German armies surrender and are disbanded, their equipment destroyed or removed. German industry is barred from war work. War criminals are punished, and the teaching of hatred and racial pride comes to an end.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d385:
Homework for the ministers fills this American delegation paper of February 8, 1945. Four items were referred to the foreign ministers. Two or three Soviet republics might join the world body as first members. The date and place of the United Nations conference needed fixing. Invitations needed a list of nations. Iran needed a policy.

An attached paper argues against seating any Soviet republics at the start. Its first point is formal: the republics had not signed the United Nations Declaration. Yet the attachment's heading shows the American view was shifting under Soviet pressure. Two days later, Ukraine and White Russia would be promised seats. The file catches the argument mid-turn.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d485:
Italy gets a refusal in Stettinius's cable to Grew of February 7, 1945. An agreed directive on Italy, the Secretary wrote, fell far short of what it should contain. It held so little of substance for the Italians that issuing it would have a disappointing and unfortunate effect, in America and in Italy alike.

America's first acceptance of a public statement, he explained, had rested on an assumption. Real help, moral and material, would follow from talks on the Macmillan proposal. That had not proved the case. So there was no reason to issue any statement now. Stettinius added that he and Matthews had gone over the matter with Ambassador Kirk.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d85:
Why did Moscow cling to the veto? Ambassador Harriman offered his answer from Moscow on 28 December 1944. His secret cable to Secretary Stettinius, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, gives his present impressions of Soviet thinking on the voting question.

Since the revolution, Harriman writes, the world has been hostile or suspicious toward the Soviets. They know they are now a great power, but they still doubt that other Council members would treat them fairly in a dispute. He adds that Moscow has future aims Washington does not yet fully grasp. One is plain: states on the Soviet border may be independent, but their governments must be “friendly.”
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d185:
General Deane proposed direct Pacific liaison links to General Antonov in a letter dated July 5, 1945. The letter is document 185 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It lays before the Soviet chief of staff, in advance, a plan the American chiefs wanted ready when Soviet forces entered the war against Japan.

Liaison through Moscow and Washington would circle the globe and be far too slow for local needs, Deane argues. He proposes swapping liaison officers and setting up radio teletype links between the Soviet Far Eastern headquarters and MacArthur's headquarters in Manila and Nimitz's on Guam. Local commanders could then swap combat intelligence fast and coordinate on submarines, air patrols, and convoys. No decision is asked now; the plan is for study before the Berlin staff talks.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d285:
A briefing paper urged holding back recognition from the satellite regimes, dated June 29, 1945. The paper is document 285 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It sets the policy the United States should follow on ties and peace treaties with the former Axis satellite states.

Word from Romania and Bulgaria shows Soviet officials and local Communists building one-party rule, the paper says. Groups that will not bow to the ruling fronts are shut out of public life. U.S. proposals on Romania's regime and Bulgaria's elections, made under the Crimea pledge on freed Europe, were curtly turned down by Moscow. Hungary is still a broad coalition, though the same pattern may be forming. U.S. and British members of the control bodies have been shut out of real say. The paper builds the case Truman took to Potsdam.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d385:
Soviet hands reached for Rumanian oil shares in a cable Melbourne sent from Bucharest on July 12, 1945. A reliable source had given him the text of a July 3 letter from General Susaikov, deputy president of the Control Commission, to Premier Groza. The letter concerns talks on creating a Soviet-Rumanian petroleum company.

Susaikov wrote that shares in Rumanian petroleum societies which had belonged to Germans now passed to the Soviet Union. They were partial compensation for damage Germany caused the Soviet Union. Groza was to turn the rights over to Moscow, which had charged an association called UCR Petrol with taking them over. Melbourne urged that Washington relay the text to Moscow.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d485:
Assurances from Poland's new rulers are sought in Grew's top secret cable to Harriman of June 22, 1945. This government, he writes, is giving careful thought to recognizing the Provisional Government of National Unity in the near future. Before deciding, it would be most helpful to have prior assurances from the competent members of that government, the more important of whom are now in Moscow.

The points listed match the facilities America extends to foreign diplomats at home. First among them stands communications. The new Polish government should grant the embassy to be set up in Poland full facilities. It should be able to communicate by mail, telegraph, radio, and courier, with the State Department and other American missions. A prompt, favorable reply would obviously ease the way.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d585:
Foreign Minister Togo cabled Ambassador Sato once more on July 13, 1945, about the Konoye mission. The secret urgent cable is document 585 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. It reports a step taken in Tokyo itself toward the Soviet side.

Togo had meant to receive Soviet ambassador Malik and tell him of the envoy plan in person. Malik, however, was sick in bed. So Togo sent Ando, his political affairs chief, to Malik's side instead. Ando told Malik that the Emperor wished to send Prince Konoye with a personal letter on ending the war. Sato was to put the same word to the Soviet government in Moscow. Malik promised to wire his government about the matter at once.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d685:
From Ankara on June 20, 1945, Ambassador Wilson relayed Britain's advice to Turkey. His top secret priority wire is document 685 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The British ambassador had just arrived from Istanbul and seen Turkey's acting foreign minister.

London held that the Turks had taken the only course open in refusing Molotov's proposals. Yet Turkey should not be wholly negative in reply. It might propose that the Montreux Convention be revised by four or five states, not by Russia and Turkey alone. Britain, Greece, and the U.S., if willing, might take part. Britain felt strongly it should intervene at Moscow without delay and hoped the U.S. would join. The Turkish minister welcomed that plan and hoped for like U.S. action. He also reported Russian troop movements toward Turkey's eastern frontier.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d85:
Ambassador Harriman gave Admiral Leahy his own reading of Stalin's likely answer on June 21, 1945. The telegram from Moscow is document 85 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. Leahy had asked how Stalin would react to the American Chiefs of Staff traveling to Berlin with the President.

Harriman is personally quite sure Stalin will not object. He expects Stalin will welcome close talks with Truman about military operations in the Far East, talks that would need the chiefs present, though the political questions would come first. Harriman also advises keeping the staffs small, unlike Yalta, and names officers he wants brought from Moscow, including General Deane. The cable shows an ambassador shaping the delegation from the field.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1085: The Acting Secretary of State sent this brief telegram to Potsdam on July 31, 1945. It reports a step just taken in Washington on the Greek-Yugoslav dispute. The Department is telling its embassies in Moscow and London to inform the two foreign offices of an American plan. A three-power commission should be named to look into Yugoslav charges against Greece, as Secretary Byrnes approved on July 28. The embassies are to ask whether the Soviet and British governments agree to take part in the inquiry.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1185:
President Truman wrote to Britain's new prime minister, Clement Attlee, on 29 July 1945. Three days had passed since the election results remade the British team. The summit had a new face across the table, and work could not pause for long greetings.

A first message to a new partner opens the working tie. Truman now had to deal with a Labour leader he barely knew, on the hardest questions in Europe. The note shows the American president greeting the new man and getting back to business. Summit history turns on such moments, when the persons change and the agenda does not.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1285:
The British Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum on 20 July 1945. It joins the British run of staff papers in the volume. London's chiefs advised their own team in the same form their American partners used across the hall.

The British services faced a world-wide bill: occupation in Europe, war in Asia, and fleets on every sea. Their papers sorted those claims for the envoys. This one dates from the first week's close. It is the British military house's view at that point, preserved through the allies' habit of sharing staff paper.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1385:
Stanisław Mikołajczyk, deputy prime minister of Poland, set down a memorandum on 24 July 1945. Mikołajczyk had led Poland's government in exile in London before joining the new Warsaw government that summer. It is printed in volume two of Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record of American diplomacy at Potsdam.

Poland's fate was the sharpest moral question at Potsdam: its borders moved west, and its government was remade under Soviet eyes. Mikołajczyk stood between the worlds, a democrat inside a regime he did not control. His memorandum gives the Polish case in a Polish voice, a rare thing in a volume of American papers. Readers should weigh it as the plea of a man who knew his country was being decided by others.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-85:
State Department staff kept these minutes of a meeting held on July 24, 1945, during the Potsdam Conference. The record belongs to the set of formal minutes printed in the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States. Minutes of this kind were the conference's memory. They fixed who met, what was put on the table, and what was decided or left open.

Readers get a plain, close record rather than a speech or a press line. The value lies in the detail: points raised, replies given, and tasks handed out. Set beside the day's other papers, the minutes help rebuild how the talks moved hour by hour.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d785:
Mosely wrote to Ambassador Winant in London on July 27, 1945, in document 785. The political adviser to the European Advisory Commission's American member reported to the embassy chief. Their shared work bound London's planning to Potsdam's choices. The letter entered the second Potsdam volume.

Letters between planners show the settlement's nervous system. Mosely and Winant had worked the Germany problem together for many months. Readers see that partnership still active in the final week. The document also shows how much of Potsdam was prepared elsewhere. The summit ratified, and revised, a structure built by men like these.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d885:
Prepared for Assistant Secretary of State William Clayton on July 29, 1945, this working paper sums up German economic matters near the end of Potsdam. Its author is not named. It notes that principles 10 through 17 already stand agreed. A short list of next steps follows.

The paper urges deleting Principle 18 and rewriting the clause on foreign credits to Germany. It also lists the open files by topic. Reparations rest on Edwin Pauley's July 24 memo. Other headings cover restitution, American property, German assets abroad, satellite assets in neutral lands, and art objects. Each heading points Clayton to the paper that holds the detail.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d985:
George Kennan, the American chargé in Moscow, cabled the Acting Secretary of State on July 19, 1945. His embassy, working with reparations aide Seymour Rubin, has sent the Soviet Foreign Office a note on German external assets. The note says Washington had to assume Soviet consent to its planned steps. No answer came to an earlier letter. Soviet moves in Ankara and Stockholm also pointed the same way.

The note stresses the need to stop German assets from being hidden or drained away. It also reports steps already taken on German official property in Spain. Kennan adds that Rubin and DuBois will carry a copy of the note to Berlin, leaving July 20.
frus-1951-54Iran-d285: The CIA station in Iran cabled the Agency in August 1953, during Operation TPAJAX, in this urgent message. The station voices horror at the weak support and guidance given to the Shah. It urges that Britain press the Shah to order the army to back Prime Minister Zahedi. Other steps include an aid cutback note and a public query from President Eisenhower. Field notes report troops breaking up a Tudeh crowd in Tehran on August 18. A garrison revolt at Sanandaj is also reported.
gao-gaoreports-b-295585:
Government Scrap Sales brought the protest in GAO file B-295585, decided on March 11, 2005. The Defense Reutilization and Marketing Service had proposed awarding Liquidity Services, Inc., a contract for the sale of scrap materials. The protester claimed a conflict of interest: a subsidiary of the winner ran a related surplus property contract. GAO denied the protest. A bare chance that a firm will act in bad faith under its contract does not make out a conflict. No other basis for barring the award was shown.

Conflicts must rest on facts, the ruling holds, not on what a firm might do. The scrap sale award could proceed.
gao-gaoreports-b-305885:
Relief for two embassy cash staff is granted in this GAO decision, B-305885, dated September 2, 2005. The case stems from the U.S. Embassy in Brazzaville, Republic of the Congo. Civil war broke out there in 1997. Staff fled the embassy amid gunfire in the city. Cash in the amount of $21,403.04 was lost.

Emery Banguid was the backup cashier on duty that day. Frank Forgione was the other officer tied to the loss. The State Department asked GAO to lift their duty to repay. GAO granted the relief. The loss came amid war and a forced flight from the post. The case shows how GAO weighs fault when cash is lost in chaos.
gao-gaoreports-b-310485:
Nilson Van & Storage, Inc. saw its protest thrown out under GAO decision B-310485, dated December 10, 2007. The Army sought moving and storage work at Fort Bragg. The work split into three lists for out, in, and local moves. The award for one list went to A+ Relocation Services, Inc. Nilson said the winner was judged fit on thin facts.

GAO dismissed the protest. The call's fact plea was no fixed test of fitness. It set no hard bar the winner had to clear. No proof showed the deal chief skipped key facts he held. Fitness calls rest with the chief, short of a red flag in the file.
gao-gaoreports-b-311385:
Phoebe Putney Memorial Hospital lost its protest. That ruling is B-311385, dated June 19, 2008. The Veterans Affairs office sought care for vets in body and mind health. The award went to Sterling Medical Associates, Inc. The hospital said the cost test was thin. It fought the tech scores of both bids as well. The deal ran at a set price for the work.

GAO denied the protest. No cost test of that kind was owed here. Set-price deals do not call for it, and this call set none. The score claims showed no harm in any case. The winner would hold the lead if the scores moved as claimed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-185: Invasive Species: Cooperation and Coordination Are Important for Effective Management of Invasive Weeds, GAO-05-185 of February 25, 2005, is held here as its own short summary text. Harmful weeds hurt range land and wild habitat and cut land yield. Most federal weed funds have gone to farm land, not wild land. GAO maps who fights weeds in wild areas and what funds they use. It reports the blocks weed chiefs named, and their views on how new funds should be split. The study drew on talks with over 90 officials.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-385:
Mutual Fund Trading Abuses, GAO-05-385 of May 16, 2005, grades how the stock watch fined the firms it caught in a trade fraud. Two frauds stand out. In market timing, pet clients trade fast past fund caps in the dark. In late trading, a client buys at the day's price after the 4:00 p.m. close has set it. Both rob the plain holder.

GAO lists the fines set in closed abuse cases. It tells of the jail-side cases that ran with them. It tests the steps by which the watch sends a case for crime probe. Fines were set by one fair path, it finds; some locks could be firmer.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-585:
Plans for who takes over key jobs are compared across four agencies in GAO report GAO-05-585, issued on June 30, 2005. Strong succession planning looks past swapping one person for another. It builds the capacity an agency will need years ahead. GAO studied the Census Bureau, the Labor Department, the Environmental Protection Agency, and the Veterans Health Administration. Each had set up its own effort to prepare future leaders and fill skill gaps.

All four gave the work to councils or boards. The health agency went further, with a subcommittee and senior posts charged with the task.  All four have begun tying the work to their strategic goals. Three have named gaps in key skills and track their progress in closing them. The Census Bureau watches its key jobs less closely, a weak spot with the 2010 count ahead.  GAO urged better coordination and sharper checks on what training achieves.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-785:
Base closures for 2005 are analyzed in GAO-05-785, dated July 1, 2005. On May 13, 2005, the Defense Secretary sent a record list of closures and shifts to an outside commission. The law told GAO to report by July 1 on the choices and the process. GAO asked if the list met the department's own goals. It also tested whether the process was logical and flagged points needing care.

GAO found mixed success. The list topped all past rounds combined in size. But most items hit reserve sites, and few closed active bases. Up-front costs were put at $24 billion. Claimed savings near $50 billion over 20 years rest on shaky ground, GAO said. Much of the yearly saving comes from jobs that will move, not vanish.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1085:
Health care for civilian staff sent to war zones is the focus of this September 2006 GAO study of the Department of Defense. The Senate Armed Services Committee required the review. DOD leaned more on federal civilians in Iraq and Afghanistan. GAO checked over 3,400 deployment records and spoke with officials. It asked whether DOD set health protection policies and whether the services followed them. It also compared special pays and benefits for civilians and troops.

DOD had policies on paper but no way to ensure compliance. Records at eight sites often lacked proof of health checks, shots, or screenings. Medical treatment rules, by contrast, had been set and carried out. Special pays and survivor benefits differed between civilians and military staff. GAO urged the Secretary of Defense to build an oversight and quality system. DOD partly agreed with that call.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-285:
Benefits eating a bigger share of the pay package is documented in GAO-06-285, dated February 24, 2006. Most workers rely on their employer for both wages and benefits. Tax breaks sweeten employer health and retirement plans. Workers and firms also pay the taxes that fund Social Security and Medicare. GAO used federal data on what private employers spend on active workers. It asked 17 experts for their read. It tracked total pay costs, the mix inside them, and what workers themselves pay or gain.

Employer spending on benefits has grown faster than wages, GAO found. Health insurance and retirement costs drive most of the rise. That shift can squeeze take-home pay even when total pay climbs. Access and worker shares of cost have moved as well. The report weighs what the trend means for private coverage over time. It gives a clear view of a quiet change in how Americans get paid.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-385:
Agencies cannot fight terror well if they cannot share what they know. GAO ruled in GAO-06-385 on March 17, 2006, on sharing terrorism-related information. Two laws drive the work. The Homeland Security Act of 2002 called for sharing policies. The Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004 called for an Information Sharing Environment.

GAO checked progress toward government-wide policies and processes. It surveyed 26 agencies on their sensitive but unclassified labels. It also reviewed the rules tied to those labels. GAO found the federal government still needs to set clear policies and processes. Readers see the label tangle that slows sharing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-485:
Prosecutors with special mandates spend public money, and their spending is audited. Financial audit GAO-06-485, issued March 31, 2006, covers independent and special counsel expenditures. The period is the six months ended September 30, 2005. One office of independent counsel and one office of special counsel were audited. Law required the audit. The statements cover Independent Counsel David M Barrett and Special Counsel Patrick J Fitzgerald.

GAO judged whether the expenditure statements were fairly stated. They were presented fairly in all material respects, GAO found. The report also gives opinions on internal control. It covers compliance with laws and regulations. Readers get both statements in full.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-785:
Guarding classified material at the Energy Department is assessed in GAO-06-785. The report is dated June 30, 2006. Congress has grown more worried that agencies misclassify information, in both directions. The department runs one of the government's most sensitive classification systems, covering nuclear weapons data. Its training, guidance, and oversight programs had been built over many years. GAO assessed a recent change in who oversees classification there.

GAO found that those programs had been effective over time. But a recent shift in oversight duty had created uncertainty about roles. Internal reviews found very few misclassified documents, GAO noted. Yet the way documents were picked for review was uneven and lacked openness. GAO urged actions so the recent changes do not weaken a system that works.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-85:
Insurers' readiness for a terrorist attack is reviewed in GAO-06-85, a report GAO released on November 18, 2005. The insurance sector is a core part of the financial system. After an attack, policyholders urgently need damage checks, claim payments, and annuity services. If insurers' own operations fail, that help stalls. GAO described the threats insurers face and tested how well large firms can protect and recover their critical work.

GAO found that insurers appear prepared to recover critical operations after an attack. Sound business continuity plans are the heart of that readiness. Firms had built backup sites, data protection, and crisis teams. Even so, GAO flagged issues that warrant further review. Some recovery plans had not been fully tested against a large, shared disaster. The report balances reassurance with caution.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1085:
Big oil spills are rare, but the federal spill fund faces risk, GAO reports in GAO-07-1085, dated September 7, 2007. Law puts the cost of a spill on the ship owner first, up to a set cap. A trust fund run by the Coast Guard pays when that party can not, or will not.

A 2006 law told GAO to study spills that cost at least $1 million. GAO counted such spills since 1990, and their total cost. It named what drives spill costs up or down. It weighed what big spills mean for the fund's health. The work drew on cost data, talks at all levels, and picked spill files.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-585:
Math beats expert gut feel at spotting crash-prone truckers, and GAO-07-585, dated June 11, 2007, shows the test. The Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration picks carriers for safety reviews with a tool called SafeStat. SafeStat was built on expert judgment. It sorts firms by crash and violation data. GAO asked whether a statistical model could sort them better.

GAO replayed the year 2004. It ranked carriers by each method, then checked crash records through 2005. A negative binomial regression model flagged the firms that went on to crash at higher rates. Data flaws in the inputs also got a look, since bad data blurs any model. Deaths per mile have stalled since the mid-1990s after decades of decline, GAO notes. Sharper targeting is one of the few cheap wins left. The report urges the agency to swap the formula for the model.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-85:
Missing alien files in citizenship cases are examined in GAO-07-85, dated October 27, 2006. U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services keeps an A-file for each immigrant. In 2002, citizenship was granted to a man whose file was missing. He was later tied to a terror group. GAO asked how often files are missing at decision time.

Files were present in about 96 percent of cases decided in fiscal year 2005. That figure comes from data on about 715,000 applications. Audits of samples found files missing in less than 1 percent of cases. The true rate sits in a range, since the agency does not log every missing file. Staff often fail to use the file-tracking system on time. GAO urged the agency to record file use in each case. It also urged a joint fix with other file users. The department agreed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-885:
Airport building needs and funding are tallied in GAO-07-885, dated June 29, 2007. The Federal Aviation Administration plans a new air traffic system called NextGen. The White House proposed deep changes to airport grants in the same law. GAO updated its picture of airport development costs and funding. It merged the agency's project data with an industry group's survey. The report holds no recommendations. The Transportation Department agreed with its findings.

Planned development costs run at least $14 billion a year for five years. That sum is in 2006 dollars. Airports got about $13 billion a year from 2001 through 2005. Municipal bonds supplied almost $6.5 billion of that yearly flow. Federal grants added $3.6 billion, and passenger fees $2.2 billion. The 67 largest airports take most of the money. They handle 90 percent of passengers. GAO set planned needs beside likely funding. It also summed up what the grant changes would do.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-185:
Emergency continuity drills across government are described in GAO report GAO-08-185 (November 19, 2007). Agencies must keep plans to run vital services in a crisis. The Federal Emergency Management Agency guides that work. It also stages a governmentwide exercise every other year. In June 2006, its Forward Challenge 06 drill let agencies test their plans live.

GAO studied eight civilian agencies with large disaster roles. It read their drill records and asked what they had tested. Agencies sent key staff to backup sites and ran core tasks. The report shows how far each one pushed its plans, people, and gear in the drill.
geschichte-der-menschlichen-narrheit-ode:
Johann Christoph Adelung published his History of Human Folly in German in 1785. Its full title promises lives of famed magicians, gold-makers, devil-conjurors, readers of signs and lines, zealots, and fortune-tellers. Adelung was a scholar of language who wrote in the spirit of the Enlightenment. The old print and worn scan make the German hard going in places.

Each life tells how a supposed wonder-worker won fame, and how the tricks or the madness worked. A first life opens with a man born in 1629 in a Silesian village, son of a country pastor. Adelung treats his subjects as warnings: folly, fraud, and pride feed on the wish to believe. The book is both a rogues' gallery and a plea for clear sight, from an age that prized reason.
gregory-thaumaturgus-dubious-or-spurious:
