Gregory Thaumaturgus, the Wonderworker, led his flock in the third century. Miracles gave him his glowing name among later Christians. An 1885 Fathers volume gathers writings ascribed to him that he likely never wrote.

The editors honestly label the pieces dubious or spurious in the title. Fame itself generated the extra literature around his revered name. Writers of later ages put their own ideas in his mouth. The gathering thus preserves thoughts that once traveled on his authority. It also teaches a useful lesson in how saints' works grow. Readers can watch reverence and invention mix across the centuries in plain view.
grose-vulgar-tongue-1785:
Francis Grose published his Classical Dictionary of the Vulgar Tongue in 1785, the first true slang dictionary in English. Grose was an artist and antiquary who collected words in taverns, markets, and army camps. He treated street speech as worthy of the same care scholars gave to Latin.

The entries record thieves' cant, soldiers' and sailors' talk, and the jokes and insults of everyday London life. Many entries are funny, and many are rude, which was part of the point. Polite dictionaries of the age ignored this half of the language. Grose preserved it, and historians of English still mine his pages for how ordinary people actually spoke in the 1700s.
hippolytus-against-noetus-macmahon-1885:
Noetus taught that the Father himself had suffered and died on the cross, collapsing the persons of the Trinity into one. Hippolytus of Rome answered him in Against Noetus, a short work in MacMahon's 1885 translation. The reply became a landmark in the Church's teaching about Father, Son, and Spirit.

Hippolytus draws clear lines between the persons while holding fast to their perfect unity. One God, he argues, yet the Son is truly distinct from the Father who sent him. The balance he strikes shaped centuries of later doctrine. Brief and sharp, the treatise rewards close reading. It shows a third-century theologian solving, in outline, problems the councils would later formalize.
hippolytus-on-christ-and-antichrist-macm:
Daniel's visions and the terrors of the last days stand at the center of On Christ and Antichrist, written by Hippolytus of Rome around the year 200. MacMahon's 1885 English translation presents the treatise. It ranks as the earliest Christian commentary on Daniel and a founding text of writing about the end times.

Hippolytus reads prophecy with confidence, laying out the signs of the end and the career of the Antichrist. Empires rise and fall in his scheme, each matched to the prophet's images. Every later work on the Antichrist stands, knowingly or not, in this book's shadow. The treatise also shows how early Christians under pressure read their own times into scripture. Its influence on later apocalyptic writing is hard to overstate.
hippolytus-refutation-of-all-heresies-ma:
Around the year 230, Hippolytus of Rome surveyed pagan philosophy and Christian sects in ten books, the Refutation of All Heresies. Long known as the Philosophumena, the work appears here in MacMahon's English version of 1885. Greek schools and Gnostic systems alike pass under his review.

Hippolytus preserves short accounts of teachings that would otherwise be lost for good. Because the sects' own books mostly perished, his summaries carry huge weight with historians. His tone can be scornful, but his information is gold. Students of the early Church still start here to learn what the so-called heretics really taught. Few ancient books hold so much otherwise vanished material.
hippolytus-the-extant-works-and-fragment:
S. D. F. Salmond translated the surviving works of Hippolytus for 1885. Hippolytus served the Church at Rome in the third century. He was the first antipope in its history, and he later died a martyr.

Comments on scripture fill much of what survives from his pen. His Refutation of All Heresies stands as his most famous work. Part scholar of the Bible and part hunter of error, he spared nothing. Truth as he saw it ruled his writing from start to finish. The fragments reveal a formidable mind and give modern readers a key voice from the early Roman Church.
history-of-the-united-netherlands-from-t:
John Lothrop Motley's History of the United Netherlands, complete in one file, runs from the murder of Orange to the truce of 1609. Fifty-three chapters trace the Dutch republic's first twenty-five years. William the Silent's assassination opens a story of offered sovereignties and refused protectors. Farnese, Leicester, Maurice, and Barneveld succeed one another as its leading figures.

The siege of Antwerp, the Armada, and the sieges of Maurice fill the military narrative. Vervins, Philip's death, Ostend, and Spinola's campaigns bring the war toward exhaustion. The conclusion finds Spain recognising an independent, sovereign, protestant republic. Motley, an American diplomat and historian, wrote the great English-language epic of Dutch freedom. This complete text holds his whole design in one place: immense in detail, dramatic in scene, and openly partisan for liberty against empire.
hoffmann-weird-tales-1885:
E. T. A. Hoffmann's Weird Tales reached English in J. T. Bealby's translation of 1885, in two volumes. Bealby's version gives Hoffmann's uncanny tales, founding texts of the fantastican literature, to Victorian readers. Hoffmann, a German composer and judge, wrote tales where dream, madness, and mechanism invade the everyday world.

The Sandman, the most famous here, turns on Nathanael's terror of Coppelius and his love for a doll, Olimpia. The Cremona Violin, The Fermata, and other tales mix music, art, and the supernatural in Hoffmann's ironic, layered frames of narration. His doubles, automata, and haunted artists fed Poe, Gogol, and the whole Gothic and fantastic tradition after him in Europe. Freud later mined The Sandman for his essay on the uncanny, fixing the tale's fame in modern thought about dread. Bealby's dress is Victorian, but the strangeness cuts through undimmed.
hoffmann-weird-tales-vol1-1885:
J. T. Bealby chose and translated the tales in Weird Tales, volume one, published in English in 1885. The selection draws on E. T. A. Hoffmann's best-known stories of the uncanny. Bealby aimed to give English readers the Hoffmann who had taught Poe and Gogol their trade.

The Sandman, the most famous tale here, turns a childhood bogey into a study of obsession and sight. Other tales bring sinister doubles, cursed gifts, and artists undone by their own gifts. Hoffmann's horror grows from the mind as much as from any ghost. His people doubt their senses, and the doubt itself terrifies. Volume one is the classic entry into his haunted world.
hoffmann-weird-tales-vol2-1885:
Bealby's second volume of Weird Tales, published in 1885, completes his English selection from Hoffmann. The tales here continue the first volume's tour of the uncanny. Music, madness, and the supernatural cross paths in tale after tale.

Readers meet enchanted instruments, fatal bargains, and lovers who may not be human at all. Hoffmann keeps one foot in daily life, which makes the strangeness bite harder. Inns, workshops, and concert rooms turn quietly wrong around his heroes. Bealby chose for variety as much as for fame, and the volume rewards browsing. Together the two volumes form the standard Victorian Hoffmann, the one that shaped English ideas of the fantastic.
howells-silas-lapham-1885:
William Dean Howells published The Rise of Silas Lapham in 1885. Silas Lapham is a Vermont farm boy who made a fortune in paint and moved to Boston. There he builds a grand house and hopes his daughters will enter high society. Howells tells the story with a close eye on money, manners, and morals.

Lapham's business falters, and bad deals tempt him to cheat a partner to save himself. At the same time, a halting courtship links his family to an old Boston clan. His true rise, Howells suggests, is moral rather than social. The novel became a landmark of American realism, prizing honest detail over romance.
ignatius-epistles-roberts-donaldson-anf-:
Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, was marched across Asia Minor under guard around 110 CE to be killed at Rome. On the road he wrote seven letters to churches and to Polycarp of Smyrna. Alexander Roberts and James Donaldson translated them for the Ante-Nicene Fathers series in 1885, with the longer and Syriac versions and the tale of his martyrdom.

Ignatius begs the Roman church not to save him: he longs to die as grain ground by the teeth of beasts. He urges unity around the bishop and defends the real flesh of Christ against teachers who called it seeming. The letters are among the earliest Christian writings after the New Testament. Their fire still startles readers.
ignatius-of-antioch-martyrdom-of-ignatiu:
Ignatius, bishop of Antioch, died as a martyr in Rome in early Christian times. Guards took him from Syria around the year 110, by the v1 account. The short Martyrdom of Ignatius preserves how the early Church recalled that death.

Wild beasts in the arena ended his life before a Roman crowd. Ignatius begged his friends not to try to rescue him from the fate. He longed, he said, to become the pure bread of Christ. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers edition carries the ancient account in English. Brief as it is, the text keeps one of the first and most revered martyrs vivid for modern readers.
irenaeus-against-heresies-rambaut-anf-18:
Irenaeus, bishop of Lyons in the second century, wrote Against Heresies to refute the Gnostic teachers who claimed secret knowledge of God. The Reverend William H. Rambaut translated the five books for the Ante-Nicene Fathers series in 1885. Fragments and a short elucidation round out the volume.

Book by book, Irenaeus lays out the systems of Valentinus and his kin, then answers them from scripture and the rule of faith. He defends one God, one Christ, and a real flesh and blood salvation. His work is our chief source for what the Gnostics taught, since their own books were mostly lost. It set the bounds of Christian doctrine for good.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-of-pinsk-: Aaron of Pinsk served as rabbi first in Kretingen, in the government of Kovno, and later in Pinsk, where he died in 1841. He wrote "Tosafot Aharon," a book that tries to solve the questions raised by the Tosafists. It treats several Talmudic tractates, among them Zera'im, Mo'ed, and Niddah. The book also holds scholastic and cabalistic talks, and was printed in 1858.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abda-servant-of: Abda, meaning servant of the Lord, is the name of two men in this short entry. The first was the father of Adoniram. Adoniram ran the tax levied by Solomon, as First Kings, chapter 4, verse 6, records. The second Abda was a Levite who lived in Jerusalem. He is named in Nehemiah, chapter 11, verse 17. In the matching list in First Chronicles, chapter 9, verse 16, this second man is called Obadiah instead.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-jud: German rabbi Abraham ben Judah Berlin died at Amsterdam on March 13, 1730. He was a son of Jost Liebman, the famed court Jew, and a pupil of Isaiah Horowitz at Posen. He served as rabbi in Halberstadt in 1692. In 1715 or 1717 Amsterdam called him, and he served there as rabbi and preacher until his death. He left no work of his own behind him. His notes in the books of others, the entry says, show little original thought.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abraham-ben-sim: Abraham ben Simeon of Worms was a Cabalist born in 1410 who died in 1440. His Segullat Melakim, or Royal Devices, holds lore on practical Cabala, magic, and natural science. He gathered the material on his travels and wrote the book for his son Lamech. In it he warned his son against magic, which he called the black art. Only part one and the contents of the rest survive, in an Oxford manuscript. He had studied under Jacob Elim in Egypt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-adda-b-simon-78: Adda b. Simon was a Palestinian amora. He is known most for moral rules quoted in the names of men before him. Cites to him sit in the Jerusalem Talmud and in Ecclesiastes Rabbah. The hosted text is two lines long. It gives his land, his rank, and the kind of words he passed on. It gives no dates, no teachers by name, and no rule in full. A reader gets the shape of his place in the chain of lore, and no more than that.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-agabus-885: Agabus was a Jew of Jerusalem and a prophet of the first church. He came to Antioch with other prophets after the first flock was scattered. Acts xi. tells that he foretold a great famine. That famine struck Judea under Claudius, between the years 44 and 48. Queen Helena of Adiabene gave much aid in it. Later, at Cæsarea, Agabus took Paul's belt and bound his own hands and feet. He said the Jews at Jerusalem would so bind the belt's owner. Paul went on and met that fate.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahimaaz-brother:
Ahimaaz, meaning "Brother of Anger," is the name of three men in this entry. The first was the father of Ahinoam, wife of Saul. The second was Solomon's commissary-general in Naphtali. He married Basmath, a daughter of Solomon. All three men appear in the books of Samuel, Kings, and Chronicles.

The third was a son of Zadok. With Jonathan, son of Abiathar, he carried news to David from Absalom's camp. After the battle he ran to tell David of the victory. He outran the Cushite, who had started well before him. He also stands in the list of high priests.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alby-albi-1085:
Alby, or Albi, is an old cathedral town in France. It is the capital of the department of Tarn, forty-two miles northeast of Toulouse. The town gave its name to the Albigensian sect. A council held there in 1254, aimed at wiping out that sect, issued savage decrees against the Jews as well.

In 1320 the small Jewish flock of Alby was wiped out in the Pastoureaux riots. Warned of the mob's approach, the Jews took refuge in Castel-Narbonnais. Word came that the Pastoureaux had been seized by the count of Toulouse, so they left the castle. A mayor's kinsman was sent to guide them to safety at Carcassonne. Out of hatred, he handed them to their enemy instead, and they were all slaughtered.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alfaquin-aaron-: Aaron Alfaquin was a physician at Pamplona. In 1413 Charles III. of Navarre granted him a monthly stipend of 9 florins. The grant rewarded certain cures he had worked with success. It was also meant as an encouragement for the future. That is all the entry records of him. No dates of birth or death are given, and no other act of his is named.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-almiliby-adam-1: Adam Almiliby was a Portuguese Jew with a royal post. In 1353 King Alfonso IV named him a farmer of the royal taxes. Isaac Belamy shared the post with him. The post freed both men from the Jew-badge. It also gave them power to force tax payments. While they held the post, one gain stood out. The Jews of Portugal were freed of all dues but the poll-tax.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anaw-benjamin-b:
Benjamin ben Abraham Anaw was a liturgical poet, Talmudist, and commentator in Rome in the thirteenth century. The entry calls him perhaps the most gifted and learned of his Roman peers, and the older brother of Zedekiah. He also studied philology, math, and astronomy, and wrote with a sharp, satirical pen.

His poetry began in crisis. In 1239 Nicholas Donin attacked the Talmud, and wagon-loads of Talmud books were burned in Paris and Rome. Anaw answered with a penitential hymn and a bitter elegy for Israel. The entry also lists his works, including a satirical poem, and notes that many of his liturgical poems entered the Roman prayer book or survive in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antinomianism-1:
Antinomianism is a term for the stance of certain Christian sects against the Law, meaning the revelation of the Old Testament. The entry sets Paul's teaching at the center. The apostles let Paul's party teach that the Law did not bind heathen Christians.

Paul went further, the entry argues. He taught that the Law was fully set aside after Jesus, against the Jewish view that the Law alone justifies a person before God. In Paul's scheme, the Law even multiplies sin, since each command adds a chance to break it. Yet breaking it also teaches people what sin is. The entry works through this clash verse by verse and follows later groups that opposed the Law.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arabic-jewish-p:
Arabic Jewish philosophy is the thought of Arabic-speaking Jews, and the entry opens with a warning. Their writing was so shaped by Mosaism that no reader can judge their gift to philosophy without keeping that in view. Mosaism itself, the entry argues, was hardly a philosophy at all.

It was, in the sharpest sense, a religion of law. Its oldest part, the Ten Words, speaks with a moral will in plain commands. Greek thought spoke in conditions, and faiths of feeling in wishes. Mosaism spoke in orders that brook no debate. The entry then traces how such a law-first faith met Greek ideas in Arabic lands and what new thought grew from the meeting.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ascension-1885:
Ascension, as treated here, means the carrying of chosen men up to heaven. Some stay there in place of dying. Others go up only to receive revelations and then come back to earth. Enoch in Genesis and Elijah in Second Kings belong to the first kind. Wide belief among Babylonians and the peoples of antiquity held that men of blameless life might be taken up without tasting death.

Babylonian tales give cases: Xisuthros, caught up for finding favor with God, and Etana-Gilgamesh, riding an eagle to a heaven from which earth looks like a hill and sea like a basin. Post-Biblical writing adds more names to those who never died, and apocryphal books tell of Baruch and others lifted up. The entry sets the Bible accounts inside that wider world of belief.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-napht:
Naphtali ben Joseph Ashkenazi was a preacher at Safed in the sixteenth century. He died at Venice in 1602. His work Imre Shefer, Words of Beauty, holds sermons and explanations on the Bible, mixing preaching with close reading of the text.

The Venice edition of 1601 prints several of his funeral sermons along with the main work. The entry rests on Steinschneider's Bodleian catalogue and on Conforte's Kore ha-Dorot. It names his city, his century, his one book, and his place and year of death. No birth date, no teacher, and no family are recorded for this Safed preacher.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-athias-atias-or:
Athias is the name of a Spanish family rich in scholars. Its members spread early: some lived in Italy and Palestine by the sixteenth century. Another branch settled in Hamburg, Amsterdam, and London. The entry walks through the family name by name, with printers, rabbis, and writers in each city.

Abraham Athias was burned by the Inquisition at Cordova on July 9, 1667, for his religion. Joseph Athias built a famed Amsterdam printing house, whose stock later passed to Proops. His son Immanuel issued fine editions of Hebrew works, among them Maimonides' code. Isaac Athias served as ḥakam in Hamburg and then Venice, where he died after 1622. A long section tells how a rival Yiddish Bible project in Amsterdam drew bans, partners, and lawsuits around the Athias press.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-awira-rab-2185:
Rab 'Awira was a Babylonian teacher of the third and fourth generations, in the fourth century. He was a fellow of Abaye and Safra. He had moved to Palestine and served as usher at the college of a great teacher there, probably Ammi. Then he returned to his native land. He brought back many rulings and tales of R. Ammi and R. Assi.

The entry warns that Awira often swapped the names of his sources as he passed their words on. Some sayings are his own. In one, he contrasts God with proud men. A great man honors only those above him, he said. God, though supreme, honors the lowly. In another, he lists seven names given to the tempter, the evil drive in man. God calls him simply Evil. Moses, David, Solomon, Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Joel each give him a name of their own.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baki-simson-238:
Simson Baki is treated here as two men of one name. The first, born in Germany or Italy and likely kin to the Bachi family, lived about 1582-84. From Safed and Jerusalem he wrote three letters, printed in recent times by David Kaufmann. Steinschneider calls him "Back." Beyond the letters, the entry tells nothing of his work or life.

The second Simson Baki was a rabbi at Casale and a mystic. His pupil Benjamin Cohen of Reggio gives his death as the 11th of Sivan, 5451, that is, 1691. A letter of Moses Zacuto from 1672 shows Baki trying to cast out an evil spirit from a woman, with poor success. He backed Shabbethai Ẓebi with fervor and sent him a letter of loyalty from Italy. His only known writing is a commentary on Lamentations and the Song of Songs, still in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baraita-of-r-el: Baraita of R. Eliezer is a title, not a separate work. The hosted entry is two sentences long and explains the name. Among the older scholars, as in Rashi and in the 'Aruk, this was the customary name for the Pirḳe R. Eliezer. Some recent scholars, the entry adds, follow their example and use this title too. Nothing about the contents of the Pirḳe is given here. The note is signed only with initials and rests on that naming practice alone.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baruch-b-samuel: Baruch b. Samuel Zanwill ha-Levi was an Austrian rabbi of the eighteenth century, born at Leipnik, Moravia. He officiated at Semlin in Croatia. His "Zera' Shemuel" (Samuel's Seed) holds novellæ on the treatise Ketubot and was published at Vienna in 1796. He also left a work titled "Le-David Baruk," with comments on the Psalms and some homilies. That second work has not been published. The entry gives those facts and his two books, with no dates for his birth or death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-be-rab-teacher-:
Be Rab is a Talmud term with several senses, at root the academy of a teacher of Mishnah or Talmud. Many citations open with the claim that a teacher taught in the academy of a named rabbi. The entry asks which schools and which books those citations mean.

Much of the piece weighs whether Be Rab points to Akiba, to the amora Rab, or to neither. It sorts the Sifra, Sifre, and Mekilta collections by school. The verdict, following Hoffmann, keeps the amora Rab apart from the older academy name. Citations drawn from those academy collections run through both the Talmud and the Midrash, the entry shows.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beiser-moses-27:
Moses Beiser was an Austrian physician and giver born in Lemberg on April 7, 1807. He died in that same city on Oct. 12, 1880. He took his medical degree at Vienna in 1835 and first served as house doctor to a noble family.

At Kolomea from 1845, Beiser sheltered exiles in his house and backed liberal politics, for which the state banished him for two years. Back in Lemberg he led cholera care in 1855 and gave money as well as treatment to the poor. The city made him an honorary citizen in 1876. Voters later put him on the city board of education and on the Jewish hospital council as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benedict-viii-1: Benedict VIII was pope from 1012 to 1024, and a harsh persecution of the Jews fell in his years. After an earthquake and hurricane struck Rome on Good Friday, 1021, many blamed the disaster on the Jews. A claim spread that they had insulted the host during Christian worship. An inquiry followed, run with the bias of the age, and the pope ordered the accused Jews put to death. The entry cites Zunz, who linked a penitential poem by Simeon ben Isaac to this persecution.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-the-sh: Benjamin the Shepherd lived in Babylonia at the start of the third century. The Talmud hands down a blessing said to be his. Knowing no Hebrew, he could not recite the set grace after meals. In its place he said a short line in Aramaic, Blessed be the All-Merciful, the owner of this bread. That plain prayer, the entry notes, is still taught to small children who cannot yet say the full grace. Rab is cited as approving the simple man's prayer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bieltzy-3285: Bieltzy is a district town of Bessarabia, Russia. The 1897 census counted 18,526 people there. Over ten thousand of them were Jews. Most Jews worked in handicrafts. Some farmed or traded instead. There were 1,188 Jewish artisans in town. A quarter of them were tailors. Fifty Jewish farmers raised tobacco nearby. They worked about 405 rented acres. Hardship grew after the 1896 liquor monopoly. Three hundred Jewish families had worked that trade. In 1898, 200 families sought charity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bloch-heinrich-: Heinrich Bloch was an Austrian philologist. He was born on February 4, 1854, at Herman-Mestec, Bohemia. His father Moses led Budapest's Jewish Theological Seminary. Heinrich studied at Teschen and at Vienna. He took his doctorate there in 1878. In 1881 he joined the Budapest seminary. He taught history and classical philology there. His book studies Josephus's sources in the Archaeology. It appeared at Leipsic in 1879. He contributed to newspapers across Europe for decades.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boleslaw-pobozn: Boleslaw Pobozny, the Pious, was duke of Kalisz and died in 1278. The entry praises his courage and his care for his subjects over war. In 1264 he issued an edict granting Jews many privileges. Its thirty-six articles show a spirit of tolerance ahead of the age, the entry says. In 1334 Casimir the Great extended those privileges to the Jews of all Poland.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boshal-bostal-m: Moses ben Solomon de Boshal, or Bostal, was a Turkish Talmudist and preacher of the seventeenth century. He wrote Yismah Mosheh, meaning Moses Rejoices. It is a homiletic commentary on the Pentateuch. The book was printed at Smyrna in 1675. The entry calls it now very rare. It gives no birthplace, no teachers, and no death date for him. Those three facts, with two source notes, are the whole record preserved here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-breslau-joseph-:
Joseph b. David Breslau was a German Talmudist and rabbi born, probably at Breslau, in 1691. He died on Jan. 22, 1752, at Bamberg. He served first at Grabfeld and then at Bamberg from 1743.

Breslau wrote three books named for Joseph, his own name. One treats the legal term Miggo in depth. A second comments on the Passover parts of the Shulhan Aruk. A third, printed after his death, gives pilpulistic notes arranged by the weekly lessons. He was a pupil of his father-in-law, Abraham Broda. The entry praises the sharpness and wit of his writing. His first book counts as the school's most important Talmudic work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-buchholz-carl-a:
Carl August Buchholz was a German Christian lawyer and author who died at Lübeck on Nov. 15, 1843. He was a doctor of laws and philosophy and served as second city syndic of Lübeck. That city was known for hostility to Jews. Buchholz, a leading citizen, still chose to champion their cause in print.

His 1814 work argued for admitting Jews to citizenship, and a second edition followed in 1816. The Jewish communities of Lübeck, Hamburg, and Bremen chose him as their voice at the Congress of Vienna in 1815. He also spoke for them at the German Diet in Frankfort. His 1815 collection of laws on the Jews carried a long plea for emancipation. The entry praises his learning, logic, and love of justice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-carthage-4085:
Carthage was an ancient city and republic in northern Africa. Its people had a Phenico-Semitic origin, and its rulers, the suffetes, recall the Hebrew shofeṭim, or judges. Jewish writings name the city from Talmudic times as Ḳarthigini. Later chronicles give variant spellings and at times treat two cities of Carthage as one question.

Josephus cites Tyrian records placing the founding of Carthage 143 years and eight months after Solomon built the Temple. He uses that count against Apion on the age of the Jewish people. Carthage itself is not named in the Bible. Many scholars link it to Tarshish, as the Septuagint, Targum, and Vulgate render Ezekiel xxvii. 12. A Talmud passage counts Carthage among the four largest cities of the Roman empire.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cerfberr-august: Auguste Edouard Cerfberr, a French author born at Epinal in 1811, died in 1858. After legal studies, he entered government service and rose to high posts. His last office was prefect and general inspector of prisons at Grenoble. He wrote two books. One, on the government of Algiers, appeared at Paris in 1834. The other, on mutual aid societies and ways to better the lot of working classes, appeared at Grenoble in 1836.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-judah-ben: Judah ben Isaac ben Moses Cohen was a Provencal philosopher of the middle fourteenth century. He studied under Samuel of Marseilles. He was also kin to Shelemiah of Lunel. At Shelemiah's request he wrote a commentary on Averroes' middle commentary on the Organon. In that work he often corrects Averroes himself. He also quotes Levi ben Gerson and defends him against Samuel of Marseilles, his own master. Part of the commentary, on the Isagoge and the Categories, still survives in manuscript at Christ Church, Oxford.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cossacks-uprisi:
Cossacks' Uprising recounts the revolt that swept the Ukraine in the seventeenth century and the massacres of Jews that came with it. The entry first sketches the Cossacks themselves. From the fifteenth century, armed bands roamed the steppes of southern Russia. They began as traveling merchants, then settled as farmers and villagers under their hetmans. Only the Ukraine branch is treated here.

Polish rule turned the peasants into serfs and set the stage for revolt. The narrative then follows town after town. At Nemirov in June, 1648, Jews who opened the fortress gates were slaughtered or tortured. Learned men, among them the cabalist Jehiel Michael ben Eliezer, died there. The account rests on chronicles and Jewish sources.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crusades-the-47:
Crusades were expeditions from western Europe to win back Jerusalem and the holy sepulcher. For Jews, the entry stresses, they were a turning point. The mobs trailing the first three Crusades attacked Jews in Germany, France, and England. Many were put to death. Legal limits grew common during and after the wars. The social place of western Jews sank for centuries, and the ground was laid for later anti-Jewish law.

The violence was foreseen. Godfrey de Bouillon swore to avenge the blood of Jesus on the Jews. French communities warned those on the Rhine, who set a fast day in Jan., 1096. Cologne and Mayence each paid Godfrey 500 silver marks for protection. The narrative then follows the massacres town by town, with forced baptisms and suicides recorded.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-danielillo-of-l: Danielillo of Leghorn is the unknown author of a Spanish defense of Judaism. The work belongs to the seventeenth century. Isaac Mendes copied it in 1738. It reached print at Brussels in 1868, as Danielillo ó Respuestas á los Cristianos. Most of the book is a debate between two speakers. It borrows many lines from an older dialogue of 1583, still in manuscript. Its chief matter is another dialogue. That one came from Juan Carrasco, a Madrid monk who turned to Judaism in Holland and wrote against Rome.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-davidov-julius-: Julius Davidov, also spelled Davydov, was a Russian physician born at Goldingen, Courland, in 1803. He graduated from the University of Dorpat in 1833 and practiced in his home town until 1838, when he moved to Moscow. At his death in 1870 he was chief physician of the Nicholas Orphan Asylum. Before leaving for Moscow he had embraced Christianity. The entry also names his two distinguished sons: August, a mathematician who wrote popular schoolbooks, and Carl, a violoncellist. Both were born at Goldingen.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dyer-leon-5385:
Leon Dyer was an American soldier born at Alzey, Germany, on Oct. 9, 1807. His parents brought him to Baltimore as a child. Self-educated, he worked first in his father's beef-packing house. He died at Louisville, Kentucky, in 1883.

Dyer won Baltimore's trust and held small public posts. During bread riots he served as acting mayor and restored order. In 1836 he sailed for Texas with New Orleans volunteers, arriving just after San Jacinto. He won a major's commission and guarded Santa Anna on his trip to Washington. Later he served under Scott in Florida and in the Mexican war.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-einhorn-max-548:
Max Einhorn was a physician born at Grodno, Russia, on Jan. 10, 1862. He studied medicine at Kiev and at Berlin. He took his medical degree at Berlin in 1884. He worked with Ehrlich and Salkowski before sailing for America. In New York he joined the German Hospital in 1885.

Einhorn soon left hospital work for private practice. He returned briefly to Berlin as Ewald's assistant in 1887. Back in New York he turned to diseases of digestion. The Post-Graduate Medical School made him professor of stomach diseases by 1899. He invented many stomach instruments, among them the stomach-bucket and the gastrograph. His writings cover nearly the whole field of stomach pathology.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliakim-ben-nap: Eliakim ben Naphtali was an Italian writer on ethics. He lived in the fifteenth century. His book Tob Shem Tob draws on the Talmud and the Midrashim. It treats reward and punishment after death. Suffering in the tomb and the rising of the dead fill its pages. The book runs to eleven chapters in all. His son brought it out at Venice in 1606. Eliakim names one more book of his, called Eben Shetiyyah. That work is no longer in hand, the entry says.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elisha-ben-abuy:
Elisha ben Abuyah was a rabbi who left the fold. He was born in Jerusalem before the year 70. He worked in Palestine at the turn of the second century. The rabbis once counted him proudly as one of their own. Later they would not speak his name at all. That ban makes his true figure hard to recover. Modern writers split on what he became. A Gnostic, a thinker, a Christian, a victim — each view has its backers.

He was the son of a rich and honored citizen. One saying of his on schooling survives in the Mishnah. Learning in youth is like writing on fresh paper, he said. Learning in old age is like writing on used paper. The entry tells of banned books hid in his clothes. His fall is tied to a famed tale of four sages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ethausen-alexan: Alexander ben Moses Ethausen was a German scholar who lived at Fulda in the seventeenth century. He wrote a Judeo-German work in two parts. The first part, Bet Yisrael, tells the history of the Jews up to the destruction of the Second Temple. The second part, Bet ha-Behirah, describes Jerusalem and both Temples in twenty-four chapters. The work was printed at Offenbach in 1719, after his time. The entry gives no birth or death dates. Its facts rest on Michael's Or ha-Hayyim, Furst, and Steinschneider's Bodleian catalogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-falaise-hebrew-:
Falaise, capital of its district in Calvados, Normandy, stood under English rule until 1206. It seems to have held a fair-sized Jewish community in the Middle Ages. Two of its Jews, Jacob and Morellus, were licensed in 1204 to live at the Chatelet in Paris. A court decree of 1220, avenging a murdered Jew of Bernai, made all Falaise citizens answerable unless they had answered his cries.

In 1299 the taxes of Abraham and his fellow Jews of Falaise came to seventy-five livres. The entry then names the town's scholars: Simson ben Joseph the tosafist, Samuel ben Solomon called Sire Morel, Hayyim Paltiel, Moses of Falaise, and Yom-Tob of Falaise. No later history of the community is given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fermosa-6085: Fermosa, born Rahel, was a Jewess of Toledo famed for rare beauty, and the entry tells her story as fact. She held King Alfonso VIII of Castile under her spell for almost seven years, though he was husband to Queen Leonora. With the clergy's consent, nobles seized Fermosa in the king's presence and murdered her, along with Jews of her circle. Older historians filed the tale as fable. But Alfonso X and Don Sancho tell it as true, and Grillparzer later made it a play.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fleischmann-jul: Julius Fleischmann was an American merchant and mayor of Cincinnati, Ohio. He was born at Riverside, Ohio, on June 8, 1872. He served on the staffs of three Ohio governors. One of them, McKinley, later became President of the United States. In the spring of 1900 the Republican party named Fleischmann for mayor of Cincinnati. He was elected on April 2. The entry notes a rare feature of that race. The candidates of both main parties were Jews. Fleischmann was reelected on April 6, 1903, by a much larger majority.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankel-albert-:
Albert Fränkel was a German physician born on March 10, 1848, at Frankfort-on-the-Oder. He took his medical degree at Berlin in 1870. He worked as assistant to Kussmaul, Traube, and Von Leyden. He then settled in Berlin and became a lecturer at its university in 1877. In 1884 he got the title of Professor. He also became director of the medical department of a Berlin hospital.

Fränkel's early work lay in experimental pathology. He studied how less oxygen reaching the tissues affects the breakdown of protein. With Geppert he studied the effects of thinned air on the body, in 1873. His later special field was diseases of the lungs and heart. He was the first to set out the theory of the micrococci of pneumonia. His large work on diseases of the breathing organs ran from 1890 to 1902. Papers on acute leukemia and bronchial asthma followed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedmann-alfre:
Alfred Friedmann was a German poet and author born at Frankfort-on-the-Main on October 26, 1845. He was brought up as a goldsmith, but gave up that trade. He studied at Heidelberg and Zurich and took his doctor's degree in 1870. He lived in Vienna until 1886, when he moved to Berlin. His song books begin with one of 1873 and Greek songs of the next year.

Three Bible idyls came in 1875 and a book of light-hearted songs in 1878. Sets of poems followed in 1882 and 1888. In 1891 he wrote a drama on Don Juan's last love affair. His novels include a tale of two marriages, turned into Italian. Four short novels of his appeared in a cheap people's library.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gallipoli-the-a:
Gallipoli, a seaport in European Turkey at the northeast end of the Dardanelles, held about 20,000 people, of whom 1,200 were Jews. Jews likely lived there from early Byzantine times. About 1162 Benjamin of Tudela found 200 Jews and a yeshibah there. The Ottoman Turks took the town in 1365 and shielded the community, as was their custom.

Many Spanish exiles found refuge there in 1492. Some families still mark a Purim of Saragossa each year. The town later had two synagogues and a Jewish school with 250 boys. A council of ten ran community affairs. Tax on kosher meat and wine paid most of its costs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gentile-6585:
Gentile is a Latin word for a people not Jewish, in plain use a non-Jew. The entry warns that it does not truly carry scorn, though some take it that way. It matches the late Hebrew goi. In the Bible goi first meant nation, and could name Israel itself. In time it came to mean nations set apart from Israel, and then a stranger or heathen.

The stranger stood under the guard of the Law. God is said to love the stranger, and the native born must love him too. Courts stood open to him. One law was to hold for native and stranger alike. Yet the stranger had to shun idols, blood eating, and Sabbath work. Edomites and Egyptians could join the fold in the fourth generation. Ammonites and Moabites were barred for good.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gross-ferdinand:
Ferdinand Gross was an Austrian writer. He was born in Vienna on April 8, 1849. He died at Kaltenleutgeben on Dec. 21, 1900. His father had come from Padua by way of Hungary. Ferdinand wrote from age fifteen. In 1872 he joined the "Extrablatt" staff. In 1877 his feuilleton won a Berlin first prize. Frankfort and Vienna papers took him in turn.

From 1898 to 1900 he presided over Concordia, the Vienna journalists' group. His output was huge and light in kind. Comedies, sketches, poems, and song collections fill the list. With Max Nordau he wrote the comedy "Die Neuen Journalisten" (1880). His last sketch volumes appeared in the year of his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-habib-joseph-ib:
Joseph ibn Ḥabib, called Joseph Ḥabiba, was a Spanish Talmudist of the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries. He followed R. Nissim b. Reuben, who had written on the halakot of Isaac Alfasi. Ibn Ḥabib wrote his own work on the same text, called "Nimmuḳe Yosef." It was printed with Alfasi's text at Constantinople in 1509.

Scholars once thought he covered only the treatises R. Nissim had skipped. Azulai showed the work in fact covered all of Alfasi, though part stayed in print only later or not at all. Some parts long credited to R. Nissim are his. Azulai also credits him with novellæ on the whole Talmud.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halberstadt-abr:
Abraham ben Menki Halberstadt was a German Hebraist and Talmudic scholar who died at Halberstadt about 1780. His "Pene Abraham," never printed, treats the hardest halakot of the Talmud and shows him an authority in that field. A set of his letters to his friend R. Jeremiah at Berlin also survives, printed in German in Auerbach's history of the town's community.

The letters show his mind at work. In 1770 he warmly defended the memory of Jonathan Eybeschütz, his teacher. In 1774 he defended the study of synonyms against R. Jeremiah. A year later he praised Wessely and Mendelssohn, and he lashed rabbis who knew no mathematics or astronomy, without which, he said, many Talmud passages cannot be explained.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hananiah-b-akas: Hananiah, son of 'Aḳashiah, was a tanna known to fame by a single remark. It runs: God wished to enlarge Israel's merits. So He multiplied Torah and commandments for them, as Isaiah xlii, 21 says. That mishnah is tacked onto each chapter of Abot in the prayer-books. That is why his name is so widely met. One halakah is also his, in the Tosefta on Sheḳalim. When he lived and who taught him cannot be fixed. He was likely a brother of Simon b. 'Aḳashiah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-abigdor-: Abigdor Hayyim was a Talmudist who lived in the eighteenth century. One book of his is named. "Peri Ez Hayyim" came out at Amsterdam in 1742. It holds his answers to legal questions. It also holds notes on Maimonides' great code and on the Arba Turim. Sermons fill the rest of the book, set in the order of the weekly Sabbath readings. The entry is very short. It names no town for him and gives no dates for his birth or death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-shabbeth:
Hayyim Shabbethai, born about 1556, was a rabbi of Salonica. He studied in that city's yeshiva under Aaron Sason. In 1607 he succeeded his teacher as head of the school and chief rabbi. He held those posts for forty years. Many Talmudic scholars and rabbis trained under him.

His answers to legal questions fill many volumes, though only four were printed. One set treats ritual law and the problem of the deserted wife. Three more cover civil law. He also wrote sermons and notes on the whole Talmud, most of them unprinted. He died in 1647.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heilbron-david-: David Heilbron, born at The Hague on July 4, 1762, was a Dutch physician. He took his medical degree at Leyden in 1784. He practiced in his home city until 1800, then moved to Amsterdam. There he sat on the board of health and worked for the rest of his life. His books, all in Dutch, treat purgatives in chest disease, the coated tongue, signs read in the eyes, and guarding cattle against plague. He died at Amsterdam in 1847.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herczel-mano-de: Manó de Szentpéteri Herczel, born in Szegedin on July 1, 1861, was a Hungarian physician whose specialty was diseases of the kidneys. He studied in several cities, ending with Paris, and took his degree in 1884. After work in Vienna and Heidelberg, he became chief of a Budapest hospital in 1892. His listed works treat drug effects, kidney stones, fixation of a wandering kidney, and bladder defects. In 1902 the emperor raised him to Hungarian nobility.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hierapolis-now-:
Hierapolis, now called Pambuk Kalessi, was a city in Phrygia, Asia Minor, named with Laodicea in Colossians. It prospered in Roman times for its medicinal springs. A Jewish community lived there in the second and third centuries. Three or four of its grave stones have been found.

One stone records gifts to purple-dyers and carpet-weavers for decorating a grave at Jewish feasts. Other stones set fines against burying strangers in family tombs. Fines were payable to the Jewish community in some cases. The entry notes that grave decoration on holy days shows how far local Jews had moved from Talmud usage.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hiyya-meir-ben-:
Ḥiyya Meïr, son of David, was an Italian Talmudist of the sixteenth century. He served as dayyan at Venice from 1510 to 1520, under a rabbi who valued him highly. He joined a famed dispute between Jacob Polak and Abraham Minz. His name stood third among Italian rabbis who gave views on it.

After 1520 Ḥiyya worked at Daniel Bomberg's printing house as an editor of the Talmud. He won praise as a corrector. Works he edited include a noted law book by Israel Isserlein and responsa by Joseph Colon. His own responsa appear in Benjamin Ze'eb's collection, the entry adds.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-homel-or-gomel-:
Homel, also called Gomel, is a district town in the Moghilef government of Russia, on the River Sozh. In 1902 its Jews numbered 26,161 of 40,446 people. Jews likely settled soon after Lithuania gained it in 1537, the entry says. In 1648 about 1,500 Jews were killed there in a Cossack rising.

A second long section gives the anti-Jewish riots of Sept. 1903 in close detail. A market fight sparked days of plunder while soldiers blocked Jewish defense, it reports. The count given is 25 Jews killed, 100 gravely hurt, and 200 slightly hurt. Some 372 houses and 200 stores were plundered and destroyed. Community leaders told a minister the official account was wrong and the riots were planned.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-horse-7885:
Horse in the Bible and Talmud is the subject here. The entry opens with the Hebrew terms for the animal. The horse was not native to Palestine and was no part of patriarchal herds. It appears first as the war-steed of enemies and as a chariot animal, not a riding animal.

Egypt supplied the first horses named in Scripture. David took up the war horse, and Solomon imported many from Egypt. Warnings against trusting in horses run beside a fine poetic passage in Job. Talmudic notes list the horse's traits, its gear, its shoes in war, and the good omen of a white horse in a dream.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-imma-shalom-808:
Imma Shalom was the wife of Eliezer ben Hyrcanus and sister of Gamaliel the Second. Raised under her brother's care, she got an education fit for a nasi's sister. One tale shows her wit. A skeptic mocked God for stealing Adam's rib in sleep. She answered with a feigned robbery in which a thief left gold for silver.

Her marriage was blessed with fine children, and her husband valued her mind despite his bar on teaching women. After his breach with Gamaliel, she kept him from a daily prayer against foes, fearing heaven would strike her brother. One morning she missed her cue, and Gamaliel soon died. A mock suit tale shows her exposing a bribed judge, first with a golden lamp, then watching her brother undo the gift with a Libyan ass.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ben-judah:
Isaac ben Judah ha-Levi was a French exegete and tosafist who lived at Sens, probably in the second half of the thirteenth century. He was a pupil of Hayyim of Falaise. Under the title "Pa'aneah Raza" he compiled a commentary on the Pentateuch. In it, plain readings sit beside word-play methods such as notarikon and gematriot.

He quoted many earlier authorities, from Joseph Kara and Joseph Bekor Shor to Judah he-Hasid and Eleazar of Worms. The "Pa'aneah Raza" was first printed at Prague in 1607, from an incomplete manuscript. Complete copies, with a postscript and an acrostic poem giving his name, survive in the Bodleian and other European libraries. Isaac also wrote tosafot to the Talmud, and he is called the Tosafist of Sens.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israel-ben-meir: Israel ben Meir was a printer and author who lived at Prague in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. He wrote "Hanhagot Yisrael," a treatise on the education of children. Its first edition, at Frankfort-on-the-Oder in 1712, came out without his name. That same year he set up, or helped set up, a printing business at Wilmersdorf. His name, though, appears on only two works of 1712: the "Bet Abot" of Moses Heilburg and the Talmudic treatise Bezah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacob-b-abba-83: Jacob b. Abba is the name of two Babylonian scholars in this entry. The first belongs to the third century and stood junior to Rab. He was a sharp debater who won arguments even against his famous senior. The second, an amora of the fourth century, was a contemporary of Abaye and Raba. His parents used to vie in waiting on him after school. Jacob asked Abaye about it, and Abaye ruled he might take his mother's service, not his scholar father's.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacobson-nathan: Nathan Jacobson, an American surgeon, was born in Syracuse, New York, on June 25, 1857. He graduated from Syracuse University and took a postgraduate course at the University of Vienna. He became professor of clinical surgery in the College of Medicine of Syracuse University. He served as visiting physician to St. Joseph's Hospital and consulting surgeon to the Syracuse Hospital for Women and Children. For more than twenty years he sat on the executive board of the Jewish Orphan Asylum of western New York, and he published papers on surgery.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jerahmeel-8585:
Jerahmeel appears in Chronicles as a great-grandson of Judah, a son of Hezron, and a brother of Caleb. David, while a refugee with King Achish of Gath, is said to have raided the south of the Jerahmeelites and sent part of the spoil to their towns. On those plain facts the entry builds two views of the clan.

The plain view makes the Jerahmeelites a Judean clan of the south country. Against it stands Professor Cheyne's bold theory of a mighty north-Arabian tribe hidden behind many Bible names by copyists' errors. The entry grants the cleverness of the method but rejects the thesis as arbitrary and unproved.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joab-8685:
Joab, in this entry, is a Jewish family name tied above all to the Roman family of Anaw. Its first named member, Aaron ben Samuel ha-Nasi, lived for a time at Oria in Apulia in the later ninth century. From the tenth century on, the name Joab recurs in one Anaw branch that calls itself Beth-el or De Synagoga.

The entry lists five early men of the name, then a family table. Most of those in the table are known only as copyists of Hebrew manuscripts. A few stand out: Benjamin ben Joab, a writer of sacred poems; a second Benjamin, a grammarian and Bible commentator at Rome; and Jekuthiel ben Jehiel, of whom twelve manuscripts survive.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jose-abba-of-ma: Jose, called Abba Jose of Mahuza, was a scholar placed in the third century, though even that date carries a question mark in the entry. He is named only once in the old sources, where another teacher passes on a single story teaching of his. The notice then turns to a puzzle of names: a like teaching is given elsewhere to a Jose with a different byname. One editor guesses that byname should read as the Mahuzan, matching this man. That guess is all the entry offers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-samu: Joseph ben Samuel ha-Hazzan, also called Joseph ha-Mashbir, was a Karaite teacher at Halicz in Galicia who died in 1700. He studied under R. Nissim. None of his books was printed. They include Porat Yosef on Hebrew grammar, Sheber Yosef on religious thought, and a work on the prayer book left unfinished at his death. He also wrote on the ten Karaite articles of faith. His liturgical poems entered the Karaite prayer book. Mordecai, who preached at his funeral, had asked his advice on Karaism's origins.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-ben-eliez: Judah ben Eliezer, called Yesod, was a Lithuanian Talmudist and giver to the poor, born at Wilna, who died there on March 18, 1762. He served as judge, town secretary, and for a short time rabbi. Though his learning was so high that both sides in a famed dispute sought his view, Wilna's Jews honored him most for his giving. He rebuilt a ruined synagogue and raised a new one that still bears his name. As secretary he kept the town's Jewish records in order.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-julius-nikolaus:
Nikolaus Heinrich Julius was a German doctor and prison reformer born at Altona on October 3, 1783. He died at Hamburg on August 20, 1862. He studied medicine at Heidelberg and Wuerzburg and settled at Hamburg after his conversion to Christianity. In the wars of 1813 and 1815 he served as a surgeon. Long trips through England and the United States fed his writing on prisons.

His books on the need to better the lot of prisoners drew the eye of the Prussian crown prince. In 1840 he was called to Berlin and posted in the Department of the Interior. Cutbacks ended his post in 1849, and he went home to Hamburg. He poured time and money into his cause, helped by his sister Henriette.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kerem-hemed-for:
"Kerem Ḥemed" was a Hebrew periodical. Its name is taken from Amos v. 11. Samuel Löb Goldenberg edited and published it. Two volumes came out at Vienna in 1833 and 1836. Five more followed at Prague from 1838 to 1843. A new series ran at Berlin from 1854 to 1856, under Senior Sachs.

The journal meant to carry on "Bikkure ha-'Ittim," which had ceased in 1832. Its pieces were cast as letters. That form, the entry says, was meant to soften the censor's hand. The contents mix Bible and Talmud criticism with poems and book reviews. The spirit of the Austrian Haskalah runs through it. It stands against Ḥasidism and against pilpul, the sharp logic-chopping of the schools.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-klein-wilhelm-9: Wilhelm Klein was an Austrian archeologist. He was born on Nov. 28, 1850, at Karánsebes, Hungary. He studied first Jewish theology and then philosophy, at Vienna and at Prague. The Austrian government later sent him to Italy and Greece. There he engaged in archeological work, studying antique pottery above all. Klein is professor of archeology at the German University of Prague. His published works include "Euphronius" of 1886. His book on Greek vases reached a second edition in 1887.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lazarus-emma-96:
Emma Lazarus, an American poet born in New York city on July 22, 1849, died there on Nov. 19, 1887. Private tutors raised her verse gift early; a first book of poems and translations came in 1867, praised by Bryant. Emerson shaped her mind. Prose tales and Heine translations followed through the 1870s.

The May Laws of 1881 and the Russian Jewish flight to America turned her gift to her own people. Essays in The Century defended the newcomers. Poems like The Banner of the Jew and By the Waters of Babylon, dated March 1887, mark her peak. A tablet with her poem went inside the Statue of Liberty pedestal in May 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lesser-louis-97: Louis Lesser was a German soldier born at Neustadt about 1850. He served in the Second Brandenburg Dragoons in the Franco-Prussian war. On Nov. 18, 1870, he was on patrol between Sens and Villeneuve. His comrades had scattered in several directions. Six enemy men surprised him alone. Lesser stood his ground. When his comrades came back, he advanced with them. Together they captured the captain of the francs-tireurs who had attacked him. The short entry cites two books on German heroes and on Jews as soldiers.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levirate-marria:
Levirate marriage, called yibbum in Hebrew, is marriage with a brother's widow. The custom appears among many early peoples, the entry notes. Among the Hebrews it was banned as a rule. Yet Deuteronomy made it a duty when a man died with no male child and the brothers shared one estate.

A brother could escape the duty through the rite of halizah. The entry says the tale of Ruth is not such a case, but Tamar's story in Genesis is. By Talmudic times the practice was seen as a burden, done from duty alone. Later schools split: Spanish authorities upheld it, while the northern school favored halizah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-gustave-98: Gustave Lévy, a French engraver, was born at Toul on June 21, 1819, and died at Paris in 1894. He studied under Geille and first showed work at the Salon of 1844. He engraved portraits of Madrazzo, Rigaud, and many others. The entry singles out his plates after Veronese, Raphael, and Caracci. His print after Rembrandt's "Good Shepherd" also wins note. Best loved were his plates of the King of the Belgians and of the poet Béranger. His last plate was framed on his tombstone at Montmartre.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lilienthal-otto: Otto Lilienthal, a German mechanical engineer, was born on May 23, 1848, at Anklam. He died on Aug. 9, 1896, at Rhinow. His theory held that built flight must follow the rules of bird flight. For twenty-five years he tested that theory with his brother. In the summer of 1891, with a pair of curved wings made for soaring, he gave the first practical proof that man could fly. He flew well several times. At last he met his death in a test at Rhinow. His 1889 book sets out the theory of his machine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-loewe-ludwig-10:
Ludwig Loewe was a German manufacturer and lawmaker born at Heiligenstadt on Nov. 27, 1837, and he died at Berlin on Sept. 11, 1886. Son of a poor teacher, he began in woolens, then became a machinist. In 1864 he set up a sewing-machine factory in Berlin.

After a trip to the United States in 1870, Loewe built a tool-machine factory using American methods new to Germany. The war office then backed a plant to make army weapons. He served on Berlin's council from 1864, entered the Prussian house in 1876, and joined the Reichstag two years later. Later charges against his firm's guns were shown to be baseless.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lumley-benjamin:
Benjamin Lumley (1811–1875) was a London opera manager born in Canada, the son of merchant Louis Levy. He is the subject of a Jewish Encyclopedia entry from 1906 by Goodman Lipkind and Joseph Jacobs. Educated at Birmingham, he took the name Lumley, became a solicitor, and wrote a standard book on passing private bills in Parliament.

In 1841 Lumley took over Her Majesty’s Theatre and remade London opera, hiring singers such as Grisi and Mario and dancers such as Taglioni. He staged the famous “pas-de-quatre” in 1845 and saved his house from ruin with Jenny Lind. Later ventures failed, and by 1863 he depended on benefit performances. The article also lists the Italian operas he brought to England, his memoirs, and a novel of a utopia on Mars. It traces a bold manager’s rise and long fall.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mapu-abraham-10:
Abraham Mapu, the Russian Hebrew novelist, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born near Kovno on January 10, 1808, he studied Bible and Talmud at the heder. His brilliance earned him the name of a prodigy by age twelve. At fifteen, driven by a mystical father, he turned to the Cabala. He died at Konigsberg in 1867.

The article tells how languages remade him. In his teacher's house Mapu found a Latin Psalter and taught himself Latin from it. A Catholic priest he met while teaching gave him a better start. From the 1840s he pursued secular studies eagerly. At Rossieny the scholar Senior Sachs deepened his love of biblical style. That style would fill his romances with ancient Hebrew color. Mapu taught at Kovno's gymnasium, but palsy struck his right hand in 1860. He went to Konigsberg for treatment and died there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-matthai-simeon-:
Adam Rudolf Georg Matthäi, born Simeon, was a German scholar whose conversion to Christianity frames his Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906, by Richard Gottheil and M. Seligsohn. Born at Fürth in 1715, he studied Talmud at Prague under his father, a lecturer there, then taught in Fürth's Jewish high school and lectured in its house of study. In April 1748 he told Fürth's clergy he meant to become a Christian, and he was baptized at Nuremberg that September.

Nuremberg made him sacristan of its Dominican church, and there he wrote book after book in German until his death in 1779. The entry is blunt about them: dressed as defenses of Christianity, they were in fact attacks on Judaism, though they showed his wide knowledge of rabbinic literature. His titles describe Jewish festivals and the Sabbath for Christian readers and collect Talmudic teachings, often to argue against them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-b-solomon-:
Meir ben Solomon ben David was a grammarian of the end of the thirteenth century. Crawford Howell Toy and Wilhelm Bacher profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His short grammar survives in a single manuscript. It was once in the collection of Halberstam and by the day of the entry was in the Montefiore Library. In his preface Meir says the author of a Hebrew grammar, the “Petah Debarai,” was his grandfather.

The book was made for private use, an aid to his study that took up problems his grandfather had left alone. In seven chapters it works through transitive and intransitive verbs. It covers the meaning of the derived stems of the Hebrew verb, the hif'il and pi'el among them. It also covers the pronominal suffixes verbs can carry. The entry leans on the study of the manuscript by Bacher in the Revue des Études Juives.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-menorah-10685:
Menorah is the candelabrum of the Tabernacle and Temple. Cyrus Adler and Judah David Eisenstein describe its rabbinic detail in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Talmud's menorah, its biblical data left to the article "Candlestick," is the one Bezaleel made for Moses. Later it was set among the ten Hiram made for Solomon, each a denarius overweight. The article measures it like an architect: eighteen handbreadths, seventy-two inches, high. The height is split among tripod, cups, knobs, and blossoms: twenty-two cups, eleven knobs, and nine blossoms.

Every ornament is glossed from the sources: The cup is shaped like an Alexandrian goblet, the knob like half an apple. The blossom is like a flower carved on pillars, with Maimonides' refinements added. It closes on the lighting arrangement. The wicks of the branches turned toward the central "western lamp." A technical entry, it models how the encyclopedia handles sacred furniture.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michael-ben-mos:
Michael ben Moses Cohen was a Palestinian rabbi and liturgist who lived at Jerusalem in the seventeenth century. Cyrus Adler and M. Seligsohn record him in a Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He is known through two books rather than through any biography. The entry gives no dates for his birth or death.

His Moreh Ẓedeḳ was printed at Salonica in 1655. It is an index to the laws of the Ḥoshen Mishpaṭ division of the Shulḥan Aruk. It shows where each rule appears in other legal works and later responsa. A second book holds prayers for the western wall of the Temple. It appeared at Venice in 1708, with additions by his son Moses, though one authority holds Michael only edited it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mitnaggedim-lit:
Mitnaggedim, literally the opponents, is the name the Ḥasidim gave to the Orthodox Jews of the Slav countries who refused Ḥasidism. Joseph Jacobs and Peter Wiernik explain it in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The entry is only a paragraph. But it tracks a real shift in the word's force. The labeled side eventually took the label for itself.

By the article's time, a mitnagged no longer had to oppose anything. The word simply meant a non-Ḥasid. It meant an ordinary Jew of the majority. The entry notes the alternative nickname, 'Olam'sher Yid, Jew of the world. That means not worldly, but belonging to the great mass of Israel outside the Ḥasidic camp. A tiny entry preserves how an insult settled into a census category.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-astruc:
Mordecai Astruc, a French liturgical poet of Carpentras at the end of the seventeenth century, is remembered for one poem and the near-pogrom behind it, as Cyrus Adler and A. Peiginsky write in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. His poems were printed in the Seder ha-Tamid, the prayer collection of Carpentras, Isle, Avignon, and Cavaillon.

In 1682 a Carpentras Jew was murdered and a crowd fell on the Jewish quarter; only the authorities' prompt intervention prevented serious rioting. The community made the day, the ninth of Nisan, a local feast of deliverance, and Astruc's thanksgiving poem, beginning Ish hayah be-tam lebabo, was read in synagogue. A minor poet preserved by a town's gratitude.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-isaac:
Moses ben Isaac was an Austrian author who lived at Bisenz in Moravia in the later sixteenth century. Gotthard Deutsch and S. Mannheimer wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry. He wrote in Hebrew at Cracow, where his books were printed in 1595.

His Darash Mosheh explains the quaint Talmudic tales gathered in the En Ya'akov. His He ha-Yediah is a prayer on the coming redemption, built as a feat of style. Every word in it begins with the letter alef. A third work, Ammude Abodah, treats the education of children and the ascetic life. The entry preserves a Moravian writer fond of learned games.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-motot-samuel-be:
Samuel ben Sa'adias ibn Motot was a Spanish commentator and translator who lived at Guadalajara in the later fourteenth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry is credited to its editorial committee and Max Schloessinger. He is best known for the Megillat Setarim, printed at Venice in 1554. It is a supercommentary on Ibn Ezra's commentary on the Pentateuch.

In that work Motot shows deep knowledge of Talmud, Cabala, and philosophy, and he defends Ibn Ezra against his critics. Yet he quietly doubted Ibn Ezra's orthodoxy himself. He also wrote cabalistic commentaries on the prayers and on the Sefer Yezirah. In 1392 he translated Ibn Daud's book of faith into Hebrew for Isaac ben Sheshet of Barcelona.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahmias-naamias:
Nahmias is the name of one of the oldest and most prominent Jewish families of Toledo. The Jewish Encyclopedia article, by several hands, traces members known from 1112 onward. Its best-known son is Joseph ben Joseph Nahmias, a pupil of Asher ben Jehiel. He wrote in Arabic an astronomical work, Light of the World, later turned into Hebrew.

The family's branches spread wide. David and Samuel Nahmias set up a Hebrew printing office at Constantinople in 1505. Abraham ibn Nahmias, a Lisbon physician there, saw his medical works printed in Latin at Venice. The record also holds martyrdom, Isaac burned at Ancona in 1556, and apostasy, Samuel becoming the Vatican librarian Giulio Morosino.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nordau-max-simo:
Max Nordau was an Austrian writer and thinker. Isidore Singer and Max Cohen wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Budapest on July 29, 1849. His parents were very poor at that time. His father, a former rabbi, taught him at home.

Latin, Greek, and Hebrew all came from that teaching. He took a medical degree in 1873. Six years of travel followed across Europe's lands. Medicine brought him at last to settle in Paris. Print, though, had claimed him since student days. His Conventional Lies of 1883 made him famous worldwide. Austria and Russia banned and seized the book. Degeneration, in 1893, stirred a fierce literary storm. It called sick much of modern art and letters. When Herzl raised Zionism, Nordau joined it ardently.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-oliphant-lauren:
Laurence Oliphant was an English traveler, writer, and lawmaker. Joseph Jacobs and Victor Rousseau Emanuel wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Cape Town in the year 1829. He died at Twickenham, in England, in 1888. He had roamed in most lands of the world.

Oliphant held many posts in a full, restless life. He served as a legation staff chief in Japan. He wrote from Paris for the London Times for a time. In 1867 he gave up his seat in Parliament. He left to study the occult with a small group. In 1879 he formed a plan for Jewish farms in Palestine. He chose the land of Gilead, east of the Jordan. The sultan of Turkey would not grant his leave, though.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-osimo-marco-117:
Marco Osimo was an Italian doctor from Montagnana. Isidore Singer and Umberto Cassuto wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born there in the year 1818. He died at Padua on May 1, 1881. He took his degree in cures at Padua in 1851.

In 1854 Marco took up the ills of silk worms. He read notes on that theme to the Padua academy. He sent such notes to the Venice institute as well. He put out two works on the silk worm ill. Both works came out in the years after 1876. He wrote a tale of a dark deed of old too. It told of Jews slain at Asolo in 1547. It gave lives of the Koen-Cantarini kin as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-panet-ezekiel-1:
Ezekiel Panet was a Hungarian rabbi from Silesia. Isidore Singer and Mathias Eisler wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Bielitz in the year 1783. He died at Karlsburg in April of 1845. He read at Leipnik, in Moravia, with a famed rabbi.

He then went to Prague for more years of study. Samuel Landau and Eleazar Fleckeles taught him there in turn. After his marriage in 1802, he read for five years. Those years were spent at Linsk in Talmud study. He joined the Polish Hasidim, a warm school of faith. He kept close ties with them all his life long. He was rabbi at Ostrik, then at Tarczal in Hungary. From 1823 to 1845 he was chief rabbi of Karlsburg.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pirke-de-rabbi-:
Pirke de-Rabbi Eliezer is a midrash on Genesis and Exodus. Joseph Jacobs and Schulim Ochser wrote the entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The book bears the name of Eliezer ben Hyrcanus. Scholars place its making in Italy after 833.

Fifty-four chapters retell the Bible with rich legend woven in. The opening tells of Eliezer's thirst for learning. Then come the six days of Creation retold. Angels, waters, lights, and beasts fill those chapters. The calendar's leap year passes from Adam to Jacob. Adam's fall and Noah's age follow in turn.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-porges-moses-be:
Moses Porges was a rabbinic author who lived at Jerusalem early in the seventeenth century. The Editorial Board and S. J. Levinson wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He later moved to Prague. There he wrote his one known book in Judaeo-German. It came out at Amsterdam in 1650 with pictures.

The book is called Darke Ziyyon, the Ways of Zion. It is built in four parts. Part one deals with the return to Palestine. Part two deals with prayer. Part three deals with teaching. Part four deals with honor for the dead. The book shows what a pious Jew of his time was urged to learn and do.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-b-nahman:
Rabbah bar Nahmani was a Babylonian teacher of the third set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in about the year 270. He died in about the year 330. His house traced its line to the priest Eli. That line came from Judea in old days.

Rabbah learned under Huna at Sura in his youth. He learned under Judah ben Ezekiel at Pumbedita as well. He shone so bright as a student that Huna paused for him. Huna would rule on no grave point without his word. That trust shows the rank Rabbah held while still young. The entry follows his rise at both great schools.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rashi-solomon-b:
Rashi, born Solomon bar Isaac, was a French commentator on Bible and Talmud. Joseph Jacobs, Morris Liber, and M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Troyes in 1040. He died there on July 13, 1105.

The article opens by clearing up errors about his name. Yarhi came from confusion with another Solomon, from Lunel. Rashi was a native of Troyes, not Lunel. It then tells legends that grew around his birth. His mother was said to be saved by a wall at Worms. The writers separate such tales from fact. Rashi studied at Worms under Jacob b. Yakar. The entry begins a life that shaped Jewish study for centuries.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-reptiles-remes-:
Reptiles are the creeping things of the Bible, called remes and sherez. Emil G. Hirsch and I. M. Casanowicz wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Genesis divides creeping things into sea and land kinds. They stand beside beasts and fowls in creation.

The article says the Talmud uses several terms for small creatures. Sherez can even cover weasels, mice, and moles. Maimonides sorts water creepers from land creepers with care. Water kinds include leeches and seals, he says. Land kinds include worms and dung beetles. All reptiles are deemed poisonous, the Talmud says. Only the snake is deadly among them. The entry mixes Bible language with old animal lore.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-robbio-mordecai: Mordecai Robbio was a Talmudist of the seventeenth century. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote this short Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906. He lived probably in northern Italy. Under the title Shemen ha-Mor he wrote responsa. They address the four ritual codices of Jewish law. An appendix holds exhortations to his son. The work was printed at Leghorn in 1793.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosewater-edwar:
Edward Rosewater was an American editor and newspaper owner born at Bukovan, Bohemia, in 1841. Cyrus Adler and Frank H. Vizetelly wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He left Prague schooling at thirteen, emigrated, and learned telegraphy.

During the Civil War, Rosewater served in the United States Military Telegraph Corps. He then managed the Pacific Telegraph Company at Omaha, Nebraska. In 1871 he entered the Nebraska legislature and founded The Omaha Bee. He edited that paper from its first issue onward. He later served on the Republican National Committee and the Mint Commission.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sacrilege-12985:
Sacrilege is the act of profaning or violating sacred things and places. Joseph Jacobs and Judah David Eisenstein wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Its ban in Jewish law centers first on the sanctuary itself.

Only priests could perform the Tabernacle or Temple services for Israel. Nothing used in the sanctuary could be turned to common purposes afterward. Even copying the sacred incense formula or the holy vessels was forbidden. A careless trespass required full restitution, plus a fifth, plus an offering. Achan, who stole consecrated spoil at Jericho, paid with his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuel-ben-abba: Samuel ben Abba was a Palestinian amora of the latter half of the third century. Wilhelm Bacher and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. A pupil of Johanan, he never received ordination himself. He declined the honor of men rising before him when he entered. He also studied under R. Assi and Ze'era, and he put legal questions to both. Later sources sometimes confound him with the great Samuel of Babylonia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-santob-shem-tob:
Joseph Jacobs and Meyer Kayserling wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Santob de Carrion. He was a Spanish poet, born late in the thirteenth century at Carrion de los Condes. That Castilian town gave him his name. He enjoyed the favor of King Alfonso the Eleventh. He kept that favor under Alfonso's son Pedro. Two works in his manuscript were long credited to him by mistake.

His real book is the Proverbios Morales, or Moral Proverbs. He began it under Alfonso and later dedicated it to Pedro. Two manuscripts survive, one at the Escorial and one in Madrid. They hold 686 and 627 stanzas. Santob drew his maxims from his own view of life. He also mined Solomon's Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, and the Talmud. His style is sharp, quick, and full of pointed sayings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schmelkes-gottf:
Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Gottfried S. Schmelkes. He was an Austrian physician. Schmelkes was born at Prague on September 22, 1807. He died at Interlaken, in Switzerland, on October 28, 1870. He studied at Prague and Vienna, taking his degree in 1837. In 1838 he became physician to the Jewish hospital at Töplitz.

Schmelkes practiced at Töplitz, a Bohemian spa town, until his death. His books describe the local coal-mineral moor and its use in baths. Others praise the Teplitz springs against paralysis and nerve pain. He gathered his case notes in Sedimente Meiner Praxis in 1867. He also proposed a hospital for invalid Saxon soldiers at Töplitz. It was founded in 1849, and he led it as chief physician. He wrote some poetry as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shahar-abakkshk:
Shahar Abakkeshka, meaning At morn I will seek Thee, is a morning hymn from about 1050. Cyrus Adler and Francis L. Cohen wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Solomon ibn Gabirol wrote the hymn, signing it in an acrostic. Sephardic prayer books quote the piece.

The hymn stands among supplications printed near Gabirol's Keter Malkut. It comes before the regular morning service for the Day of Atonement. Its tune is said to be of Morisco origin. The entry also prints the hymn's rhyme and meter scheme. Readers meet a short poem whose music and placement matter as much as its words.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shir-ha-shirim-:
Shir ha-Shirim Rabbah is a homiletic midrash, or rabbinic commentary, on Canticles. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on it. Rashi quotes it under the title Midrash Shir ha-Shirim. It is also called Agadat Hazita, from its first word.

Simon Duran called it a Palestinian collection of homilies. The sources it uses directly support that judgment. No direct borrowing from the Babylonian Talmud appears in it. Where readings match Babylonian ones, the forms often differ greatly. Both may draw on much older shared material, the entry argues. Readers get a case study in how scholars place a rabbinic text by its sources, language, and shape of argument.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sirach-the-wisd:
Sirach, the Wisdom of Jesus the Son of Sirach, is a book of the Greek Bible. Crawford Howell Toy and Israel Lévi wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Latin fathers called the book Ecclesiasticus. Greek fathers called it the All-Virtuous Wisdom or the Mentor. Jews never took it into the canon of Scripture.

Jews in Talmudic times called it the Book of Ben Sira. Its author signed his work, unlike most ancient writers. The Greek text names him Jesus, son of Sirach of Jerusalem.
