The planned scoping review will catalogue every study of a listed health app that used single questions, recording what was measured, why the shortcut was chosen, and what limits the authors admitted. Two reviewers will screen independently under standard reporting rules. No findings exist yet; the map should help regulators judge when one question is a fair measure and when it is a fig leaf.
plos-pone-0356685:
Haolun Xu and seven colleagues model a hidden flaw in the cables that carry high-voltage direct current across long distances, in this 2026 simulation study. These cables are wrapped in insulation bounded by shielding layers, and tiny bumps on that interface can concentrate the electric field, aging the insulation and shortening the cable's life. The team built a three-dimensional model of a very high-voltage cable and varied the bumps' size, shape, and the material's temperature behavior.

Height mattered far more than shape: taller protrusions distorted the field dramatically, with distortion rising roughly tenfold across the range tested. Distortion near a bump also grew as the insulation's conductivity became more temperature-sensitive. The findings give makers a clear priority, keep interface protrusions low, and offer designers a way to judge how much imperfection a cable design can tolerate.
plos-pone-0356785:
Hissah F AlMuhaysh surveys more than five hundred female students at a Saudi university about the inner skills that support learning on one's own in digital settings. Four traits anchor the study: emotional intelligence, flexible thinking, soft skills, and self-directed learning, with digital transformation of the university as a fifth force. A structural modeling method suited to tangled predictions tested how the traits lean on each other.

Emotional intelligence tied strongly to both flexible thinking and soft skills. Flexible thinking fed soft skills and fed self-directed learning directly, and soft skills in turn carried a substantial push toward self-directed learning. Digital change also tied to self-directed learning on its own. AlMuhaysh argues universities should train these human capacities alongside platforms, since tools alone do not make independent learners.
plos-pone-0356885:
Hongxiao Lv and colleagues tested a compound from the traditional Chinese herb red sage in rats with vascular dementia. They asked whether it protects the brain by policing copper. Their 2026 study modeled the disease by tying off both carotid arteries. The rats were then treated with tanshinone IIA. The team measured maze learning, hippocampal neuron damage, and the machinery of cuproptosis. Cuproptosis is a recently described copper-driven cell death.

The abstract reports the treated rats' design and assays in detail. They include water maze performance and tissue staining. Mitochondrial imaging and protein measures for a copper importer and its partner enzyme were included. Cell experiments tracked copper build-up and oxidative stress. The study extends the herb compound's known anti-inflammatory and antioxidant story into copper balance, a fresher angle on dementia.
plos-pone-0357185:
Sarah Covasso leads a team of eight listening to French teenagers who might have Lyme disease, and to their parents, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Lyme borreliosis is famously hard to pin down, and families can spend months in diagnostic limbo. Interviewing nineteen adolescents and parents across several centers in 2023, the team coded hundreds of statements into themes about how the suspected illness is lived, not just treated.

Three themes emerged. The experience was filtered through family history, including relatives' own encounters with the disease. Families felt ambivalence toward medical discourse, grateful and doubtful at once. And they hungered for clearer knowledge to fend off misinformation. Teenagers voiced confusion about what the disease even is, some indifference toward it, and a specific fear: that it lies dormant in them and might resurface to harm them later. The authors argue care pathways must explain themselves, not just prescribe.
plos-pone-0357285:
Anushree Bhagavan and three colleagues survey what mothers know about childhood hearing loss, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Two hundred fifteen mothers of children aged one to five answered a structured questionnaire at a tertiary hospital. Early hearing shapes speech and learning. What mothers recognize decides how quickly affected children get help. The survey covered causes, effects, treatment, rehabilitation, and where mothers learn about the topic.

Most mothers knew hearing loss can be present at birth or arrive later. Gaps opened on causes and on what can be done. Awareness of medical treatment ran ahead of awareness of rehabilitation services, which fewer than half knew about. A majority knew middle ear infections occur and believed they can be prevented. The authors say parent education should push past hospitals' medical framing toward hearing aids, therapy services, and screening, where ignorance currently delays children by years.
plos-pone-0357385:
Dakota R McMeans and colleagues expose rats repeatedly to methyl bromide, a fumigant still used on shipments, to check for quiet damage to nerves and muscles. Single heavy exposures are known to disturb movement, but the effects of repeated workplace-level inhalation were poorly mapped. Rats breathed the gas a few hours a day across four weeks, then took movement and behavior tests while spinal cord and leg muscle samples were examined under microscopes.

No obvious poisoning appeared: weight, walking, coordination, and activity all stayed normal, and nerve cell counts and support cell reactions were unchanged. Subtle signs did emerge, though, with the largest nerve cells shrinking and the junctions where nerves meet a fast leg muscle showing more wear. McMeans and colleagues say standard checks could miss this early damage.
plos-pone-0357485: Lenarczyk and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on how space flight strains the heart. Rats faced several simulated space stressors at once. The team tracked heart scarring, calcium signals that drive beats, immune function, signaling proteins, and gene variants. Stacked stressors may harm the heart in ways single ones do not. The work matters for keeping astronauts healthy on long missions.
plos-pone-0357585:
Hongwei Zheng and Wenbiao Chen warn that a popular score can make blood-based sepsis tests look better than they are. Their 2026 benchmark study checks gene-activity classifiers, which sort patients by patterns in blood, across four public patient datasets from different labs and machines. A test can rank patients well yet fail badly when a fixed cutoff decides who counts as sick.

That failure is exactly what they found for two common ways of scaling the data, which fell to coin-flip accuracy on one outside dataset despite glowing headline scores. A method that ranks genes within each single sample held up across all outside sets. Zheng and Chen argue that how data is prepared matters more than later fixes, a lesson for anyone building medical tests.
plos-pone-0357785:
Lea Teresa Kohl led a team of eight authors testing a parent interview for young children's behavior problems, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. Spotting disorders early in preschool children starts with asking parents the right questions. The interview under review is semi-structured and built on the DSM-5 diagnostic system, focusing on outward behavior problems.

Kohl's psychometric evaluation checks whether the interview measures what it claims and gives steady results. Clinicians need that proof before trusting it in busy clinics. Good early tools matter because help given in preschool years can change a child's path. A validated interview also gives researchers a shared instrument, so studies of early behavior problems can be compared across clinics and countries.
plos-pone-0357885:
Ard van Oosten, Mina Maharadjdin, Roland Blonk, Alex Burdorf, and Bea Tiemens published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. Its guiding question is simple, asking people directly how they would like to be helped. The study works with people who have mental-health problems and seek gainful employment, paid work they can sustain.

The method is concept mapping, where participants themselves generate and sort ideas about what helps. The authors look for factors that promote integrated approaches, support that joins mental health care and job help instead of splitting them. Employment services and mental health teams redesigning support together are the readers for this participant-built map.
plos-pone-0358485:
Fabiana Coelho Inouye led a team of eight authors who published a study protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026. Their topic was why some blood cancer patients do not take their daily kinase-blocking pills as directed. The cancers in view are the classic slow-growing types grouped as myeloproliferative neoplasms.

Inouye's group set out a plan for a review that mixes numbers with interviews and open-ended data. They focus on causes of poor adherence that can actually be changed, such as side effects, cost, or weak support. Mapping those causes first is what allows clinics to design help that keeps patients on drugs that control their disease.
plos-pone-0358785:
María del Carmen Giménez-Espert, Lucía Sanchis-Giménez, and Vicente Javier Prado-Gascó examine how nurses' attitudes toward talking with patients fit into burnout, in a 2026 PLOS ONE study. Nurses work under heavy stress, and earlier writing disagreed on whether communication strain is a cause of burnout, a result of it, or a link in between. The team set out to test those three possibilities directly.

They surveyed close to two hundred nurses at four public hospitals in Spain's Valencian Community, measuring job demands, resources, burnout, and communication attitudes. Statistical modeling showed that attitudes did not drive burnout and did not carry its effects either. Instead, poor attitudes were a consequence: when demands outweighed resources and burnout set in, nurses' approach to patient conversation deteriorated.
plos-pone-0358885:
Hunter Parsons and David G Behm compare three ways of stretching and ask what a thirty second bout changes, in PLOS ONE in 2026. Fourteen volunteers rotated through static stretching, a contract relax technique, dynamic stretching, and a no stretch control. Hip and shoulder flexibility, pain thresholds, strength, and endurance were measured before and after each session. The study also probed gains in the limb never stretched.

Static stretching won on its home turf, improving the stretched leg's flexibility by eight percent over control. The opposite leg hinted at a crossover gain that fell short of significance, and shoulders responded to nothing. Strength in the stretched limb dipped under every condition, including rest, which complicates simple stories about stretching and power. Pain thresholds did not shift. Women proved more flexible overall; men produced more force and fatigue. Thirty seconds, the authors suggest, buys local looseness and little else.
plos-pone-0359785:
Yue Yuan, Yu Liu, Jingchun Fan, and Zhen Ren published this research article in PLOS ONE in 2026. It explores key genes in colorectal adenoma-cancer, the sequence by which benign bowel growths turn into colorectal cancer. Their tool is a graph transformer, a machine learning model that reads data structured as networks.

Genes act in networks, so a model built for graphs suits the hunt for the few that drive the adenoma-to-cancer turn. Finding key genes early in that sequence could sharpen screening of polyps found at colonoscopy. Cancer genomics researchers are the audience for candidate genes raised by this method.
pmc-13198485:
Tomofumi Ishikawa and colleagues studied sedative use in early pregnancy and miscarriage risk in a 2026 Japanese study. Benzodiazepines are calming drugs also used for sleep and anxiety. Past evidence on miscarriage risk was mixed, so the team used a large health database to test dose and drug type.

They matched more than sixty thousand miscarriage cases with about one hundred ninety thousand controls. Sedative exposure was slightly more common among cases. Overall, exposure tied to a modest rise in miscarriage odds. Higher doses and longer-acting drugs showed somewhat stronger links, though estimates were imprecise. Results varied by drug, with one agent showing a clearer rise. The authors urge cautious reading of subgroup gaps.
pmc-13198785:
Shogo Narikiyo and colleagues present a 2026 case report on a benign heart tumor that seeded the brain. Cardiac myxoma is the most common benign heart tumor and surgery usually cures it. Rarely, tumor bits travel and grow elsewhere, even months later.

Their patient was a 54-year-old woman with leg weakness and several small brain strokes. Scans found a stalked tumor in her heart's upper left chamber. Full removal under heart-lung bypass confirmed myxoma. Seven months later, brief vision trouble and hand weakness led to scans showing growing brain lesions outside blood vessel zones. Brain surgery proved spread of the tumor. Beam therapy followed, and she stayed free of recurrence at one year.
pmc-13200585:
Serap Duru and colleagues followed smokers through a quit clinic with telemedicine support in a 2026 cohort study. Fear that quitting worsens depression and anxiety deters many smokers. The team measured mood over six months in routine care, with phone check-ins every two weeks for treated patients.

Five hundred adults enrolled at a specialist clinic. At six months, thirty-six percent had quit smoking. Depression and anxiety scores fell across the whole group. Both quitters and continuing smokers improved, but quitters improved more. The drug cytisine was the most used aid, and all got behavioral counseling. Side effects were mild, with no serious events. Quitting did not harm mental health here.
pmc-13201285:
Rocks formed by mineral-rich springs in northeastern Brazil hold a record of rapid climate change, examined in a 2026 study led by Tito Aureliano. The research article describes Quaternary tufa deposits at Quixeré, in the western Potiguar Basin, together with the plant fossils preserved inside them.

The team combined field description, thin-section microscopy, electron microscopy, and measurements of pore space in the rock. Fossil leaves point to an earlier humid forest, with warmer and wetter conditions than the dry Caatinga scrub that grows there today. The deposits thus record both changing water flow and the shift toward a drier climate in the late Quaternary.
pmc-13202685:
Medical students need skills for working with artificial intelligence, and a 2026 study by Hung-Che Lin builds a scale to measure that literacy. The research article develops and validates the AI Literacy Scale for Medical Students, grounded in self-determination theory and its needs for competence, relatedness, and autonomy.

A split sample of 518 students supported exploratory analysis in one half and confirmatory testing in the other. Nine factors emerged, organized under the theory's three domains, and the confirmatory models fit the data strongly. Ethics items loaded with autonomy, a result the authors say should shape how schools design and evaluate AI teaching.
pmc-13205085: A retraction notice published in 2026 withdraws a 2018 International Journal of Nanomedicine article on liposomal pemetrexed for drug-resistant breast cancer. Acting on a third party's concerns, the editors and publisher found unexpected similarities between image panels in several figures, including panels meant to show different treatment conditions. Review of the authors' raw data raised further integrity concerns, so the article was retracted and will stay online watermarked as retracted. The notice itself is all that survives here, and it names no individual findings as reliable.
pmc-13215585:
Hannah M. Moloney and co-authors introduce a 2026 method for estimating zooplankton abundance by eye, called the Zooplankton Visual Index. Zooplankton feed many large marine animals, yet their biomass is hard to measure over wide areas.

The team standardized the index and checked it against net samples, where higher index levels matched higher measured biomass and expected shifts in community makeup. They then applied it to nine years of reef manta ray sightings in the Maldives. Rays appeared more often when index levels were high, which suggests the simple score captures the food supply that draws them. The authors propose the tool for researchers and citizen science programs alike.
pmc-13216085:
Priscila dos Santos Ribas and co-authors present a 2026 preliminary study of stomach reflux during anaesthesia in dogs undergoing mastectomy. Reflux under anaesthesia is common yet silent, and opioid-based pain control may loosen the valve at the top of the stomach.

Twelve female dogs were watched with an endoscope during surgery, starting about forty-five minutes after induction. Every dog showed reflux and sphincter relaxation, with 58 percent graded mild and 42 percent severe, and one dog already had oesophageal inflammation. Because there was no comparison group, the authors cannot separate the effect of the surgery itself from that of the anaesthetic drugs. They frame the work as hypothesis-generating and call for controlled studies.
pmc-13217085:
Ounboontham and Ngoenmak test a simple picture chart against the standard symptom criteria for constipation in very young children. Functional constipation is common, yet judging it in infants and toddlers is hard. Their study enrolled 275 children at well-child visits, and parents completed both the Bristol stool chart and the Rome IV questionnaire.

Only 43 children met the full Rome IV criteria. Hard stool forms on the chart rarely appeared in children without the condition, so a positive chart strongly supported the diagnosis. Yet the chart missed about half of true cases. The authors advise using the chart to confirm, not to rule out, constipation.
pmc-13218185:
Catherina Elizabeth Naude and colleagues map chronic stroke rehabilitation delivered in primary healthcare settings in a 2026 scoping review. Stroke survivors need long-term rehabilitation, and primary care, community, and home services are where much of it must happen. The review focused on how interventions are dosed, their frequency, intensity, type, and duration, and on how they are delivered.

Searching sixteen databases plus grey literature, the reviewers included thirty-four sources published between 2010 and 2022, most from high-income countries. Nearly all interventions targeted body function and structure, usually through exercise, while far fewer addressed daily activities, participation in life roles, or the patient's context. Multidisciplinary teams delivered most programs, at home or in the community, and individual sessions outnumbered group ones. Dosage varied so widely that no best pattern emerges. The authors conclude that programs fit primary care realities poorly and call for research in rich and resource-poor environments.
pmc-13219085:
Stefanie Brehmer and colleagues report the INTRAMET phase II trial of radiation delivered during surgery for brain metastases in a 2026 paper. About a fifth of cancer patients develop brain spread, and deposits are removed and then irradiated. Giving the radiation intraoperatively, into the tumor cavity, could tighten the schedule.

Between 2017 and 2022, thirty-five adults had a suspected brain metastasis removed, and once frozen-section testing confirmed metastatic disease, a mobile low-energy X-ray device delivered thirty gray to the cavity surface. With a median follow-up over two years, local control at the site reached 94.3 percent, while freedom from new deposits was lower, at 57.1 percent. Median survival was about forty-four months, and patients moved to systemic therapy after a median of forty-five days. Radiation injury occurred in a fifth of patients, mostly mild, with no severe toxicities. The authors see a feasible alternative to postoperative radiation.
pmc-13222585:
Wenjie Wang and co-authors review immune aging in older patients with psoriasis, in a 2026 article on mechanisms and biologic therapy choices. Aging reshapes adaptive immunity and loosens control of innate responses, while skin changes feed local inflammation. Th17 and related T cell activity stays prominent in older skin, and control of antigen-presenting cells weakens.

Biologic drugs aimed at several cytokine targets have widened options greatly. Direct evidence in older patients is thin, yet available studies suggest benefit broadly comparable to younger patients. Heart and metabolic conditions complicate choices, and infection risk needs watching, especially with tumor necrosis factor blockers. Selective interleukin-23 drugs offer focused control while sparing other defenses.
pmc-13225285:
Liyang Jiang, Aixiang Yang, Jun Liu, and Jie Zhou investigate a 2026 cell study on pulmonary arterial hypertension, a fatal disease where lung artery walls thicken and narrow. A small RNA molecule called miR-661 was already known to restrain growth of the vessel wall cells involved. Serum from twelve patients and twelve healthy volunteers joined cell experiments to find the molecule's target gene.

Sequencing and reporter tests confirmed that the RNA directly binds and represses CCND2, a gene that pushes cells through their division cycle. Patient serum and oxygen-starved cells showed low miR-661 alongside high CCND2. Forcing CCND2 up drove cell growth and movement, while restoring miR-661 opposed those effects, outlining a possible treatment lever.
pmc-13225485:
Hugues Bulteau, Philippe Poidevin, and Marc Baroncini describe a 2026 surgical series testing a hinged skull flap for severe head injury with dangerous brain pressure. The standard operation removes a bone flap entirely, but that invites infection and fluid problems and later demands a second operation to replace the bone. Their semifloating version leaves the flap loosely tethered so it can bulge outward under pressure.

Twelve patients treated between 2022 and 2025 form the series, backed by a literature review. Two flaps failed to control pressure and needed full removal the next day. The rest settled back into place within weeks, with no infections, fluid complications, or bone loss, and operating time stayed short. The authors restrict the technique to carefully chosen focal injuries.
pmc-13226685:
Jason Jepson writes a 2026 first-person account of losing, and slowly regaining, control of his own mind. During his worst periods he heard voices spoken by people he knew, and he believed acquaintances could hear his thoughts through eye contact. Figures from his past seemed to stand in the room, second-guessing him, long after they had moved on with their own lives.

Police called to the family home treated him gently, and he rode to hospital in handcuffs, even sleeping in the patrol car. At the psychiatric ward he resisted the idea of schizophrenia and linked starting medication to his veterans' benefits arriving. The piece traces how slowly he grasped that the conversations were an illness, not a gift, and how central medication became.
pmc-13230285:
Evripidis Kapanidis and Keith Humphreys present in 2026 a new math framework for modeling how early breast lesions turn invasive. The model treats tumor growth as a steady process and follows people as they move between health states over time. It links screening detection, symptom detection, growth speed, and the time a contained lesion needs to become invasive.

Because the population is assumed stable, the model can be fitted using only diagnosed cases, without a separate rule for when tumors first appear. Different shapes can be swapped in for each part, so rival ideas about hidden progression can be tested. Computer simulations check that the math behaves as theory predicts. Estimates from such a model could inform debates about overdiagnosis and screening.
pmc-13230685:
Asmro Mulat and colleagues study in 2026 whether villages declared free of open defecation in Ethiopia keep using latrines over time. Fieldwork in Ebinat District in early 2017 covered seven hundred fifty-two households picked by systematic random sampling. Group talks and key informant interviews added context about habits and local support.

Only about a third of households used latrines in a sustained way, below the level programs hoped for. Homes visited in the past year by health extension workers or community health volunteers used latrines far more steadily. Having school-age children, joining a community sanitation triggering event, and latrine distance from the home also mattered. Frequent follow-up visits after a village declaration are urged to keep behavior from slipping back.
pmc-13231185:
Masato Obayashi and colleagues report in 2026 a ninety-year-old man who could not come off a ventilator while taking a blood vessel drug. He received oral beraprost for severe leg artery disease after thigh artery surgery, on top of extensive lung collapse. Every attempt to wean him from the machine ended with fast breathing and dangerous drops in blood oxygen.

Stopping the drug ended the episodes, while restarting it brought the same collapse back, a pattern that ties the drug to the problem. Beraprost widens vessels everywhere, which can send blood into poorly aired lung zones and waste oxygen matching. Teams weaning fragile patients may want to review such vessel-widening drugs when progress stalls without a clear cause.
pmc-13233585:
Sachin Malde and colleagues published a 2026 international consensus proposal on diagnosing interstitial cystitis, also called bladder pain syndrome. The condition causes long-term bladder pain and urgency, varies greatly between patients, and is often misdiagnosed. Specialists from the ESSIC network set out to replace one-size-fits-all assessment with a structured framework.

The proposal standardizes how clinicians take the history, examine patients, and report bladder scope findings, and it advises tissue sampling when appropriate. It highlights features that split patients into meaningful subtypes, including Hunner lesions inside the bladder, pelvic floor dysfunction, body-wide pain processing changes, and links to systemic disease. Sorting patients this way should let treatment match the person rather than the label alone.
pmc-13233885:
Rogelio Rojas-Rios and colleagues published a 2026 gene study tracing a hard-to-treat bacterium through Mexico City hospitals over fifteen years. Pseudomonas aeruginosa endangers burn patients, especially when it resists carbapenem antibiotics. The team sequenced two extensively resistant strains taken from burn patients in 2016 and 2021 and compared them with older local isolates.

Both newer strains belonged to sequence type 309 and sat close on the family tree to carbapenem-resistant strains isolated in the same city in 2006. Each carried a chromosomal class 1 integron, a gene cassette platform stocking resistance to beta-lactams and aminoglycosides. One strain's integron sat in exactly the same spot as the 2006 strains. The authors warn that this lineage has persisted across hospitals for over a decade.
pmc-13234485:
Gregory K. Zane and co-authors modeled in 2026 what a future chlamydia vaccine could achieve in the United States. Chlamydia is the most often reported sexually transmitted disease in the country and causes large illness and cost. Their math model followed heterosexual spread by age and sex across the people. Models ran for decades and compared vaccination plans against no vaccination.

Routine vaccination of adolescent girls alone cut projected diseases sharply by 2075. Vaccinating both sexes cut diseases by more than half and nearly removed high incidence under base assumptions. A one-time catch-up campaign for young women added only modest extra benefit. Every plan tested saved money overall in the model. Vaccinating both sexes also gained many more healthy life years than the girls-only plan. The authors call vaccination a promising prevention route despite no late-stage option yet.
pmc-13235185:
Florian Helms and colleagues analysed in 2026 whether sex affects results after minimally invasive surgery on the upper aorta. Records covered nearly four hundred patients who had replacement or repair procedures through a small-access approach at one centre. Statistical matching compared equal groups of women and men with similar risk profiles. Intensive care stay and complications after surgery were tracked closely.

Female sex, older age, and longer operation time each predicted a longer intensive care stay. Women suffered strokes around surgery far more often than men in the matched groups. Women also needed notably more transfused red blood cells during care. Short-term and long-term survival, however, showed no clear difference between the sexes. The authors conclude sex shapes early recovery after this surgery and deserves attention in planning and consent discussions.
pmc-13235485:
Sarah Uhranowsky, Dylan Perez, and Yosef Berlyand reported in 2026 an unusual cause of sudden kidney injury found on emergency scanning. A 52-year-old man with diabetes and high blood pressure arrived with fever, belly pain, leg swelling, and confusion. Blood tests showed infection markers and kidney values well above his normal level. He could not produce urine for testing in the department.

Contrast scans revealed most of his bladder, plus the tube draining his right kidney, had slipped into a groin hernia. That trapped position blocked urine flow and backed pressure into the kidney. Clinicians reduced the hernia at the bedside, after which he could urinate again. Planned surgical repair moved to an outpatient date because a separate lung clot raised operative risk. The authors note bladder involvement in hernias is uncommon and ureter involvement rarer still.
pmc-13237285:
Baek and colleagues measure the working loads an electric farm tractor must be built to survive. Swapping a diesel engine for motors and batteries changes a tractor's whole design, yet its loads still come from the field. The team fitted sensors to the engine area, drive axles, power take-off, and hydraulic pump of a mid-size tractor.

They recorded loads during plough tillage, rotary tillage, and driving in a silt loam paddy field. Each job stresses the machine differently, and electric parts must be sized for the worst of them. Real field numbers, rather than guesses, let engineers build electric tractors that are strong enough without being wastefully heavy.
pmc-13237785:
Kazuyoshi Mitta and colleagues reported in 2026 the emergency keyhole repair of a rare parahiatal hernia in a 34-year-old woman. She arrived with sudden left chest pain after two months of intermittent discomfort, and another doctor had suspected a lung abscess. Scans instead showed part of her stomach trapped through an opening beside the esophageal passage, with its blood supply cut off.

Surgeons freed the stomach through laparoscopy, closed the hernia opening with barbed sutures, and removed the dead portion of the stomach fundus. She recovered without complications, left hospital on day thirteen, and showed no recurrence a month later. The authors warn that this rare hernia can turn life-threatening when diagnosis lags. Her case had no obvious predisposing cause.
pmc-13238285:
Melemai and colleagues scope the evidence on planned surgery for people kept on long-term antibiotics after a joint infection. Replacing an infected hip or knee sometimes fails to clear the germ, and some patients gain nothing from more surgery. Those patients may instead take suppressive antibiotics indefinitely to keep the infection quiet while they live with the joint.

Their review asks what is known when such patients later receive a first hip or knee replacement at another joint. The evidence is scattered, and practice varies. Mapping it shows surgeons where confidence is possible, where it is guesswork, and which questions a proper trial should answer for a growing group of patients.
pmc-13239285:
Qiyuan Pan and colleagues reviewed in 2026 the technologies that find which protein a natural product actually binds, the step that turns a promising plant or microbial compound into a drug lead. Natural products have rich chemistry, yet their targets stay hidden because the molecules are complex and living systems are messy. The review sorts the toolkit into experimental strategies, such as chemical proteomics, and computational ones, including AI-driven prediction.

Case studies show how the methods combine into a reusable workflow that moves a candidate hit toward a validated, therapy-relevant target. Common bottlenecks, from false positives to fragmented evidence, get named alongside countermeasures. The authors aim to give mechanism hunters an actionable framework. Better target proof early, they argue, saves the expensive failures later.
pmc-13239385:
Shannon L Ferry and team report a 2026 mouse study of built T cells for melanoma. The cells carry a man-made receptor aimed at the tumour. Extra genes in the cells make two immune signals, a boosted form of interleukin-2 and interleukin-33, meant to sharpen the attack.

The team compared ways to prepare the body before the cells went in. Mice given whole-body radiation first, then the boosted cells, held their tumours down best and lived the longest. Radiation helped plain cells settle in too. The extra signals pushed cells inside the tumour toward active fighter types rather than worn-out ones. Taking the given cells away erased the lasting gain, so their staying power mattered.
pmc-13239685:
Faheem Malam and colleagues review the harms of spine injections and nerve-burning procedures for chronic back and neck pain in a 2026 systematic review. These treatments are common for pain not caused by cancer, yet rare and delayed side effects are hard to capture in trials, so the team gathered longer observational evidence.

Sixty studies covering nearly five thousand patients met the criteria, most following radiofrequency ablation, epidural injections, or joint injections. Low certainty evidence linked some procedures with temporary altered consciousness, deep infection, and accidental puncture of the membrane around the spinal cord, each affecting roughly one to two percent of patients. The review was built alongside a guideline panel.
pmc-13240485:
Lei Wang and colleagues teach a neural network to spot hidden heart wiring faults from ordinary ECG traces in a 2026 study. Two causes of racing heart episodes, concealed accessory pathways and a short circuit within the heart's relay node, often leave no trace on a resting tracing, frustrating diagnosis before ablation treatment.

Their network, CSPANet, combines two attention mechanisms that weight the most informative leads and shapes in the signal. It reached test accuracy above ninety-two percent, beating nine established networks and other attention designs. Removing parts of the design in turn showed each contributed, with the combined model gaining most in sensitivity and precision. The authors see help for planning safer ablations.
pmc-13240985:
Hohendorf's team mapped digital lifestyle programs for preschool children, comparing general and low-income groups. Five bases were searched with AI help. 77 studies on 54 programs made the cut. Food, activity, sleep, sitting time, and oral health all counted as targets.

19 programs aimed solely at low-income families, and they looked plainer by design. Texts appeared more often, pushy features fewer, and channels narrower. Results were mixed across the board, with no design trait foretelling success. Among low-income programs, the weakest ones carried more persuasive features. All of them were built for young children.
pmc-13241385:

pmc-13264885:

pmc-13264985:

The authors say network damage may start early in this group.
pmc-13265185:
Ping Lin and colleagues build a survival prediction chart for a rare pancreatic cancer subtype, in a 2026 registry study. Pancreatic signet-ring cell carcinoma is uncommon and aggressive. pmc-13266185:

pmc-13266885:
Kang Zhang and colleagues describe in 2026 patients with severe pneumonia caught outside hospital who needed intensive care in China. pmc-13267485:
Timur O Zanakhov and colleagues report in 2026 an unexpected reaction route that turns small strained ring compounds into pyrroles, a ring family common in medicines and pigments. pmc-13267785:
Ester Mascarenhas Oliveira and colleagues report in 2026 on how transgender people experience public health care in Brasília, Brazil's capital. Mental health care featured too, including rare welcoming services that worked well. pmc-13268185:

pmc-13268985:
Bo Wang and colleagues lay out in 2026 a plan to curb antibiotic overuse in newborn intensive care units in a resource-limited region of China. Main measures are how many babies receive antibiotics and for how many days, balanced against later sepsis, deaths, and restarts. The design aims to prove a model that similar regions can copy safely.
pmc-13269085:
Xinyin Liu and co-authors review in 2026 how innate lymphoid cells, a family of tissue-dwelling immune cells, may carry gut problems into the kidney. Diet, probiotics, and immune drugs aimed at this link are proposed as future treatments.
pmc-13269985:
Kevin H McLaughlin and co-authors published a journal article in 2026 sorting older surgical patients into subgroups from routine hospital data. Three groups emerged: low frailty with high mobility at 15.3 percent, high frailty with low mobility at 27.6 percent, and low frailty with low mobility at 57.1 percent. The authors suggest tailoring care by group.
pmc-13271385:
Vikas N. O'Reilly-Shah is lead author of a 2026 theoretical article examining the unfolding argument in the neuroscience of consciousness. Through mathematical proofs covering history dependence, stability, and information measures, they show such plastic systems cannot be matched by a static one-way network. pmc-13271885:
Leonie Hodel is lead author of a 2026 journal article mapping cattle densities across the Brazilian Amazon from very high-resolution satellite images. Stocking was lower on properties with more recent deforestation and on those farther from slaughterhouses. The authors note coverage and detection limits.
pmc-13272085:
Şeref Eroğlu and coauthors analyze in 2026 sleep quality among combat sport athletes using a standard questionnaire. Fighters face heavy training and strict weight control, both of which can disturb sleep. The study covered 498 athletes in Olympic and non-Olympic combat disciplines, with an average age near twenty-one.

Two thirds of the athletes qualified as poor sleepers. Male sex, competing in an Olympic discipline, and rapid weight loss above four percent of body weight each raised the odds of poor sleep. Longer time in the sport added a smaller risk. Olympic athletes also scored worse on several parts of the sleep scale than their non-Olympic peers.
pmc-13272185:
Mitchell R. Koss is lead author of a 2026 retrospective study on delays in surgically fixing distal radius fractures, breaks near the wrist end of the forearm bone. Fixation delayed beyond two weeks is linked to worse patient-reported outcomes, and the team asked whether neighbourhood disadvantage and insurance type predict such delay.

Using records from several academic health systems for 2012 to 2024, the cohort held 6,639 patients, median age 62. Median time to surgery was eight days, but 25.3 percent waited beyond fourteen days. Living in the more deprived neighbourhood quartiles, Spanish-speaking status, greater illness burden, and Medicare insurance each independently raised the odds of delay. The authors call for targeted steps to improve access.
pmc-13272885:
Parvaneh Sadeghimoghaddam leads a 2026 study of outcomes after advanced resuscitation for preterm babies in Tehran, Iran. Advanced help at birth included a breathing tube, chest compressions, or epinephrine. The team studied 444 babies born before 33 weeks at one hospital in 2020 and 2021.

They also had more breathing distress, air leaks in the chest, a persistent heart vessel, and bleeding in the brain. The authors urge caution in reading this, since sicker babies are the ones who need such help, and advise careful follow-up of survivors.
pmc-13273385:
Meizhu Gao leads a 2026 review of gut microbe products and their roles in cardiovascular disease, disease of the heart and vessels. Bile acids play a dual role, guiding fat handling and inflammatory signaling through dedicated receptors. The authors synthesize evidence on high blood pressure, atherosclerosis, and heart failure to guide new diagnosis and treatment ideas.
pmc-13273585:
Sudeshna Mondal and co-authors built an adaptive hydrogel that fights bacteria and helps wounds heal in a 2026 study. Drug resistance is rising, so materials that attack bacteria physically could bypass failing antibiotics. Their gel is inspired by nucleic acids, the chemistry of DNA.

In lab and animal tests it sped skin regrowth and wound closure.
pmc-13273985:
Enatfenta Sewmehone Endalew and co-authors report a 2026 qualitative journal article on exercise during pregnancy in Ethiopian cities. Health guidance urges at least 150 minutes of moderate activity a week in pregnancy, yet few Ethiopian women reach that level. The team asked what women knew, and what helped or blocked them.

Seven focus group talks were held with forty-five pregnant women at health centers in four cities. Most women knew activity was healthy, but some wrongly feared it could cause abortion early in pregnancy. Walking was the favored activity. Barriers included poor health, busy jobs, fear of judgment, and missing sidewalks. Partner support and access to green space helped women stay active.
pmc-13274485:
Iris M. Westra and co-authors ran controlled hydrogen release tests to sharpen emission measurement in a 2026 study. A hydrogen economy will leak some gas during making, moving, and storing it, and leaked hydrogen indirectly warms the climate. Until recently, instruments could not detect the faint plumes involved.

Their sampler and gas analysis system reads hydrogen with very fine precision alongside methane and carbon dioxide. They released a known flow from an 8 kilowatt electrolyzer and sampled the plume fourteen times by drone and from the ground. Their estimate landed close to the true rate, with error driven by how fully the plume was covered and by shifting wind. Hydrogen plumes behaved much like methane plumes, so proven methane survey tactics should transfer.
pmc-13274585:
Zhaoyuan Yao and a large team report a 2026 journal article presenting BERTH, an artificial intelligence system for watching the global water cycle. Satellites see Earth's surface well, but turning those images into rainfall, soil moisture, and runoff figures usually needs chained models with local tuning. Climate change is making water swings faster and harsher.

It converts satellite radiance directly into four outputs: evaporation from land, precipitation, soil moisture, and runoff. It maps the whole planet at thirty-meter detail, updated daily. The authors report it beat existing physics-based models on accuracy across varied conditions.
pmc-13274885:

pmc-13275285:
Weidong Xie and co-authors tested a nutrition and inflammation score as a prognostic marker in stomach cancer in a 2026 retrospective study. A chart model built on the score predicted survival with fair accuracy and added value beyond stage and regimen data. The authors say outside validation must come before clinical use.
pmc-13275685:

For surfaces, a standard swab method with buffered solution beat sponge sampling, especially on steel and silicone.
pmc-13276185:

pmc-13276285:

pmc-13276385:

pmc-13276785:

pmc-13277285:

pmc-13277585:

pmc-13278485:

pmc-13278685:

pmc-13279085:

pmc-13279185:

pmc-13279485:

pmc-13279585:

pmc-13279985:

pmc-13280085:

pmc-13280585:

pmc-13280685:

pmc-13280885:

pmc-13280985:

pmc-13281385:

pmc-13281585:
