Records for 325 patients from three Beijing hospitals, admitted between January 2019 and June 2024, split into those with and without tuberculosis. Ten factors stood out, spanning dust history, blood nutrition and sugar markers, and scan features such as cavities and fluid. Eight learning models were trained on those factors and checked with standard accuracy and usefulness curves, with an explanation tool to show each factor's weight. The work supports earlier, data-led diagnosis in chest clinics.
pmc-13317585:
Katherine Cuenca-León and colleagues developed, in a 2026 bench study, a mouth treatment blending three essential oils against Candida albicans, the yeast behind oral thrush, which increasingly resists standard drugs. The oils came from lemongrass, coriander, and oregano plants gathered in southern Ecuador.

Chemical profiling found 40 compounds, led by carvacrol at 30.01 percent of the mix in the measured profile. On agar plates, the blend at ten percent strength in alcohol cleared a zone of 77.89 millimeters, far beyond both chlorhexidine and fluconazole controls in the same test. A water version also worked, though more weakly. The authors call for strength and safety testing before any clinical use.
pmc-13318285:
Luke S. Wimpy leads a 2026 survey experiment on which short messages move public views about the safety of gene editing in farming and medicine. It closes a longer project that began with focus groups and three earlier surveys.

A national sample of 3,200 adults in the United States was randomly shown one of eight videos. Versions differed by speaker, either a researcher or a blogger, by framing around years of safe use or counts of safety studies, and by whether farming or medicine featured. Viewers generally responded well, and what they remembered depended most on the application setting, since recall was stronger when the message matched its field. Speaker and framing choices mattered far less.
pmc-13318385:
Chaimae Bekhakh and colleagues describe, in 2026, a rare intestinal lymphoma in a 34-year-old woman with poorly controlled coeliac disease. Coeliac disease raises lymphoma risk, but those cancers are usually of T-cell type. A large B-cell lymphoma in the gut, lacking the usual CD20 marker, had not been reported in this setting.

She presented with abdominal pain, weight loss and diarrhoea, and imaging showed a large mass in the jejunum. Surgery removed that bowel segment with nearby lymph nodes. Microscopy showed sheets of large abnormal lymphoid cells. Staining found other B-cell markers despite the missing CD20, and gene sequencing revealed a harmful TP53 mutation with clonal B cells. The authors stress combining tissue, staining and molecular results for such difficult diagnoses.
pmc-13319085:
Katherine A. Hirchak and colleagues present a 2026 study adapting alcohol-use harm surveys for American Indian and Alaska Native adults. Standard tools miss the history and culture of Indigenous communities. A panel of Indigenous researchers and clinicians reviewed two existing tools. Twenty adults who had drunk heavily or were in recovery were then interviewed.

The panel advised removing 20 items from the longer inventory. It added 12 items to the shorter companion tool and three new subscales. Wording based on strengths replaced stigmatising phrasing throughout. The interviews produced three themes, covering reactions to items, community-specific harms, and recovery supports. Culture, prevention, and wider social factors moved to the centre. The adapted tools will next be tested with 150 adults drawn from across the country.
pmc-13319385:
Yoshiko Toyoda and co-authors present a case report from 2026 about a rare soft tissue tumor in a young woman. The 19 year old had long been told she had a vessel tangle at her right elbow and wrist. She had mild pain, a tingling sign in her forearm, a stiff elbow, and weak turning of the hand.

Fresh scans plus a guided needle sample named the true cause as a calcifying tumor of tendon sheets, found at two sites at once. Cuts to remove both lumps confirmed the call. Nerve squeeze and a worn joint surface came with it, a rare mix. The case warns that this tumor can mimic vessel faults for years.
pmc-13319485:
Katrina Holmes à Court and co-authors explore thinking complaints in body image illness in a 2026 study across clinic and public groups. People with this illness fixate on flaws in how they look that others barely see. What they report about their own thinking speed, focus, and memory had barely been mapped before this work.

One small clinic group of 15 patients was set next to 29 healthy peers, and a far larger public group of 433 people with strong symptoms answered the same new scale. Complaints spanned speed, focus, memory, planning, and reading others, with slow speed standing out most. Clinic patients scored far above peers. Complaints rose most for social thinking when symptoms flared.
pmc-13319885:
Hsiu-Ting Chien and co-authors measure the burden of a rare severe skin illness in Taiwan in a 2026 claims study. The illness brings wide sheets of small pus filled bumps plus body wide swelling, and flares can return again and again. National insurance records were used to count cases, care use, and costs next to a matched group with common plaque skin illness.

A total of 245 people with the rare illness and no prior common plaque illness were found from 2017 onward, with more than a thousand mid to severe flares among them. Their flare rate ran higher than the matched group, and clinic, emergency, and hospital use all ran higher too. Monthly care costs ran about twice as high, which shows the heavy load this rare illness places.
pmc-13320485:
Anna E Sri and co-authors share a 2026 interview study on careful drug use in remote Indigenous communities in Australia. Fourteen nurses, doctors, Aboriginal health workers, vets, and pharmacists spoke about germs that resist antibiotics and how human, animal, and land health link together. Remote clinics face thin staffing and hard choices about when drugs are truly needed.

Staff shortages and heavy workloads made careful prescribing hard, while local health workers helped good practice take hold. Drug use in local animal care was mostly low, though preventive drugs around surgery could improve. Workers showed clear grasp of wider drivers of resistance and a wish to act jointly across health fields.
pmc-13321585:
Gaowa Ailun and co-authors report a rare ovarian cancer in a young woman in a 2026 case report. Ovarian carcinosarcoma mixes two cancer types and is highly aggressive; it mostly strikes women after menopause, so a premenopausal case is uncommon. Clear best treatment is still not settled for this rare tumour.

The patient was a 33-year-old Han Chinese woman treated with full tumour removal surgery followed by platinum based chemotherapy. Gene tests for BRCA faults and repair deficiency came back negative. After a good response, the PARP drug olaparib was started as an individual off-label choice with consent. Disease stayed controlled over 46 months of follow-up without major side effects.
pmc-13321785:
Seyed Kianoosh Hosseini and co-authors report a heart attack linked to birth control pills in a 2026 case report. Combined oral contraceptives are widely used and generally safe, but they can promote artery clots. The patient was a 28-year-old Iranian woman who did not smoke, had no major illness history, and had endured 11 hours of chest pain.

Heart tracing and blood tests confirmed a heart attack, and imaging showed a clot blocking the main front heart artery with no fatty narrowing beneath. She had taken a pill with levonorgestrel and ethinyl estradiol for 13 years. Balloon treatment reopened the artery without a stent, and scans three months later showed an open artery and better heart function.
pmc-13322385:
Mina Pashaei Ghezeljeh and Amirreza Jabbaripour Sarmadian write, in a 2026 letter, in response to a study of fat grafting combined with platelet-rich plasma for female genitourinary ageing. The original work treated thirty-eight patients and reported better genital appearance, vaginal features, sexual function and urinary symptoms at six months. A second study using a micro-fat technique reported similar gains.

The letter writers urge caution. Both studies were retrospective, small and limited to women with existing complaints, so durability and general reach are uncertain. Most women seeking fat grafting, they note, are motivated by appearance rather than symptoms, and that group deserves study. They also report clinical impressions that fat quality may depend on diet and activity, and they call for structured trials to test those ideas.
pmc-13322885:
Yiqing Wang and co-authors map how pancreatic islets remake protein production when glucose rises sharply, in a 2026 study of primary mouse tissue. Using ribosome profiling at low and high glucose, they tracked which messages were being translated and how efficiently.

High glucose altered translation for 1,680 genes in their count, lifting early response genes and building blocks for protein making while suppressing stress genes. Output for the secretion path and for mitochondrial fuel enzymes also rose, even as genes for making new mitochondria eased back. Some genes changed only at the translation level, apart from their message levels. The work shows a coordinated push toward rapid insulin supply.
pmc-13323585:
Joshua D. Mitchell and co-authors mapped who gets diagnosed with transthyretin amyloid cardiomyopathy, a rare and life-threatening stiffening of the heart muscle, and where care is available. Their 2026 study combined a geospatial analysis of amyloid centers and cardiology providers with records for 14,980 patients from a United States health care map covering July 2016 through June 2024. The goal was to expose gaps in diagnosis across place and population.

Diagnosed prevalence reached 35.68 per 100,000 people and rose fourfold over the study period, highest among Black patients and in the Northeast. Patients lived a mean 4.3 miles from a cardiology provider but 48.5 miles from an amyloid center, and large areas, above all in the Midwest, had thin coverage. The authors call for strategies that close these regional gaps and reach the many patients still undiagnosed.
pmc-13324185:
Jiayi Zhao and team found the RNA helicase DHX29 as a critical regulator of antibody output in mice. Their 2026 study began with a CRISPR screen of RNA helicases in a laboratory system of plasma cell differentiation, then tested mice lacking Dhx29 only in B cells. Protein-making control, the regulation of which message RNAs get turned into protein, is still not fully known in immunity, and DHX29 emerged as a strong candidate.

Mice without B-cell DHX29 showed severely impaired germinal center formation, plasma cell change, and antibody output. Mechanistically, DHX29 promotes translation of the transcription factors Tcf3 and Tle3 by binding their message RNA untranslated regions. Without it, B cells proliferated normally but failed to switch to IgG1 or become plasma cells, and restoring TCF3 and TLE3 largely rescued the change. The work highlights protein-making control as a lever on immune responses.
pmc-13324385:
Sumin Kang and co-authors show how faulty ICOS signalling can worsen lupus through a side door, in a 2026 mouse study. ICOS support is vital both for follicular helper T cells and for regulatory T cells, which makes blocking it a risky therapy idea for B cell driven autoimmune disease.

In lupus-prone Sanroque mice lacking the ICOS ligand, germinal centre responses collapsed, yet autoantibodies and lupus-like illness persisted. Regulatory T cells dwindled, freeing self-reactive neuropilin-1 high helper cells that outcompeted regulators for dendritic cell contact and pushed age-associated B cells outside germinal centres. The authors warn that ICOS-targeted treatment could trade one B cell route for another in systemic lupus.
pmc-13324685:
Bingrui Wang and colleagues build a neural network that sorts chaotic signals from noise in a 2026 study. Older tools often ignore time order, break down under noise, or cover only a few signal types.

The team studied 15 chaos models and tuned a Swish-modulo map with Bayesian search, checking it against Lyapunov exponents. Their network mixes learnable wavelet features with a fast cross-correlation step that respects cause and effect. Accuracy reached 96.67 percent at 20 dB of noise in tests. The correlation step beat dilated convolution by up to 5.42 percent while training 43 times faster. Reliable chaos spotting aids fields from heart monitoring to weather work.
pmc-13324785:
Nacer Bellaloui and co-authors map the genome regions that control soybean seed sugars in a 2026 field study. Sucrose adds welcome taste, while raffinose and stachyose pass undigested and lower meal quality for people and simple-stomached animals.

A cross between heat-tolerant DS25-1 and DT97-4290 yielded 201 inbred lines grown at Stoneville, Mississippi, in 2018 and 2019. Mapping with 8,445 markers found 19 sugar regions, 12 of them new. Sucrose regions sat on chromosomes 3, 5, 11, and 19 in the first year. Each region held over 50 candidate genes tied to sugar pathways. The markers could help breeders tune seed sugar balance.
pmc-13325185:
John R. Helliwell surveys how crystallography feeds open science and free teaching materials in a 2026 article. The field has shared data openly for over a century, long before the FAIR principles had a name.

W. L. Bragg published raw diffraction images in his first crystal structure paper in 1913, and the Cambridge Crystallographic Data Centre built careful archives from 1965 onward. The Crystallography Open Database allows free download of its whole collection. Open protein data in the Protein Data Bank helped make AlphaFold possible. The International Union of Crystallography supplies free learning resources to readers and authors in both rich and poor countries.
pmc-13326085:
Cassie M. Hartley and colleagues tally foodborne outbreaks from marine toxins in the United States from 2011 to 2023 in a 2026 surveillance report. These toxins resist cooking and freezing and give no taste or smell warning.

Reports to the CDC system counted 402 outbreaks, causing 1,280 illnesses, 96 hospitalizations, and one death. The national rate was 1.2 outbreaks per million people over the period. Hawaii led state rates at 25.3 outbreaks per million, followed by Puerto Rico, Florida, and Alaska. Algae make some toxins that build up through food chains, while poor storage creates others, which makes part of the burden preventable.
pmc-13326985:
Kunihiro Ishioka and co-authors report a 2026 single-center review of a blood-filtering treatment for severe leg artery disease. Their patients had chronic limb-threatening ischemia while receiving hemodialysis, a group with few good options. The device studied, Rheocarna, removes low-density lipoprotein directly from the blood.

Charts for 31 patients, average age 67 years, were checked for ulcer healing at six months and survival without major amputation at one year. Healing reached 25.8 percent at six months, while the one-year rate for amputation-free survival was 40 percent, and a leg blood-flow index improved slightly. Outcomes suggest some help with wounds and limb saving, though benefit looked limited once disease was far advanced.
pmc-13327485:
Nikolai Ramadanov and colleagues pool evidence on the learning curve for hip arthroscopy in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Keyhole hip surgery is hard to master, so they compared early cases in a surgeon's practice with later ones. Searches through the end of 2025 found eighteen studies with 2,624 procedures.

Later cases ran shorter, with operating time down by about 31.77 minutes on average and traction time down by 15.67 minutes, and patient scores improved more as well. Complication and repeat scope rates did not differ clearly, but later cases ended in full hip replacement less often. The pattern supports structured training and mentoring while surgeons climb the early part of the curve.
pmc-13327885:
In Ja Park bids farewell as Editor-in-Chief of the Annals of Coloproctology in a 2026 editorial. Park recalls taking the role with two aims: widening the journal's scope and raising its standing abroad. Reviewing manuscripts with co-editors and reviewers stands out as the most meaningful part of the term.

Under that watch, the journal grew past its regional base, building an online platform for colorectal surgeons and drawing most submissions from abroad, spanning Asia, Europe, the Americas, and the Middle East. Ties with international societies grew as well, starting with an Asia-Pacific federation and extending to an Italian society, bringing guideline work. Park thanks board members, reviewers, and authors worldwide.
pmc-13328085:
Bo Peng, Huan Xu, and Xiangjiu Che present a graph learning system that borrows language model skill in a 2026 article. Graph neural networks model linked data well but blur node differences after many rounds, while language models read text richly yet miss link structure. Their M2GNN framework joins the two for sorting nodes and forecasting links.

Language-derived meaning vectors first refine which candidate edges deserve trust, stable position codes then anchor the cleaned graph, and graph-based and language-informed forecasts are blended adaptively. Benchmark tests and part-by-part removal studies showed competitive or better results, with each piece adding value. The design is a controlled recipe for graphs that carry both links and text, not a general chat model.
pmc-13328385:
Victor B B Mello and co-authors benchmark fast deep learning pipelines for brain surface rebuilding in a 2026 study. Measuring the cortex from MRI at scale needs speed without losing accuracy, so three segmentation models, DeepSCAN, FastSurferCNN, and QuickNAT, fed an eleven-minute surface pipeline adapted from FreeSurfer. Big public datasets plus a synthetic set with known answers supplied the tests.

Judgments covered closeness to the full FreeSurfer rebuild, repeat accuracy on rescans, steadiness across ages, and tolerance of contrast shifts. The DeepSCAN-based pipeline agreed most with the reference in human data and matched synthetic truth best. A fast, dependable route for high-volume brain studies is the prize, ahead of clinical testing.
pmc-13329485:
Jack T Franchino and colleagues examine whether neighbourhood wealth shapes delays in carpal tunnel care in a 2026 study. Records covered 276 patients who had release surgery between 2022 and 2025. Home addresses were linked to deprivation and vulnerability scores at the small census tract level, plus survey data on local conditions.

Median time from first symptoms to specialist visit was 720.5 days in the reported results, and time to surgery was longer still. Deprivation scores showed no link to either delay. Adjusted models gave the same picture, and ranges ruled out delays beyond six months as a likely hidden gap. The authors conclude that no clear delay gap by neighbourhood wealth was found in this group.
pmc-13330485:
Onur Akyüz and co-authors review what is known about sexual activity, sport performance, and recovery in a 2026 narrative article. Beliefs that sex harms performance are widespread, yet proof is patchy and mixed. The review sorts body, mind, and context pathways, from hormones and heart responses to sleep and mood.

Sexual activity acts like light exertion and, when hours before contest, does not drain energy or blunt strength, endurance, or coordination in the summed evidence. Short hormone swings look too brief to harm output. Better mood and lower anxiety may aid readiness for some athletes. Harms more often trace to lost sleep or poor timing. Blanket abstinence lacks support, the authors conclude.
pmc-13330685:
Zhichao Yao and colleagues build smart microneedles that can raise or lower reactive oxygen in infected wounds in a 2026 study. Wound care faces a paradox: high reactive oxygen kills germs, yet excess blocks healing. Single materials rarely switch both ways. The patch joins vanadium carbide and iodinene inside a soft needle base.

Under laser light, the carbide makes reactive oxygen for germ killing. After light stops, it mops up leftover oxygen species instead. Lab and animal tests showed strong germ killing, calmer immune cell states, lower swelling signals, and faster closure in the reported results. Laser control plus needle delivery may dodge drug resistance issues, the authors propose.
pmc-13331285:
J Álvarez and colleagues price udder infection losses on dairy farms in Lugo, Spain, in a 2026 study. Records from 63 commercial farms in a milk quality programme for 2023 fed a cost model with literature rates. Simulation runs with 10,000 rounds tested how unsure inputs sway totals.

Average total cost reached a yearly figure of 31,643 euros per farm in the reported model, equal to about 261 euros per cow in that same output. Hidden infection without signs took 58.4 percent of losses, ahead of clear clinical cases in the shares given. Milk loss led in fixed estimates, while culling led most often under uncertainty. Reproductive delay also weighed heavily.
pmc-13332485:
Zhongyun Ning and colleagues present a 2026 case report of a rare harmless blood vessel tumor in the kidney that was mistaken for cancer. Anastomosing hemangioma has no malignant potential, but its scans carry no distinctive signature, so it is often misread as renal cancer or the dangerous angiosarcoma.

A 77-year-old woman came in with black stools for 20 days, and contrast CT showed a cystic spot about 2.0 cm across in her left renal sinus, its wall lighting up in nodules in a way that suggested cystic kidney cancer. With a R.E.N.A.L. score of 9x, she underwent laparoscopic removal of the whole kidney. Only tissue study afterward gave the true diagnosis of anastomosing hemangioma. The authors use the case to warn that this benign tumor regularly triggers cancer surgery because imaging alone cannot separate it from malignancy.
pmc-13332685:
Catherine O. Buck and Veronika Shabanova studied feeding volumes in newborns whose mothers had diabetes during pregnancy, in a 2026 prospective cohort study. Babies exposed to diabetes in the womb face higher later risks of obesity and metabolic disease, and early feeding may shape their unusual growth paths.

The cohort held 149 infants born at 30 to 36 weeks or at term, 50 of them diabetes-exposed. The exposed group had less exclusive breastfeeding on day one and took in more total fluid per day during the first week, a gap explained by their larger weight. Among late preterm babies, the exposed group gained weight faster between days 7 and 14, and that speed tracked with lower fluid intake per kilogram on days 3 and 14. The authors link the feeding pattern to feeding maturity in this at-risk group.
pmc-13332785:
Lixin Wang and co-authors built a bedside scoring chart in 2026 to predict which children with both allergic asthma and allergic rhinitis will respond early to biologic drugs. These children carry a heavy burden, and response to omalizumab or dupilumab varies widely with no practical way to forecast it.

The retrospective study covered 246 children with moderate-to-severe disease treated between January 2021 and August 2025. Early response was judged at 16 weeks from asthma control scores, nasal symptom ratings, and flare history. Of the group, 164 children, 66.7 percent, responded early. Five starting measures predicted response: exhaled nitric oxide, blood eosinophils, total IgE, coexisting atopic dermatitis, and body mass index. The chart discriminated well, with a C-index of 0.88 in training and 0.85 in validation, and calibration matched observed results closely. The authors aim it at spotting likely super-responders.
pmc-13333385:
Zhihao Qiu and co-authors pooled observational studies in a systematic review and meta-analysis from 2026. They asked whether spine disease in psoriatic arthritis is its own entity or simply axial spondyloarthritis wearing another label. The two look alike, with inflamed backs and sacroiliac joints, and classification rules leave the psoriatic form in limbo.

Fifteen studies covering 2,704 patients with axial psoriatic arthritis and 9,248 with axial spondyloarthritis were combined. Disease activity scores, spinal function scores, and inflammation markers showed no significant differences between the groups. One sharp split stood out: the genetic marker HLA-B27 was far less common in the psoriatic group, with a risk ratio of 0.37. Against classic ankylosing spondylitis alone, the psoriatic group also scored slightly better on function. The authors argue the genetic gap supports separate diseases that converge on shared inflammatory paths, possibly through a different route into the IL-23 and IL-17 axis.
pmc-13334085:
Luca Maini, Mai Anh Tran, and Josh Feng examined how market size drives pharmaceutical innovation in a 2026 economics study. The elasticity linking bigger markets to more new drugs guides pricing reform debates, but published estimates scatter widely.

Using global drug sales data, the team reran a standard period-class Poisson model while systematically changing which drugs count as innovation and which countries count toward market size. Under their preferred choices, elasticities ran from 0.21 to 0.30 depending only on measurement, and other choices pushed estimates to 0.47 in some specifications. Counting only drugs launched in the United States or similar large markets raised estimates, while revenue definitions mattered less than expected. Their message: match the estimate to the policy question.
pmc-13335485:
Hoang Thu Trang Do and co-authors used a technique called HyperTRIBE to find the RNA targets of the binding protein IMP2 inside living mouse liver in a 2026 study. IMP2, also called IGF2BP2, regulates metabolism and promotes tumors, but older cross-linking methods for finding its targets have drawbacks.

The team delivered an IMP2-ADAR fusion into mouse livers by hydrodynamic transfection; where IMP2 binds RNA, the partner enzyme edits adenosines, leaving a readable mark. Enrichment and motif analyses suggested IMP2 stabilizes its targets and confirmed methyladenosine binding motifs. Results overlapped sensibly with a fibroblast TRIBE experiment and with gene expression differences, and pointed to a link between IMP2 and autophagy. The approach maps protein-RNA contacts in native tissue without cross-linking artifacts.
pmc-13335885:
Lu Chen and co-authors found a sugar-trimming enzyme that keeps lung adenocarcinoma cells young and growing in a 2026 cancer study. Many lung tumors lack druggable mutations, so fresh dependencies matter.

The enzyme, FUCA2, limits fucosylation of the receptor ErbB3 by the enzyme FUT3 at a specific site. That restraint preserves ErbB3's partnership with ErbB2, keeping AKT signaling persistently on. Active AKT blocks senescence in both normal and mutant TP53 backgrounds, letting malignant growth continue. A low dose of the AKT inhibitor capivasertib forced senescence selectively in FUCA2-high tumors regardless of their mutation profile. Pairing it with the senolytic procyanidin C1 suppressed tumors strongly and gently across preclinical models, sketching a combination strategy for hard-to-target lung cancers.
pmc-13336485:
Syun-Hong Chou and co-authors built a self-powered electronic skin that feeds wounds healing electricity in a 2026 study. Electrical stimulation speeds repair, but wired power supplies and indifference to the wound's own state limit older approaches.

Their patch sandwiches a gelatin outer matrix over a zwitterionic conductive inner layer. It harvests energy two ways at once: body motion yields biomechanical output measured at 33.8 volts and 3.2 microwatts, while ambient electromagnetic fields from appliances add a second stream. The generated field works alongside the body's own wound field, encouraging cell migration, proliferation, and tissue regeneration. Rat studies tested the patch on living wounds. A dressing that powers itself from movement and room electronics could run continuously without batteries or leads.
pmc-13336885:
Mingyue Cui and co-authors reveal an eye-to-brain immune route that extends survival in a brain tumor model in a 2026 study. The eye extends from the central nervous system and shares neural and immune links with the brain. Pairing electrical stimulation with vaccine delivery into the eye fluid changed both immunity and nerve activity.

In mice with glioblastoma, the approach prolonged survival, with 33.3% of mice alive at day 50 in the reported experiment. Stimulation sped antigen drainage to deep neck lymph nodes, bypassing the blood-brain barrier and raising brain-specific immune responses. It also calmed abnormal neuron connections and excitability. The route suggests fresh ways to treat both eye and brain disease.
pmc-13337085:
Haolin Ye, Bangzhi Ge, Yuan Yu, and Chongjian Zhou review halide perovskites as natural heat insulators in a 2026 article. Blocking heat flow matters for thermal management and energy conversion, and these crystals conduct heat remarkably poorly. The review traces that trait from bulk behavior down to atomic vibrations.

Their soft lattice, unusual bonding, disorder, and rattling atoms scatter vibrations intensely. Heat capacity shows a boson-like peak, sound travels slowly, and conductivity barely responds to temperature, all glass-like signs. Standard vibration models break down, so coherent vibration effects must join the picture. Understanding this phonon glass behavior could guide materials that insulate or convert heat to power.
pmc-13337285:
Meghan C. Bacher and co-authors settle what builds the surface armor of a spotted-fever bacterium in a 2026 imaging study. Many bacteria wear a crystalline protein layer, and for pathogenic Rickettsia the outer protein OmpB was the suspected builder. Cryo-electron tomography let them view the Rickettsia parkeri surface in three dimensions at fine scale.

Wild bacteria showed a neat repeating layer just outside the outer membrane. Mutants with a disabled ompB gene lacked that layer entirely, proving OmpB is required to build it. Images taken inside human cells and on isolated bacteria agreed. Confirming the armor's source opens study of how it shields the bacterium and whether blocking it weakens infection.
pmc-13337485:
Jeanne Gaspar Lopes and colleagues sought a biopsy stage marker in 2026 to predict prostate cancer recurrence. Prostate cancer ranks second in incidence worldwide, yet after first treatment most tumours stay silent while some return, and clinicians cannot yet tell which patients are at risk. The team examined the enzyme cysteine dioxygenase, CDO1, as a candidate predictor.

Tumours that later relapsed showed much lower CDO1 expression, and low expression tracked with poorer survival. Methylation and androgen signalling appeared to regulate CDO1 in prostate cancer, and blocking the enzyme altered tumour behaviour in models. If validated, CDO1 testing at biopsy could help tailor follow up and treatment for men at higher recurrence risk.
pmc-13341285:
Oleic acid-rich oils fail to improve metabolic health in already unhealthy people, a 2026 meta-analysis by Junyan Hua and colleagues concludes. The team searched four databases under PRISMA rules and pooled standardized mean differences with a random-effects model.

Fifteen studies qualified. Oleic acid intake showed no link to better total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, or triglycerides, and subgroup checks by body mass index, study length, and oleic dose changed nothing. Blood sugar control, weight measures, and blood pressure also stayed unmoved. The authors note benefits seen in healthy subjects may simply not transfer to people with metabolic disorders, a population-specific response worth respecting in dietary advice.
pmc-13341585:
How much care a patient receives may itself predict line infections, in a 2026 cohort study by Na Li and colleagues. The team built a care-exposure burden score from health records in three critical care databases, covering charting frequency, number of caregivers, extra lines, and fluid volumes around catheter placement.

Critically ill adults with central lines were followed for adjudicated bloodstream infections tied to those lines. The burden score aimed to capture process complexity that ordinary catheter variables miss. Multi-source data from American and Chinese units let the authors test whether the signal holds across very different intensive care systems.
pmc-13341885:
Following safety plans changes outcomes on powerful immune drugs, in a 2026 cohort study by Li-Fong Wang's team. The Taiwan project followed 1,078 autoimmune patients starting biologic or targeted synthetic therapies between 2014 and 2023, sorting them by whether pre-treatment safety checks were done within 6 months.

Only 348 patients (32.3%) met the full risk plan rules covering tuberculosis, hepatitis, heart, and cancer screening. Those without plans suffered far more Pneumocystis pneumonia, at 11.9% of patients versus 2.3% of those with plans, and major cardiovascular events, at 8.5% of patients versus 2.6% of those with plans. Skipping set pre-checks, the data imply, is not a harmless shortcut.
pmc-13342185:
A transcription factor's possible grip on astrocyte sugar use is examined by Ping Ye's team in a 2026 review with bioinformatics prediction. Astrocytes feed neurons through a lactate shuttle, and boosting their glycolysis might slow diseases like Alzheimer's, where energy failure appears early.

ZBTB7A regulates metabolic genes in other cell types, but its role in astrocytes was uncharted. The review gathers its biology alongside glial metabolism evidence, then predicts its binding motifs in promoters of genes for glucose uptake, glycolytic flow, and lactate production and transport. The predictions nominate experiments rather than settle the question, which the authors state plainly.
pmc-13345785:
Matti Jubouri and co-authors scope bedside ultrasound in cardiovascular emergencies across ambulances and emergency departments in 2026. Handheld scanning is now routine in both settings, yet performance comparisons stayed scattered. The review covered six crises: cardiac arrest, fluid around the heart, acute heart failure, shock, collapsed lung, and aortic tearing.

Department scanning topped 85 to 90 percent accuracy and cut time to diagnosis or action by 30 to 70 minutes for several conditions, though survival did not always follow. Field crews got usable views in 70 to 90 percent of cases and often changed destination choices. Training, image archiving, and quality checks underpinned safe use everywhere.
pmc-13347785:
Mohammad Al-Harbi and colleagues link thigh muscle and fat makeup to knee arthritis severity, in an imaging study published in 2026. A total of 232 patients had knee X-rays graded by the Kellgren-Lawrence scale plus MRI scans for soft tissue measures. Results were split by sex and weight class. The aim was to hunt changeable risk factors.

Women made up 54.7 percent of patients and obesity was the largest weight group at 44.8 percent in the reported set. Muscle depth held steady across weight classes while fat depth rose with weight, more so in women. The muscle-to-fat ratio fell as weight rose, showing only a weak negative link to soft tissue wear in early results.
pmc-13347985:
Bilal Ahmad and co-authors widened in 2026 the gene map of autosomal recessive microcephaly in Pakistani families. Small head size at birth or later shows up with learning disability and slow growth. The illness varies a lot in signs and genes. Many genes play a part. This leaves many families with no gene answer.

The pairing shows what specialist training buys and how far a general model gets on its own.
pmc-13396385:
Fatmah Altaweel and co-authors describe a skin growth in a boy aged one year who has Down syndrome, a pairing they note is exceptionally rare, in a 2026 case report. The growth is a mastocytoma, a single spot where mast cells, a type of immune cell, pile up in the skin.

Such spots usually appear in infancy as firm brownish or yellow lumps and are harmless, often fading on their own. Rubbing one can bring brief redness and swelling, a reaction called Darier's sign. Some cases carry changes in a gene called KIT. Reporting this case alerts doctors that the condition, though rare with Down syndrome, belongs on the list of possibilities.
pmc-13396685:
Kayleigh S. Scotcher and co-authors produced a three-dimensional map of a nerve web that quietly runs pelvic organs, using donated human bodies. Their 2026 study examines the superior hypogastric plexus and the hypogastric nerves, which carry sympathetic signals, yet whose layout and cell makeup were poorly charted.

Specimens from body donors and organ donors were made transparent with a clearing method and photographed with a sheet-of-light microscope. Thousands of nerve cell bodies turned up inside the hypogastric nerves themselves, more than textbook accounts suggest. Surgeons who operate near these nerves, where damage can cost bladder and sexual function, gain a finer map of what to spare.
pmc-13396885:
Marin Senila and co-authors adapted a passive sampling gadget to measure traces of two toxic metals in table salt, a tricky matrix because the salt itself overwhelms most instruments. Their 2026 method targets cadmium and lead, which food law keeps under tight limits.

The technique, diffusive gradients in thin films, lets metals drift into a binding layer over 24 hours, quietly gathering and concentrating them while the salt matrix is left behind. Build-up was steady across the day for both metals, with fit values above 0.98. The enriched sample then goes to a graphite furnace instrument for precise counting, giving food labs a cheap route to sensitive salt testing.
pmc-13397785:
Lino Merlino and colleagues asked whether chronic lung disease worsens outcomes for people already living with chronic kidney disease. Their 2026 cohort study compares kidney patients with and without chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, known as COPD, on death and dementia over up to five years. Both conditions are common, yet how COPD shapes dementia risk in kidney disease had remained unclear.

Drawing on the TriNetX network, the team matched 234,317 patients in each group for age, other illnesses, smoking, and lab values. Kidney patients with COPD died more often than those without it, at 18.5 percent versus 14.5 percent, and faced higher dementia risk as well. The pattern held in a broader respiratory definition that added asthma and bronchiectasis. The work urges closer lung, kidney, and brain care for these patients, while noting that record-based studies can miss unmeasured differences.
pmc-13398485:
Katherine Power and Qiong Zhang use a climate model to ask how Atlantic swings dried the Bronze Age Mediterranean. Their 2026 study runs the EC-Earth3 model across the Holocene, the last ten thousand years or so. Proxy records show slow drying peaking in hard droughts near 1250 BCE, just as Late Bronze Age societies collapsed between 1300 and 900 BCE in the chronology used.

The model reproduces a gradual, orbit-driven drying that hit the Levant hardest while parts of the Balkans and Anatolia grew effectively wetter as cooling cut evaporation. Extreme droughts struck when Atlantic variability at several timescales lined up over an already dry land. The work ties a famous social collapse to ocean-atmosphere mechanics, with lessons for today's water-stressed region.
pmc-13400185:
Meixi Hao and colleagues reprogrammed neutrophils without touching their genes, in a 2026 study aimed at breast cancer that has spread to the lungs. They trained the cells with interferon gamma and armed them with a chemo nanoparticle. The team's answer is a sequential conditioning recipe producing what they call meta-neutrophils with a locked-in antitumor character.

The interferon gamma training first fixes the cells in their cancer-killing, immune-stimulating phenotype so the tumor environment cannot flip them. Loading them with Abraxane, the albumin-bound paclitaxel formulation, adds direct cytotoxic punch. The loaded cells accumulated strongly in lung metastases in their models. Because the recipe needs no genetic modification and works regardless of donor, the authors present meta-neutrophils as a practical route toward clinical neutrophil therapy for metastatic triple-negative breast cancer.
pmc-13400685:
Kateryna Vanivska and a large team test, in 2026, whether fenugreek seed extract affects stallion sperm in the laboratory. Fenugreek is a widely used plant supplement with reported effects on male hormones. Breeding programs care about anything that helps or harms sperm movement and survival during handling.

Sperm samples were exposed to seven extract strengths and tracked over time with computer-assisted analysis. The extract showed no overt toxicity at any tested dose. Total movement declined with time equally in all groups, but forward movement, swimming speed and head motion improved at certain doses at the final time point. Metabolic activity rose above control at most doses early on. Viability and a key sperm protein shifted in a non-simple pattern across doses.
pmc-13400985:
Kexin Xu and colleagues test, in 2026, whether erianin, a compound from Dendrobium orchids, can ease atopic dermatitis by repairing cell power stations. Eczema of this type involves chronic skin inflammation. Faulty mitochondria, the cells energy hubs, play a part. Erianin was known for antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in other conditions.

In cell and animal models, erianin improved skin condition. It reversed oxidative stress and the dysfunction of those energy hubs. Computer modeling suggested it interacts with PINK1, a protein that starts mitophagy, the disposal of worn-out mitochondria. Treatment boosted that cleanup and lowered reactive oxygen. It also reduced cell death. The findings nominate the PINK1 and Parkin pathway as central to the benefit.
pmc-13401285:
Hilal Özbek and Sibel Dilmen published a 2026 cross-sectional study of how support from a partner during pregnancy relates to anxiety, antenatal care use, and fear of childbirth. They also asked whether pregnancy-related anxiety sits in the middle of those links.

The study enrolled 331 pregnant women who completed a personal information form plus scales for perceived partner support, pregnancy-related anxiety, and delivery expectations. The team ran logistic regression for regular antenatal care use, hierarchical regression for anxiety, and a mediation analysis using the PROCESS macro with 5,000 bootstrap samples. Financial support from a partner was among the dimensions examined in the results. The design lets readers see which kinds of support matter most for mothers' mental health and care attendance.
pmc-13401685:
Muhammad Aamir and co-authors surveyed surgical patients at a large referral hospital in Lahore, Pakistan. Their 2026 cross-sectional study covers how patients perceive surgical care and what blocks their access to it. Evidence from urban Pakistani centres is scarce, which limits locally shaped fixes.

Between January and June 2025, 607 patients aged 18 and older answered a tested questionnaire, face to face, recruited by easy sampling. Just under 62 percent were male, and most were young adults between 18 and 30. Views were mixed: about 39 percent agreed that surgery helps health, while about 42 percent chose non-surgical options where possible. The team studied responses with descriptive statistics and chi-square tests. Logistic regression then separated barriers worth targeting, from cost and fear to hospital environment, so services can be made more equitable.
pmc-13401785:
Junkai Wen and co-authors are named in a 2026 correction in Biological Procedures Online for their 2024 paper on combining the herbal formula Chang-Wei-Qing with a PD-1 inhibitor. It was tested against colitis-linked colorectal tumours in mice. The correction concerns duplicated panels inside Figure 6 of the original article.

The authors explain that two magnified immunohistochemistry sections in the control group, staining for the barrier proteins ZO-1 and occludin, were inadvertently identical. Separately, magnified images for the group receiving faecal transplant plus the herbal formula and anti-PD-1 treatment, staining for ZO-1 and claudin, were mistakenly duplicated as well. Those barrier proteins matter because the paper's claim rests on restoring the intestinal barrier. A corrected figure is supplied with the notice, and the original article has been updated.
pmc-13401885:
Xin Shao, Chen Tan, Meiqi Yu, and Fan Yang reviewed how minimally invasive clot evacuation for brain haemorrhage should be used after the latest randomized trials, in a 2026 article. Bleeding inside the brain makes up only a tenth to a sixth of strokes but causes an outsized share of death and disability.

For decades, surgery trials disappointed. The ENRICH trial then gave the first positive randomized evidence: an early, protocolized minimally invasive approach improved outcomes at 180 days, mainly in lobar haemorrhages near the surface. The 2025 MIND trial, dominated by deep haemorrhages and stopped early, found no benefit on its main endpoint. SWITCH suggested decompressive skull surgery without clot removal helps little in severe deep bleeding. The authors argue the debate has shifted from whether to operate to which patients, what timing, and which platform.
pmc-13402285:
Josephine Herz and co-authors argue that oxygen shortage injury to the newborn brain should be read as a whole-body illness linking gut, brain, and immune system. Cooling therapy remains the only proven treatment, yet many infants still fare poorly. Past work stared mainly at the brain; this review widens the frame to gut microbes and immune responses that shape injury and repair.

Gut microbes help train the brain immune cells, build myelin, and seal the blood-brain barrier, and oxygen shortage upsets both the microbe mix and the gut wall. Animal work with stool transplants hints the gut changes help drive brain harm, not just follow it. Immune shifts in affected newborns can last into school age. Candidate aids such as probiotics, human milk sugars, and butyrate have early lab support only, and the authors call for long, layered clinical studies.
pmc-13402585:
Peng Peng and colleagues weigh a practical fix for hydrogen boil-off, the fuel that evaporates from liquid hydrogen tanks at airports and launch sites. Boil-off wastes money, adds indirect greenhouse emissions, and raises safety worries as hydrogen flight grows. Their techno-economic study, tuned with lab measurements, tests sorbent materials that catch and condition escaping gas at scales from 1.5 to 70 tonnes per day.

Caught hydrogen could feed engines or fuel cells directly, an option they compare with re-liquefying or compressing the gas instead. The math favored capture when delivered liquid hydrogen costs pass 0.9 dollars per kilogram at airports. At launch sites the bar sat far higher, above 10 dollars per kilogram, and only where at least 10 percent of stored hydrogen boils away. The authors present capture and reuse as a niche that pays where losses and prices run high.
pmc-13402685:
Songtao Liu and colleagues build a combined shield for power grids against false data injection attacks, where forged sensor readings mislead the operators balancing grid frequency. Multi-area grids couple regions tightly, and older estimation methods assume straight-line behavior and fixed noise, so they track such systems poorly. State guesses also blur into the noise itself, hiding attacks inside normal static.

Their framework pairs an unscented Kalman filter, which samples smart points to follow nonlinear swings, with an adaptive covariance update that relearns noise and state spread in real time. Tests under several attack scenarios gave sharper state estimates than rival algorithms, plus more accurate attack detection and stronger countermeasures once an attack was flagged. The authors pitch the joint design as a better fit for coupled grids than bolt-on detectors.
pmc-13402785:
Tang and co-authors build, in 2026, an exceptionally strong and tough polymer gel by engineering its network at three scales at once. They combine directional annealing with solvent exchange into a deep eutectic solvent. Gels normally force a trade-off among strength, stiffness, and toughness. Their polyvinyl alcohol eutectogel aligned polymer chains, packed crystalline domains, and strengthened hydrogen bonding simultaneously.

The numbers are dramatic against the starting hydrogel: tensile strength of 62.2 megapascals, stiffness of 355.3 megapascals, and toughness of 179.0 megajoules per cubic meter represent gains of 311-fold, 11843-fold, and 597-fold over the original gel in the team's measurements. Fracture resistance reached 131.5 kilojoules per square meter, the fatigue threshold 15.9 kilojoules per square meter, and impact damping efficiency 95.8 percent in their tests. The gel also kept 94.9 percent of its strength after seven days at room temperature. The authors propose the multi-scale strategy for wearables, flexible electronics, and impact protection.
pmc-13403385:
Ana Sofia V. Carvalho and team studied how cancer care speed metrics can be put to use worldwide. Their 2026 qualitative work backs All.Can, a multi-stakeholder group that proposed eight metrics on speed, teamwork, and patient-centeredness. Gauging speed is hard across varied health systems, so a hands-on guide was needed.

Forty informants from 21 countries spoke of blocks and aids in semi-structured interviews, read through the Implementation in Context frame. Rules most shaped speed metrics, while patchy or missing rules slowed uptake. End-user review shaped an Action Guide, launched in September 2024, rooted in health systems research. The work gives implementers a context-aware start point, not a one-size-fits-all scorecard.
pmc-13403885:
Navpreet Kaur and colleagues tracked chronic obstructive pulmonary disease hospitalizations in Greater Glasgow and Clyde, Scotland, from 2015 to 2022. Their 2026 retrospective cohort study uses hospital and death records covering a population of 1.2 million, with attention to socio-economic inequality and pandemic effects. COPD flare-ups signal declining health and higher death risk, yet recent trends by deprivation had been unclear.

Among 8,852 first COPD hospitalizations, mean age 70, admission rates fell 13 to 48 percent from 2017 onward, and repeat admissions also declined. Mortality after first admission, however, rose after 2020, with a hazard ratio of 1.42 in 2022 versus 2015. The most deprived residents faced higher admission and death rates throughout. The paper urges targeted, community-based care to close persistent gaps.
pmc-13404385:
Salio and colleagues issued a 2026 call for papers on preparing a health workforce that is ready for emergencies, writing as officials concerned with global health security. Recent crises showed that health systems lack enough trained staff and fast ways to mobilize them. The World Health Organization pandemic agreement now commits countries to build surge capacity and protect their health workers, and this editorial invites research that shows how.

Salio identifies four weak points that submitted work should address. They are fragmented leadership across agencies during responses, surge systems that are hard to activate, chronic understaffing and burnout worsened by rigid rules, and poor coordination across borders. Drawing on the WHO global health emergency corps framework, the authors argue that national public health agencies should anchor connected leadership and cross-trained teams. The call aims to gather practical models countries can copy before the next emergency hits.
pmc-13407585:
Mackenzie A. Simper builds, in 2026, a mathematical model of genome rearrangement using structures called double cosets. Genomes get shuffled over evolution by inversions, swaps, and moves of gene blocks. Permutation groups already model such shuffling. Double cosets extend the idea to circular genomes. Those carry repeated genes of several types.

Simper pins down how such genomes match a double coset space built from symmetry groups. Formulas follow for the sizes of single double cosets. Their counts in special cases are also derived. Those sizes yield the probability distribution expected when genomes are sampled uniformly. On that foundation the paper defines Markov chains, step-by-step random processes, capturing inversion, transposition, and translocation events for future evolutionary analysis.
pmc-13408485:
Cheng Liang, Zhi Liu, and colleagues identify in 2026 a subset of human dental papilla cells that rebuilds tooth dentin and pulp far better than the usual stem cell preparations. Regenerating the living core of a tooth has been held back by mixed cell populations whose best members were unknown. The winning subset carries the surface marker CD24.

A signalling chain explains the edge: strong BMP signalling keeps a protein called SIRT1 active, supporting mitochondrial energy production and tooth-forming capacity, and also raises a growth factor that recruits blood vessels. The marker itself does not drive the effect, which keeps the finding honest for dental engineers selecting seed cells.
pmc-13408885:
Julia Hesse and colleagues grow tiny balls of vascular smooth muscle cells in 2026 to model how blood vessel walls remodel, then read their full protein content. Flat dish cultures cannot reproduce how these cells sit inside the matrix they secrete, and that matrix decides how diseases like atherosclerosis and aneurysm progress. The same protocol also produced endothelial cell spheroids, opening the door to layered vessel models. Researchers studying vascular plasticity gain a three-dimensional system whose molecular behaviour is now charted rather than assumed.
pmc-13409085:
John Soong and co-authors describe a 2026 pilot study testing whether a dedicated acute medical unit beats an ordinary ward for unplanned medical admissions in Singapore. Such units have spread internationally on promises of smoother flow and shorter stays, yet prospective proof of clinical and economic benefit is thin, especially in Asia. Participants are followed for six months, with total acute-care bed days as the primary measure, counting both the first stay and any emergency returns. Secondary measures span readmission, mortality, and a shelf of patient-reported tools covering quality of life, wellbeing, activation, mood, and daily function. Recruitment ran from late 2024 through 2025. The pilot is designed to size up a definitive trial.
pmc-13410585:
Luise Trenkmann and colleagues compare in 2026 the formulas doctors use to estimate kidney function in healthy young people. The estimate, drawn from blood tests and body measures, guides dosing and screening. Many formulas exist, and they can disagree, especially across childhood ages.

Blood and body data from 4,776 healthy participants aged from infancy to 21 years fed the comparison. Eleven formulas were scored by how often their results landed in the expected healthy range. Four formulas, including the Schwartz and European consortium versions, stayed steady across ages without odd jumps. Others drifted far apart from the pack. Boys tended to score higher than girls under most formulas.
pmc-13411185:
Amir Ghanbari and colleagues counted American cyclist hospital stays by town size from 2016 to 2020 in a 2026 national study. Using a large hospital sample, the team tallied about 124000 stays costing over 10 billion dollars, with nearly a third ending in transfer, rehab, or death rather than a routine trip home.

Stays held steady through 2019, then jumped more than 20 percent in 2020, and older age plus car involvement most raised the odds of a non-routine discharge in both town and country. The paper gives road safety planners a clear picture of who bears the worst crash outcomes and where help is needed.
pmc-13411285:
Talebi and colleagues review what gene switches called microRNAs do after spinal cord injury, and whether medicine can use them. The review is frank about the gap to clinic: delivery to the cord, off target effects, and tangled networks still block human use.
pmc-13411585:

Gallstones, polyps, and adenomyosis are common and costly, yet hospital patients differ from people found by screening, so the team compared age, sex, and risk patterns across the three conditions.

Gallstone patients averaged about 50 years old with more women than men, polyp patients were younger with a near-even sex split, and adenomyosis patients sat between them. The paper gives digestive teams a large hospital-based baseline for spotting which patients carry higher inflammation risk.
pmc-13411885:

pmc-13412485:

This yeast causes oral thrush and invades tissue by switching into thread-like hyphal growth and secreting fat-cutting enzymes. pmc-13414585:

Testing found 297 Borrelia bavariensis, 86 Borrelia afzelii, and 81 Borrelia garinii, plus 44 Borrelia miyamotoi and 33 strains that fit the relapsing fever group but had no name yet. Lyme group species clung to Ixodes ticks, with each kind favoring its own tick host. Gene typing showed wide strain variety in the Lyme group, while miyamotoi stayed much the same. The map sharpens regional risk knowledge.
pmc-13415485:
Sarah Stewart and co-authors interview twenty-five people with gout about staying active through a disease of sudden painful flares, in a 2026 talk based study. Chats covered flares, day to day moves, work, and home roles. The team read the typed chats with care and built shared themes from them.

Four themes emerged. Wrong public views of gout shape how much people move. Lost strength means lost free choice. Moves help people win back body and self. Doubt clouds safe sport, since no one knew if strain could spark a flare or harm joints. People feared being judged, paced themselves, and found clear gout based guides for safe moves hard to find.
pmc-13415885:
Agustina Creus and colleagues review how cells keep their mitochondria healthy, in a 2026 survey of quality control systems. Mitochondria do far more than make energy: they buffer calcium, steer metabolism, and help trigger cell death. Control systems fold and clear proteins, build new mitochondria, fuse and split the network, and remove damaged units by mitophagy.

DNA upkeep, inner membrane architecture, and a permeability switch add further layers. Faults in these systems track with aging, cancer, metabolic and heart disease, brain degeneration, and autoimmunity. The review closes with therapies that tune quality control to lighten disease burden.
pmc-13415985:
Bin Zheng and co-authors test a ginger compound against heart damage from the leukemia drug arsenic trioxide, in 2026. The compound, 10-gingerol, was studied through computer network analysis plus mouse and cell experiments. Network methods found thirty-two shared targets among the compound, the drug, and heart injury, with one signaling route standing out.

Mice given the ginger compound kept better heart pumping scores and lower injury markers in blood. Oxidative stress, inflammation messages, and heart cell death all eased. The protective pathway, PI3K and AKT, switched on more strongly. A blocker of that pathway partly undid protection in cells, supporting the mechanism.
pmc-13416185:

pmc-13416385:

pmc-13417285:
Ende He and colleagues build a dual prodrug that aims cancer therapy at tumours, in a 2026 study. Toxicity fell as well, supporting the targeted design.
pmc-13417485:
Samuel Pérez Pérez and co-authors detail liver injury linked to the herbal supplement ashwagandha in a 2026 case report. A healthy woman of 27 developed jaundice and widespread itching after three days of taking the supplement, widely sold for calm and resilience. Other infection, immune, and metabolic causes were ruled out.

Scans showed no structural problem, while a liver biopsy showed a classic bile flow pattern without scarring. A formal causality score rated the link probable. Treatment with steroids and a second immune drug brought steady recovery. The case argues for structured causality checks when supplements may harm the liver.
pmc-13418485:

Over 2,000 bacterial genomes were mined for variants in that protease and in the injected cancer protein CagA.

Human relatives of the protease also mattered: three ran high in stomach tumours and tracked with matrix damage, inflammation, and spread signals. pmc-13418585:

pmc-13419185:

Themes covered risk, future focus, quality versus length of life, function versus looks, new treatments, and delegating decisions. Preferences varied widely, but patterns stood out. Patterns can start a preference talk, but never replace asking the person.
pmc-13419485:

Machine learning then distilled the set into a signature meant to sort patients by outlook and likely treatment response. Tumor makeup and cell chatter both shaped outcomes in the analysis. A score grounded in growth speed could help doctors match treatment force to the tumor in front of them.
pmc-13420385:

pmc-13420685:
Ludovico Messineo and colleagues pool studies asking whether pressure-support versions of sleep apnea therapy help patients stick with treatment better than standard CPAP. Daytime sleepiness and leftover apnea counts also failed to improve, though mask leak did fall. The authors argue the added cost and development effort lack support from outcomes. pmc-13421185:

pmc-13421285:
Anna-Maria Spektor and colleagues compared two PET tracers head to head in 2026 for cancer of unknown primary outside the neck, studying 13 patients who received both scans. Across 21 metastases, neither tracer found more primary tumors, and uptake differences varied by site without a clear overall winner. Oncologists gain a caution that FAPI's edge in head-and-neck-like disease does not automatically extend to extra-cervical unknown-primary cases outside the neck.
pmc-13421385:
Muhammad Arif and six colleagues build, in a 2026 paper, a supercapacitor electrode from barium titanate nanoparticles threaded through a carbon nanotube network. The authors propose the material for durable, high-power storage.
pmc-13421485:
Yu and colleagues reviewed in 2026 methods for growing tiny blood vessels by bioprinting, meaning printing living tissue layer by layer. Engineered tissues fail without microvasculature, the fine vessel network that delivers blood inside them. The review surveys printing approaches for vessel structures and weighs what each does well and poorly.

pmc-13422585:

pmc-13423085:

pmc-13423485:

pmc-13425585:

pmc-13425785:

pmc-13426085:

pmc-13426985:

pmc-13427185:

pmc-13427585:

pmc-13430085:

Cues may name the coming movement and the mapping ahead of time, with the cue right three times in four. Pupil size and gaze tracking read out effort and prediction.

pmc-13430185:

pmc-13430485:
Evie Z Bouma and colleagues reviewed past research in 2026 on how people with Parkinson's disease keep a say in plans for their future care. Such planning covers choices about treatment and support near the end of life. The reviewers note that talks often start late, which can shrink a person's say as thinking skills fade.

Patients asked for more backing for their own choices, and guided talks were welcome. The reviewers suggest that story-based care may help doctors open these talks sooner.
pmc-13430785:

The study names a Peripheral Instability Gradient: agreement between machines worsens steadily from the central pit outward. Eye clinics get a warning to keep patients on one machine where possible, and to read outer-zone shifts with extra care.
pmc-13431385:

pmc-13432985:

pmc-13433285:

pmc-13433785:

pmc-13434185:

pmc-13434385:

pmc-13435485:

pmc-13435985:

pmc-13436085:

pmc-13436185:

pmc-13437085:

pmc-13437185:

pmc-13438385:

pmc-13439085:

pmc-13439185:

pmc-13439885:

pmc-13440985:

pmc-13441285:
Chao and colleagues present a 2026 visual case of a 63-year-old woman. Her artificial knee joint became infected, and the surgical wound stayed chronically open. pmc-13442885:

pmc-13442985:

pmc-13443185:

pmc-13443285:

pmc-13443885:

pmc-13444085:

pmc-13444185:

pmc-13445685:

pmc-13445885:

pmc-13446185:

pmc-13446485:

pmc-13446585:

pmc-13446885:
