Days when support was actually received showed a sharper sting for bad feelings only, and the effect did not spill to the next day. People with more body limits reacted more strongly, while age itself showed no link. The authors read received help as a mixed, brief signal.
pmc-13447185:
Dong Hoon Lee weighs a two-minute step test for heart failure in a 2026 commentary. Poor exercise tolerance predicts hospital stays and death, yet the gold standard lab test needs costly equipment. The common six-minute walk needs a long clear corridor that many clinics and home services lack, which makes a small-space option attractive.

A study covered here tested sixty stable patients with a weak heart pump on the step test, the walk test and leg strength checks. Ninety-four steps marked low capacity with good accuracy and high sensitivity against the walk result. People above the mark walked notably farther and felt less leg tiredness afterwards. Lee urges caution, since the group was small, fairly young and mildly ill, leaving older and sicker patients untested.
pmc-13447285:
Zhe Li leads a team reviewing plant thorns as products of evolution under pressure in 2026. Sharp plant structures deter hungry animals and cope with harsh conditions, yet they also hinder farming of useful crops. Similar-looking points arise from different plant organs, raising questions about origins, shared controls and trade-offs between growth and defence.

Fossil evidence places thorn spread alongside the rise of large grazing mammals in recent geological eras. Development studies show thorn growth weaves together organ identity programmes, defence signals and hormone pathways, including two named hormones that also govern growth. Breeding thornless varieties needs that control map, the authors argue. Their synthesis joins anatomy, ecology and genetics into one account of how a defence innovation evolved repeatedly.
pmc-13447485:
Viet Nam Huynh and colleagues measure match running in Vietnamese professional football across a full season in 2026 GPS work. Top-level football demands repeated high-speed efforts, and local players had never been profiled against league level, position and European benchmarks in one dataset. A combined score was also built to grade overall running performance.

Fifty-seven matches from six clubs in the top two divisions yielded close to five hundred player-match records from one hundred sixty outfield players. Top-division players beat second-division peers on high-speed running, sprint distance, top speed and sharp speed changes, while total distance matched. Forwards produced the strongest high-intensity outputs, while defenders covered the most ground overall. Most records graded as average, with elite grades rare, and high-speed outputs trailed elite European levels.
pmc-13448085:
Dae Hee Kim and coauthors weigh a 2026 study of bending errors in children with on-off outward squint against the general Korean public. Drawing on 2,744 clinic patients aged 5 to 18 and 1,224 national survey people, the team weighed round values, uneven sight, and eye-turn angles.

Bending spread largely matched the general public, and the non-main eye did not exceed general myopia levels. Yet uneven sight ran higher by a wide margin in outward squint patients, most of all after age 9, while bending readings barely tracked turn angle. Screening should watch unequal bending in outward squint, not myopia alone.
pmc-13448385:
Echeverria-Ortegon and colleagues pooled published evidence on whether tumor DNA found in spinal fluid predicts outcomes for lung cancer patients with spread to the central nervous system. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis focused on non-small cell lung cancer. In that cancer, brain sampling is risky, and liquid biopsy, meaning gene testing on body fluids, offers a safer window on the disease.

Echeverria-Ortegon found three studies covering roughly 700 patients that reported survival by spinal fluid tumor DNA status. Patients with detectable tumor DNA in spinal fluid faced more than double the combined risk of death or disease progression compared with patients whose tests were negative. The pattern held across all three studies despite moderate differences between them. The authors present spinal fluid tumor DNA as a promising risk marker while calling for larger prospective studies to confirm its clinical use.
pmc-13448485:
James J Prisciandaro and coauthors report a 2026 swap trial testing N-acetylcysteine and gabapentin as glutamate and GABA tuners for paired bipolar and alcohol use ills. Fifty-four patients cycled through one-week rounds of each drug and placebo, with brain scans gauging cingulate glutamate and GABA plus drinking and mood results.

Only N-acetylcysteine lowered cingulate glutamate versus placebo and cut heavy drinking days, while gabapentin changed neither brain measure nor drinking. Neither drug lifted low-mood symptoms by a wide margin. The results support mechanism trials aimed at glutamate fault in this hard-to-treat dual illness.
pmc-13448785:
Yuchan Li, Meichao Yi, and Bing Liu pool in 2026 the trial evidence on combining overnight corneal lenses with atropine drops to slow childhood nearsightedness. Their meta-analysis gathered 18 randomized trials covering 1,669 children. The comparison was orthokeratology lenses alone against the same lenses plus atropine, a drug that relaxes the eye's focusing muscle.

Across trials, the combined treatment slowed eye elongation more, with a standardized difference of −0.66, and reshaped the cornea more strongly. It gave no clear advantage in unaided vision or in the thickness of the tear film's oily layer. Children on the combination also had wider pupils and weaker focusing power, known effects of atropine that parents and clinicians must weigh against the slower growth of the eye.
pmc-13449085:
Gregor Maier and co-authors compare in 2026 two modern diabetes drug classes head-to-head on serious liver outcomes in people who have both type 2 diabetes and fatty liver disease. German claims data from 2005 to 2024 yielded 45,256 such patients starting either a GLP-1 receptor agonist or an SGLT-2 inhibitor. Statistical weighting balanced the groups, and patients were followed a median of 4.3 years for major adverse liver outcomes.

Those starting GLP-1 drugs had a somewhat lower hazard of the combined liver outcome, with a hazard ratio of 0.91, and the gap widened in on-treatment analyses. Lower hazards also appeared for cirrhosis, at 0.88, and liver cancer, at 0.76, while all-cause mortality did not differ, at 1.04. Confidence intervals still crossed no-effect for the main outcome, so the authors frame the liver advantage as possible rather than proven.
pmc-13449285:
Mengqi Liu and Lei Feng survey in 2026 art students in China to test whether outdoor landscape sketching does more for them than sharpen technique. Their model extends the stimulus-organism-response framework with two perceived outcomes, emotional healing and personal growth, and places artistic creation in the middle as the mechanism. The sample held 350 art and design undergraduates from three institutions who had taken outdoor sketching courses.

Feelings from natural surroundings fed both creation, with a path coefficient of 0.351, and healing directly, at 0.197. Cultural surroundings fed creation still more strongly, at 0.495, but reached healing only through the act of making art. Creation itself linked to healing at 0.692, and healing to personal growth at 0.879. The authors recommend building such sketching courses deliberately into higher art education for their psychological payoff.
pmc-13449385:
Xiang-yang He and co-authors test in 2026 a simple blood-based index, TyHGB, as a predictor of cardiovascular disease in older adults. The index blends triglycerides relative to protective cholesterol with fasting glucose and body mass. Their data come from a large community cohort in Shenzhen, China, covering 26,603 elderly participants, of whom 1,968, or 7.40 percent, suffered cardiovascular events during follow-up.

Each standard-deviation rise in the index carried a hazard ratio of 1.12 for cardiovascular disease overall, 1.09 for stroke, and 1.30 for heart attack, after adjustment. People in the highest quarter of the index faced still larger risks, up to 1.72 for heart attack against the lowest quarter. Flexible curve models showed the relationship was a straight climb rather than a threshold effect. Since every ingredient comes from routine laboratory work, the authors propose the index for cheap risk sorting in clinics.
pmc-13449585:
Francesca Rodriguez and colleagues set out a 2026 protocol for bringing brief behavioral therapy to low-resource primary care for anxious and depressed youth. Anxiety and mood disorders in young people are common and impairing, and untreated cases risk lasting harm and suicide. Youth of color and families facing social risk are least likely to receive care.

The protocol tests STEP-UP, a primary-care therapy expanded for digital delivery and Spanish-language use, in 220 youths aged eight to sixteen. Participants will be assigned at random to STEP-UP or to assisted referral to usual care. Effectiveness and implementation outcomes will both be tracked. Clinics serving low-resource families gain a tested route to care that fits their setting.
pmc-13449685:
Xinyuan Hu and colleagues profiled sugar tags on blood proteins across teen depression subtypes in 2026, seeking biological clues to a varied condition. Protein N-glycosylation, the attachment of sugar chains after a protein is made, affects immune signaling and brain communication. It had not been mapped across depression subtypes in young people.

Serum from teens with major depression, depression with non-suicidal self-injury, depression with suicide attempts, and healthy controls was analyzed by mass spectrometry with pooled samples. All depression groups shared some changes, including fewer bi-antennary glycans and Lewis structures and higher levels of other forms. The exploratory design cannot support firm statistical claims, but it points to pathways worth testing in larger, individual-level studies.
pmc-13450485:
Jana Khawandi and colleagues reviewed blood and urine markers for polycystic kidney disease in 2026, seeking better ways to predict who worsens fastest. Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease is the leading single-gene cause of kidney failure, yet its course varies widely. Reliable markers could guide trial selection and day-to-day care.

The team searched three databases through April 2025 for longitudinal studies with at least ten patients and a year of follow-up, assessing bias and grading evidence. Fifty-eight studies were included, covering thirty-three urine markers and twenty-nine blood markers. Urine osmolality, copeptin, proteinuria, MCP-1, and uric acid were most studied, against kidney function and kidney volume outcomes. Clinicians gain a ranked map of which markers have real prognostic support.
pmc-13451285:
Jiaojiao Han and others mapped gut vessel swelling in lupus in 2026, a rare but deadly gut twist of the disease. The ill state inflames gut blood tubes, gives gut pains that can kill if missed, and is easy to miss as cases pass from ward to ward. The team read files for 174 cases seen in Zhengzhou from 2015 to 2023.

Cases were split by first ward, rheumatology or other wards, and by how many gut signs they had and how long they lasted. Blood tests, disease scores, and scans were checked for links to how bad the case was. The work aims to keep doctors alert for gut vessel swelling when lupus patients show gut pains. A fast catch could save lives and cut deaths from this rare twist.
pmc-13452185:
Yufan Tong and Min Wang hunt in 2026 for natural antioxidants in wampee fruit using learning models and physics checks. They built a bank of 474 compounds from the fruit and ran a stack of tools: group learning models, docking, shape grouping, motion runs, and quantum math. Model scores ran high across eight antioxidant tests.

Screening left 47 candidates, and 30 varied ones went to motion runs. One compound bound a cell guard switch firmly across a long run, with a quantum gap a quarter below that of vitamin C. Its close twin, on hand in labs, showed dose-tied antioxidant power in bench tests. The work backs fruit-based finds for food use.
pmc-13452285:
Xiaoting Zhang, Shuai Tang, and Haoliang Lu argue in 2026 that party balloons are a missed source of tiny plastic risk. Balloons are made to be brief, then burst or drift off, and their latex, film, or foil skins can shatter into micro and nano bits. One burst can shed from tens to thousands of such bits in minutes.

That pulse pattern sets balloons apart from goods that leak slowly, and it can seed hot spots where crowds gather, such as schools and squares. Skin touch, breath, and swallowing give the bits near routes into people. The authors call for balloon waste to join the counted sources in plastic risk work.
pmc-13452785:
Yusuff Adebayo Adebisi and eighteen co-authors pool published studies on vaping and blood sugar problems, covering diabetes, prediabetes, and insulin resistance. Their 2026 review searched three databases through December 2025 and kept ten studies with more than 2.8 million people in all. Users were split into current vapers, dual users who also smoke, and former vapers, each compared with never users.

For prediabetes, odds ran higher in every user group, with current vapers at 1.34 times the odds of never users. For diabetes itself, only dual users showed a clear rise, while current and former vapers did not differ from never users. One long term study found no link at all between vaping alone and new diabetes. The authors warn that most data are one time snapshots, which cannot prove vaping caused the sugar problems.
pmc-13453285:
Tagurum and a large team explore why rural residents rarely join cancer clinical trials in this 2026 qualitative study. Trials drive progress in cancer care, yet rural enrollment stays low because of distance, workforce shortages, and mistrust. Through a Florida cancer institute's Research Navigator program, the team ran five focus groups with 30 rural participants, including survivors, caregivers, advocates, and patients in treatment.

Most participants had heard of clinical trials, but discussions exposed misconceptions about their purpose, process, and accessibility. The commonest barriers were unreliable transportation and financial worries. Mistrust of doctors and the healthcare system ran close behind. Four themes organized the findings, from lived experience and how trial information spreads to enrollment obstacles and possible fixes. The authors recommend navigator-led outreach and patient-centered technology so trials feel like routine care.
pmc-13453585:
Evangelia Maria Tsapakis and eight co-authors ask whether a stress hormone like protein in blood tracks the diagnosis of psychiatric inpatients or their body wide strain. The protein, GDF-15, rises with swelling and kidney stress. Their 2026 study drew blood within 12 hours of emergency admission from 190 inpatients, 126 with schizophrenia spectrum disorders and 64 with mood disorders.

Diagnosis itself did not predict GDF-15 levels once other factors were weighed. Older age, higher urea, and two swelling markers, IL-6 and suPAR, each tracked higher GDF-15, and together they explained 40.2 percent of its spread. Checks that added smoking, heart disease, and thyroid problems changed nothing. The authors present GDF-15 as a marker of total body burden in acute mental illness, not a fingerprint of any one diagnosis.
pmc-13453685:
Zuodong Yang and six co-authors build a blood test panel from four tiny RNA snippets to catch prostate cancer that the standard PSA test misses or overcalls. PSA testing gives many false alarms and false all clears. Their 2026 study ran in three phases: picking candidates from databases, training on 28 patients and 28 controls, then validating on 84 of each.

Five snippets separated patients from controls well in the validation round. The team settled on four of them, weighing accuracy against test cost. That panel scored an area under the curve of 0.825, catching 83.33 percent of cancers at a set threshold. Gene analysis pointed to one shared target gene, NFASC, tied to cancer pathways. The authors offer the panel as a cheap, needle free aid beside PSA.
pmc-13453785:
Ang Li and four co-authors tune the prompts given to a large language model so its mental health texts persuade readers to trust professionals. Low trust in such professionals feeds the treatment gap for depression. Their 2026 pilot first had 168 people rate pairs of texts to find which features persuade, then ran a small randomized test with 40 readers.

Three features made texts feel more credible and more persuasive: source credibility, argument quality, and smooth readability. Warmth and empathy, by contrast, were dropped for failing to move readers. Readers of the tuned texts improved their trust in professionals clearly more than readers of plain texts. The authors offer the feature set as an early recipe for AI written health education at scale, pending larger trials.
pmc-13453885: Kaneda writes to question a study that reported lower Mini-Mental State Examination scores in stable COPD patients without low oxygen. He notes the groups were badly lopsided on education. The COPD group held 27 illiterate patients versus 12 among controls, and only 1 highly educated patient versus 17. The groups also differed clearly in age, yet no correction was made. Since the test is strongly swayed by schooling, he argues the roughly 3-point gap may be too big. He asks the authors to clarify the separate contribution of lung disease.
pmc-13454685:
Morales-Alonso and colleagues compare the journeys of two related sedge lineages across South America's Southern Cone. Their 2026 paper studies the Carex phalaroides group and Carex section Bracteosellae. These independent lineages share strikingly similar ranges centred on the eastern coast. Both have offshoots in central Chile and the Andes. Herbaceous plants of this region are rarely studied this way.

Using DNA sequencing across many genes, the team dated divergences, rebuilt ancestral ranges, and modelled climatic preferences. The phalaroides group showed a clearer vicariant pattern, its earliest splits falling on opposite sides of the Arid Diagonal that bisects the continent. Both groups diversified in step, moving between the Pampa-Atlantic region, colonising the northern Andes, and differentiating in the Yungas forests. Only the phalaroides group showed a clean east-west split in climate preferences, including one species' shift in temperature tolerance.
pmc-13455085:
Taylor Kissel, Miranda Murray, Josh DeClercq, and Autumn Zuckerman track, in a 2026 study, how smoothly bowel disease patients move from clinic infusions to self-injected versions of two biologic drugs. Under-the-skin forms of vedolizumab and infliximab were newly approved in the United States. One center reviewed referrals from September 2023 to December 2024.

Of 248 patients analyzed, about 72 percent won approval, over half of those through prior authorization fights. The median wait for access was 11 days, though the full range stretched past a year. One in five approved patients never started, most often by their own choice. Commercial pharmacy coverage tripled the odds of a long wait. The authors note that payer hurdles and patient hesitation together leave over a quarter of referred patients without the new format.
pmc-13455185:
Hirakawa and team asked how much early out-of-bed activity protects heart surgery patients stuck in intensive care for three days or more from losing independence by discharge. Their retrospective cohort covered 610 such patients, with mobilization dose tallied in 20-minute units of standing-level activity per day.

After matching 196 low-dose patients against 196 high-dose patients on baseline characteristics, functional decline struck 31.6 percent of the low-dose group versus 19.9 percent of the high-dose group at discharge. That gap translated to an odds ratio of 2.03 for decline with low mobilization in the matched analysis. Adverse events during mobilization were rare at 1.2 percent overall and did not differ significantly between dose groups in the safety comparison. Spline modeling showed a nonlinear dose-response curve, supporting a threshold message: reach an adequate daily dose and function is preserved without added risk.
pmc-13455385:
Yifang Lin and colleagues sort brain-wave markers for arm recovery after stroke in a 2026 systematic review. Arm weakness often lasts after stroke, and brain-wave recording offers a cheap window on recovery, yet scattered studies made it hard to know which signals matter for what. The team searched five databases to March 2026 and kept 42 studies of adults linking quantitative EEG measures with arm motor outcomes, sorting markers by role.

For assessment, a brain symmetry index, beta-band links between hemispheres and network efficiency tracked how severe impairment was. At baseline, asymmetry and connectivity hinted at future recovery, while shifts in wave power, connectivity and network shape over time paralleled gains. The symmetry index recurred most often, but mostly fair study quality limits clinic use until standard methods and large trials validate these markers.
pmc-13455685:
Yunpeng Xu, Qiaolan Liu, and Jian Liang survey, in a 2026 study, how the shape of risk communication moves people to protect not just themselves but the group during health crises. Past work explains private precautions well, yet cooperation-minded acts that also serve the public are less mapped. The team surveyed 1,417 residents across eleven Chinese provinces.

Felt risk sat in the middle, passing much of the influence from message to action. Trust in official sources played a double game: high trust actually dampened the path from official sources to felt risk, a filtering effect the authors call high-trust attenuation. Their framework extends a classic warning-response model for officials planning crisis communication.
pmc-13456485:
Qi Ding and colleagues investigated whether ionomycin, a compound that carries calcium into cells, can make breast cancer cells die more readily under radiation. Radiation works partly by creating reactive oxygen species, damaging molecules that push cells toward death, yet many tumors resist it. Their 2026 study treated two breast cancer cell lines, including a triple-negative type that lacks the usual drug targets, with ionomycin, radiation, or both together.

The combined treatment worked best on every measure the team checked. Cell survival dropped to about 42.5 percent of untreated levels in one line and 36.9 percent of untreated levels in the other after pairing the drug with radiation. The drug opened a pore in the mitochondria, the cell's power stations, releasing a flood of reactive molecules.
pmc-13458285:
Yu and colleagues investigate why the anesthetic sevoflurane can dull thinking after surgery in this 2026 study of aged rats and neurons. Sevoflurane raised PRKCD levels in neurons, and blocking the enzyme restored cell survival, mitochondrial voltage, and breathing capacity while lowering damaging reactive oxygen output. In aged rats, silencing PRKCD after sevoflurane exposure improved performance in maze, object-recognition, and fear-conditioning tests and reduced tissue damage. Extra PINK1/PRKN pathway activity partly undid this protection, placing the pathway downstream of PRKCD.
pmc-13458485:
Chuan Song and colleagues pool the research on whether exercise can pry attention away from the negative. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis searched eight databases and pooled 32 studies across anxious, depressed, stressed, addicted, obese, and healthy people.

Training reduced negative bias in people with anxiety, depression, and high stress, easing symptoms along the way. It dulled the pull of addiction-related cues and cut craving, and it built positive bias in healthy adults. Two exceptions stood out: no reliable benefit showed in overweight or obese groups, and intensity flipped the effect. Moderate exercise performed best, while a single hard workout worsened negative bias. Cue type mattered too, emotional images beating words. The authors advise moderate programs as a mental-health tool and warn against thinking harder is better.
pmc-13458685:
Guibing Ren and colleagues turn the tumor's immune districts into a forecast for stage III lung cancer. The pattern was coherent: more mature, denser, larger, stroma-placed ones meant longer progression-free survival, and patients reaching a major pathological response harbored clusters alongside heavier lymphocyte presence. The team fused the features into a merged score; a good score of four predicted better survival with an area under the curve of 0.82. pmc-13458785:
Lina Sahnoon and colleagues show how two immune signals jointly scar asthma airways, and how dupilumab blocks them, in a 2026 study. pmc-13459285:
Samuel Reynolds and co-authors present MouseRS-CMD, a software tool that counts immune cell types in mouse blood using DNA methylation patterns instead of physical cell sorting. Methylation marks differ by cell type, so a reference library can deconvolve a mixed sample mathematically. In their 2026 paper, the team purified six immune cell types, from neutrophils to B and T cells. They measured methylation at over 285,000 sites and used an algorithm to pick the 300 most informative sites, validating the tool against flow cytometry in real blood samples.

The 300 site library estimated cell proportions with errors under 2.7 points for four cell types and under 3.5 points for all six. Because the method works on stored DNA, it enables immune profiling in archival samples collected long before anyone planned the analysis. It also lets researchers correct studies for shifts in cell mixture that would otherwise masquerade as gene effects.
pmc-13459385:
Fateme Behmaneshpour and colleagues build a model for training public-minded nurses from faculty and student views in a 2026 talk-based study. Colleges are asked to meet local health needs, yet public duty rarely grows on its own during training. Fifteen nursing faculty members and students were interviewed until no new views came up, with collection and content analysis of transcripts at once.

Five barrier groups emerged, spanning workplace factors, weak positive feedback, course limits and built-in support gaps. Seven helper groups covered school and legal support, faculty and student help, hands-on learning networks, course blending, own and local pulls and outside teamwork. Boosting helpers while easing barriers offers policy chiefs a roadmap for public-minded nursing courses.
pmc-13460185:
Mitsue Kawahara and a multicenter Japanese team charted in 2026 when lung adenocarcinoma returns after complete surgery in patients whose tumors carry an EGFR mutation. Their cohort held 787 patients operated on at four institutions between 2010 and 2020, before preventive EGFR drugs became standard; 295 tumors carried the mutation. Competing-risk methods tracked recurrence timing across a median follow-up of about five years.

pmc-13461285:
Hak-Loh Lee, Seong-Min Choi, Soo Hyun Cho, and Byeong C. Kim separated in 2026 the cognitive fingerprints of depression and anxiety in 149 patients with early to mid-stage Parkinson disease. Depression's link with weaker verbal recognition memory faded under the same correction. Patients carrying both conditions fared worst of all, with broad deficits across visual memory and frontal executive skills. The additive pattern argues for screening and treating mood early to protect thinking.
pmc-13461385:
Xianzhe Zhang and colleagues tracked metabolic health in psoriasis patients treated for 48 weeks with IL-17 blocker drugs. The patients had moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis plus metabolic conditions, a pairing whose drug effects on metabolism were poorly mapped.

The single-centre series covered 30 patients treated between June 2023 and December 2024, with checks every 12 weeks. Skin severity scores plunged on average, from 18.6 before treatment to 2.8 after 48 weeks of therapy. Fasting glucose also fell over the same period, moving from 6.2 down to 5.3 units by the final check. Triglycerides, uric acid, and homocysteine all fell too, and two body-wide inflammation indices roughly halved. A drop in one inflammation index independently predicted better glucose control in the analysis. pmc-13461485:
Aryadi Aryadi and colleagues built in 2026 a dental emotion corpus and a hybrid recognition system that reads patients' feelings from what they say during treatment. Twelve restorative dentistry consultations were recorded, transcribed, and split into 2,160 patient utterances, each labeled by three trained annotators into six emotions: neutral, fear, sad, happy, angry, and disgust. Agreement between annotators was high.

Neutral remarks led the corpus, followed closely by fear and disgust, an honest portrait of the dental chair. Fear proved both common and the hardest category for machines to classify. The hybrid design lets a recurrent neural network decide confident cases. It then asks one of three open-source large language models to re-rank the shaky ones, aiming to give dentists a live read on patient distress.
pmc-13461585:
Michael Courtney and co-authors ask, in a 2026 study, whether the local stage of prostate cancer seen on a magnetic resonance scan can predict spread to nearby lymph nodes. The men studied had high-risk prostate cancer not yet treated. Node spread was checked with a PET scan that targets a protein found on prostate cancer cells. Knowing who likely has node spread helps doctors plan staging and care.

Records for 152 men who had both scans were tested with statistical models using stage, a blood marker, tumor grade, and age. Cancer that had grown into the seminal vesicles, stage T3b, strongly predicted positive nodes on its own. The same held in one tumor grade subgroup. The final model sorted patients well overall. One low-risk mix of marker, stage, and grade showed no positive nodes at all, which may help guide who needs the PET scan most.
pmc-13461685:
Afrooz Arzehgar and co-authors benchmarked large language models, with and without a document retrieval add-on, on the hard job of classifying inborn errors of immunity from patient records. Their answers were scored for accuracy and consistency against expert classification.

Performance varied widely by model. The most reliable were Gemini-1.5-Pro and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, each scoring a kappa of 0.98 for agreement in the testing reported, and Gemini led without any retrieval help. Adding retrieval raised average classification performance across all models, and DeepSeek-R1, reasoning over retrieved material, achieved the best weighted score overall. Retrieval augmented systems are credible decision support for rare disease classification, the authors conclude.
pmc-13462585:
Yajuan Chen and colleagues examined a protein called FAM111B in 2026 in lung squamous cell cancer, a harsh form of lung cancer that recurs and spreads more than its glandular cousin. The protein, a cancer-linked enzyme found in cell nuclei, already showed ties to glandular lung cancer. Here the team asked whether it also drives the squamous form and could serve as a drug target.

Across patient samples and lab models, FAM111B ran high in squamous tumours and its removal slowed growth, movement, and invasion while stalling cells mid-cycle. The protein seemed to push a shape-shift that lets cancer cells wander, and its growth effects ran through the PI3K signal path. Blocking FAM111B may thus offer a fresh angle on a cancer with few targeted options, though human trials remain distant.
pmc-13462685:
Jian Zhou leads a 2026 climate study on how lake ice in the Northern Hemisphere responds once winter air passes critical warmth thresholds. Ice cover steers northern lake ecosystems, from mixing to nutrient cycles, and is shrinking fast. More than half of Earth's lakes freeze each year. Nearly nine in ten large lakes sit in the far north band that is warming about twice as fast as the global average. The team set out to find the temperature points where ice behavior changes abruptly.

Spring thaw proved far more volatile than autumn freeze-up. Past the winter thresholds, the ice calendar's sensitivity to warming jumps by more than tenfold, a rapid nonlinear acceleration. The finding supplies a way to predict which lakes will lose ice fastest. The authors urge climate impact studies to build in such threshold jumps rather than assuming smooth change.
pmc-13463185:
Miwa gave in 2026 a clinical update on orthostatic intolerance in myalgic encephalomyelitis and chronic fatigue syndrome, where patients cannot stay upright without severe symptoms. Standing shifts about 800 millilitres of blood toward the pelvis and legs, and healthy bodies answer with faster heart rate and tighter vessels. Most patients with this illness show the intolerance, and it is the main limit on their daily function.

Miwa reports that many patients have a small left ventricle, the heart's main pumping chamber, with low output to match. pmc-13486885:

pmc-13487385:

pmc-13487485:

pmc-13487985:

pmc-13488285:

pmc-13490385:

pmc-13490585:

pmc-13493785:

pmc-13493885:

pmc-13495185:

The main curve's apex barely turned, held back by its stress pattern, while other curve tops turned well. pmc-13495285:
Amy L Perry and Richard P Steel examine, in a 2026 study, how gender, smartwatch use, and diagnosed illness combine to shape health anxiety. For women the pattern flipped: the watch went with lower anxiety when a condition existed and higher when none did. pmc-13495485:
Abdul Razak Abubakari and colleagues study, in a 2026 mixed-methods paper, how babies in Northern Ghana are first fed foods beyond milk. Clinic visits and ethnic group shaped timing; child age and household size also mattered. Talks showed early starting driven by grandmothers and a sense the child was ready. pmc-13499685:

pmc-13499985:

pmc-13500385:

pmc-13500785:

pmc-13501685:

pmc-13501785:

pmc-13503785:

pmc-13505085:

pmc-13506585:

pmc-13507785:

pmc-13508285:

pmc-13508385:

pmc-13509185:

pmc-13511085:

pmc-13512585:

pmc-13513885:

pmc-13514785:

pmc-13515585:

pmc-13517885:

pmc-13518085:

pmc-13518885:

pmc-13518985:

pmc-13519785:

pmc-13520285:

pmc-13520385:

pmc-13521885:

pmc-13522285:

pmc-13522485:

When the new index rose by a typical spread, the linked increase in excess risk was consistently larger than the increase tied to the standard air quality index. The advantage held across sex, age, and season groups, suggesting the tailored index better reflects combined pollution harm for local residents.
pmc-13522585:
Fadi G Alnaji leads a team tracking defective flu genomes over repeated passages in a 2026 study. Influenza populations contain many genomes with large internal deletions, which cannot replicate alone yet compete with normal genomes and may soften disease. Serial passage combined with deep sequencing followed how these deleted genomes emerged and changed over time.

Early passages held a highly diverse set of deleted genomes, which then collapsed sharply until only one or two persisted at high frequency. A recurring mutation was found that boosted the replication and interfering power of a deleted genome. The findings show that defective genomes evolve under their own selective pressures and actively shape the wider viral population, with implications for disease severity.
pmc-13523185:
Hermano Alexandre Lima Rocha and colleagues relate anemia in mothers and children to early development in a 2026 population study from Ceará, Brazil. More than two thousand four hundred children up to six years old were assessed. Hemoglobin was measured by a portable device, and development was checked with a standard parent questionnaire. That tool covered motor, language, and problem-solving domains.

Overall, neither maternal anemia nor child anemia tracked development scores or delays after adjustment. Severity mattered, however: mild child anemia linked to more fine motor delay, while moderate to severe anemia linked to more gross motor delay. In older preschool children, anemia at either severity linked to lower motor and problem-solving scores. The authors argue that timing and severity should shape targeted interventions for young children.
pmc-13523385:
Pingping Xue and colleagues engineer a smart wound dressing for diabetic wounds in a 2026 study. Chronic diabetic wounds stall under oxidative stress, inflammation, poor vessel growth, and infection risk. The dressing combines a gelatin-based nanofiber mat with a metal-organic framework carrying the drug saracatinib. The framework breaks down in response to peroxide, a marker of the wound environment, releasing the drug where it is needed.

Released drug stabilized a protective protein by blocking its tagging for destruction, switching on an antioxidant pathway. In cell tests the dressing lowered oxidative damage, protected three skin and vessel cell types, and sped migration and growth. It killed a broad range of bacteria, including drug-resistant strains. In diabetic rats, wounds closed faster with better vessels, collagen, and skin regrowth.
pmc-13524985:
Patryk Rogaczewski and colleagues map, in a 2026 scoping review, evidence for taking vitamin B12 by mouth after total stomach removal for gastric cancer. Losing the stomach removes intrinsic factor, a protein needed to absorb the vitamin, so lifelong supplementation is required. Injections are standard, yet oral dosing could be simpler if it works.

Seven studies covering 449 patients were included, 310 of them receiving oral B12, mostly a form called mecobalamin at daily doses between 500 and 1,500 micrograms. Oral treatment consistently normalized blood levels and eased symptoms in most patients, and comparisons suggested biochemical responses no worse than injections. Weaknesses included inconsistent symptom tracking, short follow-up under six months, only one randomized study, and sparse Western data. Trials with standard outcomes are needed.
pmc-13525185:
Andrew J Day and G. Peter Sarantopoulos present a case of thyroid dermopathy, a rare skin thickening tied to Graves' disease, an overactive thyroid condition. The patient was a 40-year-old woman whose skin disease grew worse over years despite treatment.

The condition builds up jelly-like sugars in the skin and strikes under 5 percent of Graves' patients, mostly with severe eye disease. Shots of steroid and an enzyme into the skin helped only partly over three years of care. Lasting relief came only when immune-calming drugs, started for her other autoimmune illnesses, also eased her leg pain and swelling. Day notes no approved therapy exists, so the case hints systemic immune treatment may help advanced disease.
pmc-13526785:
Zeng and co-authors reprogram how cement hardens in this 2026 materials study, attacking a structural weakness at the atomic scale. Cement's two main hydration products form badly coordinated: calcium hydroxide grows as lopsided layered crystals while the binding gel nucleates where it pleases. The team synthesized a positively charged, disordered precursor of calcium hydroxide by steering proton transfer during grinding.

The charged precursor acts as a seed that triggers both products to nucleate, forming an intergrown composite instead of split phases. Calculations showed hydroxyl vacancies on crystal surfaces spontaneously grab water to create the charged sites that stabilize silicate clusters. The payoff was large: hydration ran faster and gave off more heat, stiffness rose, and early compressive strength at twelve hours rose 5.4-fold over the control mix in the experiments. The authors present protonation control as a general atomic-scale design lever for cementitious materials.
pmc-13527285:
Charith Perera and colleagues develop, in a 2026 mouse imaging study, a dynamic MRI protocol that watches manganese ions cross the blood-cerebrospinal fluid barrier at the choroid plexus. That barrier controls the fluid bathing the brain and moves essential ions, and manganese serves as a stand-in for calcium. Earlier methods blurred the fast early transport window.

Their heavily weighted FLAIR sequence sampled every four minutes at high spatial detail in anesthetized mice given manganese or a gadolinium tracer. Manganese crossed rapidly, with uptake into the choroid plexus far steeper and higher than into ventricular fluid. The gadolinium tracer cleared faster and arrived later in the fluid, showing that tracer choice strongly shapes measured barrier kinetics. The authors promote manganese for probing plexus transport by compartment.
pmc-13527685:
Anne-Sophie Jung and others set out, in a 2026 conceptual article, a transdisciplinary research agenda for resilience in health systems. Resilience is usually framed as absorbing and recovering from acute shocks, and interest surged after the COVID-19 pandemic. Critics warn the label can become technocratic, celebrating adaptation while ignoring political choices and unequal resources.

Drawing on a collaboration spanning institutions in Brazil and three other countries, the authors argue the center of gravity should move from shocks to the ordinary. Everyday services live under chronic, accumulating stress rather than isolated crises, and that persistent pressure demands continuous recalibration. Their agenda asks how chronic stressors interact with system functioning over time, and they call for concepts and measures built around that everyday reality.
pmc-13527985:
Daiki Takekawa and six colleagues ask in a 2026 pilot study whether telomere length before surgery predicts depression right after surgery in older patients. Telomeres are caps on chromosome ends that shorten with age and stress. The study enrolled 48 patients aged 65 or more. All needed intensive care for at least two days after major surgery. Depression was scored on day seven with a standard scale.

Twenty patients, about forty-two percent, met the depression cutoff. Their telomeres were slightly shorter on average, but the gap was not significant in the full group. Type of surgery was the strongest predictor. In a side analysis that removed head and neck cases, shorter telomeres did link with depression. The authors call that finding exploratory only. They blame the small sample and mixed surgery types for the weak main result.
pmc-13528085:
Yizhang Zheng studies the lying flat attitude among Chinese university students in a 2026 paper. Lying flat means opting out of striving and competition. An online survey gathered 2,323 valid replies from thirty provinces. Students rated social support, meaning in life, resilience, and lying flat. A structural model tested how the four connect.

Lying flat ran against all three positive measures. More support meant less lying flat. Part of that link ran through meaning in life. Part ran through resilience. Together the two formed a chain that carried about seventy percent of the total link. The model explained about half the variation in lying flat. Zheng argues support works partly by feeding purpose and bounce-back strength. Programs building those inner resources may matter as much as direct support.
pmc-13530185:
Dominika Kapuścińska and co-authors examine in 2026 how a green alga defends itself against common painkiller drugs that pollute water. Four painkillers of differing strength and structure entered the cultures. Every drug raised hydrogen peroxide inside cells, a sign of chemical stress and redox imbalance.

Defense tactics split by drug strength. Gentler drugs switched on a broad set of protective enzymes across the cell. Harsher drugs leaned on a chloroplast-focused cleanup route. One gene rose under all four drugs, marking it as a possible water-quality warning signal. Overall defense efficiency faded as drug toxicity climbed.
pmc-13531785:
Elif Kocak leads a 2026 follow-up of children who lived through the 2023 Türkiye earthquakes, focusing on lasting sleep problems. A total of 132 mother-child pairs, with children aged 8 to 12, were assessed at three months and again at twelve months. Mothers reported their own depression, anxiety, and trauma symptoms on standard scales.

Child sleep improved over the year, yet about two-thirds still slept poorly at the second check. Mothers trauma symptoms eased, while depression and anxiety barely moved. Early child sleep trouble, mother symptoms, quake exposure, and mother schooling together explained 38 percent of later sleep quality.
pmc-13531885:
Jie Dai and co-authors build in 2026 a prognosis model for throat cancer based on genes tied to R-loops, DNA-RNA tangles that disturb gene reading. Public tumor data supplied the starting gene pool, narrowed by survival modeling to a three-gene score. Outside datasets checked the score, including one on pre-surgery immune therapy.

The score split patients into risk groups with steady accuracy and matched immune therapy response patterns. One gene, EIF5A2, stood out as the core driver, sitting mainly in tumor cells. Single-cell data linked high levels to worn-out killer T cells through a dominant signaling pair.
pmc-13532785:
L Cummins and colleagues report in 2026 partial regrowth of a hind toe in an eastern grey kangaroo. The fourth hind toe bears most weight and push during hopping, so harm to it often means a poor outlook. After trauma the tip was lost, yet the nail bed stayed intact and no surgery was used.

Skin closed over the site, the nail bed held, and a new hard nail formed in time. The animal moved normally, kept good condition, carried a pouched young, and lived past two years after release. Readers see why function, not full anatomy, guided the release choice.
pmc-13534385:
Zhiqiang Zhu and colleagues evaluate in 2026 simpler electronics for high-resolution PET detectors used in small-animal imaging. PET scans help move lab findings toward clinical care, yet detector cost and complexity limit access. Their design squeezes 64 sensor outputs into four signals that a shared commercial chip can process.

Two crystal arrays were tested with sensors read from both ends. All crystals resolved clearly in flood maps, energy scores stayed near the mid-teens in percent, and depth scores beat three millimetres. Readers gain a cheaper route to sharp small-animal scans without losing key performance.
pmc-13534585:
Maryam Hataminejad and colleagues develop in 2026 a home-made ELISA test for cystic echinococcosis, a parasitic disease that forms cysts in organs. Diagnosis by blood tests can vary with cyst stage, so cheaper reliable options matter in affected regions. Their test uses a small purified piece of a parasite antigen from sheep cyst fluid.

Testing held 51 confirmed patients and 50 healthy controls. The new test caught most cases with perfect specificity and matched a commercial kit closely. A DNA test on blood caught a similar share, supporting the home-made test as a low-cost option.
pmc-13534685:
Krzysztof Bartnik and colleagues test in 2026 whether automated body composition measures from CT scans predict survival in liver cancer patients receiving artery-directed chemotherapy. Muscle and fat traits may reflect body reserve, yet their value in this setting was not well studied. Two separate cohorts held 230 and 100 patients with scans before treatment.

Muscle density at the lower spine was the strongest independent predictor of survival in both cohorts. Adding muscle data to clinical scores gave modest gains in one model type and a clear gain in forest models. The measures add objective biological detail for risk sorting.
pmc-13536585:
Maria Teresa Bruno and colleagues ask in 2026 whether active surveillance is always right for CIN2, a mid-grade cervical cell change, in HPV-positive women. Watching instead of cutting can avoid overtreatment, mainly in young women. Records followed women whose lesions were confirmed and then monitored for up to 48 months.

About six in ten lesions cleared on their own, while a quarter progressed and the rest stayed put. High-grade cell test results and HPV types 16 or 18 marked higher progression risk. Careful risk sorting is needed rather than one rule for all.
pmc-13538485:
Laura Zellner and colleagues present a multi-step workflow for analyzing metal complexes in a 2026 methods study. Metal-carbon compounds drive catalysis and drug research, yet mass analysis struggles with their fragility and tangled isotope patterns. Liquid separation was paired with tunable spray conditions and a drift-based separation that yields size descriptors for each compound. Group-six metal complexes served as test cases across varied mixtures.

Drift data revealed orderly metal-linked trends matching expected structural gaps. Those trends let analysts assign the central metal even for faint species lacking clear isotope fingerprints. Tuning spray harshness also let users dial fragmentation up or down by need. The authors offer the combined platform as a flexible toolkit for untangling complex organometallic mixtures.
pmc-13538685:
Masoumeh Hajizadeh and colleagues test light-based therapy as a booster for a standard melanoma drug in a 2026 cell study. The drug dacarbazine faces growing resistance in melanoma care. A melanoma cell line received light therapy, the drug, or both in sequence, with viability, cell cycle, death genes, movement, and colony growth all measured.

Pre-treatment with light therapy made cells markedly more sensitive to the drug. All treatments stalled the cell cycle and raised programmed death, with the combination strongest and death gene shifts confirming the pattern. A major growth pathway quieted while its natural brake rose. Migration and colony formation fell across treatments, most under the combination. The authors propose the pairing for further melanoma research.
pmc-13538785:
Eva Svehlikova and eleven colleagues published this 2026 pharmacology study of AT278, an insulin aspart concentrated five-fold at 500 units per millilitre, for people with type 2 diabetes needing large doses. Concentrated insulins act slowly, a problem for mealtime use. In a randomised, double-blind crossover clamp study, 41 overweight and obese patients received doses of AT278 and standard-strength insulin aspart. A concentrated human insulin was studied for comparison, while glucose was held steady to time the action.

AT278 absorbed fast: it reached half its peak level in 9 minutes, against 35 minutes for standard aspart and 55 for concentrated human insulin. It delivered double the first-hour glucose-lowering effect of standard aspart. That speed held regardless of body mass, whereas standard aspart's early effect faded as BMI rose. Total exposure and effect were comparable. The authors present AT278 as the first ultra-rapid concentrated option for prandial dosing in insulin-resistant patients.
pmc-13540285:
Bai and colleagues published a 2026 study charting one immune sensor across human diseases. CLEC5A is a sensor on immune cells that can amplify inflammation fiercely. The team mined over 42,000 human samples using gene and protein data. They mapped where the sensor sits in health and how it shifts in disease.

The sensor concentrates in macrophages and neutrophils, the first-responder immune cells. It stays low in most healthy tissue but surges in inflamed and infected states. Macrophages rich in it made more alarm chemicals yet ate germs worse. A computer knockout test showed wide ripples across immune pathways. The sensor may serve as both marker and drug target. Sex differences in its levels appeared in some organs as well.
pmc-13542285:
Kara Zivin and colleagues published a 2026 analysis of mental health care around childbirth for women covered by Medicaid, the United States programme that pays for more births than any other insurer. The team used national Medicaid claims for live births from 2017 to 2021. They tracked diagnoses of perinatal mood and anxiety disorders, antidepressant prescriptions, and psychotherapy visits, state by state and year by year.

The cohort held nearly 4.6 million women, and about 13.9 percent received such a diagnosis during the study window. Diagnoses grew across almost every age, racial, and regional group, and in all but one state. Prescribing patterns varied widely between states even while national treatment trends stayed fairly flat. The authors present the state trajectories as a baseline for understanding why recognition and treatment differ so much by place.
pmc-13543385:
Ahmet Tarık Harmantepe and colleagues published a 2026 study of low anterior resection syndrome, the bowel dysfunction many patients suffer after sphincter-saving rectal cancer surgery. They asked whether surgical approach or join height changes the risk. Records of 115 patients operated between 2012 and 2024 without a diverting stoma were reviewed, and patients were grouped by a validated syndrome score. Open, laparoscopic, and robotic operations were compared, along with the distance of the bowel join from the anal verge.

Overall syndrome scores did not differ significantly among the three approaches, though open surgery scored worse than the two minimally invasive approaches combined. Join height mattered greatly: a join within four centimetres of the anal verge was strongly tied to worse syndrome. Urgency and clustering of bowel motions were the severest complaints, and symptoms levelled off around four years. Functional outcomes deserve a place in surgical planning, the authors conclude.
pmc-13543485:
Can Xie and colleagues published a 2026 paper describing TxMicroSim, a web toolkit that helps doctors compare treatment-timing strategies when a disease moves through several states. Choosing when to deploy a therapy, not just whether, can maximise benefit while limiting harm, and no single schedule fits all patients. The tool runs microsimulations: thousands of virtual patients matched to a real patient's data are played through a multistate model under each candidate strategy.

They then fit flexible transition models from uploaded data or typed-in parameters, and finally enter one patient's details and start point. The output compares strategies by restricted mean survival time, the average time lived within a chosen horizon. Built as a browser app, it aims to put formal decision analysis within reach of ordinary clinical teams.
pmc-13544485:
Dahna Choi and colleagues published a 2026 study of empathy in major depression, separating the pain of feeling with others from the warmth of caring for them. Earlier work mostly compared patients with controls as two blocks. This preregistered analysis of a German cohort study covered 499 patients and 670 healthy controls. It related three self-reported traits — empathic distress, empathic concern, and perspective-taking — to family risk, current symptoms, and lifetime illness burden.

Empathic distress, the self-focused discomfort at another's suffering, ran higher in patients and rose with both acute symptom severity and cumulative burden across the illness history. Its apparent link to family risk faded once age and sex were counted. Patients also reported more empathic concern, likely coloured by their current state, and slightly weaker perspective-taking. Heightened emotional attunement during depression, the authors suggest, is a treatment-relevant feature, not a simple deficit.
pmc-13546585:

Such chemotherapy can improve the odds of clean surgical margins, yet many patients gain little. Their study used advanced spectral CT scans from 150 patients treated between 2019 and 2025, combining three-dimensional scan measurements with clinical features.

Three factors carried independent weight: a normalized atomic number measure from the scan, the tumor marker CA19-9, and a measure of fluid space within the tumor. The combined chart predicted response more accurately than scan or clinical models alone, in both the group used to build it and a held-back check group. Larger multi-center testing is still needed, the authors note.
pmc-13547285:

The genes, qacA and qacB, code for pumps that push chemicals out of the cell and differ by only a few building blocks. Each gene was inserted into a clean laboratory strain on a small DNA carrier, and the drug level needed to stop growth was measured again and again.

The qacA gene quadrupled tolerance in nearly every repeat, while qacB doubled it, a real though smaller effect. Computer modeling showed the two pumps share the same overall shape, with differences confined to small local spots. The authors argue for continued monitoring where these genes circulate widely.
pmc-13547385:

Working with Ordovician rocks from the western Ordos Basin in China, they distilled five log curves into two combined components. The first separates clay from carbonate content, and the second tracks the balance between calcite and dolomite.

Plotting the two components against each other produced clean clusters for each rock type, including the in-between lithologies that usually blur together. Element measurements from a live borehole confirmed the assignments. Because every step keeps a geological meaning, the authors argue the method beats black-box classifiers for practical field use.
pmc-13547685:

A robot loaded each ankle in its native state, after injury with only a fibula plate fitted, and after adding either a syndesmotic screw or a repair of the torn deltoid ligament. Both additions restored sideways stability about equally well. Rotational and tilting stability told a different story: the screw left large deviations from the native ankle, while ligament repair stayed far closer on both measures. The authors conclude that repairing the ligament gives the more complete stabilization in this fracture model, a result with direct surgical relevance.
pmc-13548485:
Lise R. Lothe and colleagues recorded single motor units in 2026 from a deep back muscle of nine patients with fresh low back pain. Recordings came before and after a high-velocity spinal manipulation at the painful level. Fine wires in the lumbar multifidus captured the firing of individual muscle fibers' control units while patients stood and sat, in recordings made back in 2007 for this hard-to-study question.

Coordination between the two sides of the muscle stayed weaker than within one side, matching the pattern seen before treatment and unlike pain-free standing. The authors frame the study as a methodological base and call for recovery follow-up.
pmc-13548585:
Jorge Miguel Santacruz-Monzon and colleagues test leaf extracts from the African tulip tree as a rinse for infected root canals, in a 2026 laboratory study. The target bacterium, Enterococcus faecalis, survives inside teeth and resists standard treatment, so plant-based alternatives interest dentists. Six extracts made with different solvents were screened for the lowest doses that stop or kill the bacterium, then compared in dishes against bleach solution.

The water-based extract failed, while the others halted the bacterium at low concentrations. Ethanol and acetone extracts matched the bleach in dish tests at high strength. In extracted human teeth carrying four-week-old bacterial films, the ethanol extract cut living bacteria far more than the bleach rinse did. Rich plant compounds such as flavonoids and tannins may explain the effect, the authors suggest.
pmc-13549385:
Dougherty and colleagues ask whether a diabetes drug class improves cancer immunotherapy outcomes in this 2026 analysis. They matched 573 patients with advanced cancers who received an SGLT2 inhibitor alongside immune checkpoint inhibitors. The comparison group was 573 similar patients on immunotherapy alone.

The combined group lived a median of about 27.4 months, compared with about 17.4 months for immunotherapy alone in this dataset, and stayed on immunotherapy longer. Benefits were clearest in non-small-cell lung cancer and renal cell carcinoma. The survival edge shrank when the analysis corrected for a timing bias favoring late starters, but it persisted in patients already taking the drug when immunotherapy began.
pmc-13550485:
Laura Pasquardini and colleagues build a pocket-sized optical sensor that detects antibodies against polyethylene glycol in blood plasma within fifteen minutes, in a 2026 device paper. PEG coatings help many modern drugs last longer, but some people's immune systems learn to attack PEG itself, causing reactions or wiping out the drug's benefit. Calibration curves in buffer and diluted serum reached detection in the nanomolar range for both major antibody classes, and the chip could be reused. Plasma from healthy controls and hemophilia patients on PEG-linked factor treatment was measured against a commercial instrument and a standard laboratory assay with agreement. The authors aim at cheap point-of-care screening before PEGylated therapy.
pmc-13550585:
Xinpeng Li, with five colleagues, published a 2026 study of a ginseng compound in lung disease. The disease, called COPD, causes long-term airway swelling and harm. The compound, ginsenoside Rg1, fights swelling and cell stress in lab work. The team asked how it might help, using computer tools and cell tests.

Computer screening found 105 targets shared by the compound and the disease. Two signaling routes stood out, both centered on a protein called EGFR. In airway cells stressed by smoke extract and a bacterial toxin, the compound cut swelling and mucus output. Protein tests showed lower activity on both routes. The results point to a clear path for more tests.
pmc-13551385:
Gabriele Simonetti, leading seven colleagues, published a 2026 review of patch testing for drug hypersensitivity reactions in children. The review weighs evidence by drug class and reaction type, especially where a drug challenge test would be too risky.

Yield is low for penicillin-type and most other antibiotics, limiting its stand-alone value in common rashes. Results look better for anti-seizure drugs, where testing can also flag cross-reactivity. The authors call for standard protocols and prospective studies in children.
pmc-13551685:
D C Preethu, leading six colleagues, published a 2026 field study of how the insecticide fipronil breaks down in tropical rice paddy soil. Fipronil controls rice pests, yet its persistence under different water conditions was poorly known.
