Added organic matter prolonged persistence, with half-lives stretching toward two weeks in cropped soil and longer in uncropped soil in the reported values. Plants took the chemical up quickly, mostly into roots, while organic matter lowered plant levels, a balance the authors flag for food safety.
pmc-13551985:
Godfrey Zari Rukundo, with thirteen colleagues, published a 2026 review of a training model for health students in Uganda. The model is called micro-research. Small mentored teams run local studies on HIV and related diseases. The program ran from 2018 to 2024 under a partnership scheme. The team counted trainings, study plans, and papers. They also interviewed participants and scored the model on a five-part frame.

Over half the expected papers reached publication despite the pandemic. Interviewees called recruitment fair, open, and broad across fields. Most voiced satisfaction with the chances the program gave. The team presents small local projects as a workable path to research skill. Such skill is scarce where disease burdens are highest, they note.
pmc-13554185:
Xiaoliang Hu and Yun Lin design a self-tuning regulator for fairness in pro sports leagues in a 2026 study. Set rules for pay caps and shared income cannot track how leagues shift season by season. Their system maps each league as a web of clubs linked by results, money, and dominance. A learning agent then adjusts caps, sharing rates, and draft odds over many seasons.

Trials replayed twenty seasons of English football and American basketball data in simulation. Balance improved by about a third in football and about a fifth in basketball, beating fixed rules clearly. The agent pushed harder when gaps grew severe and eased off when fairness overshot. Checks against real past data supported the setup, though the authors plan fuller real-world tests.
pmc-13554285:
Mengyuan Jiang, Xiyuan Mao, and Lu Zhang combine a graphene-collagen gel with vesicles from dying fat stem cells to calm raised scars in a 2026 study. Raised scars grow from overactive scar cells that lay down too much collagen. The gel alone turned down collagen and other scar markers in those cells, and slowed their growth and spread. Vesicles from the stem cells gave similar calming effects on their own.

The gel's pores soaked up vesicles well, making it a handy carrier. In animals, gel loaded with vesicles lowered scar height and a key scar marker. Healing tissue showed more of the calm macrophage type and signs of controlled cell turnover. The pair forms a two-pronged platform the authors offer for scar care research.
pmc-13555185:
Ingeborg de Rover and three colleagues write to the editor about light shielding during surgery for a rare light-sensitive disease in a 2026 letter. The disease, erythropoietic protoporphyria, loads the body with a compound that turns visible light toxic to skin and organs. The letter answers a case report on shielding for a mastectomy in such a patient. Risk planning, they stress, should rest on liver health and compound levels for each patient.

Three fronts matter: blocking light injury, avoiding liver-harming drugs and iron, and lowering the compound before surgery when needed. Their own cases include a home-built filter that cut operating light sharply and halved its blue share. Risk rises with liver trouble, long open surgery, strong lights, and high compound levels. Shielding alone usually suffices for short procedures.
pmc-13555885:
Shuai Zhang leads a seven-author team mapping the immune layout of melanoma tumours in a 2026 study. Checkpoint drugs often fail in this skin cancer because the tumour's spatial order is poorly understood. Single-cell and spatial gene mapping split the tissue into two zones with different outlooks: an immune region and a pigment-cell region. One gene, CORO1A, stood out as a hub inside the immune zone.

Silencing that gene in a humanised mouse model teamed with a checkpoint drug to suppress tumour growth. The drug itself also lowered the gene's expression in dish tests. Two molecular bridges carried talk between the zones. The authors nominate CORO1A as a target for combination therapy and stress that tumour geography shapes treatment success.
pmc-13556085:
Tianxi Wang and seven colleagues reported in 2026 that a receptor called TREM2 protects light-sensing cells in mice with inherited retinal degeneration. Immune cells in the retina react fast when photoreceptors are stressed, and their response can either help or harm. The team used the rd10 mouse model, in which photoreceptors die progressively, and compared animals with and without working TREM2.

Mice lacking TREM2 lost photoreceptors faster, with thinner retinal layers and disturbed support tissue. Single-cell profiling showed that immune cells without TREM2 switched on inflammasome machinery, a protein complex that drives a fiery form of cell death. Blocking a key executioner protein in that pathway rescued many photoreceptors. The authors identify the inflammasome route as a drug target for retinal diseases where TREM2 control fails.
pmc-13558585:
Mina Moradi and eight colleagues built in 2026 a machine learning framework that estimates hypertension risk from routine blood tests and basic clinical measures. High blood pressure drives heart disease worldwide, and cheap early warning tools are valuable. Data came from a long-running cohort study in Mashhad, Iran. About five thousand adults were followed for new hypertension. Predictors spanned blood counts, cell size measures, age, body mass, kidney function, and habits.

Ten algorithms were trained and ranked. The gradient boosting model XGBoost performed best, though its discrimination was modest, correctly ranking pairs of future cases and non-cases about two thirds of the time. Age, body mass, red cell count, and red cell size carried the most signal across models, and performance held steady between training and test data. The authors frame the model as exploratory signal finding, not a diagnostic.
pmc-13560285:
Mingkai Zhao, Shiqi Pan, and Yuanming Song apply machine learning to forecast healthcare resource needs in China's primary care system. Their 2026 study tunes two neural network types, a backpropagation network and a long short-term memory network, using the sparrow search algorithm to optimize their settings. Predictions cover the number of institutions, personnel counts, and total health costs.

The tuned memory network clearly beat the tuned backpropagation model. For forecasting institution numbers, its root mean squared error fell by forty-five percent on the test set, and absolute error by over a third. Averaged across all tasks, error reductions ran near a quarter for squared error and a sixth for absolute error. Training data echoed the same advantage. The authors offer the model as decision support for staffing, facility planning, and budget distribution aimed at closing regional gaps.
pmc-13560385:
Yan Lü and colleagues survey Chinese adults with type 1 diabetes using a novel two-in-one insulin pump that switches between a tubeless patch form and a tubed portable form. Their 2026 multicenter real-world study gathers forty-seven patients who had used the device at least three months by the end of December 2025. The questionnaire covered glucose control, quality of life, and product experience, all self-reported.

Average glycated hemoglobin sat at 7.2 percent in the month before the survey. Sensor data showed time in range at seventy-four percent, within target, while time below range missed the safety goal in the reported metrics. Over half the patients reported fewer high and low episodes than before pumping. Comfort and overall quality of life improved for most respondents. The authors credit the switchable design with easing skin problems from long-term wear, and they point toward closed-loop automation next.
pmc-13561185:
Abu Thiab and colleagues report a 14-year-old girl whose brain infection was first mistaken for meningitis, in a 2026 child health case report. Subdural empyema, a pus pocket between the brain and its outer membrane, is life-threatening and mimics meningitis closely. The healthy teenager arrived with severe headache, neck stiffness, light sensitivity, and vomiting after an upper airway illness with foul-smelling nasal discharge. The picture pointed toward a sinus source for the infection spreading inward.

Blood tests showed marked inflammation, with C-reactive protein above 320 milligrams per liter, while scans showed a 6-millimeter subdural collection shifting the brain's midline. Surgeons performed endoscopic sinus surgery plus a bilateral craniotomy to drain the pus, and cultures grew Streptococcus constellatus, an abscess-forming bacterium unusual in teenage brains. Targeted antibiotics and rehab followed, and she improved steadily. Abu Thiab urges imaging whenever meningitis-like illness comes with focal nerve signs.
pmc-13562485:
Rishi Bhandari and nine colleagues ask what rules govern the microbes living on an invasive fruit fly and on the grapes it damages. Spotted wing Drosophila spreads sour rot through vineyards, yet the fly and the fruit might assemble their microbial communities in very different ways. The 2026 team sampled flies and rotting grapes at seven California vineyards and sequenced bacterial and fungal marker genes. Fly communities from males and females looked alike, and both differed sharply from grape communities.

Modelling showed chance processes dominated inside the fly, with a neutral model explaining 40 percent of the variation. Grapes mixed chance with strict filtering by the fruit itself. Microbes that broke the neutral pattern, hinting at selection, were mostly rare kinds. The authors cast the fly as a wandering reservoir that scatters microbes, while low-abundance species may steer how rot develops.
pmc-13562585:
Najah Afina Mohd. Harun and six colleagues ask what shapes staff well-being at a Malaysian public university, with self-confidence as the middle link. The 2026 study surveyed 522 academic and non-academic employees, then interviewed eight of them. Leadership, workplace social contact, and felt support were measured against self-efficacy, which means the belief that one can handle the work, and against overall life satisfaction and mood. Structural modelling mapped the paths between them.

Feeling supported raised self-efficacy, which in turn raised well-being and carried much of the effect of both support and leadership. Leadership itself showed a surprising negative link to self-efficacy, and everyday social interaction showed none. Interviews explained the twist: supportive bosses helped, while heavy monitoring, fuzzy expectations, and workload pressure eroded confidence. The authors conclude that management's effect on well-being depends on style and setting, not on leadership.
pmc-13563785:
Ridong You and four colleagues pool randomised trials to put numbers on a known worry: the antipsychotic olanzapine disturbs blood sugar. The drug serves schizophrenia and bipolar disorder well, yet its metabolic shadow is long. Their 2026 review searched four databases to July 2025 and kept only randomised trials against placebo or no treatment that reported fasting glucose, fasting insulin, or the long-term marker HbA1c. Fifteen trials with eighteen comparison arms qualified, and quality and certainty were graded formally.

Olanzapine raised fasting glucose by a pooled 2.618 milligrams per decilitre and fasting insulin by 3.636 units, both statistically firm. HbA1c did not move significantly. Doses of ten milligrams or more and courses past twelve weeks hinted at larger shifts, though unevenly. The authors read the pattern as early insulin resistance rather than established diabetes, and they urge routine glucose and insulin checks plus lifestyle support from the first prescription.
pmc-13563885:
Elana Forman and eight colleagues ask how syringe services programmes keep care centred on the people who use drugs, not on the system funding it. These programmes run on harm reduction values: no coercion, no judgement, autonomy first. Yet as they add services, funders and hospital partners press for standardisation. Their 2026 qualitative study interviewed 41 representatives of 27 programmes across United States jurisdictions between May 2023 and February 2024, working within a recognised framework.

One theme organised everything: recipient-centeredness, practised through three facets. Accessibility meant low-barrier entry and outreach that goes to people. Consistency meant schedules clients can plan around, kept even in hostile policy weather. Non-coerciveness meant referrals offered, never imposed, so trust survives a refusal. Staff treated the three as one culture, not a checklist. The authors offer the trio as guidance for a service trying to grow without losing the values that make people walk in.
pmc-13564085:
Decheng Li and colleagues use, in a 2026 mouse study, single-cell gene sequencing to examine memory T cells that live permanently in inflamed muscle. The model mimics autoimmune myositis and is triggered by a human disease-linked enzyme fragment. Such resident cells are suspected of keeping muscle inflammation going in people with inflammatory myopathy.

A clear population of resident helper T cells appeared in muscle, carrying the expected stay-in-tissue gene pattern and matching human muscle profiles. Those cells were heavily expanded from a few cell clones and stayed stable over weeks, while also feeding inflammation-linked pathways involving two major immune signals. The findings nominate resident memory cells as a possible treatment target in autoimmune muscle disease.
pmc-13570485:
Madeleine Louise Kelly and colleagues report a scalp melanoma that announced itself by turning white hair brown, publishing the case in 2026. A 78-year-old man presented with a patch of light-brown hair on the crown amid otherwise white hair, decades after childhood scalp radiotherapy for ringworm. Examination found a tan pigmented patch with darker spots, and biopsy showed lentigo maligna, a melanoma in situ subtype.

Wide excision with skin grafting revealed a tiny invasive component limited to the upper dermis, and follow-up showed no recurrence. The case highlights hair repigmentation as a rare warning sign of melanoma and past scalp irradiation as a possible risk factor. Clinicians should weigh both when assessing new pigment changes on irradiated scalps.
pmc-13571385:
Trinca and colleagues report in this 2026 case study how a brief pause in blood thinners nearly cost a new heart valve. A 70-year-old man received a catheter-delivered replacement for his leaking tricuspid valve using a 56-millimeter EVOQUE prosthesis, and the implant itself went without complications.

Days later he developed complete heart block, so intravenous heparin was stopped for about sixteen hours around a pacemaker implantation. Three days after that he crashed into cardiogenic shock with severe oxygen failure, and ultrasound showed extensive clot choking the fresh prosthesis even though therapeutic anticoagulation had been restored. Surgeons removed the clotted device, but its anchoring had damaged the native valve, forcing a full surgical replacement. The authors warn that early anticoagulation gaps after this procedure can be catastrophic in high-risk patients.
pmc-13572385:
Faguang Wang and colleagues built a rigorously verified image dataset to help computers catch stomach cancer early. Gastric cancer often goes undetected until advanced stages, when survival plunges, yet diagnostic AI has lacked large, trustworthy training sets. Their dataset, EndoWLI-NBI, holds 11,971 magnifying narrow-band imaging pictures from 868 patients, covering the full precancerous cascade from chronic gastritis and intestinal metaplasia to early cancer. A 2026 data paper describes it.

Every image is mapped to a biopsy-confirmed diagnosis, giving the labels a gold standard that most public datasets lack. Benchmark tests with modern deep-learning models confirmed the dataset's quality, while also showing how hard it is to separate high-grade neoplasia from early cancer by eye. The authors offer it as a resource for finer lesion classification, adaptation research, and endoscopy training.
pmc-13573385:
Mei Jin, with six colleagues, reports a 2026 case of a rare epilepsy type in a child, paired with a review of past reports. The condition pairs absence seizures, brief blank spells, with rhythmic twitching around the mouth. It is easy to miss, since the mouth signs are subtle and standard tests may not catch them.

The patient was a 10-year-old boy with spells of 10 to 15 seconds that grew from weekly to several a day over six months. Video brain-wave tests caught the classic three-per-second spike pattern, and a muscle sensor at the mouth logged the twitching. A daily dose of valproate stopped the seizures within two weeks, and he stayed free of them for eight months. The authors urge mouth muscle checks when absence spells come with lip twitching.
pmc-13573485:
Jiaxi Liang, with six colleagues, reports a 2026 study that reads leaf nitrogen in orchard trees from drone images. Nitrogen in leaves flags how well a tree is fed, and in dry Xinjiang oases, exact feeding saves cost and water. Ground sampling is slow, so the team fused colour spectrum data with image texture from drone flights.

Walnut, jujube, and apricot trees in one river oasis gave 50 leaf samples per species. Three model types tried the task, and a random forest that joined both spectrum and texture won. Its fit scores ran high across species, and texture added a clear lift in accuracy and a cut in error. Maps showed jujube leaves rich in patches, apricot even, and walnut low overall. Small sample size tempers the claim, the authors note.
pmc-13574885:
Tali Amir leads a 2026 study asking whether how clearly a breast lesion stands out on contrast-enhanced mammography predicts cancer. Radiologists graded each lesion as low, moderate, or high in how much it stood out from nearby tissue. The work used scans from one centre gathered between 2019 and 2021.

Across 476 exams in 455 women, readers found 563 lesions, of which 55 proved malignant. Cancer rates were close for all three grades, near nine to eleven percent in each group. Most cancers showed only low or moderate prominence. The authors warn that a faint lesion should not be read as harmless, since many such lesions appeared only on the contrast images.
pmc-13575185:
Soyoun Won and six colleagues build neural networks that forecast vision after treatment for a blocked retinal vein, in a 2026 study. Branch retinal vein occlusion can leave lasting sight loss, and results after anti-VEGF injections vary widely between patients. The team asked whether scans plus basic clinical facts could sort patients by likely outcome.

The best model combined two kinds of retinal scans with starting vision, retinal thickness, age, and sex. It sorted patients into vision classes 12 months ahead with modest accuracy. A side test on a diabetic eye swelling dataset was treated only as a rough feasibility check. The authors stress caution: the study was small, single-centre, and backward-looking, so prospective testing comes next.
pmc-13578285:
MacAulay Harvey and colleagues test whether software alone can sharpen a special kind of laser microscope, in a 2026 optics study. The microscope builds images from doubled and tripled light signals, a trick that reveals fine tissue detail. Like all light based tools, its sharpness stops at a hard physical limit, and past fixes needed costly custom parts.

Several programs first built for glowing dye images were tried on these harmonic images instead. On lone tiny structures the software sharpened detail by more than threefold, with no change to the microscope at all. Two of the programs also kept the way the signal swings with light direction, which lets users read fiber alignment at fine scale. Dense scenes stay tricky, since brightness and crowding blur together.
pmc-13579185:
Leila Pourtalebi Jahromi and colleagues lay out a chemistry guide for refitting the surface of extracellular vesicles, in a 2026 review. Vesicles are tiny parcels cells shed, and drug makers covet them as natural delivery trucks. The snag is control: a raw vesicle shows sticky, changeable surface proteins that steer where it lands and how fast the body clears it.

Borrowed lab tricks from antibody coupling and bioorthogonal chemistry let makers graft homing tags, cloaks, and sensors onto the shell. The authors widen the menu with chemistries borrowed from protein and cell surface work, still untried on vesicles. Lipid engineering rounds out the toolkit. The closing call is for shared yardsticks, since matching how teams describe these grafts is what will let results add up.
pmc-13579885:
Elaheh Zarean and colleagues hunt DNA methylation marks that forecast breast cancer survival, in a 2026 pooled study of 2,157 tumors. Methylation is a chemical tag layer on DNA that can silence genes. Data came from a Melbourne cohort plus nine public sets, and the scan covered five year survival in close to two thousand cases.

Thousands of tag sites linked to survival before adjustment, and hundreds held after hormone receptor status was counted. A signature built from 228 sites sharpened five year forecasts beyond standard clinic facts in the test cohort. The same score also predicted cancer free time in a harder to treat tumor subgroup. Pathway checks pointed to the biology under those tags, and the authors pitch the score for risk talks after diagnosis.
pmc-13580185:
Anqi Tu and colleagues find a precise blood style marker for whether a new cancer drug is hitting its target, in a 2026 study. The drug blocks an enzyme called PRMT5, but only in tumors missing a partner gene, a pairing that kills those cancers while sparing healthy cells. Judging the block by total enzyme output is blurry, so the team hunted single marked protein pieces in preserved tumor samples.

A mass reading scan of treated mouse tumors weighed one hundred forty five candidate pieces. One piece, a doubly tagged spot on a stress protein, stood out for its plenty and its dose tied fall. At the top dose the mark dropped by over ninety percent, repeatably, across the target tumor models. The assay needs no extra enrichment step, a plus for clinic labs.
pmc-13585985:
Petronela Rezbáriková and colleagues compare plant compounds that jam a calcium pump in muscle cells. The pump, SERCA1a, hauls calcium back into storage after each contraction and is a drug target in cancer, heart, and metabolic disease. Their 2026 study set the classic blocker thapsigargin beside a cousin, trilobolide, and two altered versions of that cousin, using lab vesicles that carry the pump.

All four compounds slowed the pump more as dose rose. Trilobolide beat even thapsigargin, the long-standing benchmark, while one altered version kept fair strength. Each drug lowered the pump's top speed without much changing its calcium grip, which points to a stuck, slow shape. Computer fitting added a twist: the winner did not bind tightest on paper, so fat-liking and charge fit mattered as much as raw grip.
pmc-13586685:
Thomas Cluzeau and a large team report a leukemia trial that was stopped early because the added drug was not helping. The patients had acute myeloid leukemia marked by high levels of a receptor called RARA, and most were older or unfit for hard chemotherapy. Standard care paired two drugs, venetoclax and azacitidine. The trial added a third, tamibarotene, which switches the RARA pathway on and had shone in earlier, smaller work.

The three-drug mix was tolerated well enough, yet it did not beat the standard pair on response or survival in this 2026 report. The study was halted for futility, a planned judgment that more patients would not change the answer. The authors draw a wider lesson. A bright marker like RARA on its own may not pick out who gains from a targeted drug, so future trials need finer ways to select patients.
pmc-13587285:
Lei Chai and Xuejie Ding follow money worry, loneliness, and sleep in British households over time. Worrying about future finances, before any bill is actually missed, is a strain of its own. Their 2026 study used two waves of a long UK household survey, covering more than twenty thousand people, and tracked changes inside each person rather than comparing strangers.

Expecting to be worse off went with feeling lonelier and with worse sleep quality and more broken sleep. Loneliness carried part of that link, acting as a bridge between money worry and poor sleep. Other sleep troubles, such as taking long to fall asleep or using sleep medicine, showed no firm tie. Men and women looked much alike in the pattern. The authors suggest that easing money uncertainty and strengthening social ties could both protect sleep.
pmc-13591285:
Michael C McKelvey leads a large team testing two mucus loosening treatments for bronchiectasis, a lasting lung disease where widened airways trap thick sputum. Patients were assigned at random to salty mist, a drug called carbocisteine, both, or usual care. Sputum was gathered at the start and at two and eight weeks. The team measured its stretch and flow, its irritant markers, and its mix of bacteria.

Neither treatment thinned the sputum or shifted its markers or bacteria in this sub study, with small groups of 6 to 15 per arm. At the start, thicker sputum tracked with higher levels of a key irritant signal and with one bacterium taking over. McKelvey and the team conclude the data do not back these drugs for changing sputum traits.
pmc-13591685:
Ning Liu leads a 2026 study of a skin test that may help spot mental illness in teenagers. When niacin, a B vitamin, touches the skin, most people flush red as blood vessels open. That flush is often weak in people with schizophrenia and some mood ills. The team tested 51 adolescents with mental disorders against 18 healthy peers, then checked how flush strength lined up with blood results.

Patients flushed less and reacted more weakly, above all those with depression or bipolar disorder. Flush scores sorted the groups with fair accuracy. Weaker flush also tracked with thyroid hormone levels, uric acid, and red blood cell traits. Liu and the team offer the test as a cheap aid beside standard diagnosis, not a stand alone proof.
pmc-13591885:
Hatice Eğilmez and two colleagues test, in 2026, a care bundle meant to stop pressure injuries during bone surgery. Long operations, fixed poses, and numb bodies put surgical patients at high risk of skin breakdown. Their study at a Turkish public hospital covered 190 patients: 68 who received the bundle and 122 who received standard care. The groups started out much alike in age and health.

Pressure injuries struck under six percent of the bundle group, against over eighteen percent of controls. Three days after surgery the bundle group also reported less pain, less fear of falling, and greater comfort. Eğilmez and the team urge wider use of bundled checks, padding, and repositioning in operating rooms.
pmc-13592585:
Gang Ren and six colleagues survey why high schoolers keep using AI learning devices, gadgets such as study tablets and teaching robots with chat built in. Their questionnaire drew 726 first year senior high students who had used such devices. Items covered device traits like personalization and friendliness, basic psychological needs, enjoyment, and intent to continue. A structural model sorted the web of links.

Feeling socially connected to the device fed enjoyment most strongly, while friendliness was the trait that fed that connection best. Feeling free and capable linked to continued use both directly and through enjoyment. Two expected links failed: personalization did not feed felt freedom, and fast replies did not feed connection. Ren and the team advise designing past raw responsiveness.
pmc-13594885:
Antoine Gardin leads a nineteen-author multicenter study of a paradoxical complication after liver transplantation in children and adults born without a working bile salt export pump. The immune system can learn to attack the transplanted pump protein. That causes a disease like the original one. The team screened thirty-five transplanted patients for the responsible antibodies in their 2026 report.

Ten patients, nearly a third, tested positive and all developed the alloimmune disease, typically about five years after transplant. Strong immune treatments brought remission in nine, though six relapsed; relapse-free stretches lengthened with maintenance therapy. Three of the ten died, and six needed a second transplant, against far better outcomes in the unaffected group. A severe form of the underlying gene change predicted the complication, and the authors urge routine antibody screening for such patients.
pmc-13595485:
Cristina Bosetti and co-authors audited how completely European cancer registries record the stage of a cancer at diagnosis. They worked with the ECIS Working Group. Stage information guides treatment and lets countries compare their results fairly. Their 2026 report covers eighty-six registries feeding the European Cancer Information System and focuses on six common cancers.

Sixty-seven registries from eighteen countries supplied stage data spanning 1990 to 2022, and nearly all used the standard TNM system. Reporting improved steadily over the decades. In the late 2010s most countries had stage on more than eighty percent of breast, cervical, colorectal, and lung cases. Stomach and prostate cancers sat above seventy percent. A few countries still staged under half their cases. The authors credit registries' commitment while pressing for harmonized reporting to close the remaining gaps.
pmc-13595685:
Ling Su and co-authors reviewed the hospital records of 129 children treated for COVID-19 at a Xiamen hospital during 2025. They checked how the children fared. They also checked whether every drug received was justified. Their 2026 retrospective analysis sorted cases into mild, moderate, and one critical case, and audited prescriptions for correct indication and correct route of delivery.

Nearly every child recovered or improved, with fever, cough, and runny nose the typical picture. Moderate cases were older and heavier and received markedly more symptom drugs, steroids, and antibiotics than mild ones. The audit found irrational prescribing in fifteen children, covering inhaled steroids and antibiotics given without a matching indication, plus an interferon given by the wrong route. One child developed the rare multisystem inflammatory syndrome. The authors urge tighter prescribing discipline for pediatric COVID care.
pmc-13596085:
Khushi Khandelwal, Eleanor Jones, Connor O'Farrell, and Hannah Katharine Batchelor compared four laboratory systems for predicting how a drug tablet releases its contents in the human colon. Their 2026 study tracked a modified-release theophylline tablet in two standard pharmacy apparatuses and two advanced gut simulators, using the dynamic colon model as the reference standard.

Release swung widely with stirring speed in the paddle apparatus and with flow rate in the flow-through cell, and in both the gentlest settings matched the colon model best. A simplified version of the other simulator showed the same lesson. Slower, gut-like movement gave the closest profiles. Removing water, as the colon does, improved every system's match. The authors recommend keeping the simple tools for quality control while letting the simulators guide predictions, possibly at even gentler settings than those tested.
pmc-13597085:
James S White and co-authors filmed living fruit fly pupae to watch a surprising wound response: nearly half the skin cells near an injury fuse into giant multinucleated cells called syncytia. Conventional healing relies on cells dividing and crawling, and this fusion behavior's contribution was unclear until their live imaging study.

When the team knocked down an autophagy gene, fewer syncytia formed and wounds closed more slowly, and a tissue model estimated fusion speeds closure by about a third. The fused cells help three ways. They race ahead of ordinary cells to lead the first sealing. They reduce the cell shuffling needed as tissue reshapes. They also pool their contents toward the wound edge. The authors suggest the same tricks likely serve syncytia in development and disease, where fused cells are common but poorly understood.
pmc-13604585:
Eman H Yousef leads an eight-author team testing milk thistle extract and zinc oxide nanoparticles against colon cancer in rats. Chemotherapy remains the mainstay for colon cancer, but toxicity and resistance push the search for gentler options. Thirty male rats were split into five groups: healthy controls, DMH-induced cancer, and cancer groups treated with silymarin, zinc oxide nanoparticles, or both daily for four weeks.

Each single treatment lowered a tumor marker, restored mucus production in the colon wall, and improved tissue appearance. The combination worked best of all. The two agents eased oxidative stress by different routes, one restoring protective enzymes and the other cutting lipid damage. Together they reined in β-catenin, a growth driver, by restoring its natural brake, and normalized a regulatory RNA, miR-192, and its partner PKCα. Markers of proliferation, spread, and cancer stem cells also fell. The authors back further study of the pairing.
pmc-13612485:

Mycobacterium tuberculosis forms cellulose-rich biofilms that shield it from immunity and drugs, yet the metabolism behind them was murky. The team first showed fermentable fuels, glucose, glycerol, and pyruvate, grow thick biofilms while other carbon sources lag. Attention then fell on pyruvate carboxylase, an enzyme feeding carbon into the TCA cycle.

A mutant lacking that enzyme failed at every biofilm style tested: floating pellicles, submerged films, and macrocolonies all came out defective. Microscopy showed the mutant biofilms lacked cellulose and carried less biomass. Restoring the gene fixed the defect, and adding glucose or pyruvate rescued it too. The authors conclude that controlled carbon flow supplies both the bricks and the power for the biofilm's protective matrix. The enzyme emerges as a candidate drug target against the bacterium's most stubborn lifestyle.
pmc-13612585:

Patterns emerged quickly. Groups diverged sharply across fifteen oral and eight airway sites. Airway bacteria carried more antibiotic resistance genes and varied more between people. Across twenty-five case-control studies spanning twelve diseases, disease status reshaped them in nineteen datasets, and classifiers beat 0.70 accuracy in twenty. Shared signatures surfaced for periodontitis and pneumonia, some belonging to uncultured species. About an eighth of catalog species also turned up in the gut, where they linked to multiple diseases. The authors offer the catalog as shared infrastructure for the field.
pmc-13613585:
Bernard Appiah leads a team weighing the cost-effectiveness of a radio campaign meant to raise full vaccination rates among young children in Ethiopia, in a 2026 study set in the Jimma Zone. The campaign, called 10+10+30, mixed a ten-minute radio drama about vaccines, ten minutes of talk led by a community health worker, and a thirty-minute listener phone-in, run over three months. Getting children vaccinated on time stays hard in many lower-income countries.

The team modelled the campaign using results from a trial in two districts and priced it at about four United States cents per person reached. They counted extra children fully vaccinated, lives saved, and healthy years gained for the money spent. Such figures help health ministries judge whether lively radio formats deserve a place beside clinics and door-to-door work.
pmc-13614985:

Steroids control immune and inflammatory disease, yet prolonged use brings diabetes, weak bones and muscles, weight gain, and mood trouble that blunt exercise gains. Their review, built on a systematic search to May 2025, pooled 19 studies covering 663 patients, mostly women with rheumatoid arthritis or lupus.

Exercise consistently improved muscle power and daily function, while bone, heart-metabolic, thinking, and mental-health evidence stayed thin or mixed. Strength plus aerobic training emerged as the essential pairing, with adherence and safety plans alongside. Etayo-Urtasun and colleagues call structured exercise a promising add-on that may cut extra drug use, pending firmer guidelines.
pmc-13615485:
Basil Mahfouz, Licia Capra, and Geoff Mulgan ask in 2026 whether COVID-19 education policy kept up with the newest research, or leaned on older studies out of habit. They used a language-model method that matches policy documents to studies with similar content, then checked whether closer, newer work already existed when each policy was written. School policy during the pandemic is a sharp test case, since research poured out at record speed.

The pattern was clear: policy papers kept citing settled pre-pandemic research even when similar studies from after 2020 were already available. The lag suggests policy systems absorb new proof slowly, even in a crisis with fast science. The matching approach itself can be reused in other fields to measure how quickly decisions absorb fresh findings, a useful health check for evidence-based government.
pmc-13615985:
Hüseyin Ender Gürmeriç, Mustafa Şengül, and Burhan Basaran measure in 2026 the levels of potentially toxic metals in 84 cheeses gathered from seven regions of Türkiye. Cheeses were sorted by milk source, ripening stage, and whether they came from factory or traditional making. After dissolving samples in acid, a mass spectrometry method read metals from aluminium and zinc down to cadmium and lead, some present only in traces.

The team then estimated how much of each metal a cheese eater takes in daily and converted that into standard risk scores for non-cancer harm. Wide ranges between samples show that region and making style shift the metal load a lot. Shoppers and regulators get a fact base for judging which cheeses deserve closer watch, instead of treating a national food as one uniform product.
pmc-13616385:
Xinyi Qian and colleagues name a long non-coding RNA, called GSLR, as a driver of lung adenocarcinoma, the commonest lung cancer type, through control of the cancer's energy supply. Such RNAs do not build proteins but steer gene activity, and cancer's metabolism is a growing target. GSLR runs high in these tumours, and patients with more of it fare worse. Starving cells of glucose or glutamine shut the RNA's gene down through changes in its DNA packaging.

The RNA grabs a helicase protein and walks it to the switch of creatine kinase B, an enzyme that buffers the cell's energy currency. More of that enzyme kept energy steady and the cell's power plants stable, feeding growth. GSLR's sensitivity to nutrients makes it both a sensor and an engine of the tumour's hunger.
pmc-13616585:
Miguel A. Woodham, Anthony DeMaria, and Prerana Bhatia present a 2026 case report of a woman recovering from takotsubo syndrome. In this stress-triggered heart failure, the tip of the left ventricle balloons and stops squeezing. Recovery usually unfolds over days to weeks. Three weeks after diagnosis, this patient's middle ventricle segments had become overactive, squeezing so hard they blocked the chamber's middle, and she developed new symptoms on standing.

Serial ultrasound scans tracked the shift from a limp tip to a blocked middle, then to full recovery at six months. The authors propose that healing muscle can overshoot in patches, and that this contractile reshuffle explains symptoms that return during an otherwise good recovery. Patients and doctors who expect a straight climb back may misread such a dip without this picture in mind.
pmc-13617685:
Erçin Samunahmetoglu and Arzum Yilmaz compare five artificial intelligence models on dentistry exam questions in a 2026 study. They used two hundred fifty-eight multiple-choice questions from the Turkish Dental Specialty Examination held between 2012 and 2021, split between factual knowledge items and harder analytical ones in oral radiology and surgery. Each model answered every question once under default settings.

Accuracy differed significantly between models overall and on both question types. Gemini scored highest on knowledge questions, while Claude scored lowest, and no model clearly beat the others on analytical questions in head-to-head checks. Agreement between models was low by one measure and moderate by another. Overall success mostly mirrored factual recall, leading the authors to conclude that these systems recall dental facts well but reason clinically less reliably. That suits them as study supports rather than independent decision makers.
pmc-13618385:
Tasnim Nafian and five colleagues report a nineteen-year-old Bangladeshi woman whose Plasmodium vivax malaria, long dismissed as the benign form, erupted into three life-threatening complications at once. Previously healthy, she arrived after five days of high fever with rigors, weakness, and upper abdominal pain. Blood tests showed collapsed blood counts across all cell lines, a ferritin level in the tens of thousands, clotting failure markers, and raised pancreas enzymes, while a rapid test confirmed vivax malaria.

Intravenous artesunate plus team supportive care produced steady improvement, and she never needed the immune-suppressing therapy the blood syndrome often demands. Oral artemisinin combination treatment and primaquine ended the cure, and she stayed well at follow-up. The authors urge vigilance for such complications in endemic regions.
pmc-13619985:
Vaishnavi Vivek Chiddarwar and ten colleagues reviewed research on exercises that switch on one lower-body muscle more than its neighbors. Trainers and therapists want such selective moves to rebuild weak muscles after injury or to prevent imbalance. The team searched three databases for studies in healthy, active people that measured muscle recruitment during specific exercises.

From more than two thousand five hundred initial hits, 106 studies qualified, and just over half rated as high quality. Twenty-nine muscles of the lower quarter and trunk appeared across the literature. Skin-surface electrical recording was the standard measuring tool, and the biceps femoris, a hamstring muscle, drew the most study by far. Many leg muscles still lack good evidence for any exercise that isolates them. The authors call for work that fills those gaps so prescriptions can get more precise.
pmc-13623385:

The study drew 1,028 officers, mostly men with an average age near forty-two. Three quarters scored in the moderate-to-very-high burnout range on a standard assessment tool. Burnout ran lower with age, longer service, and regular physical activity. It ran higher among women, White officers, degree holders, those on fixed shifts, and those using long-term medication or with a history of psychological care or addiction. The authors read the pattern as demands outrunning the support the institution supplies, and they urge combined policies for healthier workplaces and accessible mental health care.
pmc-13623985:
Sarah Schill and colleagues published a 2026 German-language review of immune and cell therapies for type 1 diabetes, an autoimmune disease where the body destroys its own insulin-making beta cells. The disease can now be spotted before symptoms, when at least two islet autoantibodies appear in blood. That early window opens the door to treatments that slow the attack.

The review, built on a 2025 overview by Ziegler and colleagues plus current guidelines and trials, centres on teplizumab, the first disease-modifying drug for the pre-symptom stage. It delays the arrival of full diabetes by two to three years on average. Other immune drugs preserved remaining beta cell function after diagnosis in trials, though none is approved for that use yet. Stem-cell-grown replacement beta cells are in early testing for advanced cases. The authors expect combinations, and protection of transplanted cells, to decide the field's future.
pmc-13624885:
Niranjan Bista, Patrick Shenjere, and Demeesh Oudit write to the editor about an infant treated for melanoma that had spread to the neck. Their letter follows the child across sixty years, an unusually long window for so rare a cancer. Treatment at the time joined radiation given before surgery with a radical operation that cleared the lymph nodes of the neck.

The child stayed free of melanoma for the long term, a result worth noting because options then were few and rules for judging childhood melanoma were unsettled. Infant melanoma is hard to spot, since children's spot-like growths often mimic harmless moles. The letter uses the long survival to show how far diagnosis and care have come in six decades.
pmc-13626085:
Lonnie G Thompson and colleagues defend an old age for ice drilled from the Guliya ice cap on the Tibetan Plateau. Two long cores, one pulled in 1992 and a twin in 2015, carry matching oxygen isotope layers, a climate diary written in ice. Building the shared timeline took three kinds of evidence. Rare isotopes pinned a known flip of Earth's magnetic field about forty-one thousand years ago. Layer matching tied the cores to a dated summit core. A cave deposit shaped by the Asian monsoon gave a final comparison.

The lines of evidence converge past one hundred thousand years, reaching about 128 thousand at the deepest dated layers, the oldest yet from Tibet. The isotope record sways with Earth's orbit through the last ice age. Margin ice dated by radiocarbon backs the great age, settling a long dating dispute.
pmc-13628285:
Zhaoping Liu and five colleagues surveyed 680 nurses at three large hospitals in Wuhan, China, between October and December 2025, sorting them by patterns of problematic short-video use. Presenteeism, meaning showing up for work while functioning below par, was the outcome of interest, with work spilling into personal life examined as a possible middle step.

Statistical grouping produced four profiles, from low-symptom use to generalised heavy symptoms. Nurses in the heavier profiles reported more presenteeism, and work interference with personal life carried part of that link for every heavier group. Because the survey captured one moment in time, the authors avoid causal claims, and they suggest protecting off-duty recovery and healthier digital boundaries as strategies worth testing.
pmc-13630385:
Jinghan Qiao and seven colleagues watched the contractile machinery of cells shuttle back and forth during the building of a siphon tube in the sea squirt Ciona. The tube forms in two rounds of inward folding, and the puzzle was how one tissue choreographs two different force programmes in sequence.

Live study showed the actomyosin network first moving from the cells' sides to their tops, squeezing the sheet inward, then relocating back to the sides to power a faster second phase. Genetic tweaks to muscle-like myosin strengthened or abolished the first fold, and light-based inhibition stalled the second. Computer vertex models supported the coupled mechanism. The authors propose this two-way redistribution as a general trick of organ formation.
pmc-13630885:
Thi Nhien Hao Nguyen and six colleagues mapped the genetics of cucumber aroma. The fresh scent rides on two dozen volatile compounds. Using several breeding groups grown in greenhouses and open fields, they hunted genome regions that set scent levels. Such regions are called quantitative trait loci. Each one helps set how much of a scent chemical a fruit makes.

Single-compound analysis found 284 such regions. Many huddled into fifteen clusters. A combined view added 52 more. Two clusters stood out as stable across groups and settings. One governs the major six-carbon alcohols. The other governs the nine-carbon aldehydes behind the fruit's signature freshness. Genes for transcription factors are prime suspects inside them. The authors discuss how breeders might select for flavour directly.
pmc-13631085:
Wiâme Mokkedem and fourteen colleagues add a new gene to the catalogue of inherited male infertility. Their study appeared in 2026. One man's sperm were immotile and deformed in the pattern called MMAF. Sequencing across a 168-patient cohort found both copies of his LRGUK gene carrying a truncating variant. The variant cuts off the gene's tail domain.

Protein staining confirmed the gene product was missing from the patient's sperm. Microscopy showed wrecked inner structure in both tail and head. The nuclei were oversized, the chromatin loosely packed, and the DNA fragmented. The authors conclude LRGUK is required to build sperm correctly during growth. Affected families gain a concrete genetic answer and a counselling target.
pmc-13631285:
Dodzi Kwaku Jnr Senoo and two colleagues review how built gut communities pin down what diet does to the microbiome. Their review appeared in 2026. Real gut systems are too tangled to prove cause and effect. So researchers build synthetic communities. These are defined sets of cultured microbes whose membership is known exactly. They then feed them controlled diets.

The review walks through how such sets are designed. It covers the lab fermenters and germ-free animal models they run in. It covers the multi-omics and computing tools used to read the results. Those show who grows, who fades, and what chemicals change as foods shift. The authors propose reporting standards for repeatable work. They look ahead to sets spanning bacteria, fungi, and other kingdoms, designed with AI help.
pmc-13631485:
Lee traces in 2026 the troubled birth of Korea's two-year premedical course, the standard gateway into medical training, between 1945 and 1979. The article asks why the system kept facing proposals to move, abolish, or merge it.

Working from United States military government and University of Minnesota records, Lee focuses on Seoul National University while noting differences across institutions. His sources also include university documents, journals, newspapers, and student publications. The Korean model fused an American principle, general education and basic science at university level, with direct progression into the four-year medical phase directly, without a second competitive selection. While the legal two-plus-four framework survived, coordination across admissions, quotas, records, curriculum, teaching, and progression decisions never settled into durable form. Lee calls this failure to institutionalize coordination the system's core instability.
pmc-13631685:
Nandaki Keshavan leads a large international panel behind these consensus guidelines for pyruvate dehydrogenase complex deficiency. The rare inherited condition weakens an enzyme complex that turns a sugar breakdown product into fuel for cells. Its effects range from dangerous acid buildup in newborns to learning delay with epilepsy in children and milder nerve problems in adults. Care had varied widely between hospitals and countries.

Experts from Europe and North America reviewed the published evidence and voted through a structured Delphi process until they agreed. They produced one hundred ninety-nine recommendations, each graded for strength and quality of evidence. The guidance covers diagnosis, diet and other treatments, watching for complications, genetic counseling, and the move into adult care. The panel also lists the biggest gaps in knowledge, pointing to where new treatments are most needed.
pmc-13632685:
Adrian Troya and six colleagues describe two new turtle ant species from Ecuador. Turtle ants live in trees and carry armor-like bodies. One new species comes from lowland forests in the Chocó and Amazon regions, and the other lives in Amazonia. The team based the descriptions on careful body measurements of workers and soldiers, supported by high-resolution images. DNA barcode readings confirmed that both differ from their closest look-alikes.

The finds raise Ecuador's known turtle ant count to thirty-three species. The paper also gives the first description of the soldier caste of a rarely collected relative. A fully illustrated key and checklist cover every species known from the country. Both new species live in well-preserved forests that face fast clearing and mining pressure. The authors argue that combining body evidence with DNA gives a solid framework for sorting this complex genus.
pmc-13634685:
Dental work in dogs and cats raises a practical question about infection risk. Weese and three colleagues review what evidence exists. Dental procedures disturb the bacteria-rich lining of the mouth, so bacteria can briefly enter the bloodstream. Vets worry about rare but serious outcomes such as heart-valve infection or sepsis. The team searched the literature for local and whole-body infectious complications and for the effect of antibiotics given around the procedure.

No study clearly reported rates of sepsis or heart-valve infection after dental work. Pooled data put post-procedure bacteria in the blood at about forty-seven percent. Two controlled studies found no clear link between the procedure and blood bacteria, and no study tested whether preventive antibiotics changed serious outcomes. Weese and colleagues conclude that the evidence base is severely limited, which hampers sound guidelines for a very common treatment.
pmc-13638785:
Robert Sean Tyler and nine colleagues describe a 2026 training curriculum that teaches infectious diseases trainees how to handle donor calls. When an organ becomes available, doctors must judge quickly whether it is safe for a transplant patient, yet trainees often get little practice at that decision.

The course offers twelve case modules based on real donor situations, released step by step online. Twenty-nine trainees from twenty-two medical centers finished all modules, and most reported stronger confidence in judging donor suitability. Gains were largest for trainees with the least transplant experience, which supports wider use of the approach.
pmc-13640185:
Laura Tasson and five colleagues present a 2026 scoping review of the thinking-aloud method in health questionnaire design. In this technique, people say their thoughts out loud while answering survey items, revealing how they understand each question.

From 1,678 records, 210 studies qualified, and only eighty-four described their methods completely. Most involved patients, face-to-face sessions, and frequent prompts from the researcher. Approaches varied widely in analysis, coding, and theory, and about a fifth cited no framework at all. The authors call the method versatile but fragmented, and they recommend fuller reporting so studies can be compared.
pmc-13643785:
Maria Dolores De Donno and co-authors report a newly characterised locus on the fruit fly Y chromosome linked to the crystal and Suppressor of Stellate system. In this classic system, small RNAs called piRNAs from the Y chromosome silence the Stellate repeats on the X chromosome. Their 2026 study re-annotates these sequences in the fly genome.

Using the current genome release plus heterochromatin-enriched scaffolds, the team mapped two distinct crystal regions with different organisation. Beside the known orderly tandem region, they found a disorganised region mixing fragments in both orientations from crystal repeats and transposons, mobile DNA elements. This region looks like a piRNA cluster that regulates both Stellate and transposons. They also found at least four more organised crystal-like loci and two new repeat types carrying parts of the HetA and gypsy12 transposons.
pmc-13646785:
Wei Yang and three colleagues test whether early-morning classes wear down university students' positive mental health, using survey data from 1,437 students in Sichuan and Yunnan, China. Exposure meant weekdays whose first class began at or before eight in the morning. The team modeled a chain in which schedule strain creates social jetlag, a mismatch between body clock and social clock, which strains emotion control. Bedtime procrastination was tested as an amplifier, and students were sorted into risk profiles.

More early classes went with lower positive mental health, and the serial chain through jetlag and emotion difficulties carried part of that link. Delaying bedtime strengthened the first link in the chain. Five student profiles appeared, and those pairing frequent early classes with shaky sleep and weak emotion control fared worst. The authors argue timetables are a fixable institutional factor in student well-being, not a fixed hardship to endure.
pmc-13649285:
Alexander Muacevic and six colleagues report a deadly brain infection by cytomegalovirus in a man with a sound immune system. This virus lies quiet in most adults and strikes hard mainly when immune shields are down. The man had long headaches, then stroke after stroke in the back of his brain.

Spinal fluid held the virus at high counts, and blood tests pointed to a first-ever catch of it. Scans showed tight spots in two big brain arteries. A virus drug cleaned the spinal fluid, but bleeds in the brain's skin, gut, and urine tract took his life. The authors urge virus tests when long headaches pair with repeat strokes and hot spinal fluid.
pmc-13649485:
Winston Tse-Hou Kwok and two colleagues report a 38-year-old woman whose first sign of a rare inherited syndrome was a full-body seizure. She had no past illness and no family history of nerve disease. Brain scans with a high-power magnet showed a benign growth pattern in the cerebellum on both sides, a hallmark of Lhermitte-Duclos disease.

Gene testing found a known harmful change in the PTEN gene, which confirmed Cowden syndrome, a trait that raises cancer risk across the body. Prompt screening then found an early breast cancer in place and odd thyroid cells. She chose removal of both breasts and her whole thyroid. Her seizures stayed controlled on one drug, and the growth itself needed no surgery.
pmc-13649685:
Tristan Baumann and Oxana Eschenko tracked brain signals in rats as they learned a complex maze over many days. Two hubs, the hippocampus and the prefrontal cortex, must talk to each other for spatial memory, and a small midline relay called the nucleus reuniens links them both. The team read signal strength, sync, and the direction of flow in all three areas.

As learning grew, one path clearly strengthened: flow from the hippocampus into the relay rose across three rhythm bands. Flow back the other way fell, and direct links between the two hubs stayed much the same. Sync between the prefrontal cortex and the relay even dropped. The relay, they argue, is no passive pipe but an active player.
pmc-13649985:
Yalin Hu and six colleagues present BiSpikeNet, a computer model built to spot pests and diseases on tea plants quickly and cheaply. Fast, accurate identification matters in smart tea gardens, yet strong image models often need heavy computing, while very light models can miss the features that separate one leaf problem from another.

BiSpikeNet joins ordinary convolutional networks with spiking networks, which process signals in pulses, and adds an attention step that highlights key features. The base model reached a reported accuracy in the low ninety percent range, and a fusion version that merges the two network types scored higher still in the team's tests. The authors argue the design balances accuracy against computing cost, which suits field tools with limited power. Code for the model is posted in a public repository named in the article.
pmc-13651185:
Colton R Kessenich and five co-authors, in 2026, offer a hands-on framework for reading genome sequencing data when regulators describe gene-edited crops. Safety review must show what DNA was put in, where, how many copies, whether stray plasmid pieces came along, and whether the insert stays stable across generations. Sequencing can answer all of it when the patterns are read right.

Working from mock paired-end datasets that mimic many edit outcomes, the team defined five classes of mapped reads whose mixes form signatures. A clean single insertion signs itself one way. Added copies, backbone contamination, and structural rearrangements each sign differently, with coverage shapes and read-pair orientations as supporting proof. Worked examples walk users through the reading without requiring any set software. The authors aim the framework at newcomers and regulators alike, to steady judgments and make sequencing-based checks clearer.
pmc-2586385:
Dethlefsen, Huse, Sogin, and co-authors track how one antibiotic course affects the human gut microbiota. Gut microbes are essential partners in nutrition, growth, metabolism, defence against germs, and immune control. Antibiotics can disturb those long-evolved partnerships, sometimes with lasting harm.

Using deep sequencing of a marker gene, the team followed gut communities before, during, and after treatment. Their detailed view shows which groups fall, which survive, and how fully the community recovers. Such evidence informs wiser antibiotic use and interest in restoring gut microbes after treatment.  Recovery, when it lagged, left lasting room for harmful germs to settle.
pmc-3004885:
Jolley and Maiden present BIGSdb, a platform for analysing bacterial genome variation across whole populations. Parallel sequencing created new chances for population genomics of bacteria. Those chances demanded software able to store, retrieve, and analyse genetic data linked with traits of each strain.

BIGSdb was designed to scale with that flood of genomes. It keeps sequence and descriptive information together so users can ask population-level questions. Public health teams use such platforms to track outbreak strains, vaccine targets, and the spread of drug resistance between hospitals and countries.  Outbreak teams adopted the platform to share strain data across national laboratories.
pmc-3828585:
Blencowe, Cousens, Chou, and co-authors review the global epidemiology of preterm birth in the Born Too Soon series. Worldwide, more than one in ten live births in 2010 were preterm, amounting to roughly fifteen million babies born too early in a single year. Preterm birth is a leading cause of newborn death.

The paper reviews how rates vary between countries and sets priorities for improving the data itself. Better counting is a first step toward prevention and care. The series framed preterm birth as a global emergency requiring action before and during pregnancy.
pmc-4383985:
Amberger, Bocchini, Schiettecatte, and their colleagues presented OMIM.org in 2014. OMIM, Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man, is a curated catalog of human genes and genetic disorders. It describes each gene and trait and sets out the relationships between them.

The paper marks the launch of OMIM.org as the official web site for the resource. Entries are written and updated by experts as new evidence appears. Doctors use it to check a rare condition, and researchers use it to link a gene to a disease. It remains a first stop for questions in human genetics.
pmc-4489285:
Drozdetskiy, Cole, Procter, and their colleagues released JPred four in 2015. JPred is a popular server that predicts protein secondary structure, the local folds such as helices and sheets within a protein. Its predictions come from the JNet algorithm, among the most accurate methods of its kind.

Version four updated the service and kept its simple web access. Knowing secondary structure is often the first step toward grasping a protein's full shape and function. Many proteins will never have a measured structure, so prediction fills a real gap. Students and researchers use JPred as a quick, trusted check on new sequences.
pmc-5079585:
Houben and Dodd re-estimated the global burden of latent tuberculosis infection in 2016. The existing estimate, that one-third of the world population carries latent TB, was nearly twenty years old. Controlling latent infection is central to the End TB Strategy, which aims to eliminate TB by mid-century.

Using mathematical modelling, the authors updated the figure with current demography and science. Latent infection means the bacteria live quietly in the body without symptoms, yet can activate later. A modern estimate shapes how much treatment and testing programs must plan for. The revision gave global TB policy a firmer number to work from.
pmc-8844085:
Lei Wang and colleagues reviewed in 2022 the state of therapeutic peptides, short chains of amino acids used as medicines. Peptide drug development advanced quickly over the previous decade, helped by better ways to make, modify, and analyze these molecules. Peptides can now be built by chemical or biological routes, and new design and delivery strategies have widened what they can treat.

The authors survey current uses, from diabetes and hormone disorders to infections and cancer. They then look at the directions the field is heading, including peptides that cross barriers once thought closed to them. The review captures a class of drugs sitting between small pills and large antibody medicines, with room still to grow.
polycarp-epistle-martyrdom-roberts-donal:
Polycarp, bishop of Smyrna and a hearer of the apostle John, wrote one surviving letter, to the church at Philippi. With it stands the Martyrdom of Polycarp, the account of his death by fire and sword around 155 CE. Roberts and Donaldson translated both texts for the Ante-Nicene Fathers series in 1885.

The letter urges faith, patience, and care for widows, strangers, and the poor, with warnings against greed and false teaching. The Martyrdom tells how the old bishop refused to curse Christ, and how the flames bent around him. It is the earliest full martyr account outside the New Testament. The two texts show the second-century church in word and deed.
polygraphice-or-the-arts-of-drawing-engr: Polygraphice, 1685. The arts of drawing and engraving. This book preserves that manual. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
price-observations-american-revolution-1:
Price published his Observations on the Importance of the American Revolution in 1785, after Britain had accepted American independence. He had defended the colonists from the start, and Congress had thanked him and even invited him to help the new republic's finances. The new pamphlet greeted the American dawn with a prophet's hopes.

Price hails the revolution as the opening of a new age for mankind, in which free states might show what liberty can do. He also warns the Americans plainly: avoid public debt, standing armies, and the corruptions that ruined Britain. The warnings give the praise its weight. The pamphlet was the Old World's blessing on the New, from the English writer Americans most trusted. It completes the story begun by his civil liberty tract of 1776.
reid-essays-intellectual-powers-1785:
Thomas Reid's Essays on the Intellectual Powers of Man, from 1785, give the full system behind his earlier Inquiry. All eight essays stand here, in the order Reid planned. He treats perception first, then memory, conception, and the forming of general ideas, called abstraction.

Judgment and reasoning follow, and taste closes the set, as the mind's powers unfold in sequence. Reid's rule throughout is trust in the plain beliefs nature gives every person. He writes against Hume's skepticism with patience rather than scorn. The Essays form the most complete statement of Scottish common-sense philosophy. Generations of students in Britain and America learned their logic from this book.
renouvier-esquisse-vol1-1885:
Charles Renouvier spent years mapping every major system of thought into one ordered scheme. Volume one of his Esquisse, a systematic classification of philosophical doctrines, appeared in French in 1885. Renouvier led the French neocritical school, which rebuilt Kant's legacy for his age. The Gallica scan from the French national library preserves this original text.

Renouvier sorts doctrines by the deep choices each one makes on core questions. Free will or fate, the finite or the infinite: such choices, he shows, drive whole systems. His map lets readers place any school and see its kin. No English translation from his era exists. Scholars still consult the French volumes.
royce-religious-aspect-1885:
The Religious Aspect of Philosophy, published in 1885, was Josiah Royce's first book, written when he was a young Harvard teacher. It is a critique of agnosticism, the fashionable doubt of his day, and a first sketch of his idealism.

Royce argues that doubt itself rests on faith in an ideal of truth, so the skeptic cannot escape the religious aspect of thought. Morality and knowledge alike point toward an absolute mind in which our partial views are completed. The argument is dense but fervent. The book launched the career of America's leading absolute idealist of the next decades.
sbe-20-vinaya-texts-3-1885:
Book Twenty of the Sacred Books of the East came out in 1885. It ends the Vinaya Texts with Part Three, in the dress of Rhys Davids and Oldenberg. The Vinaya sets the rule of life for the monks of the Buddha. Parts One and Two stand just past in the set.

The Kullavagga runs here from Book Four to Book Twelve. The Patidesaniya rules close the text, a short set of faults to be owned. Tales tell how each rule came to be laid down by the Buddha. The three parts give the whole monk rule in English for the first time.
scientific-american-supplement-no-481-ma: The Righi Railroad, with three engravings, leads Supplement No. 481, dated New York, March 21, 1885, in Volume XIX. The Chinese pump in one figure, the water clock in three figures, and new self-propelling and steering torpedoes follow. Dobson and Barbour's improvements in Heilmann's combers and a machine for polishing boots and shoes complete the engineering list shown. Technology gives T. Fletcher on the use of gas in the workshop, covering placing of lights, best burners, light lost by shades, the blowpipe, gas furnaces, and gas engines.
scientific-american-supplement-no-483-ap: Volume XIX, Number 483, dated New York, April 4, 1885, opens its chemistry contents with J. B. Mackintosh on determination of graphite in minerals. Sulphocyanide of potassium, sugar nitro-glycerine, remelting of cast iron, and the hardness of metals follow. Engineering lists the jet ventilator in four figures and feeding boilers at the bottom in two figures. The Honigmann fireless engine comes next, explaining fireless working of steam engines by means of a solution of hydrate of soda, with several figures and diagrams.
scientific-american-supplement-no-484-ap: A bridge over the Blaauw Krantz Ravine in Cape Colony, in two engravings, leads Supplement No. 484, dated New York, April 11, 1885, in Volume XIX. Torpedo ships follow, then Dugald Clerk on the gas engine, covering combustion engines, the first cylinder and piston engine, Watt's experiments, the first gas engine, and principles of the gas engine. E. T. Abbott on rapid construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway, the Osgood mammoth excavator in three figures, and capstan navigation on the Volga in four figures come next.
scientific-american-supplement-no-492-ju: The new Spanish artillery, in two engravings, leads Supplement No. 492, dated New York, June 6, 1885, in Volume XIX. L. Tetmajer on qualitative tests for steel rails, A. Trappen on a new form of small Bessemer plant, and A. E. Seaton on triple compound engines, read before the Institution of Naval Architects, follow. Early history of the steam jack, a bridge over the River Adige at Verona in thirteen figures, and E. D. Leavitt on pumping machinery, covering mine pumps and direct acting steam pumps, come next.
scientific-american-supplement-no-497-ju: Making sea water potable, by Thomas Kay, opens the chemistry contents of Supplement No. 497, dated New York, July 11, 1885, in Volume XX. The acids of wool oil, a new absorbent for oxygen, and H. B. Slater on depositing nickel upon zinc follow. Engineering gives foundations in quicksand and a lift bridge over the Ourcq Canal in three figures. St. Petersburg as a seaport follows, covering a canal cut from Cronstadt to St. Petersburg and its opening by the Emperor and Empress, with a full page engraving.
scientific-american-supplement-no-508-se: The Cowles electric smelting process, in five figures, leads Supplement No. 508, dated New York, September 26, 1885, in Volume XX. Eugene H. Cowles, Alfred H. Cowles, and Charles F. Mabery write on the electrical furnace and reduction of oxides of boron, silicon, aluminum, and other metals by carbon. Chemical action of light follows. So do eutexia with cryohydrates and eutectic alloys, and chinoline. A method of rapid estimation of urea and an assay of earthenware glaze complete the chemistry list shown, with page numbers in the 8100s.
scientific-american-supplement-no-514-no: Chlorides in the rainfall of 1884 open the chemistry contents of Supplement No. 514, dated New York, November 7, 1885, in Volume XX. Apparatus for evaporating organic liquids, with description and three figures, follows. Engineering lists relative costs of fluid and solid fuels and the manufacture of steel castings. Don Arturo de Marcoarter on science in diminishing casualties at sea, from a paper read before the British Association, comes next.
scientific-american-supplement-no-520-de: Steel structures, on the best use of different grades of steel from a paper by James Christie, lead Supplement No. 520, dated New York, December 19, 1885, in Volume XX. Andrew Carnegie on natural gas fuel follows. He read the paper before the Iron and Steel Institute. It covers first use of the gas and wells near Pittsburg. It also covers the extent of gas lands, cost of piping, and gas tests. A gas engine water supply alarm, Professor W. H.
sinclair-satans-invisible-world-english-:
George Sinclair, a Scottish professor of philosophy, published Satan's Invisible World Discovered in 1685. The book is a choice collection of relations, accounts offered as proof of spirits, witches, and apparitions. It became the Scottish classic against Sadducism, the doubt of the spirit world.

Sinclair gathers Scottish cases with names and places attached. Witches, ghosts, and second sight all testify in his pages. His purpose is polemical, but his relish for a good story shows through. Northern ghost lore here marches under a professor's banner. The collection preserves tales that might else have vanished. It also shows Scotland answering the skeptics in kind, story for sworn story.
slave-narratives-a-folk-history-of-slave:
Volume VI of the Slave Narratives holds the Kansas accounts, drawn from talks with former slaves. The typewritten records were made by the Federal Writers' Project in 1936-1938 and put together by the Library of Congress project. The Washington issue is dated 1941. Just three names appear as those who spoke: Clayton Holbert, Bill Simms, and Belle Williams.

Holbert's account, taken at Ottawa, Kansas, by Leta Gray, opens the set. He states that he is eighty-six years old and an ex slave, born and raised in Linn County, Tennessee. His master, Pleasant Holbert, held a fairly large farm with, he thinks, around one hundred slaves. He was working the fields as the Civil War wound down.
spr-proceedings-vol3-1885:
Parts eight and nine make up volume three of the SPR Proceedings, issued in 1885. The Society for Psychical Research printed its findings here for members and critics alike. Telepathy tests continue from the earlier volumes, with tighter controls. Cases of apparitions and haunted houses enter with sworn statements.

Investigators weigh each report for error, fraud, and coincidence before printing. Trance mediumship receives long, careful write ups from sittings. The society's habit of publishing doubts beside wonders marks every part. Volume three deepens the archive of the great evidential debate of the era. Researchers still mine it for early cases. Its caution is as notable as its claims.
stanley-congo-free-state-vol1-1885:
Henry Stanley returned to the Congo in 1879 in the service of King Leopold of Belgium. Volume One of The Congo and the Founding of Its Free State, from 1885, tells of his five years there. Stanley had traced the Congo River to the sea two years earlier.

He built stations, cut a road around the falls, and signed treaties with hundreds of chiefs. Steamers were hauled in pieces past the rapids to the upper river. Stanley presents the work as commerce and civilization. Later history judged Leopold's Free State a horror, which gives this proud volume a grim second meaning today.
stanley-congo-free-state-vol2-1885:
Volume Two of Stanley's Congo narrative, also from 1885, continues the founding of the Free State. Stanley's crews were opening the upper Congo to steamers and trade posts. The volume runs to the year the Berlin Conference blessed Leopold's claim.

Stanley describes new stations, river surveys, and his dealings with Arab traders and local rulers. He also argues Europe's case for taking the Congo basin, in the blunt language of the Scramble for Africa. The Emin Pasha relief trip, his last great expedition, lay just ahead. Read now, the volume documents both exploration and the start of a catastrophe.
stevenson-childs-garden-verses-1885:
Robert Louis Stevenson had been a sickly child, kept in bed for long stretches in Edinburgh. As an adult he turned those years into A Child's Garden of Verses, published in 1885. The book holds sixty-four poems, complete, and it has never been out of print since.

The poems see the world at a child's height: a bed becomes a ship, a shadow follows like a friend, and trains and foreign lands feed daydreams. Stevenson remembers both the fun and the loneliness of childhood without talking down to young readers. Adults often love the book as much as children do. It set a new standard for poetry written for the young.
stories-from-the-italian-poets-with-live:
Leigh Hunt opens Volume I of his Stories from the Italian Poets with a warm letter. The letter dedicates the work to Sir Percy Shelley, the poet's son. It praises his mix of love for romance and cool good sense. The volume is dated MDCCCXLVI, or 1846.

In his preface Hunt states the plan. He would add to the stock of tales drawn from Italian writers. He would take them from the poets, not the prose tale-tellers. He would keep as much of the verse's poetry as prose can hold. He would also furnish careful lives of the authors. Earlier sets had mined the novella writers; Hunt argues the poets offer a richer store.
tatian-the-diatessaron-of-tatian-anf-188:
Tatian wove the four Gospels into one smooth narrative around 170. He called the work the Diatessaron, a Greek phrase meaning through four. The 1885 Ante-Nicene Fathers presents the harmony in English.

For centuries the Syriac Church used it as its standard gospel text. Preachers read from its blended story in place of separate gospels. The work thus served both as devotion and as history. It also witnesses what the Gospels looked like in early copies. That value holds for scholars long before the canon was fixed. Few books shaped daily worship in the East as deeply as this one harmony did.
tennyson-idylls-of-the-king-1885:
